PREFACE 

The report of the American Historical Association on the social studies carries this significant statement: "Being convinced from the study of history that national policies, arising from narrow intolerant nationalism and aggressive predatory imperialism, were largely responsible for the World War, as well as for the intense rivalries among nations before 1914 and after 1918, and that the pursuit of such policies can only lead in the long run to national ruin, the Commission believes that-in keeping with the true interests of civilization in general and of American society in particular-nationalism should be infused with enlightenment, reason, and tolerance. . . ."

In the preparation of this text the authors have made conscientious efforts to apply the principle set forth by this authoritative body. To lead American youth to an unbiased appraisal of racial, national, and political problems has been an objective held constantly in view. "It should not be considered unpatriotic to examine our shortcomings in a calm, judicial fashion."

This text presents all the essential facts of American history. They are worthy of the best efforts of the pupil in their mastery. Among essential facts are those which deal with the achievements of common people. Whenever the emphasis is placed upon sensational and spectacular episodes and events, a full appreciation of the forces which have made America is not possible. "History is having difficult going in our junior high schools. It is made too encyclopedic. Too much is attempted and, therefore, too little becomes an integral part ¹ American Historical Association, Report of the Commission on the Social 

Studies: Conclusions and Recommendations. 

2 Department of Superintendence, N.E.A., Fourteenth Yearbook, 1936.

of the pupil's intellectual possession." The judicious selection of the material in this text and the subordination of the trivial to the important has afforded opportunity to set forth with definite emphasis the really great and significant aspects of our national development. "Clearly the reading difficulty of most social studies material is too great for the grades for which planned."4 

Throughout the preparation of the material for this text great care has been exercised to eliminate language and vocabulary difficulties. Of equal importance is the selection of subject matter within the range of interest and comprehension of pupils of this grade. The large space and sympathetic treatment given to the materials selected for emphasis has been made possible by the decision of the authors to set narrow and rigid limits to the space given to such inherently difficult matters as intercolonial controversies, military strategy, and partisan politics.

UNIT I THE DISCOVERY AND EXPLORATION OF AMERICA 

Five thousand years ago the civilized way of life developed in the river valleys of northern Africa and southwestern Asia. Slowly civilization spread westward across 

Europe. In the western part of Europe, five hundred years ago, several strong nations appeared. In these nations were to be found intelligent, gifted people. Architects, artists, and poets found opportunities to use their talents. Skilled workers produced articles of use and beauty. Trade flourished. 

But this busy European world was, after all, a small world. Ice and snow, burning deserts, and unknown oceans hemmed in this little civilized world on all sides. What lay beyond these boundaries was shrouded in mystery and doubt.

Our story will tell how the people of the Old World came to learn about the New World beyond the seas. It will tell how and why the men of Europe explored the new lands, made settlements, and laid the foundation of a new civilization in America.

From Quennell's History of Everyday Things in England, Chas. Scribner's Sons, publisher OLD FARM SCENES. Six hundred years ago the grain fields of Europe saw activities like these. In the upper panel the farmers are preparing the soil. 

In the lower are pictured the sowing, the reaping, and the threshing of the grain. Can you name each step shown in the pictures?

CHAPTER I THE WORLD MEN KNEW FIVE HUNDRED YEARS AGO 

The purpose of this chapter is to give a picture of the Europe of five hundred years ago. From this Europe came the men and women who laid the foundations of our country. It is important to know a great deal about them. What the people of those faroff times were like, how they lived and what they thought about, this chapter tries to make clear. 

America unknown to the Old World. It seems strange to think that for thousands of years the people of the eastern and western halves of our world should have been wholly ignorant of the existence of one another. It is hard for us to imagine how it would be to live in the world and not know what lies beyond the oceans that border our continent. But for long centuries men were ignorant of these things.

Long before the beginnings of civilization in western Europe trading ships had crept out into the Atlantic Ocean from the Mediterranean (měd-i-tě-rā'ně-ăn) Sea. Some of them skirted the shore of Africa for some distance southward. Sailors of ancient times grew familiar with the shores of Spain, France, and Britain. 3

But we have no record that any of these mariners turned the prow of his ship to the west and sailed boldly away from the well-known shores of Europe. There is only the merest hint, here and there, that in ancient times men of the white race actually crossed the Atlantic and stood on the soil of America. All through the years when our ancestors were building a civilization in Europe, what we know as America lay in utter darkness. What lay beyond the ocean to the west of Europe? When this question was raised, these ancestors of ours could make no answer. 

1. EUROPE'S DEBT TO THE ANCIENT WORLD 

The peoples of western Europe did not create their civilization. They inherited much of it from peoples who had lived about the shores of the Mediterranean Sea and had there built a civilization while the natives of western Europe were still savages. Back of these ancient, civilized dwellers about the Mediterranean were thousands of years. of human life on our earth when progress upward toward a better way of living was slow and halting. But there was always progress, and on the foundations laid by early men developed the first truly civilized people to appear in the world.

Two ancient river valleys. Certain groups of ancient men thousands of years ago made their homes in the valley of the Nile River, in northern Africa, and in the Tigris- 

Euphrates (ti'gris-û-frā'tēz) Valley in western Asia. Here both climate and soil helped them to leave old, savage ways behind and to develop what we call civilization. Theirs were the oldest civilizations to influence the people of Europe, and, through them, to influence the growth and development of our own country. 

In both valleys written languages came into use. Books and libraries appeared. Farming, weaving, pottery, glassmaking, and other useful arts were practiced. Architects,

THE WORLD MEN KNEW FIVE HUNDRED YEARS AGO 5 

engineers, astronomers, poets, and sculptors developed skill in their professions and arts. Trade flourished and by means of ships and caravans the beautiful and useful products of the river valleys found their way into the hands of less civilized peoples. Slowly the new and better ways of life spread northward and westward into new lands.

The Phoenicians. The Phoenicians (fé-nish'ǎnz) lived along the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea. The 

Lebanon (leb'a-nun) Mountains hemmed them in on the east. In these mountains grew quantities of fine timber. 

The Phoenicians began to build ships and to engage in commerce as a means of livelihood. East of the Phoenicians lay the rich cities of the Tigris-Euphrates Valley. South of them lay Egypt. Westward along the shores of the Mediterranean Sea lived uncivilized tribes. Phoenician ships in ever-increasing numbers engaged in carrying the products of the civilized East to the uncivilized West. The Phoenicians were the carriers of civilization to new lands and new peoples.

The Hebrews. The ancient Hebrews built a small kingdom near the eastern end of the Mediterranean. The kingdom was short-lived, but the Hebrews themselves gave the growing civilized world an idea that has never since been forgotten. Early men, even the civilized dwellers in the two river valleys, held the belief that many gods, having different characters and duties, looked after the affairs of men. The Hebrew leaders taught monotheism, the belief in one God. To them God was a just, merciful 

Father, anxious that men should lead good, upright lives.

Long after the Hebrew kingdom had disappeared this idea about God spread to all civilized lands. 

The alphabet. One gift to Europe carried in the vessels of the Phoenicians was not listed in the cargoes of goods shipped to the western shores of the Mediterranean. This was the alphabet. Among the uncivilized peoples who

crowded down to the shores to meet the traders from the east were the Greeks. They bought the Phoenician goods and at the same time learned from the Phoenicians the meaning and use of their alphabet. They fitted this to the 

Greek language, improved upon it, and, much later, passed it on to the Romans. From the Romans the use of this

SINUS GANGET Cus CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY'S MAP (150 A.D.). Ptolemy was a famous scholar who lived in ancient times in Alexandria, Egypt. His map is known as the first scientific map of the ancient world. He assumed that the earth is a globe. 

Translate some of the names on the map into modern names: Albion, Italia, Mare Internum, and others. alphabet spread into western Europe and from there to America.

The gifts of the Greeks. Two thousand years before 

America was discovered, the intelligent Greeks developed the best civilization the world had yet seen. In many ways it has never been improved upon. The Greeks believed in personal freedom for Greek citizens. They loved beauty and were able to give expression to their appreciation of the beautiful in sculpture, painting, poetry, and music. 

They have continued to be the world's teachers in almost every fine art. The Greeks did not build a strong empire. 

The small Greek states fought with one another, weakened

THE WORLD MEN KNEW FIVE HUNDRED YEARS AGO 7 

themselves, and fell under the control of powerful neighboring states. But Greek ideas lived on and spread, first to the older eastern lands, and then to Rome and to western Europe. No other people have equaled the Greeks in the gifts made to the widespread civilization in the world today. 

Acme Newspictures, Inc. 

CATHEDRAL AT MILAN, ITALY. This church building with its many sharplypointed spires is a good example of the cathedrals which were erected in 

Europe five or six hundred years ago.

The empire of the Romans. The Romans conquered the civilized ancient world. They gave most of their attention to practical affairs. Because they ruled so many lands and peoples, they were obliged to learn to govern well and to work out just laws for all. They admired the Greeks and copied Greek ideas, but they could not improve on the arts of the Greeks. In the great Roman Empire the knowledge and the culture of the Greeks had a good chance to take

root. In time the people of western Europe came under the influence of Greek ideas.

Besides helping to save Greek civilization, the Romans made gifts of their own to western Europe and to us. Two of the greatest of these are the Roman law, used in many countries today, and the Latin language, which has influenced many important modern languages. 

The rise of the German peoples. A thousand years before the discovery of America, barbarous tribes of German peoples broke into the great Roman Empire from the north and took possession of much of the land in the western part. 

At first they destroyed Roman cities and looted Roman churches and temples. But slowly the conquerors came under the influence of civilization. The Dark Ages, as the centuries following the coming of the Germans are called, passed away. Life and property became safer, cities again grew up, and trade revived. Civilization spread once more through western Europe. It was not exactly like the older civilization, for the Germans themselves had added much to it. Among their gifts were new ideas about personal freedom, the importance of family life, and respect for womanhood. 

How Christianity influenced our European ancestors.

About five hundred years before the western part of the Roman Empire was invaded by the German peoples, Jesus was born near Jerusalem (jê-roo'sȧ-lěm), the old capital of the Hebrew kingdom. Before the coming of the Germans

Christianity had spread through most of the lands of the empire. In the early years of the Dark Ages the leader of the Christians at Rome came to be recognized as the head of the Christian Church in all western lands. He was given the title of Pope. 

The incoming Germans soon gave up their pagan beliefs and became Christians. The new religion did much to make the warlike Germans more kindly and law-abiding. As

THE WORLD MEN KNEW FIVE HUNDRED YEARS AGO 9 

Christians they could be led to see the values of civilization. 

In time all of western Europe adopted the Christian religion. The leaders of the church had great influence over the people. Even the rulers of the growing countries were usually glad to take the advice of the Pope. The beautiful ceremonies of the church, and its steady efforts to keep peace and order among the people, gave the church and its leaders a high place in the love and respect of all. The picture on page 7 shows one of the beautiful churches of that time.

The crusades furnish a good example of how earnest the people of Europe had become about the Christian religion. 

The Mohammedan (mt-hămě-dăn) Turks had captured Jerusalem, the scene of the teachings and death of Jesus. 

Christian pilgrims had been in the habit of making the long journey to Jerusalem to pray and to seek blessings at the holy places there. The Turks made it dangerous to undertake this journey. As a result the kings, lords, and knights of western Europe began a long series of wars to rescue the Holy Land from the Mohammedans. In spite of the long distance they had to march and the many hardships they met, they succeeded for a time in making Jerusalem a Christian city. In the end the crusades were not successful, but they had important results. The crusaders saw that the people of eastern lands produced many articles of comfort and luxury which they had never before even heard of. 

In Constantinople (kon-stǎn-ti-no'p'l) they had a chance to see what the great cities of ancient times had been like. 

The travels of the crusaders broadened them and made them eager to have better living conditions in their home countries.

The crusades caused a great new commerce to spring up between the towns of western Europe and the lands to the east. From the time of the crusades onward an increasing number of people in the west were eager to have closer rela-

tions with the ancient eastern lands in which were produced such rich and luxurious articles as those described by the returning crusaders.

We see, then, that western Europe was a civilized region at the time of the discovery of America. It is clear, also, that this civilization had largely come from the ancient lands near the eastern end of the Mediterranean, from Greece, and from Rome. In two ways the civilization of western Europe was better than any that had grown up in ancient times. It was a Christian civilization, and it had been improved by the ideas of our freedom-loving ancestors from western and northern Europe. 

1. Name and locate the river valleys where civilization began. 

2. Tell about the importance of the Phoenicians. 

3. Contrast the religious ideas of the Hebrews with those of other early peoples. 

4. What special gifts did the Greeks make to civilization? 

5. Tell the purpose and results of the crusades. 

2. HOW THE PEOPLE OF EUROPE LIVED 

What was Europe like five hundred years ago? How did the people live, and what ideas did they have? Why were they ready, at last, to search for new lands and to conquer and settle them? Let us try to imagine what the old European world was like just before its people discovered and colonized America. 

How the people were governed. Western Europe was occupied, four or five hundred years ago, by the nations that are found there today. England, France, Portugal, and Spain, which were among the best organized of the nations, were ruled by kings. Each king was assisted by the great nobles and the important church officials of the nation. 

The common people had almost no voice in the affairs of the country. In local matters the ordinary people of England had a number of important rights and privileges.

THE WORLD MEN KNEW FIVE HUNDRED YEARS AGO 11 

Courtesy Bibliothèque Royale de Belgique AN OLD-TIME FAIR AND MARKET. Here we have a scene in the late Middle 

Ages. Most of the exchange of goods in the Europe of that day took place at such fairs.

In central and eastern Europe the people were not grouped in nations at all as they are today. There was no united 

German or Italian nation. There were many small, weak states whose rulers quarreled among themselves over questions of lands and power. Important kings and petty princes

were alike in their belief that it was their right to rule their subjects as they saw fit. Few people in those days questioned this right.

Religious ideas. The Christian church had a strong hold on the people of western Europe. All the people belonged to the same church organization and looked to the Pope at Rome as their spiritual leader. In the East were Christians who did not follow the practices of the western churches nor accept the rule of the Pope. These people were members of what is called the Greek Orthodox (ôr'tho-dŏks) Church. 

In Africa and in many ancient eastern lands the Mohammedan faith was held by millions of people. 

Farm life. Life in the country was far different from what it is today. The number of farmers, when compared with the number of people engaged in other occupations, was much greater than in our own time. Few of the actual farmers owned the lands they tilled. These were the possessions of great landlords who not only controlled the living conditions of their tenants but had the power to try them in private courts. The tenants planted their crops on narrow strips of ground assigned to them by the manager of the estate. The farming was carelessly done, and only the crudest of farm implements were in use. The crops were small, and the cattle, horses, and other livestock raised on the estates would appear thin and stunted if placed alongside the farm animals of today. The millions of farmers in the Europe of that day must have led hard, povertystricken, uninteresting lives.

Life in the growing towns. The cities were crowded, busy places. The streets were narrow, winding, and dirty. In most of them there was no general provision for either sewage or garbage disposal. Common people went about on foot. The merchants went from town to town with their goods piled in long trains of carts or on the backs of horses. 

Rich men rode through the streets on horseback, while the

THE WORLD MEN KNEW FIVE HUNDRED YEARS AGO 13 

ladies of that day, if they traveled about, rode in couches with shafts, called litters, carried by servants. There were no paid policemen or firemen.

The business of buying and selling was conducted at fairs and markets. Here might be found the products of other lands as well as articles produced on some near-by farm or in some shop in the city. The strange garb of the traders from faraway countries and the open-air performances of wandering groups of players made the fairs exciting events in the lives of the people. The picture on page 

11 gives some idea of how the fairs were conducted. 

Manufacturing was done by hand in little shops presided over by the owner, or master. His skilled helpers were called journeymen. Boys who worked in a shop while they learned the trade were known as apprentices (ă-prĕn'tĭs-ěz). The masters engaged in making a particular article were banded together in organizations called guilds. The guilds made careful rules regarding the workmanship and price of each article produced. Usually the shops were grouped in the cities according to the craft they carried on; the goldsmiths were to be found on one street, the saddlers on another, and the bakers on another. 

The cities of five hundred years ago were crowded, noisy, dingy places. But in the better towns there were points of beauty as well. Splendid churches and cathedrals, more beautiful in many ways than our finest buildings today, towered above the crowded roofs and the filthy streets. 

The halls or meeting places of the guilds were often places of great beauty. In many of the cities of that day the leading citizens bought from the king, or from some powerful neighboring lord, the right to manage local affairs.

A changing Europe. Europe was going through great changes in the years just before the discovery of America. 

Printing by means of movable types had been invented, and the process of paper-making had been learned from

the Arabs. As a result, books for the first time became fairly cheap and plentiful. Knowledge began to spread among large numbers of people. Gunpowder and guns were coming into general use, and the mounted knight in his armor found himself no match for the common foot soldier 

 PRINTING FROM MOVABLE TYPE. Here we see John Gutenberg looking at the first proof sheet as it comes from his printing press. armed with one of the new weapons. The power so long possessed by rich nobles began to crumble. Better and stronger ships were being built. Ship captains, with a compass to give them the directions, and a new invention, the astrolabe (ǎs'tro-lab), to help them get their "position" on the sea, were becoming less and less afraid to venture out of sight of familiar shores.

The men of that time were beginning to think new and interesting thoughts. Some of them found and read books

THE WORLD MEN KNEW FIVE HUNDRED YEARS AGO 15 

written by ancient Greek thinkers. The study of the Greek language became popular. Greek ideas helped to turn the thoughts of the people of Europe toward the world around them. They became inquisitive about the surrounding lands and oceans and about such questions as the size and shape of the earth and the movements of the heavenly bodies. Books appeared which were written not for a few scholars but for all classes of people. Italians, Frenchmen, Spaniards, and Englishmen now had the opportunity to read new and interesting books written in their own language.

The new literature and art of Europe, the fresh energy displayed by the people, and the growing interest in travel and trade carried Europe from the long period known as the Middle Ages into the modern age. This period of great change is called the Renaissance (ren'ě-säns), the rebirth of civilization.

3. FORERUNNERS OF A CENTURY OF DISCOVERY 

The story of the Vikings. A thousand years ago, in Norway, power was slipping from the hands of the nobles and into those of a king, Harold Fairhair. To many nobles this change was not to be endured. With their faithful followers they began sailing away to other lands in search of wealth and adventure. Some of the adventurers joined their kinsmen in England and made war on the hard-pressed King Alfred. Others sailed southward to the coasts of France or passed through the Strait of Gibraltar (jĬ-brôl'tēr) into the

Mediterranean Sea. Still others among these northern sea rovers, or Vikings (vi'kings), sailed toward the west and made settlements in Iceland and Greenland. These settlements on the threshold of America grew and prospered. 

Norwegian Travel Information Office A VIKING SHIP. This old vessel was found on the coast of Norway in 1904. 

In such a ship Leif Ericson visited our shores nearly a thousand years ago. 

But the wanderings of the hardy Vikings did not end here. One Viking captain, bewildered by the fogs, steered his long, narrow craft far to the south and west. When the fogs lifted he saw a hilly, forested coast on his right hand. When he returned to 

Iceland and Greenland he reported what he had discovered. Leif Ericson, (ĕr'ik-sun), another captain, determined to explore the lands that had been seen. With thirtyfive men on a single vessel he took the route southward. Ericson's ship was probably much like the one shown in the picture on this page. He and his com- panions sighted land and steered their ship into the mouth of a river which led into a lake. Leif Ericson named the country Vinland. He and his men spent one winter in cabins they built on the shore of the little lake. 

Where was the Vinland of Leif Ericson? Probably somewhere on our North Atlantic coast. It seems certain that several other Viking ships visited the region. Timber was cut and carried back to treeless Greenland. No doubt plans

THE WORLD MEN KNEW FIVE HUNDRED YEARS AGO 17 

were made for a permanent settlement in the new land. 

But for some reason interest in the discoveries waned. 

Presently Vinland was only a dim legend. 

It seems likely that the discoveries of the Vikings, or Northmen, had no influence on the plans of later explorers and discoverers. This may seem surprising until we remember that in the year 1000, which is the date of the discovery of Vinland, books were almost unknown in Europe, and few people traveled about. It is doubtful whether the 

Europeans outside of the Scandinavian (skăn-di-nā'vĭ-ản) countries had any knowledge of the western adventures of the Vikings. Modern scholars have given us the story. 

Marco Polo's book. Europeans of five hundred years ago had some knowledge of lands stretching away to the eastward from Europe. They knew that certain luxuries purchased by the rich came from lands far beyond the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea. Some of the church leaders had heard the reports of missionaries who had traveled widely in the East. But to most of the people of Europe the lands and peoples of eastern and southern Asia must have seemed as vague and mysterious as the possible inhabitants of another planet seem to us. 

Then a book, called The Book of Marco Polo Concerning Kingdoms and Marvels of the East, appeared. It told of the adventures of a Venetian lad, Marco Polo, who had traveled with relatives to the court of Kublai Khan (kōo'bli kän') in northern China. As a trusted envoy of the great eastern ruler, Polo had had opportunities to travel widely through eastern lands, returning at length to his native city after an absence of twenty-four years.

Polo told his story to a fellow prisoner-of-war after his capture in a naval battle in which the fleet of Venice was engaged. Polo's listener wrote the story. But two hundred years passed before it appeared as a printed book, in the year 1477. It was then set up in the new movable type and

To the eager and inquisitive men of the fifteenth century, Polo's book was exciting, even though the events it told about were two hundred years in the past. 

While the readers did not believe all that they read in the book, it is probable that many of the things which they doubted the most were the truest. Polo's book of travel was translated into many languages. The story was so vivid and

real that never again could the East be the vague land of mystery it had formerly been. 

Most important of all, Polo told of a sea lying east of Asia. 

The account of his return journey from the East seemed to prove that the sea beyond Asia could be reached by a water route all the way from the Persian (pûr'zhản) Gulf. 

A great idea began to take shape in the minds of certain thinking men in Europe: If there was an ocean east of Asia, and an ocean west of Europe, might they not be the same body of water? To intelligent people, who were accepting the old Greek theory that the earth is a sphere, it was not hard to believe that a single ocean touched the shores of the two continents. Who would put this belief to the test and sail westward away from the coasts of Europe? 

Henry the Navigator. Henry was a prince of Portugal.

He turned his back on affairs at the Portuguese court and on what promised to be a successful military career and gave his life to the study of ocean navigation. He gathered about him scientists, geographers, and brave sailors. They studied maps and charts and read the books that told about regions to the south and to the east. They experimented in shipbuilding. Portuguese captains sailed southward along the coast of Africa. The Cape Verde (vûrd) and other small groups of islands were discovered. Gold and ivory were brought back to Portugal from Africa. At last, in the year 

1486, Bartholomew Diaz (dē'ǎs) reached the southernmost tip of the continent. Twelve years later Vasco da Gama (då gä'mȧ) sailed across the Indian Ocean and reached India. The Portuguese had found their way by water to the rich lands of the East. Lisbon (lĭz'bun), the capital of 

Portugal, was soon the center of a flourishing trade with India.

CHAPTER II  

This chapter tells the story of the life and work of one of the great men of history, Christopher Columbus. You will learn of his years of patient and persistent effort to secure aid in carrying out his plans and of how Queen Isabella of Spain was finally won to his support. Here are related the circumstances of the remarkable voyage of Columbus across the Atlantic Ocean, and of his final triumph in the discovery of America. 

1. THE LIFE AND PLANS OF COLUMBUS 

Boyhood of Columbus. One of the most beautiful of 

Italian cities is Genoa (jen'ô-ȧ), the birthplace of the discoverer of America. It is built on the slope of the Apennines (ǎp'è-nīnz), and as one approaches it from the sea, its palaces and cathedrals, rising tier above tier, make a striking picture. When Columbus was born Genoa was a bustling seaport, her wharves crowded with merchandise, 23

and the sails of her ships dotting the waters of the Mediterranean.

Dominico Columbus, the father of Christopher Columbus, was a wool comber by trade, as his father had probably been before him. Not much is known about the Columbus family except that they were good, respectable people who had to work for their living. 

 COLUMBUS. This is a sup posed likeness of the great explorer. What means were at hand, five hundred years ago, for preserving, for future generations, the appearance of some famous personage? 

The young Christopher went to school, where he learned to read and write and possibly got a few ideas about astronomy and other sciences. He was always a student, never giving up his studies of the ocean and the art of sailing until he had learned all that was known about these things at that time. 

Columbus as a sailor. When only fourteen Columbus became a sailor, and by the time he was twenty-one he was a brave and hardy mariner. Sometimes he served on peaceful merchant vessels plying the Mediterranean, and at other times he fought in the wars between the jealous

Italian cities. Once, so the story goes, he commanded a fighting ship which had a duel to the death with a big Venetian galley. For hours the two ships lay close together, their crews fighting hand to hand until many of the men had been killed. Then the ships took fire and most of those who were still alive perished in the flames. Columbus saved himself by leaping overboard and swimming to the nearest land, six miles distant.

A little later the young sailor moved to Lisbon, in Portu-

gal, then the center of learning in all things that had to do with the art of the sailor. Columbus was a fine looking young man at this time, being tall and muscular, courtly in manner, and a ready speaker. In Lisbon Columbus spent a busy life, now going on voyages down the coast of Africa or out to the Cape Verde Islands, and now up along the coasts of France and England. When at home he spent all his time studying and making maps and charts and learning all he could about the sea.

Europe's luxuries from the East. The Europe of five hundred years ago produced its own necessities of lifeplain foods in abundance, clothing, materials for building purposes, the utensils of the home, the farm, and the shop. 

But its luxuries had been coming for many years from that mysterious East of which the average man knew so little. 

On the "luxury list" of that day were many of the commonplace articles found in the poorest homes today. We should scarcely call cloves, cinnamon, sugar, or ginger "luxuries."

But many articles brought in from the East, such as fine fabrics, diamonds, rubies, and pearls, are luxuries now as then. 

The enterprising Italian merchants of Venice and Genoa, bringing these articles into Europe over long and dangerous routes, controlled this eastern trade. Now the merchants of other countries—of England and Portugal and Spainwere growing rich and powerful and were constantly seeking new fields for their enterprises. Why not get a part of this valuable eastern trade? This was easier said than done, for the Venetian and Genoese (jěn-ô-ēz') merchants controlled, between them, all the known routes of trade from the Mediterranean eastward. Then what about finding new routes?

Thus you see that the day had arrived when daring sailors, with fresh ideas and novel plans, would find willing listeners, if not ready helpers.

The problem of the eastern trade. Then suddenly the problem of the eastern trade took a new turn. It became less a question of who should share in this trade and more a question of how these finer goods could be brought into Europe at all. The warlike Turks had been for years extending their conquests over the lands about the eastern end of the Mediterranean. As they did so they made the old routes Spine 13 تا 10 Decidis

Orits TOSCANELLI'S MAP. It is said that Columbus studied this map. Can you see how the map confused and puzzled him after he had made his discoveries? to the east constantly more dangerous and expensive to the merchants of the Italian cities. When the Turks finally took Constantinople, in 1453, they cut off the last clear, open road into the East. Did this mean that the well-to-do and the rich of Europe would be obliged to get along without those luxuries they had learned to love? Or were there new ways to bring them in? 

You see, then, an additional reason why geographers and sailors began to have a new prominence in the life of Europe. 

The ideas of Columbus. Christopher Columbus threw his whole mind and heart into the study of these new questions. Gradually a great thought came to him: he became

convinced that the East with all its rich products could be reached by sailing westward; that the earth is round and that a sailor could, by sailing far enough to the west, come finally to the very lands of spices and jewels reached by the toiling caravans and by the adventurous feet of Marco 

Polo by going eastward.

This idea of Columbus was not a new one. Many learned men, as we have seen, had held the same belief. But Columbus was the first man who was ready to spend his life and to risk everything in trying to prove that his belief was correct. For this he deserves a place among the great men of history.

From this time on Columbus never swerved from his one great idea. He spent every minute of his time planning for the great voyage he believed God intended him to make. 

But Columbus was poor and could not fit out an expedition himself. So he applied to King John of Portugal for help. But the king, after talking it over with the wise men of his court, decided against Columbus. When Columbus learned, a little later, that the king had secretly sent out an expedition to test the idea of a journey to the west, he grew angry and left Portugal in disgust.

In Spain Columbus for a long time had no better success. 

King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella were busy driving the Moors out of their country, and they had no time to listen to the plans of a poor dreamer. So at last, with his little boy, he turned his back on the Spanish court. He had now waited seven years for help. He had been jeered at on the streets as a crazy man. But he was just as firm in his purpose as ever. He would not give up.

Spain aids Columbus. On the long road out of Spain 

Columbus and his son one day stopped at a monastery to ask for food and water. Then almost a miracle happened. 

The prior listened to the great plan of Columbus and believed. "Why," cried he, "should not Spain undertake this

great work and win the great reward?" Best of all, the good man knew the queen well and had great influence with her. 

 THE TRIUMPH OF COLUMBUS. This scene, called "Columbus' Triumphal

The prior, Perez (pā'rāth), sent a messenger in haste to the queen, begging an interview. The request was granted, and the good prior hastened to plead for Columbus before the queen. He spoke so eloquently of the grand views of Columbus and of the glory that would come to Spain if the venture succeeded that Isabella was convinced. In a little while

Columbus was called before the king and queen and the assembled court to tell about his great plan. After some trouble over the details, the royal pair agreed to send three ships into the unknown western seas with Columbus in command. 201321

2. HOW COLUMBUS SOUGHT THE EAST AND FOUND AMERICA 

The sailing of Columbus. On the morning of August 3, 1492, the most famous of all sea voyages began. The three small vessels of Columbus pointed their prows westward and soon left the familiar shores of Spain behind. On board were ninety sailors-a motley crew of men, some of whom had been forced to go on the journey, while others had been liberated from prison in order to help man Columbus' ships. 

The sailors dreaded the voyage, for that unknown sea ahead held grim terrors for them. Had they known the great distance they were to go, it is doubtful if anything could have coaxed them even to set foot on deck. 

Day after day the three ships held their course to the west. More and more uneasy grew the sailors. Once they saw a broken mast floating on the waters. To the sailors this was an omen of the ruin that was awaiting them. The compass behaved queerly and no longer pointed to the 

North Star. Were the very laws of nature changing? Columbus kept two reckonings of the distance-one much "Behind him lay the gray Azores, Behind, the Gates of Hercules; 

Before him not the ghost of shores, Before him only shoreless seas." shorter than it really was and another for himself, accurate as he could make it. But even he must have become uneasy, for he had been sure that the coast of Cipango (si-pǎng'go), or Japan, would be reached at the end of 

2,500 miles. But here they were, 2,700 miles from home, and still no land in sight. Columbus was too wise to show his fears, and before his men he appeared confident and cheerful.

At last all the men grew interested in watching for land, for Columbus had promised a reward equal to about four hundred dollars to the man who should first see land. Once or twice it was thought that land had really been sighted; but each time the discovery proved to be only a low-lying bank of clouds. 

Paul's Photos "THE CHIPPEWA FAMILY." This famous statuary group stands in Lincoln 

Park, Chicago. The sculptor is John J. Boyle.

America discovered. At last, however, there was no longer any doubt that land was near at hand. A branch containing berries, a carved stick, and some weeds that do not grow at sea were picked up. That night not an eye closed in sleep on any of the three little ships. The next morning, October 12, 1492, before the sailors lay a verdant shore with fine trees swaying in the wind. To Columbus it seemed that the great journey had ended successfully.

Columbus and his men went ashore, set up a cross, and took possession of the land in the name of the sovereigns of Spain. They soon found that they were on a small island. 

After exploring it and naming it San Salvador (sän säl-väthôr'), they sailed away in search of other lands. Other islands appeared, often very small, and at length the great islands of Cuba and Haiti (ha'ti) were discovered. But as the days passed Columbus and his sailors must have grown more and more puzzled. Here were lands about where 

Columbus had expected to find them, beautiful islands with luxuriant forests and myriads of brilliant birds, but where were the towered cities and the great rivers described by Marco Polo? Here were naked savages-in whom Columbus was greatly interested, to be sure-but where were the kings and princes in their gorgeous robes of state? Poor 

Columbus! He was groping among those savage islands for kingdoms that lay ten thousand miles away. He named the islands, as might be expected, "The Indies," and their inhabitants "Indians." Shortly after this one of the ships of Columbus was wrecked, and a second was taken away by a disloyal captain. Columbus at length reached Spain with one ship, some of his men being left on one of the newlydiscovered islands.

The triumph of Columbus. True, Cathay (kă-tha') had not been found, and there was no rich store of jewels to lay at the feet of the Spanish sovereigns. But new, strange lands had been discovered, a new race of men, and strange birds, animals, and plants. Was that not enough for the first expedition? As for Cathay-surely it could be only a little farther on. Columbus was satisfied-and so were the rulers and the powerful nobles of Spain. The returning captain marched in triumphal procession from Palos (pä'lōs) to the capital, where Ferdinand and Isabella gave him a splendid reception and listened attentively to his story. Look at the picture (page 28). This is an artist's

conception of the scene in Spain following the return of Columbus.

The last years of Columbus. It was easy, now, to find 

Spaniards ready to sail with the great navigator. Columbus made three more voyages with noblemen, gold-seekers, and colonists crowding his ships. He found more islands, touched the coast of South America, and carefully explored 

Courtesy Milwaukee Public Museum AN INDIAN HOME IN THE SOUTHWEST. This is a museum reproduction of the various rooms in the house of a Hopi Indian family. Notice the furnishings, and the occupations that are going on. the shoreline of Central America. But nowhere did he find lands or people such as Polo had described. Always that savage tropical shore barred his way. 

Behind Columbus, in Spain, his enemies were busy. They belittled his discoveries and criticized his management of the colonies springing up in the newly-discovered islands.

He brought no gold to fill the coffers of the Spanish government. The sailors of Portugal, sailing south along the west coast of Africa, had at last rounded the cape at the southern end of that continent and, under Vasco da Gama, had reached India. They had won the race to open a new sea

route to the East. Columbus, returning from his fourth voyage, found his old benefactress, Isabella, dying. Ferdinand, indifferent, cast the aging mariner aside. Neglected and in poverty, Columbus died in 1506, ignorant, as were all others, of the greatness of his work. 

Naming the new lands. For many years the name of 

Christopher Columbus was almost forgotten. Other mariners rose rapidly into prominence, and one, Americus Vespucius (ȧ-mer'i-kus vès-pu'shus), wrote so well of his explorations in South America that Professor Waldseemuller, of the college of St. Die, suggested that the new lands, particularly the southern part, which was seen to be a new continent, be called America. This idea met with approval, and soon the new name came to be applied to all of the 

New World as North America and South America. Thus it may be said that Columbus was robbed by an accident, due to ignorance, of the honor of having the new continents named for him.

Greatness of Columbus' work. In time, of course, men saw that the great new continents were the same lands first discovered by Columbus. Then it was that his name was given the place it deserves among the world's great discoverers. Today his fame is secure, though as one writer says, "His discovery was a blunder, his blunder was a new world, and the new world his monument."

CHAPTER III  

In this chapter you will learn of the work of the three great rivals in the exploration of America: Spain, England, France. The character and purposes of these early explorations are explained, and the regions explored are indicated. The rise of English sea power and the decline of Spain, with the effects on the future colonization of the American continent, will be clearly understood from these narratives. 

1. SPAIN IN AMERICA 

Spanish enterprise. Spain was better prepared than any other country to follow up the great discoveries of Columbus. The Spanish people were flushed with success from their victories over the Moors. The land was filled with bold and warlike men who, now that the Moorish wars were over, wished for new fields of excitement and glory. The 36

rulers were alert to push any plans that seemed to promise more fame and riches for Spain. 

In addition to all this, Spain was spurred on by her rivalry with Portugal, whose mariners, as we have seen, had already reached India. One Portuguese captain was driven by a storm to the coast of Brazil (brȧ-zil'), in South America, and Portugal made claim to that region. The rivalry between the two countries became so bitter that the Pope suggested drawing a line around the world giving Brazil and the new eastern lands to Portugal and the rest to Spain. The two countries made a treaty carrying out this idea.

In the course of the first fifty years after the voyages of Columbus, Spanish captains with their bands of bold adventurers had overrun a territory in the New World greater by far than the whole of Europe. The story of the adventures of these Spaniards fills many large books whose pages glow with interest. Only one of these stories can be given here.

The expedition of Ferdinand de Soto. This famous expedition was unsuccessful, and its results were not specially important. But it took place within the present boundaries of our country and well illustrates the spirit and daring of the Spanish explorers. For these reasons it is well worth knowing.

De Soto (dě sō'tō) was born in the year 1500. By the time he was a young man Spain had a firm hold on the West Indies, Central America, and parts of the coast of northern South America. Ponce de León (pōn'thā dā là-ōn') had discovered Florida and had made a pathetic search for a fountain of youth he had heard about. Magellan had sailed around the southern point of South America, had crossed the broad Pacific Ocean, and his ships had come home to Spain by traversing the Indian Ocean and passing around Africa into the Atlantic. Cortez (kôr'těz) had

888 

marched into the interior of Mexico and had conquered and robbed the partly civilized Indians living there. Little towns were springing up on the islands and on the coasts of the mainland; everywhere the Indians were being destroyed or enslaved; and treasure ships, bearing the loot of plundered Indian cities, were beginning to make Spain the richest country in the world. 

The young De Soto was just the kind of man to throw himself into this exciting life in the New World. Adopted into the family of a proud Spanish nobleman, he had been taught all the accomplishments that a gentleman of that time needed. He was dashing in appearance and was said to be the best rider and swordsman in the Spanish army. 

His first chance for fame and fortune came when Pizarro (pĬ-zärʼrō), who was forming an expedition to go to 

Peru, in South America, chose De Soto as his lieutenant.

This cruel expedition, in which the rich king, or Inca (ing'ka), of the Peruvian Indians was killed and his fine kingdom almost destroyed, made De Soto rich. In Spain he was received as a hero. He married a Spanish lady, but lived in such style that in two years half his fortune had been used up. So he decided on a second visit to America to restore his fortunes. 

De Soto had heard of Florida, a name used at that time by the Spaniards to mean not only the Florida of today, but all of the vague country lying north and west of the lands discovered by Ponce de León. De Soto believed that somewhere in this region there must be other rich countries like Mexico and Peru, where gold might be gathered in great quantities. So he secured permission to fit out an expedition to conquer this northern country, and in May, 1538, he set out. Leaving his faithful wife, Isabella, to rule 

Cuba in his absence, for he had been made governor of that island, De Soto and his men sailed gaily away for Florida. 

His little army was as fine a one as Spain could offer.

From every side the brave and the daring from the finest families in Spain had flocked to De Soto's standard, eager to share with him the glorious search for riches. There were 570 men and 223 saddle horses. The men were armed with the heavy guns that were beginning to be used at that time, and with fine swords which they knew how to use with great skill. They had metal breastplates and gloves, while their heads were cased in steel helmets. Blacksmiths and surgeons and priests were with the expedition. To be sure of a supply of food, a large drove of hogs was taken along. 

Can you imagine the excitement on board the ships when at last a faint blue line on the far horizon told the adventurers that their land of gold was just before them?

The men broke into songs and shouts of joy. Here was the land of eternal spring, the land of flowers and fountains of youth. Here they would surely find another Mexico or Peru, from which they would return laden with wealth. Thus thought the followers of De Soto that spring day in the year 1539.

The landing was made on the west coast of Florida, at 

Tampa Bay. On the first night the Spaniards had their dreams of easy conquests and sudden riches disturbed by a sudden Indian attack. They sprang up and fled to their ships. Now they began to realize that there was plenty of grim, hard work ahead of them. But these Spaniards were as brave as they were greedy. Soon men and horses and supplies were all set on shore, and the best of the ships sent back to Cuba. In a little time the army was ready for the march, and the great forest swallowed them.

De Soto's explorations. De Soto may not have been at heart a cruel man. But his desire for gold made him desperate. He would not let any feelings of gentleness stand in the way of success. So he kept his men prepared to fight the Indians every step of the way if necessary and to rob and enslave them if that would help his plans.

One thing he soon learned. A cruel Spaniard, Narvaez (när-vä'ath), had visited these regions a few years before, and he and his men by their evil deeds had taught the red men to hate the white strangers. Once they had cut off the nose of a chief and stood by while the chief's mother had been torn to pieces by the Spanish bloodhounds. This chief, and most of the other Indians who had heard of 57 

From Inman's The Old Santa Fe Trail CORONADO CROSSING THE DESERT. Note the armor worn by men and horses as the Spaniards searched for the fabled cities of the Southwest. 

Narvaez, were ready for war the moment they heard of De Soto's coming. The cruelties of Narvaez made De Soto's work doubly hard and dangerous. 

One piece of good fortune fell to De Soto. A Spaniard who had come to Florida ten years before to help search for Narvaez had been captured by the Indians and held a prisoner all these years. Now he came to De Soto's camp and became the interpreter and guide of the expedition. 

Eagerly the Spaniards plied this man with questions concerning the places where gold might be found, but he could give them no information. He spoke, however, of a great

chief to the northward, and thither De Soto's men turned their steps.

His hardships. This was the beginning of a three years' search for the rich cities and the gold which somehow remained always just out of the reach of the greedy Spaniards. Most of the Indians fled at the approach of the invaders. Often those who remained were seized and made

4, scene of his death; 5, point where he and Coronado were near each other; 6, the wanderings of the remnants of De Soto's army. to act as guides through the endless forests. Sometimes these guides had their revenge by leading the Spaniards into great swamps. Whenever the native chiefs came out of the woods to parley with De Soto, he seized them and made them go with him to the edge of the lands they ruled over. Each day was filled with hardships. But beyond a few pearls and trinkets there was nothing to take back to Spain.

Finally De Soto's wanderings led him to the lands of an Indian queen. He seized her while his men went to some

mines she told them of. Here at last was their Peru, thought they. But, alas, the metal which the men brought back to camp proved to be only a worthless alloy of copper. So the expedition toiled on and on through the wilderness. 

Turning back towards the coast near where Mobile now stands, the adventurers met Tuscaloosa, head of a warlike tribe. He greeted the white men with a smile, and De Soto and a part of his men went into the main Indian village. 

Here the war whoop suddenly rose, and the Indians rushed upon their surprised visitors. For a time the Indians drove the Spaniards back, but the veteran soldiers of De Soto's band rallied and held their ground. For hours the battle raged. In the end, the good Spanish swords and the Spanish armor were too much for the Indian arrows and war clubs, and when night came the Indian army was destroyed. But a hundred or more white men had fallen, and many of the horses had been killed, while a fire had destroyed most of 

De Soto's baggage and medicine.

At this point the white leader showed his courage. He knew that some of his relief ships were on the coast waiting for him. His little army was ragged and footsore and discouraged after their year and a half of wandering. But 

De Soto had not found what he sought, and proudly turning his back on the chance for escape from the wilderness, he led his men again northward.

Discovery of the Mississippi River. The discovery that makes De Soto's name sure to live in history was still before him. One day the Spaniards came out on the bank of a mighty river two miles wide which carried timbers and uprooted trees along in its resistless progress toward the south. De Soto had discovered the Mississippi River.

This was in the year 1541. Notice on page 36 an artist's idea of this event.

The yearning for gold blinded the Spaniards to the greatness of their discovery. Crossing the great river, the white

men wandered about on the plains of Arkansas for a year and then dragged themselves back to the Mississippi. A slow fever was burning in De Soto's veins, and his face was wrinkled and drawn from pain and hardship. He was not ready yet to give up, but the fever grew worse and he died on the banks of the great river. 

Courtesy Southern Pacific Railway SAN XAVIER MISSION, TUCSON, ARIZONA. This famous old mission looks today almost as it did when it was built. Much of the work on many of the old Spanish missions was done by the Indian converts. 

Burying the body of their leader in the depths of the river, the three hundred fifty survivors of the brilliant army that had landed so gaily on Tampa Bay three years before hurriedly built some crude boats and floated away down the river. Reaching its mouth they sailed along the gulf shore to the westward until Spanish settlements in Mexico were found.

Coronado in the Southwest. While De Soto was making his fruitless search, another Spaniard, Francisco Coronado

(kō-rô-nä'thō), was leading a band of adventurers through what is now the southwestern part of the United States. He sought the fabled "seven cities" which existed only in the imaginations of men. He found Indian villages, but no rich cities whose walls were studded with precious gems. Some of Coronado's men, however, made an important discovery. 

They found the Grand Canyon of the Colorado River. On page 40 is a picture by a famous artist showing Coronado's march.

The stories of De Soto and Coronado enable us to understand how the Spaniards frequently wasted their energies in fruitless expeditions in search of precious metals. Treatment of the Indians was frequently cruel and heartless. 

The Indians were often enslaved. Compelled to work on plantations and in mines, many died, and in a few years the Indian population of Cuba and Mexico was greatly reduced. We must not assume, however, that the Spanish conquerors in their treatment of the native population were greatly different from other members of the white race. 

The Spanish established many prosperous colonies in Cuba and other islands of the West Indies and in Mexico and parts of South America. Not only did they work the mines of those countries, but they also developed large plantations. When the native labor supply was exhausted they imported negroes from Africa to do the work. 

The failure of De Soto and Coronado to find gold in the southern parts of what is now our country led the Spaniards to spend their time and energies in the richer and more easily conquered lands farther to the southward. This left most of North America open to exploration and settlement by other nations.

2. Describe the relations between De Soto and the Indians.

2. DRAKE AND THE RISE OF ENGLISH SEA POWER 

For almost a hundred years after the discovery of America, Spain had everything her own way in the New 

World. The plundered cities of Mexico and Peru made her rich, but all this sudden wealth began to ruin her real prosperity, for her people gave up much of their farming and manufacturing and bought most of the things they needed from other countries. Still, for many years, Spain was regarded as the most powerful nation in the world. 

England indifferent to America. The island kingdom of 

England was just recovering from long and cruel civil wars at the time Columbus sailed to America. But powerful kings now sat on the throne, and England was prosperous. 

There was some interest in the great news of Columbus' discoveries, and King Henry VII sent out John Cabot (kǎb'ut) to make discoveries beyond the Atlantic. He kept far to the north, in order not to conflict with Spain's claims, and discovered land in and about the Gulf of St. Lawrence and southward as far as Cape Cod. Setting up the flag of 

England in the lands he had found, he returned, reporting that he had seen immense numbers of cod and herring in the shallow waters near Newfoundland. From then on fishing vessels of England and France crossed the sea regularly to the famed "Newfoundland Banks" for the fishing season.

But little attention was paid to the discoveries of Cabot, and for half a century, while the people of England were engaged in a great religious quarrel, the work of this discoverer was almost forgotten, and no attempts were made to rival Spain in the New World.

The awakening of England. After the year 1550, a great change began to take place in England. Under their queen, Elizabeth, Englishmen began to feel that their country should be the leader in commerce and power on the sea. 

Most Englishmen were by this time members of Protestant churches, while Spain considered herself the champion of

the Catholic church. This situation added to the growing dislike between the two nations, and soon they were bitter enemies. For a long time there was no open war between them, but this did not prevent the bold English sailors, such as Frobisher (frō'bish-ēr), the daring explorer, and Sir John Hawkins, who won fame as a slave trader, from doing all they could to injure the rich commerce of their enemy. 

But among all the daring sailors of this age none equaled Sir Francis Drake, the Dragon, as the Spaniards learned to call him.

The English sea dogs. Drake's career as a sea rover began when he was a boy and continued for more than thirty years. The easiest way for Elizabeth's sailors to cripple

Spain was to lie in wait for and capture the great treasure ships which crossed the Atlantic from the New World to Spain laden with the gold and silver taken from the rich mines of Mexico and Peru or captured from the natives. 

This was also an easy way for the English sailors to get rich, for much of the treasure captured was kept for their own use. All this was much like piracy, but in those times nobody thought much about how wrong this method of warfare was. 

Drake's first adventure was as a captain on board one of

Sir John Hawkins' ships. Hawkins' fleet was driven into a 

Spanish harbor on the American coast, where it was set upon by the Spaniards. They knew very well why the English commander was prowling about the "Spanish Main," as that part of the coast was called. Drake's ship was one of the two that escaped, but the ship and its crew had been sadly battered. Drake never forgot this early defeat at the hands of the men of Spain, and he spent the rest of his life in evening the score.

Drake's exploits. Soon, in command of three ships, Drake appeared off the coast of America near the Spanish towns, and seizing some of them, captured "a pretty store of

money" as an old historian puts it. Once he crossed the Isthmus of Panama (pån-¿-mä′) and gazed out on the Pacific, upon which no European, save the Spaniards, had sailed a ship. Drake at once decided that an English vessel should soon sail that great ocean. 

In England, where Drake was already hailed as a hero, he set about making his preparations for what proved to be the greatest voyage an Englishman had yet undertaken. 

In the fall of 1577 his five ships slipped out of Plymouth Harbor, in England, and turned their prows for the distant shores of South America. Drake's flagship, the "Pelican, was richly fitted up and was a strong, swift vessel. Coasting along the shore of South America, Drake at last arrived at the Strait of Magellan. All the other ships had returned to 

England or had been wrecked. Renaming his ship the "Golden Hind," Drake braved the stormy strait, and soon the "Golden Hind" was plowing through the waters of the Pacific on its voyage northward along the coast of South America. Not long after that the English craft was among the great galleons (găl'è-unz) of Spain, laden with silver from Peru, on their voyage to Panama. Drake captured the 

Spanish ships, and soon the gold and silver bars of the Spanish treasure fleet were safely laid away in the hold of the "Golden Hind."

In his story of his adventures Drake says that in one harbor he captured three small Spanish ships. In one he found "fifty-seven wedges of silver, each of them weighing about twenty pound weight and every [one] of these wedges was of the fashion and bigness of a brick." At another point they found a Spaniard asleep on the shore with thirteen bars of silver beside him. Drake says, "We took the silver and left the man.' 

The stanch ship found a safe harbor somewhere on the coast of California; after naming the land New Albion, Drake soon put to sea again.

He feared the great Spanish warships might lie in wait for him if he tried to go back to England the way he had come, and so he resolved on a bold course. He would follow in the wake of Magellan and get home by sailing west across the Pacific and completing his journey around the world.. 

With Drake, to think was to act, and he finished the long 

 SIR FRANCIS DRAKE, England's most daring "sea dog." The Spaniards called him the "Dragon." Does he not look capable of dangerous exploits? journey in November, 1580. An Englishman had circumnavigated the globe. 

Queen Elizabeth had been requested by King

Philip of Spain to surrender 

Drake to the Spaniards to be punished as a pirate, should he ever return to his native land. Instead, she knighted him and wore in her crown the splendid jewel he had presented to her. His revenge on the 

Spaniards might now have been considered complete, for it was more than a hundred years before the Spanish sailors ceased to speak of him as the "Dragon." 

Destruction of the Spanish Armada, 1588. But Drake's work was far from done. Spain and England were soon at open war, and the Spanish Armada (är-ma'da), one of the most magnificent fleets any nation had ever gathered together, sailed from Spain for the coast of England. Philip was bent on punishing the saucy islanders who dared dispute with him the command of the seas. It looked as if he would do it, too, but at last the English people were roused to their peril. England's finest sailors, among them Drake

and Lord Howard and Frobisher and Hawkins, in light, quick-moving vessels, awaited the approach of the great Spanish fleet. Size and numbers of ships were on the side of the invaders. Skill and daring and good fortune were with the men of England. Through the rough waters of the 

English Channel the two fleets battled. The English ships darted in, struck their damaging blows, and were away before the heavy Spanish warships could turn to destroy them. At last the battered Armada was cooped up in the 

North Sea, with the homeward passage blocked. Then, as the Spanish captains sought to work around the British Isles to the northward and westward, a great storm struck them. Scores of ships were wrecked, and the bodies of thousands of soldiers and sailors were washed up on the shores of Scotland. Only a feeble remnant ever crept back to Spain.

This was the beginning of the end of Spanish control of the sea. After that great day Spain grew steadily weaker, and from that time to the present England has had few dangerous rivals on the seas. So Sir Francis Drake and the other sea rovers of Elizabeth did much to change the history not only of Europe but of America, as we shall see.

3. WHEN Cartier PlanTED THE FRENCH FLAG IN AMERICA 

France and the New World. During all the years that 

Spain was growing rich from her conquests in America, France, like England, was giving almost all her time and attention to affairs within or near her own borders. A great

religious quarrel, similar to that in England, broke out, and led to much civil strife. France gave little thought, during most of this period, to discovery and exploration beyond the sea.

Still, the name of at least one great French sailor of this time should be known and remembered by Americans.

Jacques Cartier (kȧr-tyā') was an energetic seaman of the bustling port of St. Malo, France. He was sent out by his king in 1534 to seek a northwest passage to the coasts of Asia and to take possession, in the name of France, of any new lands discovered. To keep clear of the lands claimed by Spain and to reach the region where, as he believed, this water passage to the East was most likely to be found, he steered his ship west and northwest in his voyage across the Atlantic.

Cartier's was by no means the first French ship to cross the Atlantic. In 1524 Verazzano (vĕr-rät-sä'no), an Italian sailing under the French flag, had coasted along the shores of what is now the United States, and had strengthened the belief of many people that at a point about where Maryland is, North America narrowed down to an isthmus, like the one at Panama. So Cartier, like many others, believed that a water route might easily be found through North America to the ocean beyond. This belief led to some careful explorations of our coast in the early days, and the belief in this famous "Northwest Passage" died slowly in men's minds. 

Cartier's voyages to the St. Lawrence River. On his first voyage Cartier sailed half way around Newfoundland and explored the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the mouth of the 

St. Lawrence River to a point "where land could be seen on both sides." Soon he was in these waters again with a fresh ship and supplies, for he felt that the mighty St. 

Lawrence might indeed be the sought-for passage through to the lands of Asia. Up the river pushed the adventurous ship,

Always the Indians said "Canada" when the Frenchmen asked for the names of the villages along the shores. "Canada" meant "village" in the Indian tongue, but this word in time was applied by the French to all of the great country along the St. Lawrence and north of the Great Lakes. At last the water became so fresh that Cartier knew he was on a river and not a channel of the sea. But he explored the river banks and looked over the ground carefully where one of Canada's chief towns, Montreal, was later to be established.

Cartier spent a dismal winter on the shore of the river, doing his best to make friends with the Indians by giving them presents of knives and beads and having his trumpeters give loud blasts on their instruments.

Cartier's third voyage was a colonizing enterprise, but in a short time the settlers were glad to escape from the cold country and return to France. 

Results. Cartier was a good sailor and a careful explorer, and his work on the St. Lawrence gave France her claims to this region when she began the work of settlement in earnest seventy-five years later.

UNIT II EARLY EUROPEAN SETTLERS IN NORTH AMERICA 

On the heels of the daring explorers who quickly made large part of our continent known to the people of Europe came those who planned to make their homes in the newfound lands. Settlers from the leading countries of Europe crossed the ocean to America. Some men planned to fish along the shores for a living, some to engage in the fur trade, and still others to help their country make good its claims to a part of America. As time passed, more and more men left Europe to escape conditions which they did not like, brought their families with them, and took up farms on the edge of the American wilderness. Here they struggled to make their homes, suffered from famine and disease, fought the Indians, and learned how to live and even to prosper in the new land.

The three chapters of Unit II tell the story of some of these earliest immigrants to America. Here we learn that in the end it was the people from England who took possession of the eastern part of what is now our United States, making it certain that the English language, customs, and ideas of government would be established in this country. 55 55

Courtesy National Park Service RUINS AT JAMESTOWN. Jamestown never became a thriving town. This shows an old foundation after the rubbish had been cleared away. Today the place is in charge of the National Park Service. In the distance can be seen the Jamestown Monument.

CHAPTER IV  

In Chapter IV is told the story of how groups of people from England first gained footholds in America. Here you learn of the conditions in the mother country which stimulated the settlement of the American wilderness. You are told of the first years of hardship in the new land and of the means the settlers took to improve their condition. At the close of this period the English occupied a continuous strip of territory reaching from the present state of Maine on the north to the peninsula of Florida on the south.

The New-World home. Now that Englishmen, and after them the people of other European countries, were ready to make their homes along the eastern shores of North 

America, let us see what the surroundings of the new homes were to be like. These first immigrants found them- 57

selves on a low coastal plain, cut into by many good bays and harbors and crossed by numerous rivers. It can be said that "America faced Europe" and seemed to invite the newcomers to her shores. The soil was capable of producing the crops of grains and vegetables with which the settlers were familiar in Europe. Almost everywhere there stood 

HENNEPIN'S SKETCH OF NIAGARA FALLS. This is without doubt the first drawing ever made of the famous cataract. above this good soil a heavy forest of hardwoods. The new settler would need to be a woodsman before he could become a farmer. The axe and the gun would mean more to him, at first, than the hoe or the plow. 

Along the northern coasts and in the rivers the water teemed with fish. Deer, feathered game, and fur-bearing animals were to be found in countless numbers in the forest and along the marshes and swamps. No man who had a

gun or who could contrive a fishline and a hook need starve in this wilderness.

Off to the westward a few days' journey the hills billowed up into the long parallel ridges of the Appalachian (ǎp-ȧ-lǎch'ĭ-ăn) Highland. This highland served as a barrier to the west and confined the settlers in compact groups nearer the sea. It was many years before any one needed to worry about this mountain barrier or what lay beyond it. The climate of the new home was not greatly different from that of western Europe. Still, it produced some unpleasant surprises. The weather changed suddenly. The summers were hotter and the winters colder than in the same latitudes in Europe.

The Indians. Of course these early settlers had the greatest curiosity about the red dwellers in the forest, the Indians. But their dread of the natives was even greater than their curiosity. The red men, however, were few in number and were widely scattered. They were generally inclined, at first, to be friendly. There were troubles enough in store between the red men and the white; they would have been fewer had the white men striven harder to understand their red neighbors. We must remember that the 

Indians had much greater cause to fear and dread the "palefaces" than the latter had to fear and dread them.

This new American home for the people of Europe was a beautiful country. Its stately forests took on magic hues when autumn came. Its rivers were sparkling green ribbons as they rolled toward the sea. There was a quiet beauty in the gently rounded hills and in the smiling valleys between. There was vigor in the air that drifted in from the mysterious west; there was hope in the vivid sunshine of th's new land. In spite of dangers and hardships and poverty, the newcomers soon learned to love their homes on the edge of the great American wilderness.

2. List the ways in which the new land made a good home for Europeans. 

1. THE VIRGINIA SETTLEMENT 

Sir Walter Raleigh. During the years when England and 

Spain were fighting to see which should command the seas, one Englishman, Sir Walter Raleigh (rô'li) was giving his time and fortune in attempts to colonize Virginia, as the land between Florida and Maine was then called. He succeeded in planting a colony on Roanoke (rō'ȧ-nōk) Island off the coast of North Carolina. The war with Spain was then going on, and the Spanish were still strong enough to prevent supplies and fresh colonists from joining the little group of Englishmen on the island for several years. 

When help did arrive the colony had disappeared. Nobody to this day knows what became of the lost colony of Roanoke.

But Raleigh's attempt was not in vain. His ships brought back to England two American products, tobacco and the potato. Raleigh was soon raising the potato on his estate in Ireland, while the gentlemen of England were soon smoking tobacco and wondering where they could get more of it. But Raleigh's greatest work lay in the fact that his years of effort to plant a colony in America finally roused the people of England to a keen interest in colonizing enterprises. He should be remembered as the father of English colonization in America. 

Hard times in England. By 1600 Englishmen no longer greatly feared the Spanish ships. To many it seemed that 

America was intended by God as a place for distressed Englishmen. Times were hard in England at that time. The great landlords had decided that they could make more money by pasturing sheep on their estates than by raising crops. Thousands of tenants were driven off the land, and shepherds with their flocks took their places. The poor farmers were reduced to the verge of starvation. To many

Englishmen it seemed that their homeland was overcrowded. 

Then, too, there was a great increase in the amount of money in use in that country, as well as in the rest of Europe. The gold and silver from Spain's mines in America was constantly adding to the supply of coins in circulation. 

 GOVERNOR CALVERT AND THE INDIANS. The first governor of Maryland is here shown meeting the Indians near the place where he wished to plant his colony. He was successful in gaining the good will of the red men. 

This caused prices to go up. But the wages of those employed did not rise with the rise in prices of the things they had to buy. Their situation became almost as bad as that of the tenant farmers.

Stirring times in England. But if the times were bad they were also stirring. Thousands of Englishmen disliked the claim of the king that he ruled them because God had given him that right. Some feared that the English Parliament would lose the powers it had been so long in winning.

Some of the leaders in England saw that their country had a chance to take the place of Spain in New World colonization. Merchants and manufacturers, with more money at hand for carrying out their plans than they had ever had before, saw, in English colonies beyond the ocean, new and profitable uses for their ships and new places to sell their goods.

With stout ships, eager leaders, money to finance their plans, and thousands of Englishmen ready to brave the dangers of the wilderness rather than remain in England, there was no reason why the nation should not plant colonies in the New World.

Remembering how much money Raleigh had spent in his unsuccessful attempts to establish a colony, the Englishmen interested in the plans for a colony decided to put their money together in a trading company and let the company manage the enterprise. A group of "knights, gentlemen, merchants, and others" who met in London, in 1606, formed the London Company. They went to King 

James I for a charter. He granted them lands along the coasts of what are now Virginia and Maryland. In this charter it was stated that those who went to the new land were to be governed by English law. They took "the rights of Englishmen" with them. Plans were at once made for sending out a group of settlers. 

Jamestown founded, 1607. On December 20, 1606, three ships, the "Susan Constant," the "Goodspeed," and the "Discovery," sailed down the Thames (těmz) River from

London with one hundred twenty people on board. The passengers were all men. Captain Christopher Newport, commander of the fleet, had charge of the settlers until the landing was made in Virginia. Captain Newport took the old route by way of the Canary Islands and the West Indies.

It was not until April 26, 1607, that the coasts of Vir-

ginia were sighted. Here two points of land reached toward one another across a broad channel, and these were at once named Cape Charles and Cape Henry in honor of the king's two sons. Somewhere within these capes on Chesapeake 

Bay the officers of the London Company had decided that the colony should be planted. 

The men first landed on Cape 

Henry, and here the sealed instructions which Newport carried were opened, and the names of the seven men who were to rule the colony as councilors were learned. Captain John Smith was one of the seven named.
