At once the search for a suitable place for the settlement was begun. It was springtime, and the shores were beautiful with vegetation. The men were in high spirits. It seemed to them that planting a colony for the London Company was going to be a pleasant, easy task. The little fleet lay at the lower end of Chesapeake Bay, which has four large, broad rivers entering it from the west.

Any one of these rivers could be navigated by the ships of the time, and the long narrow tongues of land lying between the broad river mouths looked fertile. Heavy forests covered the land except where patches had been cleared away for the Indian cornfields or had been desolated by fire. serve the dress and equipment of the early seventeenth-century soldier and adventurer.

The colonists had been directed to go up one of the rivers some distance and settle on high ground where the forest was not dense and where good water might be had. Finally, after two weeks' search, a place was selected for the settle-

ment thirty-two miles up the James River, which had been so named in honor of King James. It was a peninsula reaching out into the river from its north bank. But it was low and marshy and covered with trees and high grass. 

There was no water to drink, except the river water. 

Here the colonists were set ashore with their provisions and tools. They were put to work building a three-cornered fort near the neck of the peninsula. Cannon were mounted on the rude walls, and within the enclosure were marked off the beginnings of a town which was named Jamestown. 

Most of the men were not used to such rough toil as this. 

But they were really servants of the Company and had to do as they were ordered. The picture on page 57 shows that this early English settlement never developed into an important town.

Hard times in the colony. Newport had been directed by the London Company to hunt for gold. He took a small vessel and sailed away up the James. He returned in a week with no gold and learned that while he had been away the Indians had made an attack on the unfinished stockade of the fort. After aiding the settlers in completing their stockade he sailed away for England, leaving one hundred four men in Virginia.

Only a few weeks had passed when things began to go badly. There was little to eat except barley meal, and there was only a small ladle of this for each man each day. The colonists had a few poor log cabins and holes in the ground for shelter. Soon they found that the climate did not agree with them and the water from the river seemed to poison them. One after another they died, until in September more than half the little band of homesick and desperate men had found graves in the wilderness of Virginia.

Captain John Smith. In such times men of strong character come to the front to take charge of affairs. Captain 

John Smith, who was given the work of caring for the sup-

plies and handing them out to the men, now began visiting the Indians along the rivers and buying corn from them. 

In this way he warded off starvation from the little colony during much of the next year or so. 

The Virginia Indians. Whenever he could, Smith explored the shores of Chesapeake Bay and sailed up some of the fine broad rivers flowing into it. He had many adventures with the Indians. Most of the Indians living on the lands granted by the king to the London Company were banded together in a confederacy which was ruled over at this time by Powhatan (pouha-tǎn'), who had his principal village on the York River fourteen miles across the peninsula from Jamestown. Powhatan was a wily chief and seems to have had much more power than most Indian chiefs. He had friends acting as chiefs of the tribes in the confederacy. These men collected the taxes for him. As a bodyguard he had fifty huge savages always near him. The Virginia Indians raised corn, tobacco, and vegetables. They lived in oval-shaped wigwams made of bark fastened on a framework of poles. The tribesmen resented the coming of the white men, and their hatred was one of the greatest difficulties in the way of planting a strong colony. Smith and Powhatan came to know each other well. It was Powhatan's daughter Pocahontas (pō-kȧhon'tȧs) who, according to Smith's story, saved his life when as a prisoner he was about to be executed in the old chief's council house.

Mistakes of the London Company. After a while Smith became actually the absolute ruler of the band of wretched men in Jamestown. Many of the colonists had never known how to do hard work and did not care to learn. Besides, they were so weakened by sickness that they had little strength or ambition. The Company was trying hard to do well by its colony, but many mistakes were made. Fresh bands of settlers and supplies of food were sent out each year, but often the supplies for the men in Virginia were nearly all consumed on the voyage across the ocean. Thus the newcomers often added to the distress by helping eat the provisions Smith had worked so hard to gather. Then, too, the company wanted immediate returns on the money it had invested. The ships sent out to Jamestown were expected to carry a cargo back to England. Sometimes it was worthless ore and sometimes it was timber, but in either case the poor, feeble settlers were compelled to do the work of gathering the cargo and putting it on board the ships. Another great weakness in the company's plans was the arrangement to have all the settlers work on the same piece of land, when they farmed, and put the crops raised into a common storehouse from which enough was handed back to the men to enable them to live. For this reason the men who might have done well enough on little farms of their own became discouraged and worked no harder than they were compelled to, while those who were naturally lazy grew still lazier.

Captain Smith saw all these things and wrote angry letters home to the company officers urging them to make changes in the conduct of the colony. He said that real farmers were needed, and that the company should hasten to make farms in Virginia and not waste the strength of the people in foolish efforts to find gold or other riches. 

Smith also set the men at clearing more land and constructing better buildings. In 1609 this energetic man, who had

really saved Virginia, was injured and returned to England. 

Better times. Gradually the sound advice Smith had given began to be heeded. Three acres of land was given to each settler for his own. Then it was made possible for men to buy a hundred acres. The Company sent governors to rule the colony, in place of the seven councilors. Some of the governors were very harsh, but the Indians were cowed by them, and there was order in the colony. Sickness and death were still common, but gradually the older settlers became accustomed to the climate, and the danger of starvation and failure lessened.

Of the many interesting things that happened in Virginia during the next ten years, only a few can be mentioned here. 

A great day in the colony was that on which a ship arrived bringing to Jamestown more than ninety young women to become the wives of settlers. The colony needed homes perhaps more than anything else. It was not long before most of the young women had had proposals of marriage from some of the lonesome men. If the proposal was accepted, the man paid the cost of the voyage to Virginia for the girl who had consented to marry him. Other groups of women followed the first band and most of them found good husbands in Virginia. During the same year in which the first women arrived, some negroes were brought to Jamestown and sold to the white settlers. This event was the beginning of negro slavery in the United States. 

An assembly of the people. For the first time in the history of Virginia, the colonists were given a share in the government of the colony. They had had in England a right to choose their own local officers. They could not see why they should not have the same right in Virginia. 

The Company granted the wish, and a legislature, or House of Burgesses chosen by the people, began holding regular meetings at Jamestown. This pleased the colonists, and 

Virginia continued to grow and prosper. The House of

Burgesses was a fine model for the legislatures of other colonies. It will be interesting, later, to see how careful the 

House of Burgesses was to protect the rights of the people against governors who often wanted to rule the colony in high-handed ways.

All three of these events-the coming of the women, the landing of the first negroes, and the first representative assembly of the people-happened in the same year, 1619. 

This date should be remembered.

Virginia farms. By 1624, when King James, angry with the Company, took away its charter and began to rule Virginia through governors he selected himself, about 1,000 white people were living in Virginia. The settlers were in scattered groups along the James River and on the York River to the north. Most of the men now owned land, and the more prosperous of them were steadily adding to the size of their farms. Those who had been servants of the 

Company and others who came over as servants, bound to work for some master for a term of years, were also taking land of their own as soon as they were free to do so. 

The towns and villages in Virginia remained small. 

Jamestown and a number of other early villages have disappeared. The people scattered out over the land on separate farms. Those who were able took up lands along the rivers which served as the only roads of the early Virginians. 

Practically all the men were either farmers raising some special crop to be sold in Europe-planters they were called -or the servants of planters.

Life in early Virginia. Most of these features of Virginia life were due to one thing-tobacco. The use of tobacco, which Raleigh had introduced into England, had become very popular. In 1612 the Virginians began raising it. The price was high and there was a great demand for all the tobacco the Virginians could raise. Soon every patch of cleared ground, and even the streets of Jamestown, were

used for raising tobacco. Every one who owned land spent more time on his tobacco fields than on any other crop. 

The planters were what might be called "one-crop" farmers. 

Now one-crop farmers need to sell this single crop in order to get the clothing, furniture, and implements which they need. The Virginians sold their tobacco in England and got the supplies they needed from England. The broad, deep rivers helped in this arrangement because the ships of the time could come up the rivers right to the planter's landing. This, you see, was the chief reason the planters wanted land that fronted on the rivers. There was little need of towns in Virginia, for the planter and his wife did their "shopping" in England. They sent over to England lists of the supplies they needed, and an agent there made the purchases and shipped the goods back to them. Since tobacco used up the fertility of the soil very quickly, it seemed easier for the planter to open up new tobacco lands than to try to keep the old lands rich enough for his crops. 

This explains why the plantations grew larger and larger, and it also helps to show why the planters felt they needed great numbers of servants or negro slaves to carry on their farming.

But tobacco made many Virginians prosperous, and soon fine homes began to spring up along the rivers. As the years passed people poured into Virginia rapidly, and the colony flourished. The Virginia which has been such a famous state throughout much of our history was beginning to develop.

2. THE PILGrims at PlyMOUTH 

The Plymouth Company. When the London Company was formed, in 1606, another company called the Plymouth

Company was also organized. The lands granted to this company for colonization lay to the north of those of the London Company. The motives of the Plymouth Company in wishing to plant colonies were like those of the London Company. Both the Plymouth Company itself and men to whom they granted lands tried to set up colonies in the years between 1606 and 1620. But nothing came of these 

 ON BOARD THE MAYFLOWER. Before the Pilgrims landed in America they drew up a set of rules by which to govern themselves. Here they are seen making the rules, or "Mayflower Compact," as the finished document is called. attempts to establish commercial colonies on the North Atlantic coast. In the year 1620, while fishermen knew these coasts very well, and the region had already received the name New England from Captain John Smith of Virginia, there were no permanent settlements in this territory. It was a religious reason that was to bring the first permanent settlers to these shores.

Religious disputes in England. You will remember that a great religious quarrel was going on in England during

the half century after the year 1500. Even during the glorious reign of Elizabeth, when the Spaniards were being humbled, the religious quarrel went on. The church supported by the government was now the Church of England, or Established Church. But there were thousands of Englishmen who were not satisfied with this church or with many of the conditions in 

English life. They desired the Established Church to make itself still less like the Catholic Church which had so long been the state church in England. They believed in stricter rules of conduct for members of the church. They felt that the morals of the people should be better. These discontented people were called 

Puritans. Some of the qualities of character of the Puritans are shown in the statue pictured on this page. 

d, supialis

THE PURITAN. This picture was made from a famous statue by the sculptor, St. Gaudens. What traits of character did the sculptor wish to bring out? What book is being held 

But there was another group of people in England firmly under this Puritan's arm? that was even more discontented with the church arrangement. This group wanted no state church whatever. Each church congregation, so they thought, should be independent of the state and of all other churches. These people were called Separatists (sĕp'ȧ-ra-tists). 

In England all the other religious bodies felt that the Separatists were a dangerous sect, and it was impossible for the latter to carry on their religious meetings without suf-

12 

fering persecution from all sides. Some of the congregations, among them the congregation in the village of Scrooby, fled to Holland, where for a number of years the members earned a hard living in the mills and shops of Leyden (li'den).

The idea grew in the minds of these Separatists, or Pilgrims as we should now call them, that America would offer them a better home than they could hope for in Holland. In the New World living conditions might be easier, the children would be free from the Dutch influence, and they could all be Englishmen under the English flag. Plans were accordingly made, and in December, 1620, the "Mayflower" landed its famous little band of Pilgrims on the shore of 

Plymouth Harbor, Massachusetts.

Before they went ashore, the Pilgrims drew up a simple plan by which they were to govern themselves. This agreement, which was the first charter of self-government in 

America, is known as the "Mayflower" Compact. Under it the first successful settlement in New England began, a settlement planted by a band of people who had made themselves outcasts and wanderers for the sake of their religious beliefs. John Carver was the first governor, and 

Miles Standish was their military leader.

Because the Pilgrims made the first permanent settlement in New England, we speak of them as the "Pilgrim 

Fathers," the founders or fathers of all the colonies planted by Englishmen in that region. 

Plymouth, 1620. The colony at Plymouth lived and grew, but it never became a great and flourishing commonwealth. 

It is not important because of its size or wealth or the stirring events of its history. The Pilgrims themselves were plain, simple Englishmen of the poorer class. But it was their heroism, their steadfastness in the things they thought to be right, and the fact that they pointed the way for a greater migration of Englishmen to those shores that will

keep the memory of the Pilgrim Fathers—of Miles Standish, the soldier of Plymouth, and William Bradford, an early governor and the historian of the colony-ever fresh in our minds.

3. THE GREAT PURITAN COLONY 

The largest and most famous of all the colonies founded in New England was the Puritan colony of Massachusetts Bay. It grew rapidly; its early leaders were men of influence and education; its laws and government are well worth studying; and it became the mother of still other colonies. 

Later on its influence on other English colonies in America was great. For all these reasons the colony of Massachusetts 

Bay needs to be studied carefully. 

It will be remembered who the Puritans in England were and why they were dissatisfied with conditions in their country. In contrast with the Separatists, the Puritans were a powerful party and included many men of wealth and culture. When King Charles I came to the throne of 

England, in 1624, a long quarrel between him and the Puritan party began. For a number of years the king ruled 

England almost as he pleased. It was then that thousands of the Puritans decided that they, too, would seek homes in America.

Massachusetts founded, 1628. The Puritans obtained land from the Plymouth Company, and in 1628 a band of them under John Endicott (ĕn'di-kot), an energetic but stern and narrow-minded leader, crossed the ocean and settled at Salem on the shore of Massachusetts Bay, sixteen miles north of where Boston is now. A few settlers who had come earlier and had settled along the near-by coast joined Endicott at this place.

Two years later John Winthrop, a rich and well-educated Puritan, and a man of fine, sturdy character, led a party of eight hundred across the Atlantic to join Endicott. Winthrop became the governor and held that position for many years. Within a few months Puritans had settled eight little towns on and near Massachusetts Bay-among them Charlestown, Dorchester, Cambridge, and Boston. After a short time Winthrop moved to Boston because of a fine spring located there, and this town soon was made the capital of the colony. 

Freeman's Oath, Massachusetts Bay Colony "I do promise to give my voice for the election of such person or persons unto voide places as I shall thinke to be the wisest, godliest and ablest for the discharge; men of wisdom and courage-fearing God and hateing covetousness."

Government of the colony. Even people living in a wilderness cannot get along well together and prosper without some form of government. When the Plymouth Company sent over Endicott and his settlers, it had very much the same relation to its colony that the London Company had to Jamestown. It was supposed to be a trading company looking for profits in the enterprise. But when Winthrop sailed for America the charter of the company was transferred to America also. From that day on, the company and the settlement became one and the same, Massachusetts Bay becoming a self-governing Puritan colony. At first the government was in the hands of Governor Winthrop and his assistants. After two years Massachusetts Bay Colony had a legislature, called the General Court, made up of representatives from the scattered towns. The governors were elected once a year by the General Court, while the

assistants held office during good behavior. But the freemen, or citizens with the right to vote, had to be church members. A member of the colony gained the privilege of voting only when those who were already freemen formally granted that right. Thus for many years the government

DRUMBEAT INSTEAD OF CHURCH BELL. It mattered little to the Puritans whether they were called to worship by the boom of a drum, the notes of a horn, or the peal of a church bell. They came cheerfully to listen to the lengthy sermons. was really in the hands of a few church members. It was not a democratic government in the sense that we use that word today. For instance, when the first General Court met, in 1630, there were only eight voters to attend it, while there were more than a hundred heads of families in the colony who could not vote. 

The towns. In New England each settlement was called a town. In the towns all affairs were managed at town meet-

76 ings, held annually. Here the church members of each town. talked over all matters of interest to the town, elected a long list of town officers-including selectmen, clerks, hog reeves, fence viewers, pound keepers, overseers of chimneys, and overseers of the village almshouse, and told them exactly what they were to do. Each town was thus a selfgoverning little community in which the church members had all the political power. In time the various towns sent representatives to the General Court at Boston, and the individual freemen stayed at home. Thus representative government came to be familiar to the people. 

Church matters. Once out of England the Puritans, who had never left the state church there and who said that they did not wish to do so, really became Separatists. Many of their ministers, in particular, had been badly used by the state church at home, and these led the colonists still farther away from the Church of England. In this way the 

Puritans of Massachusetts Bay became more like the Pilgrims of Plymouth. But though the Puritans had come to 

America to secure religious freedom for themselves, their troubles in England did not make them gentle in their treatment of the people who did not agree with them. They had strong, settled opinions on the subject of religion, and they insisted that every one living in Massachusetts should adopt exactly the form of religious worship which the leaders approved. But nearly all men were narrow and selfish in their religious opinions at that day, so the Puritans may be in part excused for their intolerance toward others. 

A study of the pictures of the Puritans in this book helps us to understand the strong feelings of the Puritans on all matters relating to their church. 

Schools in early New England. It is in educational matters that the Puritans are seen in the best light. Almost from the first they had small private schools. In 1636 the 

General Court voted about $2,000, a great sum when we

consider the poverty of the colony, to found a college at Cambridge that, as they said, "the light of learning might not go out, nor the study of God's word perish." This college grew into the great Harvard University of today. In 

1647 the General Court decreed that every township containing fifty or more families should open a public school

The terms of school held were short-no more than four months a year-and some of the poorer towns refused to obey the law and organize schools. But this humble beginning in public schools shows the fine spirit of the Puritans and their determination to make their colony a fit place in which to live and to bring up families.

How the people lived. Times were hard in the New England towns at first. Scurvy and other diseases caused sickness and death. Once or twice the eight towns about the 

Bay were actually threatened with starvation. The climate was much colder than that of England. The thin, stony soil yielded scant crops. It was only by a life of steady toil and thrift that both ends could be made to meet. 

Courtesy Edison Institute

But from the first the settlers here were better adapted to their task than were the men of Virginia. They had made careful plans for their settlements. They brought over a good supply of hogs and cattle with which to stock their farms. There was no time wasted in searching for gold and sudden wealth. Then, too, not all the New Englanders had to farm for a living. Fishing and shipbuilding and other occupations gave profitable employment to many of the settlers, almost from the first.

The near-by Indians were friendly. But above all, the Puritains had come to America, almost every one of them, determined to stay, no matter what happened. It is this feeling that makes the best settlers in a new country. 

A GRAIN CRADLE. With such a cradle most of the grain on

American farms was cut less than a century ago. The wooden fingers parallel to the scythe helped to lay the cut grain in a smooth swath behind the man who "swung the cradle."

For many years after the founding of Massachusetts Bay, affairs in England went from bad to worse for the Puritans who remained there. This led thousands of the sturdiest of Englishmen to cross the ocean with their families to the thriving new commonwealth in New England. 

After ten years fifteen thousand people were in the country.

4. THE DUTCH "WEDGE": NEW AMSTERDAM 

The colonies whose history we have now traced were all planted by Englishmen. We shall next notice one, destined in time to outstrip all the others in wealth and population, which was planted by a different nation, The Netherlands, or Holland.

The rise of Holland. With the decline of Spain, Dutch power increased, and on the sea Holland rivaled England for almost a hundred years. In the Far East the Dutch sailors took control of lands bordering on the Indian Ocean; 

Dutch navigators introduced coffee and tea to Europe; they planted a colony in South Africa; Australia was discovered by the bold sailors of this same nation. But it was an 

Englishman, Henry Hudson, sailing under the Dutch flag, who made the one notable discovery for the Dutch in 

North America. 

In 1609 Henry Hudson, searching for the Northwest

Passage along the bays and river mouths of the North Atlantic coast, sailed up the broad river that now bears his name. Returning to Holland he reported his discovery of "as fair a land as was ever trodden by the foot of man.' 

Holland laid claim to all the land between Chesapeake Bay and the Connecticut River, giving it the name New Netherlands. In a few years her great Dutch West India 

Company had established trading posts on Manhattan Island and along the Hudson, and a little later, as far eastward as the Connecticut. Most of the trade was carried on with the Iroquois (ir'ô-kwoi) Indians in the northern and

central parts of the present state of New York-a group of Indians tribes whom we shall need to notice more carefully a little later.

For a number of years there were no actual white settlers in New Netherlands. In 1623, however, a group of refugees from Belgium was sent over by the Company to settle in the colony. Some of these people settled on Manhattan

Island while others sailed up to Fort Orange, now Albany, and established homes there. The Dutch were making good their claims to the country. 

New Amsterdam. Peter Minuit (min'a-it), who came over to govern the colony in 1626, purchased the whole of Manhattan Island (22,000 acres) from the Indians for twentyfour dollars' worth of beads and ribbons. Today perhaps 

1 When New Netherlands was fifteen years old its population numbered only 270.

there is no equal area on the face of the earth worth so great a sum as this island purchased by this shrewd Dutchman, Minuit. The governor built a fort at the lower end of the island and called it New Amsterdam. This was the real beginning of the history of the greatest city of the New World.

To attract settlers the Company now agreed that any member of the West India Company who would bring or send to the colony at least fifty settlers more than fifteen years of age should have an estate fronting on a river or bay and extending sixteen miles along one shore, or eight miles on each shore, and extending as far inland “as the situation of the occupiers will admit." The Hudson Valley was soon dotted with vast estates, the proprietors being called patroons (på-troonz'). These patroons were granted such rights as the old feudal barons had had in Europe centuries before. Each patroon had full control of the government and courts within his grant. The tenants on the lands of a patroon were temporary serfs, as they were obliged to remain there for at least ten years. They had to sell their produce to the patroon, to grind their corn in his mill, and to pay him a small annual rent. In return the patroon was obliged to provide each tenant with a farm ready stocked, and each settlement with a schoolmaster and a minister.

This system was so different from what emigrants to America desired or would put up with that it did not last long. But it is one of the most interesting experiments tried in America and should be remembered in connection with early New York history. Besides, the patroons were the founders of some of the great families of New York, the men of which have played an important part in the affairs not only of that colony but of the American nation. 

The government of New Netherlands was harsh and undemocratic. The people, particularly the English who came

28 

to the colony, constantly complained of their lack of rights and there was quarreling and even bloodshed over these political matters. Very early the inhabitants of New 

Netherlands were of many nationalities. 

How New Amsterdam became New York, 1664. During all this time England claimed New Netherlands, basing her claim on the discoveries of the Cabots. She did not like the idea of a Dutch colony between her northern and southern colonies. But for many years the two countries were acting together against Spain, and neither cared to open the question of the ownership of New Netherlands. It was not until after Spain had been successfully dealt with and England had recovered from her Civil War that the quarrel between England and Holland began. The war that followed was really a war to find out which of the two nations was to be the ruler of the seas.

The fate of New Netherlands was soon settled. An English fleet with five hundred veterans and several hundred 

New England volunteers appeared before New Amsterdam in 1664, and the colonists, tired and disgusted with Dutch rule, refused to rally around stubborn old Peter Stuyvesant (stī'vě-sănt), the governor. He fumed and stamped about on his wooden leg, but in the end had to surrender without striking a blow. New Netherlands with its wonderful harbor at New Amsterdam, its great river reaching to the north and west, and its ten thousand colonists passed into the hands of England. The town and colony were both renamed New York. From Maine to Florida the entire coastline was now an English possession. 

Growth of the Middle Colonies. Under English rule the colony of New York grew rapidly, the laws became more liberal, and the people prospered. The colonists were of many races; it is said that before the city of New York was fifty years old at least eighteen different languages were spoken there. As time passed the town prospered and took on still more the features of our great metropolis of today.

Outside the city the settlements extended up the Hudson to Albany, and by the time the Revolutionary War began, these settlements reached many miles westward along

5. PENN AND HIS QUAKER COLONY 

Pennsylvania, one of the last English colonies to be founded in America, was also one of the most successful. 

The name of one man, William Penn, is more closely associated with the founding and early history of this colony than is the name of any single individual with the history of any other colony, except possibly Maryland, Pennsylvania's neighbor on the south. 

William Penn and the Quakers. William Penn, whose father was an admiral and a close friend of the King of England, surprised and grieved his relatives and friends by joining the Quakers, a despised religious sect, then suffering persecution in England and in the Puritan colonies for their peculiar views and practices. Penn, grieved at this persecution, decided to found a colony in America where his Quaker associates, as well as persecuted people of any other religious belief, might be free to do as they pleased. 

At the time of the death of Penn's father the government of England owed him eighty thousand dollars. In payment of that debt, arrangements for a grant of land to Penn for his colony were soon made. The colony was named Pennsylvania by the king. The Pennsylvania of that day was almost identical in size and shape with the great state of

that name today. It was as fair and rich a land as was to be found in all America.

Founding of Pennsylvania. The proposed colony was well advertised, and from 1680 to 1682 several thousand people, from widely separated parts of Europe, sailed to make their homes there. English, Welsh, Swedes, Germans, and French were in the colony almost from its beginning. Most of the early settlers found homes along the fertile river valleys of eastern Pennsylvania. 

Karl F. Lutz O

OLD QUAKER MEETING HOUSE. The Quakers in Philadelphia held their meetings here.

Penn visited his colony in 1682 and stayed two years. He was both ruler and landlord, and on his arrival the settlers gave him a royal welcome. At New Castle, a village in 

Delaware, the Dutch, Swedes, and English, dressed in their holiday clothes, met the great visitor and presented him with the keys of their little fort.

The first settlers in Penn's colony made their homes in caves near the shore of the Delaware River. Here Penn found them at the time of his visit. At this place he began

the building of a city and gave it the name it has since borne-Philadelphia, the City of Brotherly Love. Penn laid out some of the principal streets, arranging them to cross one another at right angles a plan followed in most of our cities and towns today.

The Great Law of Pennsylvania. While in his colony, Penn met with the representatives of the various settlements, and it was here that the Great Law was drawn up and accepted. The Great Law provided, among other things, that (a) the colonial government must not act in an oppressive manner; (b) all taxpayers might vote and any Christian might hold office; (c) every man might worship as he saw fit, and need not attend or help support any church; (d) prisoners in the jails were to learn trades, and efforts were to be made to reform them; (e) only treason and murder were to be punished with death (heavy penalties were laid on swearing, lying, drunkenness, scolding, and cruel sports); (f) children over twelve years of age were to learn some useful trade or occupation; (g) all laws were to be obeyed by high and low alike. 

These generous laws give one the best insight into the character of the great man who had founded the colony of Pennsylvania. Some of the regulations of the Great Law are seen to be as fine and humane as the best of our laws today; and yet William Penn lived at a time when religious persecution was general, the laws were harsh and inhumane, and the death penalty was exacted for scores of petty offenses. 

Penn's third fine action for his colony was his treaty with the Indians. Meeting the tribesmen under their own treaty tree, a fine elm which stood within the present limits of Philadelphia, he arranged a treaty with the red men. 

After much speechmaking and much solemn smoking of the peace pipe, the Indians promised to be the eternal friends of these gentle Quakers, and large tracts of the tribal lands were sold to the white men. This Indian treaty

was kept better than almost any other treaty ever made between the red men and the white.

Ever after it was known as the Great Treaty. 

After Penn returned to England there was much discontent in 

Pennsylvania over the rental system, and the many nationalities did not always get on well together. But the colony grew and flourished as Ohio St.Lawrence Connecticut

CHAPTER V  

In this chapter you will learn that the original English settlements in America gradually spread back from the seashore and up the river valleys. The reasons for this expansion will be found in the quarrels over religious matters and in the desire for better land and other opportunities for making a living. By the close of this period, about 1700, the English settlements had gained a position of comparative prosperity and permanence. 

1. THE EXPANDING SETTLEMENTS OF NEW ENGLAND 

If the first white child born in New England, at Plymouth, for instance, in 1621, lived to a good old age, he saw great changes in the new land and lived through some stirring events. 

You will remember the first two colonies in New England were Plymouth, planted by the Pilgrim Fathers, and the great Puritan colony, Massachusetts Bay, some distance 90

northward along the coast. Plymouth had a slow but steady growth; and her people, farming the old corn grounds of the 

Indians, fishing along the shore, and trading with the natives, prospered and paid off the English merchants who had furnished them the money to come to the New World. 

For the most part they lived at peace with their neighbors, red and white. After a time, by action of the king, their colony became a part of Massachusetts. 

Religious disputes. Massachusetts Bay grew grew most rapidly during the years 1630-1645, the years when the Puritans were having the hardest time in England. The narrow views of the leaders of the colony, many of whom were ministers, caused much trouble among the settlers. 

Those who did not agree with the leaders had a hard time of it, and their discontent led to the founding of other New 

England colonies.

Rhode Island. Rhode Island was settled by Roger Williams, who was driven from Massachusetts Bay in the dead of winter because he disagreed with those in power. He thought that people should be free to carry on their religious worship as they pleased. He believed that the colonists should pay the Indians for their lands. These ideas were contrary to the ideas and practice of the New Englanders of that day. Williams obtained lands from the Indians and began a settlement. Other people who liked his views about religion joined him. The growing colony was named Providence. In time it took its present name, Rhode Island. 

Pioneering in Connecticut. The settlement of the Connecticut Valley is of especial interest. Driving their stock before them and carrying their household goods along as best they might, the emigrants traveled from the neighborhood of Boston almost a hundred miles through the wilderness to reach their new home. Each night the travelers camped in the woods. The journey lasted nearly two weeks. Besides their dissatisfaction with things in the old home in Massa-

chusetts, they believed they could do better on the rich lands of the Connecticut Valley. They wanted to be freer and to better their condition. Those are the reasons that have kept the people of our country moving westward ever since. So, in a way, this movement to Connecticut may be 

International News Photos GATHERING SAP FROM THE MAPLES. Collecting the sap and boiling it down into maple syrup or maple sugar is still an interesting spring industry in many northern and eastern states. It began in early colonial times. said to be the beginning of that pioneering movement which has been going on from that day to this. These people were our first American frontiersmen. Led by 

Thomas Hooker, a minister, they settled in three little towns, Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield. About the same time other settlements were formed on the coast of Connecticut, and for a time there were two colonies within the present boundaries of that state-Connecticut and New Haven. Later they were united.

Beginnings of Maine and New Hampshire. Toward the end of the seventeenth century Englishmen were living in every one of the present New England states except Vermont. In Maine there were merely dots of settlements on the coast. From New Hampshire to Cape Cod there was a solid belt of settlement along the coast, in places its western edge being fifty miles from the sea. Settlement was almost continuous westward from Buzzard's Bay to the western end of Long Island Sound, while along the Connecticut and the other rivers, broad belts of settled country extended for many miles inland. After a few years people were grouped under four separate colonial governments— 

New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut.

Everywhere in New England the people were settled in villages. Along the coast it was natural for the colonists to cluster about the good harbors, of which there were many. 

When the people moved back into the interior of the country they often went as church congregations, taking their minister with them; and in order to keep up their religious worship together they settled in villages. Most of the soil in New England was poor, and a farmer could do better by farming a small piece of ground carefully than by attempting to develop a large farm. Besides, much of the land was hard to clear, and labor was scarce. Fear of Indian attacks also aided in keeping the New Englanders in compact groups.

The New England village. For the reasons given, then, the most important feature in the life of these people was their village life. Whether the men were fishermen or traders or farmers, they and their families lived in little villages. 

The countryside was dotted with these villages, the church being one of the first buildings visible as one approached. 

In the early days a blockhouse, with its second story projecting over the lower one so that the men inside could fire

down upon the heads of an attacking party, was also usually found in each village. Sometimes four blockhouses were placed in the form of a square and connected by a stout wall of timbers sharpened and stuck in the ground close together. 

This formed a fairly strong stockaded fort within which the people were reasonably secure from Indian attacks. The streets in time were lined with neat houses, well shaded by fine trees, and each in a spacious yard. The lands of the farmers who lived in the village usually lay at the outskirts of the town, the individual plots of ground being separated from each other by stone walls often built with the stones gathered from the land. Then there were common village lands where all the cattle and sheep were pastured and where wood for the fireplaces was cut. 

New England colonial homes. The first homes of the colonists were simple rough shelters, being little more than camps. Soon, however, more substantial homes were built, generally of squared timber, that is, logs squared with the axe. The roof at first was usually thatched but later was covered with shingles, which in early times were made by hand. The floors in these early houses, called "puncheon (pun'chun) floors," were made of logs split in halves with the flat side turned up. The log cabin, with walls laid up of logs, was not used in early colonial times. It was the common type of building used later by settlers on the new lands. 

It was not many years before small sawmills were operating along the swift streams. A supply of lumber for building purposes was soon available. Notice the picture of one of the colonial New England houses on page 95. Many homes of the well-to-do, especially in the towns, were made of brick.

In the home the chief feature was the great fireplace, built usually of stone and, later, when brick could be readily obtained, of brick. The fireplaces were used for cooking as well as for heating purposes. The furniture at first was as

crude as the houses, being made by the settlers on the spot from logs cut in the forest. Even plates, spoons, and bowls at first were made of wood. It was not long until skilled workmen made good furniture of excellent design for use in colonial homes. Chairs, beds, bureaus, chests of drawers, Halliday Historic Photograph Co. in ONE OF THE OLDEST HOUSES IN NEW ENGLAND. The old Fairbanks house at Dedham, Massachusetts, shows the kind of home built by well-to-do 

New Englanders before 1650. and other pieces were made from oak, birch, maple, and mahogany. In frontier cabins, pine was a favorite wood not only for furniture but for the making of household utensils. 

Furnishings of colonial homes are illustrated on page 112 and facing page 98.

In the homes of the poor and the well-to-do alike, candles were commonly used for lighting. They were made by dipping long wicks into melted tallow or by pouring the tallow into molds containing wicks. Often the only light used dur-

ing the long winter evenings was that furnished by the wide fireplaces, where knots of pitch pine blazed brightly. There were no matches, and it was often hard to start a fire with flint and steel. To make sure that fires would not go out during the night, settlers found it convenient, before going to bed, to cover them with ashes.

Making a living. Making a living on the small 

New England farm was difficult; hence, each farmer had to be jack-of-all trades, making his own sleds and even wagons, and pounding out nails and iron implements at his own forge. See the nailmaker at his anvil on this page. The whole family had to help in making the living, and around the great fireplaces during the long winter evenings much spinning, knitting, and weaving were carried on. Only the finer clothes were purchased, these coming from England. On the farms corn, wheat, barley, and vegetables were raised, but no staple crop, like tobacco, was raised for export.

Where all the people worked hard, and mostly at manual labor, there was bound to be much equality in social position. And yet, on a Sunday in the church, where everybody gathered regularly to hear the long sermons of those times, the well-to-do and the magistrates had the better seats and the poorer sort of people the worse. There were laws, too, decreeing that the people should dress according to

their station. So after all, the social classes were pretty well marked off from each other even in the New England village. 

Life in the coast towns. In the seaport towns life was much more varied and interesting. Here as time went on more and more of the time and money of the men went into commercial pursuits. Splendid timber and fine, straight trees suitable for masts grew almost to the water's edge, and the colonists could build a ship for about half what it cost in England. Soon the shipping industry of New England took three distinct forms: first, fast schooners, designed and built here, were sold abroad; second, these ships were used by the colonists themselves in the fishing industry; third, the colonists engaged in commerce. Great quantities of fish, lumber, oil, and rum were sent to all parts of the world, and New England ships carried most of the goods that passed up and down the coast between the colonies. 

In these days the trade with the French West Indies was very profitable. It was in these islands that the molasses was obtained from which the rum was manufactured. The shipowners also engaged in the slave trade. Cargoes of rum were taken to the African coast and cargoes of negroes were brought back. These captives were sold in the West 

Indies and in the English colonies on the Atlantic seaboard.

Few slaves were used in the North, chiefly because they were of little use on the small farms where each man could do his own work.

The chief imports to New England were the better grades of clothing, luxuries for those who could afford them, and the higher classes of manufactured articles of various sorts. 

Dolls were imported for the children, china and fine silks for the women, and silks, velvets, and wine for the men. 

The fishing industry did two important things for the people of New England: it gave many of them cash for the

things they needed to buy, and it made of thousands of them as expert seamen as could be found anywhere.

The Indians. When the settlement of the New England coast began, the country was inhabited by numerous tribes of Indians. They were, like most of the Indian people the early settlers had to deal with, a race of hunters and fishermen, but depended in part for their living on crops of corn, squashes, and beans which were cared for by the squaws, as the Indian women were called. The New England Indians were not organized into a confederacy, like those of Virginia under Powhatan, and so were not usually in a condition to threaten the destruction of the colonies.

The white men came in contact with the Indians in at least four ways. At first, as in the case of Plymouth, where the Pilgrims early became acquainted with friendly Indians like Samoset, the white men learned from the red men how to find and make use of the products of the wilderness, and it was the abandoned Indian corn fields that enabled the Pilgrim Fathers to plant and raise a crop the first year in the new land. In the second place, the white men traded with the Indians. The Indian had one thing that the white man was willing to pay for-that was the fur of wild animals. From the first many traders wandered about among the Indian tribes trading guns, blankets, kettles, beads, and rum for the fur. The guns which the Indians learned to use made them more nearly a match for the white men in battle. 

The rum debased them almost to the level of brutes. A third way in which the white men and the red came in contact was through the efforts of a few fine men to convert the Indian to the Christian religion. John Eliot, apostle to the 

Indians, was the greatest of these. He translated the Bible into the Indian tongue and labored all his life among the tribesmen. Several thousand converts were made, these "praying Indians" sometimes being gathered by the missionaries into little settlements by themselves. But the evil

effect of the rum of the traders probably more than offset the good work of Eliot and his friends. Then, lastly, the white men fought with the Indians for the possession of the country.

The Puritan had little regard for the Indian claims to the land. As the red men felt the pressure of the white settlements increase, it was natural that the two races should come into conflict. The Puritan was a stern and merciless fighter, and his wars with the Indians were often wars of extermination. Indian men, women, and children were often shot or burned in their villages.

The Pequots (pē'kwŏts) were displeased to find white men starting settlements in their tribal lands in the Connecticut River Valley. In the war that followed, in 16361637, the tribe was destroyed. But the greatest of all the 

New England Indian wars came in 1675-1676, when Philip of the Wampanoags (wŏm'păn-ôgs), in Rhode Island, called "King" Philip, roused most of the southern New England Indians to try to destroy the English settlements. The war raged more than a year, and it looked for a time as if the Indians might succeed. No less than thirteen towns were destroyed, and the area held by the white men dwindled month by month. But soon Philip's warriors were beaten and grew discouraged, and finally he himself, deserted by most of his followers, was shot down by one of his own race. This war destroyed the Indian power in New England and opened wide areas to the advancing New England pioneer.

But there were many years of peace between the Indians and the settlers. At such times the white men found the 

Indians harmless and friendly neighbors, much inclined to beg for food at the cabin doors. 

The New England plan to act together. For about forty years Massachusetts Bay Colony, Connecticut, New

Haven, and Plymouth attempted to work together in im-

portant matters affecting them all. They saw the need of united action against the Indians and thought there might be need to protect themselves from the Dutch or the 

French. Representatives of the four colonies held meetings and laid plans as to how they would furnish men and 

A COLONIAL KITCHEN. Here we have a good view of a very old kitchen fireplace. Notice the heavy kettles and the cranes by which they were swung over the flames. Can you name some of the other utensils shown here? supplies when needed. Massachusetts Bay Colony was so much larger and stronger than the others that there was fear and suspicion of her on the part of the others. This 

New England Confederation showed two things: that the colonies in America could unite when some common danger threatened them, and that the small colonies feared the power and influence of the great ones and disliked the idea of a

union with them that would decrease their own importance. 

Ministers and squires. Feelings of equality and democracy were not strong, even in New England. We have already noticed how few of the men could vote. As the settlements grew, two classes of men came to be looked upon as the "upper crust" in society. The ministers were in that class from the first. Gradually there joined them the men who had made money as shipbuilders, as successful seacaptains, or as merchants, or who had developed large farms. These "squires" had great influence in their towns, and no doubt managed to have political matters handled much to their liking. When these people had lived in England they had been accustomed to have "the gentry” manage everything. It was natural, in those times, for even colonists living in a new country to divide into an upper and a lower class. Only as they moved away from the seashore and became true pioneers did they lose this sense of being either superior people or common people. 

The New Englanders and their king. The New England people had set up forms of government based on the charters granted to them by the king. Sometimes they had these charters before actual settlement began, as in the case of Massachusetts Bay, and sometimes they made their settlements and then sought a charter in England, as in the case of Connecticut. But in all cases, owing largely to the troubles in England, the colonists did almost as they pleased much of the time. Several times, when the king got ready to break the independent spirit of a colony, troubles at home caused him to forget his unruly and liberty-loving subjects beyond the sea.

The most formidable attack on New England liberties came in 1686. James II was on the throne of England and was trying the foolish experiment of personal rule in a country that was well past the point where it would tolerate anything of the kind. James sent Edmund Andros to rule

all the colonies from the Jerseys northward. Andros kept the colonists greatly wrought up for two years by his efforts to destroy the precious charters and to take the government of the colonies into his own hands. In 1688 his royal master in England was driven out of his kingdom, and the New Englanders, when they heard the joyful news, eagerly laid hands on Andros and clapped him into prison.

Though some of the colonies lost the right to name their governors, yet for many years after the fall of Andros they were given almost complete freedom to manage their own affairs and to develop the kind of governments needed by large and thriving settlements on the edge of the wilderness. 

By the year 1700 the English colonies of New England were strong and populous commonwealths. The people were keen, sturdy, honest, and law-abiding. They were becoming more and more absorbed in making their lives comfortable and their surroundings cheerful. Nearly every one worked hard and was his own master. Everywhere there was an earnest desire for self-government, and interest in public questions was keen.¹ It is people such as these who will be ready to fight for their rights if kings or parliaments in the home country try to oppress them.

If the plantation was located far from deep rivers the hogsheads were rolled toward the distant wharf in the manner shown here. veloping along the rivers while towns and villages were few and small. It is now necessary to notice the later development of Virginia, and show how, in time, neighboring colonies grew up to the north and south of Virginia until the whole southern Atlantic coast line was occupied by the colonists of England.

Tobacco raising. Tobacco continued to be the leading export crop in Virginia. Most of the planters depended on tobacco, which was sold in England, to furnish them with the necessities as well as the luxuries of life. The work of raising and caring for the tobacco was done by members

of the family and by slaves and servants. We have seen how negro workers were introduced into the colonies at an early day. In time these black people became slaves and were depended on almost entirely for work on the plantations. 

For a time a few Indians were used as slaves, but these were surly and revengeful and died soon if kept at work in the field. The picture on page 104 shows how the hogsheads of tobacco were sometimes rolled from faraway plantations to the docks on the rivers. 

Servants. There were also many white servants whose labor was in great demand. In fact, these people outnumbered the slaves for many years. Some of these white servants were men taken from the jails of England and sent to the colony to work for a term of years. Others, often respectable men, voluntarily sold themselves to a ship captain for their passage on his ship to America, the captain in turn selling the "redemptioners," as they were called, to a planter for a period, usually, of five to seven years. These white servants, when they became free, often moved with their families to a piece of land and became farmers. These lands were usually far up the rivers where the ships could not go, and here small farms, devoted to a variety of crops, were developed. Many people believed that slaves and servants could not be employed profitably on these small farms.

There were in Virginia, and through the South, a large number of planters on small plantations. These owned only a few slaves and lived in a modest way, but they, too, were interested in raising tobacco.

Plantation owners. Holding the best social position in the South were the great planters, living on farms covering often as much as a township of land. 

It was the rich planters who made life in the colony interesting and picturesque. Colonel William Fitzhugh is a good example. He owned fifty-four thousand acres of land and

raised flax, hemp, and tobacco, which he sold, and bought more land and more slaves. He lived in "a very good dwelling house with many rooms in it, four of the best of them hung & nine of them plentifully furnished with all things River Potomac Rappahannock Richmond

wheat and corn. His income was about $15,000 a year, besides the increase of his negroes. He shipped his tobacco to England direct from his own wharf.

Each plantation, while dependent on England for many things, was nearly independent of all the other plantations. 

Much of the clothing for the slaves was made on each plantation, and a great deal of blacksmithing and woodworking was carried on. The master rode over his wide fields and superintended the work, while his wife supervised the many activities in the great plantation home with its broad chimneys and pillared porches, and in the village of negro huts placed at a little distance. 

The planter and his wife entertained hospitably the families of the other great planters, house parties, fox hunts, and dancing being the usual forms of entertainment. They and their friends were the aristocrats of the colony. They owned good homes, well-bred horses, and fashionable clothing. They carried out quite successfully the kind of life some of them were accustomed to and most of them had seen on the country estates of England. The picture of the Byrd mansion on page 108 gives a good idea of what some of the best homes of the planters were like.

Maryland. Virginia's first neighbor colony was Maryland, on Chesapeake Bay. The life of the people there came, in time, to be much like that of the people of Virginia. The colony was established by Lord Baltimore, a Catholic, who, anxious to find a home for the persecuted Catholics in England, founded the colony and opened it to Catholics and all other groups of Christians. This was unusual in those times; and while there was much trouble in the colony over the claims of Virginia to the shores of Chesapeake Bay, and among the colonists themselves, Maryland grew rapidly, and Baltimore, the chief city, came to be one of the largest towns in America. 

The Carolinas and Georgia. South of Virginia, North

Carolina and South Carolina were settled about sixty years after the founding of Jamestown. North Carolina had no good harbors, and the rivers were shallow. Most of the farmers raised a variety of crops and depended little on the outside world. The people here were much like the people 

Cook Photos A PLANTATION HOME. Westover, on the James River, Virginia. Here many generations of the Byrd family lived. Richard Byrd, of "Little America" fame, is a descendant of the family whose early colonial home was Westover. far up the rivers in Virginia, and because their farms were small, they consumed most of what they raised, and they had few slaves. They were real frontiersmen. In time the pine forests were used for the production of three articles of export-lumber, tar, and turpentine. 

South Carolina was very much like Virginia and developed an aristocracy of rich men whose wealth consisted in land and slaves. Rice and indigo were raised for export.

The slaves outnumbered the white men in many communities, overseers being employed to manage the very large plantations. The plantation owners themselves lived in 

Charleston much of the year to avoid the malarial climate in the regions where the rice and indigo were grown, and to enjoy the social life of the city. Charleston was one of the leading cities in the English colonies.

The colony of Georgia was founded in 1733 by James Oglethorpe (ō'g'l-thôrp), but was a small, weak settlement during colonial times.

3. THE THIRTEEN ENGLISH COLONIES 

Colonial surroundings. For many years after their settlements had been founded, a large number of the New Englanders continued to see a great deal of the ocean. It was almost at their doors. They could look out upon it from their homes on the many safe harbors along the shore. As more and more of them journeyed westward to seek new homes, they became better acquainted with their rivers. 

These were found to be rough and rapid within a few miles of the sea. They were useful, however, for floating timbers down to the coast and for the water power they furnished the many small mills that were set up along the banks. 

The soil in the river valleys was generally fertile. In time the advancing pioneers of New England found themselves in rugged and mountainous country to the west and north of the earlier settlements. Pine and hardwood forests covered much of the land.

From the first the people of New York and Pennsylvania

and the other middle colonies made much use of such great rivers as the Hudson and the Delaware. In places the valleys of these streams were deep and picturesque. The rolling country was well timbered. In Virginia and on to the southward, as we have already seen, the broad, slow rivers had much to do with shaping the activities of the settlers. West 

Courtesy Lexington Historical Society WINNOWING BASKET AND FLAIL of the early American farms. The flail was the threshing machine, and the basket the fanning mill of later times. of them they discovered, as they pushed up the streams, the continuous crests of the Blue Ridge. 

From the northernmost English settlement in America to the most southern was a distance of thirteen hundred miles. At the end of a hundred years of pioneering in the wilderness practically all of the people were living still within seventy-five miles of the seashore. 

The people. In the 

South most of the white people were from England. There were a few Scotch and Scotch-Irish here and there, particularly along the western frontier. In the middle colonies there was a greater mixture. Not only were there settlers from Scotland and north Ireland, but there were Dutch, Germans, and Swedes as well. In the North the people were practically all of English blood. They were all sturdy, hard-working people, bent on making good homes and good communities.

Colonial ideas. It was the common opinion that the governments set up in the colonies should be largely under the control of the people themselves. They felt quite capable of managing their own affairs. In many respects each family was a little, self-sufficient community. Religious matters were taken seriously by all, and church attendance was general. Many had brought with them from the old home odd beliefs about the powers of evil spirits over the lives of people. They thought it quite possible for a person to be bewitched by these dark powers. The "witches" were shunned, or, as happened at Salem, in Massachusetts, were for a time punished without mercy. The list of other "crimes" was long, and the punishments were severe. The stocks, the whipping post, the pillory, and the ducking stool were to be found in many of the settlements. 

Amusements. Most of the settlers in the New World worked so hard clearing their farms or managing their shops or plying their trades that they had little time for amusements. In the frontier settlements, in particular, the men sometimes combined work and play. They often gathered to "raise" a barn or to help some neighbor clear a patch of ground. When the work was finished they sometimes stayed to take part in wrestling or shooting matches. The women had their "quilting bees," and at these they managed to have the quiet enjoyments open to women in those days. 

The Puritans of New England frowned upon most of the things that we should call pleasurable today. The children, however, had many quiet little games, such as hoop-rolling, spinning tops, and "prisoner's base." In the South those who had the time for it were much freer in their amusements. Dancing, fox hunting, and horse racing were all popular. 

Contrasts. There were many contrasts in the lives of the people in the various colonies. Some of these we have already noted. The farms in the North were small, and the

work was done largely by the owners themselves. In the 

South the leading men managed their large plantations but did little actual work themselves. The poorer men worked, of course, but they, too, hoped some day to become large landowners. Opportunities to go to school were much more 

Halliday Historic Photograph Company A CORNER IN A COMFORTABLE COLONIAL HOME. Pleasant, well-furnished homes became fairly common in later colonial times. The New England men gave their town governments much attention, and were active in the annual town meetings. This close community life with the opportunities it offered for active civic work trained large numbers of the men to be good local leaders and aided many others to become keen and intelligent citi-

zens. The people of the South, scattered widely as they were, relied chiefly on their county governments for the management of local affairs. These larger units gave a few men in each county excellent training for leadership in both military and civil affairs. The colonies of the middle section had both counties and towns, and these units of government played important parts in the development of the settlements. Later on they were widely adopted in the new states that developed west of the mountains. In all the colonies the leadership and intelligence gained in the management of county and town governments were of high value when colonial rights were threatened. 

Relations among the colonies. The thirteen colonies had little to do with one another. The roads were poor and there was little occasion for the people to travel about. Each colony felt itself to be almost an independent little nation, with a few ties binding it to England and none at all between it and the other colonies. This feeling of separateness made it hard for the colonies to work together, as it became necessary for them to do later. Even after the colonies had united and become a single nation, this old feeling affected the history of our country for many years. Fortunately common blood and a common language were able to overcome at last the barriers between colony and colony, state and state.

CHAPTER VI HOW THE FRENCH BUILT A WILDERNESS EMPIRE AND LOST IT 

In an earlier chapter you read a brief account of French exploration in the Lower St. Lawrence River valley. We shall now see how the fearless explorers and adventurers of this nation followed up these early efforts and, by 1700, occupied not only the 

St. Lawrence-Great Lakes basin, but the Mississippi River valley as well. You will then learn of the rivalry between the English and the French which resulted in a great war. At the close of that struggle France lost to England all her possessions in 

North America. 

1. CHAMPLAIN, THE FATHER OF NEW FRANCE 

Laying the foundation. During all the years that the 

English colonies were growing up along the Atlantic coast, France, a rival of England, was laying the foundations of 

New France along the St. Lawrence River and westward on the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. The story 115

of New France is one of the most interesting in all American history. Much of it can be told by relating the stories of a few of the great Frenchmen who helped to make New France. 

Cartier, you remember, explored the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the lower parts of the St. Lawrence River and spent a few winter months on those bleak shores. This kept the interest of France centered on this northern region, and nearly all their early colonizing attempts were made in or near the great northern river.

Champlain (shăm-plan') was the father of New France. 

In the year 1608, just a year after the settlement at Jamestown, he founded the town of Quebec on the north bank of the St. Lawrence and hundreds of miles inland from its mouth. Champlain was well fitted by long experience as a soldier and sea captain to be the leader of the colony, but his experiences and those of his men were almost as terrible as those of the Englishmen at Jamestown. The next spring more men and supplies came to Quebec, and Champlain found time to go on an interesting exploring expedition. 

All the Indians along the St. Lawrence, as well as those near the English colonists, belonged to the Algonquin (ǎl-gŏng'kin) race. Those near the St. Lawrence Champlain soon made the firm friends of France. But to the south, in what is now the central part of New York state, lived the Five Nations of the Iroquois. These tribes loved war above all things. The squaws raised much corn and many vegetables; the long houses in which groups of families lived were more comfortable than wigwams. The 

Iroquois warriors had good weapons, and sometimes they built forts almost as strong as those of the white men. The 

Five Nations, or tribes, were banded together so well that they were more than a match for their much more numerous enemies. Even the Indians on the faraway Mississippi feared the Iroquois.

HOW THE FRENCH BUILT A WILDERNESS EMPIRE 117 

Iroquois enemies of Champlain. Champlain's friends, the 

Algonquins, were usually at war with the Iroquois. When an Algonquin war party set out in the spring of 1609, Champlain and a few other Frenchmen went with it. Up the Richelieu (rē-she-lyû') River went the canoes until the beautiful lake that now bears 

Champlain's name was reached. To the eastward 

Champlain could see the 

Green Mountains, while to the west were the pine-clad slopes of the Adirondacks (ǎd-i-ron'dăks)—the hunt- ing grounds of the hated

Iroquois. 

Soon a large party of Iroquois was seen coming down the lake. With wild whoops of defiance the two parties landed and got ready for the fight. As the Iroquois warriors advanced, Champlain, clad in his armor and carrying his gun, stepped out be 

Courtesy Canadian Pacific Railway SAMUEL DE CHAMPLAIN. This pic ture was made from a portrait of the famous French colonizer. What place is suggested by the background? fore the Algonquins. The Iroquois paused in surprise, for this was the first white soldier they had ever seen. Then 

Champlain fired and two warriors fell. After another shot the braves of the Five Nations fled in terror, and the warriors from the St. Lawrence were almost ready to worship 

Champlain for giving them so easy a victory.

But it was a dear victory for the French. The Iroquois fighters hurried to their villages vowing vengeance on the white men. From that day on the Five Nations hated the

Frenchmen, and at times it seemed as if they would succeed in driving the white men from the country. Then, too, the

keen Iroquois saw a chance for great profit for themselves in the fur trade. They wanted the fur from the country of the Great Lakes to pass through their hands to the Dutch traders on the Hudson River. They fought to keep the 

French away from the routes leading to the west. The 

French were obliged to give up their plans to explore and plant colonies along Lake Ontario and Lake Erie and to the southward. In fact, a Frenchman hardly dared set foot on the shores of Lake Ontario, while no Frenchman even saw Lake Erie for many years. Instead, the French went westward along the Ottawa River and carried their canoes and supplies (portaged) across to the waters of Lake Huron. 

From there they journeyed on to Lake Michigan and Lake 

Superior. 

Effects. Thus the whole course of French exploration was changed, with important results, as we shall see. Champlain, while he laid the foundations of New France, made it hard for this colony to prosper because he had gained for his countrymen the hatred of the warlike Iroquois.

2. THE FRENCH FUR TRADERS AND MISSIONARIES 

The inland waters of New France. The French on the St. 

Lawrence were not long in discovering that the fur trade offered them the best chance to make money. Soon almost every one was engaged, directly or indirectly, in this business. Dozens of parties in the birch canoes of the Indians were threading the watercourses in every direction to trade with the Indians for their furs. 

Radisson, the forest ranger. The most venturesome of all these early traders was Pierre Radisson (răd-is-on'). In the fall of 1659 he and a companion beached their canoes

HOW THE FRENCH BUILT A WILDERNESS EMPIRE 119 

on the shore of Lake Superior near where the town of Ashland, Wisconsin, is now located. The two Frenchmen built an odd little fort at this point and adopted so bold an attitude toward the many Indians living along the lake shore that the red men treated their visitors with the greatest respect.

The white men spent the winter among the Ottawa (ŏt'ȧwȧ) Indians, somewhere south of the lake in the depths of the forest. Radisson won the gratitude of these Indians by giving many presents. Radisson's journal tells about this. The gift to the men of the Ottawa village was a kettle, two hatchets, six knives, and a sword blade. Radisson told what each gift meant. The gift to the women was twenty-two awls, fifty needles, two "graters" to clean beaver skins with, two ivory combs and two wooden ones, some red paint, and six little looking glasses. Said Radisson, "The combs and the paint are to make you beautiful; the looking glasses that you may admire yourselves." Then the children were gathered together and the Frenchmen tossed some brass rings over their heads and distributed bells and mugs among them.

After a winter of famine among the Indians Radisson wandered far to the southwest, and to the wild country north of Lake Superior. No white man had ever seen the streams and lakes he traversed. Finally he returned to the 

St. Lawrence with many canoes loaded to the water's edge with bales of fur.

Later on Radisson, angry at the rulers of New France because they had seized his cargo of peltries, went to England and helped to organize the great Hudson's Bay Fur Company.

This story may give you some idea of the bold, fearless qualities of these forest rangers and will partly explain why the Frenchmen made such lasting friends of the northern and western Indians. The picture on page 115 gives a

good idea of the Indian canoe and of the voyaging Frenchmen on the western waters. 

French missionary zeal. The French people had a warm interest in the Indians and desired to convert them to the Christian religion. For this reason it was natural that New 

France should number among its people many missionaries whose duty it was to bring the red men to the Christian faith. 

THE JESUIT AND THE MISSION. In such humble little buildings as the one shown in the background of this picture the missionaries carried on their work among the Indians. Often the walls were of bark, much like those of the Indian wigwams themselves.

Father James Marquette (mår-kět') was one of the heroic missionaries of New France. He worked among the Indians on the shore of Lake Superior. In company with Joliet (jō'li-ět), the explorer, he later made a canoe voyage from Lake Michigan up the Fox River, across a portage there to the Wisconsin River, down that river to the Mississippi, and down the Father of Waters as far as the mouth of the

On the return journey the travelers turned their canoes up the Illinois River, and finally, paddling and portaging, came out on the shore of Lake Michigan again, on the present site of Chicago. Here Marquette tarried among the Indians, for he felt the call to go on with his missionary work. Although sick and weak from disease, he managed to survive a winter in a hut at this place. In the spring he started on a journey down the lake toward the mission of St. Ignace, but died on the way. 

The influence of the missionaries seems pitifully small, if we consider the numbers of the red men who were then and there actually made over into kindly Christian people. 

But they worked hard to improve the condition of the Indians and tried to prevent the fur traders from bringing intoxicating liquors to the Indian villages. No more courageous band of Christian workers ever went into the wilderness to labor among savages than the "black robes" and the "gray robes" of New France. These missionaries are pictured on pages 120 and 126.
