3. LA SALLE IN THE VALLEY OF THE MISSISSIPPI 

"For the glory of France." Patriotism was one of the motives that brought some of the best sons of France to the New World. Among these patriots who spent their lives in the wilderness in order to build up a great dominion for the French throne was La Salle (lå sål'). 

In La Salle's time all the Great Lakes except Lake Erie were well known to the Frenchmen. Fur-trading posts and missions were scattered along the streams and lake shores. 

On the St. Lawrence were the thriving towns of Montreal, Three Rivers, and Quebec. Farther east Nova Scotia (nō'vȧ

HOW THE FRENCH BUILT A WILDERNESS EMPIRE 123 

skō'sha) and the near-by islands were well settled. Farming and fishing were the main occupations around Nova Scotia, but on the St. Lawrence and to the westward the fur trade still held sway as the chief business of the population. 

La Salle's dream was to reach and explore a great southward flowing river of which the Indians often spoke. But before he could carry out his plans two other Frenchmen, as we have seen, had traveled southward along this mighty river, the Mississippi, for hundreds of miles. La Salle determined to reach the mouth of the river and claim for France the whole region drained by it.

 Work of La Salle. After many starts and many journeys back to Montreal for supplies, La Salle finally crossed from Lake Michigan and the Chicago River to the Illinois River and started southward. Here and there he built little forts. For a long distance his course took him over the route traversed by Joliet and Marquette a few years before, but finally he neared the mouth of the great river, and, in April, 1682, the party came to the open sea. New France had been extended to the Gulf of Mexico. 

The new region was named Louisiana for Louis XIV of France.

LA SALLE, famous French explorer of the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys.

La Salle hurried back to Canada, and thence to France, for he now planned to plant a colony and forts at the mouth of his great river so that the new empire of France in the

basin of the Mississippi might be held against the attacks of another nation.

Soon the expedition sailed, but La Salle missed the mouth of the river and landed his people on the coast of what is now Texas. He searched long for the Mississippi but could not find it. His colony dwindled away, and the men became discouraged and rebellious. At last La Salle started on foot for Canada but was killed by one of his companions. The little fort in Texas was destroyed by the Indians. 

La Salle was ambitious and enthusiastic and planned much more than he had the means to carry out. But he was the first man to see the importance of the Mississippi Valley, and his work opened up trade between the Great Lakes and the Gulf of Mexico. His dream of a great French dominion in the heart of America influenced French plans for nearly a hundred years.

4. HOW ENGLAND GAINED NEW FRANCE BY CONQUEST 

English and French rivalry. England and France were enemies during the years that their colonies were being planted in the New World. So it was only natural that the colonists of the two nations should regard one another with suspicion and dislike. When the French built their line of forts down along the Mississippi and finally, about the year 1700, founded Mobile and New Orleans to defend their claims to the Mississippi Valley, there was a further cause for trouble between the two nations. The English had always claimed all the lands westward from the Atlantic coast to the "South 

Sea"-wherever that might be—and the charters of many of the colonies had been worded in such a way as to give to each colony a strip of land running to the west as far as the continent extended. The French in Canada might be con-

HOW THE FRENCH BUILT A WILDERNESS EMPIRE 125 

sidered only troublesome and disliked neighbors, but the French in the Mississippi Valley were another matter; they were on the lands claimed by the English. Many of the 

English colonists were eager to engage in the western fur trade. These men feared that the French would cut them off from this profitable trade. This fear furnished another reason for disputing the claims of their rivals. 

Three wars, which reflected greater ones being fought in Europe, took place between the English and French colonists before the year 1750. Nothing important came of these minor conflicts except further bitterness and hatred between the two peoples. Almost anyone could see that a great war would have to be fought sooner or later to settle whether the French or the English were to control eastern 

North America.

English and French settlements compared. The English settlements in America were close together along the Atlantic seacoast. The French had well-developed settlements in only a few parts of the large territory they claimed. One of these lay along the St. Lawrence River between Quebec and Montreal. Another was in Nova Scotia-Acadie, (å-kȧ-dē'), the French called it. A third settlement stretched along the lower Mississippi River. Here large plantations had been laid out. New Orleans, the chief town in the settlement, carried on a flourishing trade. 

Between the groups of French settlements were wide stretches of untouched forest. Scattered about in the wilderness were many small forts, trading posts, and missions. One fort, Frontenac, stood near the eastern end of Lake Ontario. 

There were other forts at Niagara, at Detroit, in southern Illinois, and along the Mississippi River. Small groups of 

French traders and farmers lived near these forts, the largest being at Detroit and on the rich lands in southern Illinois. One of the most permanent of the missions was at 

St. Ignace, near the northern end of Lake Michigan. The

French government claimed a vast territory in America, but they had a firm hold on only small parts of the lands they claimed. 

Differences between the English and French colonists themselves. People of nearly all races and beliefs were welcomed in the 

English colonies. As we have seen, the settlers in the colonies of England were given the chance to manage their local governments and, through the representatives, were able to take a hand in colonial affairs as well. As a result of these fair and just arrangements the English colonies rapidly filled with settlers. 

The French government tried hard to build up the population of the French colonies. The king sent out young women to become the wives of the settlers. To each couple married in Canada he gave a wedding present of "an ox, a cow, a pair of swine, a pair of fowls, two barrels of salted meat, and eleven crowns in money." The modern idea of giving prizes to the parents of large families was also tried. 

But the sturdy French farmers and the skilled French workmen could not be coaxed or bribed to move in large numbers to the colonies of their king. Fur traders and explorers and adventurers came, but they were not the kind

of people to clear the land and make prosperous settlements. 

Some of the rules laid down by the French government worked against the success of their colonies. Only Frenchmen who were also Catholics were allowed to live in New 

France. The French Protestants, or Huguenots (hu'ge-nots), would have been glad to find homes in French America, but those who came were hunted down and imprisoned. 

The common people in the French colonies were given no part in the government. The rulers managed everything. 

No detail was too small for them to make rules about. What rents were to be paid, what fees were legal at the small gristmills, what clothes could be worn, what pew was to be sat in at church, how many dogs the settler could own, what crops he could plant, and scores of other small matters were all settled by some official of the French colonial government. The colonists never voted, never held any offices, and had practically no chance to send their children to school. 

As we know, the English colonists grew strong and selfreliant through the neglect of the mother country. The 

French, on the other hand, lost the ability to think and to act for themselves because they had too much done for them. In 1750 the English colonists outnumbered the 

French twenty to one.

Sides taken by the Indians. The northern and western 

Indians liked the French and had many dealings with them because of the fur trade. Most of them were ready to help 

France against England. But you will remember how and why the strong tribes of the Iroquois had learned to hate the Frenchmen. Still, they were suspicious of the Englishmen and their intentions and might have joined forces with the French in the coming war except for the work of Sir William Johnson. He was one of the few Englishmen who knew how to deal with the red men. He built himself a great house in the midst of the Iroquois lands, kept it open at all times to Indian and white alike, and succeeded

in keeping the haughty warriors of the Five Nations on the 

English side.

The French and Indian War, 1754-1763. The great war for the possession of eastern North America was brought on when the French began building forts along the upper waters of the Ohio River. The colony of Virginia claimed the land in that region and made a protest against the action of the French. George Washington, then a young Virginia planter and surveyor of twenty-one, was sent by Governor Dinwiddie (din-wĭd'i) to warn the French that they were trespassing on Virginia lands. But the French finished their forts, the most important of which was Fort Duquesne (doo-kān'), at the point where the Alleghany (ǎl'ê-gā-nî) and the Monongahela (mô-nong-gå-he'lȧ) rivers unite to form the Ohio.

The next year, 1754, Washington and a small army of Virginians lost a fight with the French at Fort Necessity, in the Pennsylvania wilderness. This was the beginning of the war in America. The conflict soon spread to Europe, where it was called the Seven Years War. 

Braddock's defeat. In 1755 General Braddock, with an army of British regular soldiers and colonial frontiersmen, tried to capture Fort Duquesne. The French and their

Indian allies met this army in the woods nine miles from the fort and defeated it. The remnants of the British force fled back along the road they had made, leaving hundreds of dead and wounded behind them. George Washington was present at this terrible battle and with his Virginians did good work in protecting what was left of Braddock's army.

After the defeat of the British near Fort Duquesne, the Indians spread out along the frontier and attacked the settlers. Hundreds of log-cabin homes went up in flames, and men, women, and children were either killed or led away into the northern forests as prisoners. Three years passed

HOW THE FRENCH BUILT A WILDERNESS EMPIRE 129 

before the armies of England were able to capture Fort

Duquesne and drive the French out of the Ohio Valley. 

The French fort was renamed Fort Pitt (Pittsburgh). 

William Pitt, General Wolfe, and the end of the war. William Pitt, one of England's greatest statesmen, and at that time her prime minister, took charge of the war after it had been waged unsuccessfully by 

England for two years. He sent able British generals to America. He encouraged the colonists to work harder to win the war. The French forts fell one by one. At last the one strong post left in French lands was the fort at Quebec. 

 los A MONUMENT TO GENERAL WOLFE. At Quebec, Canada, stands this shaft in memory of the English captor of Quebec. 

Today Wolfe is honored not so much because he defeated a brave enemy in battle, but because of the courage and patience he displayed in overcoming weakness and disease in his own frail body. 

General James Wolfe was given the task of capturing 

Quebec. The well-fortified town was on a cliff overlooking the broad St. Lawrence 

River. The best of the French commanders, General Montcalm (mont-käm'), defended it with his army. It seemed impossible for the British to draw near enough to the French fort to begin their attack. But Wolfe found a narrow path leading up from the edge of the river to the level ground back of the city. During a dark night his men scrambled up the steep path dragging their cannon with them. When daylight came the British army was ready for battle. 

The battle on the Plains of Abraham was brief. The

French were defeated. Both Wolfe and Montcalm received wounds from which they died. Quebec surrendered to the British.

Results of the war. The fall of Quebec really meant the end of the war. The French had lost the contest. When the treaty of peace, in 1763, ended the great war which had been raging in Europe, France gave up all Canada and the eastern half of the Mississippi Valley to England; while Spain, the ally of France, received the French lands west of the 

Mississippi. In all North America France had left only two small islands in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

Thus the great work of Champlain, La Salle, Montcalm, and the other brave and patriotic Frenchmen was lost. The war decided that the English language, customs, and forms of government, and not the French, should prevail in all of eastern North America.

Pontiac's War. A hard task for the Englishmen after the war was to come to terms with the northern and western Indians. The Indians, dismayed at the defeat of their friends, the French, more than ever feared and disliked the cold Englishmen who now came among them. Under 

Pontiac (pon'tĬ-ǎk) the warriors began a sudden attack on the scattered British posts. For a time it seemed as if 

English rule in the country of the Great Lakes would be destroyed. But some forts held out bravely, the red warriors became discouraged, and peace was finally made. British agents made treaties with the tribes, carefully fixing the boundaries of their lands. British traders went into the wilderness to buy the Indians' peltries. Soon the Indians learned to like the British and decided that their true enemies were the American settlers who were just beginning to move over the mountains into the Indian country. 

Other results of the French wars. In the early years of the English colonies the settlers had felt dependent upon the mother country. So long as the French and their Indian

The colonists had helped the soldiers of Great Britain win many of their important victories in the war. These successes gave them a sense of their own strength. They felt able to fight their own battles.

During the war the colonists had many times been obliged to act together. Men traveled from Virginia and

UNIT III FROM COLONIES TO NATION 

With the close of the long French wars all the lands of eastern North America came under the control of England. 

The growing British Empire now spread over rich eastern lands as well as over the scattered settlements and the forest areas of America. British statesmen began the planning of measures to unite the scattered parts of the empire into closer relations with England. 

The new plans were distasteful to the people of the thirteen colonies along the Atlantic seacoast of America. They had always been left to manage most of their own affairs. 

Now that the French were gone they felt still less dependent on England. The efforts of England to set up a closer control over the American colonies brought on a quarrel which deepened into a war. In the midst of the war the united colonies declared their independence of England and fought on to make their independence real. 

At the end of the war the thirteen English colonies became thirteen American states. After long years of weakness and discord they at last formed a strong and enduring union, the United States of America. 

The story of this greatest event in our history will be told in the next four chapters. 135

CHAPTER VII THE QUARREL BETWEEN COLONIES AND MOTHER COUNTRY 

In this chapter you will learn of the bitter dispute which arose between the colonies and the mother country, which at last led to war and the winning of American independence. The many causes of this war will require close study. Behind the many points at issue was the fundamental difference of opinion as to the purpose for the founding of colonies. England, like other countries in Europe, believed that colonies were established for the profit of the home country. The colonists considered themselves as free Englishmen and entitled to the same rights and privileges as were enjoyed by the people of England. 

1. HOW THE ENGLISH COLONIES WERE Governed 

Each English colony was entirely independent of the others. There was no general government in America over all the colonies. Each had its own separate relations with the mother country. 137

Royal governors. A governor, a legislature, and a system of courts was to be found in each colony. In most of the colonies the governors were appointed by the king. Some of them were good men and worked for the interests of the colony they had been sent to govern. But many of them were short-sighted and vain and selfish. These spent much of their time quarreling with their legislatures. So many of the governors were so thoroughly disliked by the colonists that getting rid of royal English governors was one of the motives for starting the Revolutionary War. 

Lawmaking in the colonies. Each colony had a legislature, the members of which were elected by the voters in the colony. Although colonial laws had to be approved in 

England before they went into effect in America, the colonial legislatures made laws for the colonies. They raised money by taxation for the expenses of the government of the colony, such as the salaries paid to the governors. Sometimes a bad governor was brought to terms by the refusal of a legislature to pay him his salary until some abuse had been corrected. In each colony the people became accustomed to having their legislature lay and collect all the taxes they were required to pay, and to handle all financial concerns of the colony. 

Courts. There were courts in all the colonies, and they worked well. The courts of England seldom interfered, although they had the right to hear appeals from the colonial courts. Just before the Revolutionary War a law was passed in England providing that colonists charged with certain offenses should be tried in England. 

2. HOW ENGLAND RESTRICTED COLONIAL TRADE The Navigation Laws. Some of the chief causes of the separation of the colonies from England are to be found in the way in which the British government tried to regulate trade and industry in the colonies. That we may better

Restrictions on farm products and fish. In New England, as you have learned, the soil was not fertile except in the river valleys. Yet the New

Englanders carried on a great deal of farming. Maize became an important food product. Vegetables and hardy apples and cherries were grown in abundance. 

Cattle and sheep grazed on the steep New England hillsides. In New York and 

Pennsylvania agriculture was carried on more extensively than in New England. 

So well had the farmers of 

New England and the middle colonies prospered that, by the year 1760, they were producing many things in greater quantities than they needed for their own use. The surplus products they sold abroad. We must remember that England at this time produced most of her food supply and thought it best to continue to do so. 

Therefore, when colonial farm products came to be offered for sale in large quantities in England, the English farmer objected. He saw that he would not have as good a chance to sell his products if English people bought farm products raised in America. He therefore asked Parliament to pass laws which would keep these colonial products out of

England. This parliament did. Wheat, corn, barley, oats, pork, beef, butter, and cheese were the leading farm products kept out of England by these laws. 

Fishing was an important New England industry. Large quantities of mackerel, cod, and herring were caught, prepared for the market, and shipped to England. But English fishermen, like English farmers, objected to the importation of food supplies. The British government, therefore, refused to admit fish products to English ports. Soon these products began finding their way to the West Indies. 

Some of the West Indian Islands belonged to England and some to France. The French West Indies bought large quantities of foodstuffs from the northern colonies, giving in exchange sugar and molasses. Of course, the people in the British West Indies did not like this because they wanted the chance to sell these products to the northern colonies themselves. To secure this opportunity for them, Parliament in 1733 passed a celebrated law known as the Sugar Act. This law placed a high duty on all sugar and molasses brought into the colonies from the French West Indies. 

The triangular trade. You may well ask how the colonists used so much molasses. Large quantities of this product were used in distilling rum. Now at this time there was a growing demand for slaves in the West Indies to work the large plantations. Adventurous sea captains took cargoes of rum to the coast of Africa. Here the rum was exchanged for negroes captured in the wilds of that continent by slave hunters. These negroes were exchanged in the West Indies for molasses. Then the ships went back to New England with the hogsheads of molasses to be made into more rum. 

This was called the triangular trade. It was very profitable since a ship was loaded on all parts of its voyage. Therefore, the Sugar Act which aimed to cut off this profitable trade was unpopular with the Americans.

QUARREL BETWEEN COLONIES AND MOTHER COUNTRY 141 

While the British government was passing laws which kept certain colonial products out of England, she at the same time passed other laws which forced the colonists to send certain other products to England and to England only. This list of goods was called the "enumerated list." 

The enumerated list. Cotton, indigo, and dyewoods were used by the English manufacturers in cloth making. Tar,

All these goods and many others were placed on the enumerated list. This requirement in practice forced the colonists to sell these products to English buyers at practically whatever price was offered.

You will remember that the Virginia settlers found the tobacco crop so profitable that they raised little else for sale. Now tobacco was placed on the enumerated list. This was not because the English wanted all the tobacco for their own use but that by this arrangement the British merchant got control of this product and sold it to the rest of Europe,

making, of course, a profit on the sales. This certainly was taking an unfair advantage of the tobacco grower. 

You can see from these examples what a selfish policy was followed by the British government. The English farmer was to be protected at the expense of the American farmer; the colonists were to be made a source of wealth to 

English merchants.

3. HOW ENGLAND RESTRICTED COLONIAL MANUFACTURE 

Manufacturing in the colonies. As you may suppose, there were many things the colonists needed that they could not readily make themselves. They needed agricultural implements and tools of all kinds, chains and anchors for their ships, firearms, and traps. Machinery was needed for their sawmills and gristmills. Since such things were very expensive to buy from English manufacturers, the enterprising colonists set about providing themselves with the things they needed. They found iron ore deposits in many places. They set up smelting furnaces and forges. Soon the colonists were making machinery for their mills as well as tools and domestic utensils of various sorts for use on the farm and in the home. Most of these things were made in 

New England. Small furnaces were set up in the New England kitchens, and during the winter season the men and boys hammered out on their anvils large quantities of nails, horseshoes, and other iron products.

At first the colonists were unable to make their own clothing. They did not raise the raw materials from which clothing is made. But soon they began to raise flax. At first there were few sheep, but the number was rapidly increased. 

Cotton was brought from the West Indies. As soon as these

Dutch of New York and Pennsylvania were not far behind their New England neighbors in this household industry. 

Fine hats, in those days, were made from beaver fur, which was plentiful. The hatters of New England and New 

York sold their hats in nearly every country of Europe. 

Restriction on manufacturing. England was a manufacturing country. Her manufacturers wanted to sell the colonists their cloths, their tools and implements, and their shoes and hats. They were, therefore, opposed to having the people of the colonies make these things for themselves. 

Parliament, accordingly, passed laws limiting in some cases, and prohibiting in others, the manufacture and sale of articles made in the colonies. This of course retarded colonial manufacture and compelled the colonists to buy English-made goods at English prices. 

We now understand how laws were passed to benefit the English farmer, the English merchant, and the English manufacturer. We shall next see what laws were passed to benefit one other class, the English shipowner.

There was a steady demand in Europe for many American products. Shiploads of grain, fish, rice, and tobacco were sent abroad. Whale oil, whalebone, rum, and cider found ready sale in Europe. Returning ships brought linen and woolen goods from England and Holland, wine and fruits and spices from southern countries, sugar and molasses from the West Indies. English shipowners wanted this carrying business. Several laws called Navigation Acts were passed. One of these measures required that all goods brought to American ports or shipped out of American ports must be carried in ships owned by "English subjects.” 

This term included colonial shipowners. Another measure

QUARREL BETWEEN COLONIES AND MOTHER COUNTRY 145 

stated that all goods purchased abroad must come through an English port. That is, a ship could not bring a cargo to 

Boston direct from Holland or Spain, but must stop at some port in England, where the cargo would be reshipped to America. These laws were made so that English shippers and merchants would get the business of handling goods going to the colonists. The British government also got a chance, by this arrangement, to collect a duty on goods bought abroad by the colonists.

How some of the Nav igation Acts helped the colonies. In two ways the laws of England on these matters actually aided the colonies. (1) .

(2) In some cases the laws in the mother country were planned to stimulate certain kinds of production in the colonies. For example a bounty of about thirty dollars a ton was paid for the production of hemp, and twenty-five dollars a ton for tar and pitch. 

How the colonists evaded the laws. The British govern ment for many years made no serious attempt to enforce her many laws on colonial trade and manufacture. Many a

hogshead of tobacco found its way to Holland without first going to England. Molasses from the French West Indies still came to New England in the holds of the ships of shrewd Yankee sea captains. These smugglers on dark nights would anchor their ships off some lonely coast. 

Boats from the land would come off, and the cargo of sugar, or whatever it was, would soon be transferred to shore. 

Teams would be waiting for it, and before daylight the smuggled goods would be safely stowed away in the cellars of farmhouses or in innocent-looking warehouses. The laws appeared to the colonists to be unjust, and otherwise honest people, as so often happens, became lawbreakers. 

Because of some of these laws, and in spite of others, the colonists had prospered. On the whole they had a much kindlier and more liberal mother country than the colonists of any other nation of that day.

4. ATTEMPTS TO TAX THE COLONIES 

George III was king of England during the years following the last war with the French. He was a good man but a poor ruler. He was courteous and kindly to his family and his friends, but he did a great many things as king which we should not approve. His mistaken views as to his duties and rights as king made trouble. For many years the kings of England had not really ruled the country. Parliament and the king's ministers, who had seats in Parliament, governed the realm in the king's name. Now George III wanted to be a real king and govern in person. This desire led to a quarrel between the king and certain leaders in Parliament who were opposed to the king's views. The most

QUARREL BETWEEN COLONIES AND MOTHER COUNTRY 147 

noted of these leaders were William Pitt, Edmund Burke, and Charles Fox. We are able to understand why these men sympathized with the colonists when they opposed the king's policies in America; they were fighting for about the same things in England.

Writs of Assistance and James Otis. One of the first things the king decided to do was to enforce rigidly the laws which the colonists had been disregarding. In order to prevent smuggling he sent more ships to America. The 

British officers had trouble in finding the smuggled goods, which were hidden away as soon as landed. These officers were, accordingly, given authority to search any place they wished, including private houses. The papers which granted this general authority were called Writs of Assistance. To have their private houses thus subject to search at the whim of a British officer made the colonists very angry. James 

Otis, a leading lawyer of Boston, made a great speech against the Writs of Assistance. While many colonists, including even some prominent citizens, were engaged in smuggling, the great body of the people were entirely innocent of any offense, and they justly considered their personal rights violated by the writs. 

The Stamp Act, 1765. Another thing the king and his ministers decided to do was to make the colonies raise part of the money to pay the debt incurred by the British government in the French and Indian War. Also it was proposed that the colonies raise money to support British troops that were to be stationed in America. While the reason given for these garrisons was that the colonies should be protected against the Indian outbreaks, the colonists suspected these troops might be used against them in case a dispute arose with the British government. 

To raise the money for these purposes the king and his ministers decided to tax the colonies. Accordingly in 1765

Parliament passed a law known as the Stamp Act. This

act required that, to be legal, all papers such as deeds, mortgages, licenses, and certificates of all sorts should have stamps placed on them. Even newspapers must be printed on stamped paper. Our government has frequently used this kind of tax, and it is considered a fair form of taxation. 

The colonies objected to the tax because it was passed by the British Parliament. The colonists had always voted 

 THE NEW MARKET IN COLONIAL PHILADELPHIA. Notice the pump at the left. Do you find anything interesting about the advertising sign at the right? their own taxes in their colonial assemblies. No resident of the colonies had a seat in Parliament. The colonists said, "Taxation without representation is tyranny." They decided that they would not use the stamps; their lawyers said that they would consider papers legal without them. 

This was disobeying the law, but many people in the colonies did not have much respect for the laws made by the English Parliament. They seized and destroyed the stamps whenever they could. The British tax officers were roughly treated, and some of them were forced to resign. Since the colonists would not buy the stamps, no revenue resulted.

QUARREL BETWEEN COLONIES AND MOTHER COUNTRY 149 

The British government, therefore, repealed the tax. But at the same time Parliament declared that it had the right to tax the colonists. 

Townshend Act, 1767. Another way of taxing the colonies was then tried. The Townshend Act was passed in 

1767. This act provided that glass, paint, paper, tea, and a number of other articles should be taxed upon entering the colonies. The colonists objected to this tax for the same reason that they objected to the stamp tax; they had had no voice in levying it. They refused to use the things that were taxed. In some cases they refused to allow the ships to land their cargoes. Again the British government gave up its scheme of taxing the colonies. This tax was also repealed, except the tax on tea, which was kept to show the colonists that the British government had not surrendered the right to tax them.

CHAPTER VIII  

You will be introduced in this chapter to one of the great characters in our history, Samuel Adams. This man, more than any other individual, provided the leadership which brought on the revolt of the colonists. Around this revolutionist center the events and incidents in Massachusetts which led to armed resistance and to the Declaration of Independence. In Virginia the oratory of 

Patrick Henry fired the colonists to resist England and to fight if need be for their liberties. 

1. SAMUEL ADAMS, THE FATHER OF THE REVOLUTION 

In the events leading up to the Revolutionary War, Massachusetts led the colonies, Boston led Massachusetts, and Samuel Adams led Boston. Samuel Adams was a poor man. He neglected his own affairs to work for Boston and 151

Massachusetts and for America. The Boston of his time was quite unlike the great city we know today. Shipping and fishing engaged the interest of most of the people. 

Adams was popular with the rope-makers, shipmasters, fishermen, and other groups of working people. 

Samuel Adams belonged to a family which has produced many great men. As you read the history of our country 

 SAMUEL ADAMS. This picture was made from a painting by John 

Copley. Does he not look capable of stirring up a revolt among the you will meet this family name frequently. In these events about which you are now reading, John Adams, a cousin of 

Samuel Adams, played a prominent part. These two men usually worked together in the undertakings of that time. 

The "Boston Massacre," 

1770. The resistance of the colonists to the Stamp Act and the Townshend Act was met by the British government by sending two regiments of soldiers to Boston. It was thought that sight of the "redcoats" would frighten the colonists into obeying the laws. 

Instead, their presence irritated the citizens, and frequent quarrels occurred between them and the soldiers. 

Finally, one winter evening, a crowd of men and boys from the wharves set upon the sentry before the customs house. 

A file of soldiers came to his aid and tried to press the crowd back. The bold sailors and shipbuilders, refusing to yield, pressed forward against the very muzzles of the soldiers' muskets and assailed them with clubs and pieces of ice. In the confusion and tumult the soldiers fired upon the crowd, discontented colonists?

killing three citizens and wounding eight others, two of whom soon died. Excitement ran high in Boston that night.

For a time it looked as if a battle might be fought in the streets. Samuel Adams placed himself at the head of the people and demanded that the troops be withdrawn from the town. After several days of controversy the royal governor, Thomas Hutchinson, did as Adams demanded, and the troops were removed to Castle William in the harbor.

This riot is known in American history as the "Boston 

Massacre." Do you think it a fair name?

The Committees of Correspondence, 1772. So many bitter things were said against the king and so many of the acts of Parliament were resisted that the royal governors would not allow the assemblies of some of the colonies to meet. Without meetings it seemed impossible for the colonists to confer and arrange plans by which they would oppose the king's measures. But Samuel Adams found a way. In 1772 he had committees appointed in all the towns of Massachusetts. These committees corresponded with each other and advised together and carried out whatever seemed to be for the best interests of the patriots. A little later in the same year, Richard Henry Lee in the Virginia Assembly saw the need of a similar arrangement among all the colonies. Accordingly a committee was appointed for the purpose of carrying on correspondence, and soon there were similar committees in all the colonies. This was an important arrangement. By it the colonies were somewhat drawn together. The leaders became better acquainted with each other than they had ever been before. The foundations of a union of the colonies were being laid. 

Resistance in other colonies. While Boston was the center of the rebellion against the authority and acts of Parliament, the other colonies were also engaged in the quarrel. 

In Pennsylvania, John Dickinson wrote a series of letters

known as the "Farmer's Letters" in which he explained to the people what the colonies were contending for and urged them to resist unjust laws. Patrick Henry and others in 

Virginia were fighting the king's tyranny. Henry had opposed the Stamp Act. He claimed that the people of the colonies could not rightly be taxed by the British Parliament.

BOSTON TEA PARTY. In this old sketch, one boatload of "Indians" seems to be late for the "party." 

The Boston Tea Party, 1773. You will remember that the British government left the tax on tea when it repealed the tax on other articles. A scheme was now devised by which it was thought that the colonists would be tricked into paying the tax. It was so arranged that the tea could be bought at a lower price in the colonies, even with the tax added, than it could be bought in Holland. The real test of the scheme was to be made in Boston. It was thought that the Yankee, who is so eager to make a good bargain,

would surely buy the tea at this very low price. The colonists thought that some of it would probably be sold. It was therefore decided not to allow the ships to unload their cargoes.

The committees of correspondence informed the towns of Massachusetts and the other colonies of the situation. 

A band of men was ready to resist any attempt to land the tea. Beacon fires were ready to light on the hilltops, and riders had their horses saddled ready to carry the news to the surrounding country. So matters waited. 

At length the governor was asked to arrange for the ships to leave the harbor without unloading the tea. 

N. Y. 

N. X. 

A great mass meeting to await the governor's answer was held in the old South Church, where the patriots were accustomed to hold such meetings. The crowd overran the church and filled the adjoining streets. Nothing like this meeting had ever been known before in Boston. Excitement was at fever heat. What would the governor's answer be, and what would be done in case it was a refusal? The crowd waited through the afternoon and until darkness came at the end of the short December day. Candles were lighted in the church. At length the messenger from the governor arrived. His answer was "No, the ships should not depart." Then Samuel

Adams arose, for it was he who had been presiding at the meeting, and exclaimed, "This meeting can do no more to save the country." This was a signal for action. Evidently the governor's refusal had been expected. Outside the war

Other leaders. Samuel Adams doubtless planned this affair. In his frequent acts of resistance he had some able helpers. During the earlier years of this struggle James 

Otis, the brilliant orator, lent his talents to the cause. It was he, you will remember, who spoke so effectively against the Writs of Assistance. He was very popular with the people. It is said that a gathering of people in Boston would break out in hand clapping and cheers whenever he appeared. His health was poor, and his mind was finally so enfeebled that his fine talents were early lost to the patriot cause. Another trusted and able worker through these years was Dr. Joseph Warren, who, a few years later, gave his life for the cause of American independence. 

It was important that some man of wealth be connected with Adams' plan for stirring up resistance to England. By skillful management John Hancock, a wealthy and aristocratic merchant of Boston, was drawn into the struggle. 

During the critical times of the contest over the tea ships, Hancock was in front like a brave man. He and Samuel

Adams were held chiefly responsible for the leadership of affairs in America, and it was not long before they were accused of treason, and orders were given for their arrest.

2. OPEN REVOLT THE GREAT DECLARATION 

Whigs and Tories. King George III took matters more and more into his own hands. He found his prime minister,

Lord North, ready to do his bidding. Many people in England thought the colonists had done a very high-handed thing in destroying the tea. They upheld the king. There were many people in America, especially among the wealthy, who supported the king's policy. These people, both in America and in England, were called Tories. In 

England a strong party called the Whigs opposed the king's measures. The patriots in America also were called Whigs. 

The Retaliatory Acts, 1774. It was now decided that the people of Boston should be punished for their many offenses. At the king's direction the Retaliatory Acts were passed by Parliament in 1774. One of these acts, known as the Boston Port Bill, closed that port until the tea that had been destroyed should be paid for. This act was a serious blow to Boston, since it cut off all shipping from that city. 

Another of these acts took away nearly all the rights of self-government, which the colonists prized most highly. 

They could no longer make their own laws. The royal governor was given all the power and was to rule the colony according to instructions received from England. You must remember that Massachusetts had been making her own laws and governing herself pretty largely for about one hundred fifty years. You can perhaps realize how this act made the colonists feel. General Gage was made governor and with several additional regiments of troops came over to Boston in 1774. 

Patrick Henry. In the meantime, the committees of correspondence were busily at work. The other colonists were told of what was going on in Massachusetts. They were made to realize that this colony was fighting the battles of all of them. Consequently they stood ready to help Boston.

Provisions of all kinds were sent in abundance to the people of Boston. The people there would have suffered severe hardships without such help since many of them depended upon commerce for a living, and the commerce of the town had been destroyed by the Port Bill. Perhaps the expres-

sions of sympathy and support from the other colonies did more than anything else to nerve Boston and Massachusetts to stand firm. In support of those who were resisting the English government, Patrick Henry made a great speech in the Virginia House of Burgesses. He is supposed to have said: "The next gale that sweeps from the north

First Continental Congress. The dispute between the colonies and the king's government had now become very

serious and threatening. Samuel Adams and other leading men saw the need of further united action. A convention of prominent men of all the colonies was called at Philadelphia. This meeting was called the First Continental Congress. 

It drew up and issued a Declaration of Rights which told the world what the colonists were contending for. They demanded the right to tax themselves.

They condemned the laws which interfered with their shipping and asked that they be repealed. This meeting was another important step in unifying the colonies. It was felt more and more that all were standing shoulder to shoulder in opposition to the king's tyranny. 

Courtesy Lexington Historical Society THE MINUTEMAN. This statue is perhaps the best known memorial to the little band of men who gathered in the colonial towns to fight for their rights against the mother country, England. 

The "minutemen." During this time the people of the colonies, particularly of New England, were busily preparing to fight if the need should come.

Many of the men in the colonies had fought in the French and 

Indian War. These veterans got the men and boys together and organized them into companies and taught them something of war. As most Americans were used to firearms, they learned readily. These men were called minutemen since they were supposed to be ready at a minute's notice to drop their work at the call to arms. The picture of the minuteman on this page was made from one of our country's most famous statues. 

War supplies, rifles, powder, and ball, were collected and

stored in convenient places. Close watch was kept upon 

Gage and the British troops in Boston. Messengers kept horses in readiness to spread the alarm in case the troops should make any hostile movement.

In April, 1775, Hancock and Adams were preparing to attend the second meeting of the Continental Congress at Philadelphia. Gage realized that he must make the effort to seize them at once. Learning that Adams and Hancock would spend the night of April 17 with a friend in the village of Lexington, about twelve miles from Boston, he decided to march troops out secretly by night and make the arrest. A few miles farther on, at Concord, the patriots had collected a supply of rifles and ammunition. Gage thought that at one blow he could

The battle of Lexington. When the British troops arrived at Lexington at daylight, April 19, they found about sixty minutemen under arms drawn up in line on the common near the village church. Captain Parker, an old soldier who had been with Wolfe at Quebec, was at their head. 

About eight hundred men were in the British column. There was a fight. We do not know who fired the first shot-"the shot heard round the world." After the minutemen were driven from Lexington, the British troops moved on to Concord and destroyed a part of the military stores. As the 

British soldiers marched back toward Boston they were fired upon by the Americans who now came hurrying up with their muskets in their hands. The British, leaving

many dead and wounded behind them in the road, were glad to get back to the protection of the cannon of the British fleet.

Even after the battle of Lexington few patriots thought of making the colonies into an independent nation. Benja- 

Karl F. Lutz "DECLARATION CHAMBER." Famous events have occurred in this room in 

Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Here the Declaration of Independence was adopted, the design for the first American flag accepted, and the Constitution of the United States drafted and adopted. min Franklin, who returned from England about this time, thought it possible to secure justice and remain colonies of 

England. Thomas Jefferson, of Virginia, and John Adams were not yet ready to seek independence. But Samuel 

Adams from the first wanted to make the war that had now begun a war for independence. Thomas Paine was another leader who felt that the colonies should fight for their freedom. In his pamphlet, "Common Sense," he urged the colonists to take this step. 

The Second Continental Congress. A second meeting of the representatives of the colonies began shortly after the

battle of Lexington. The chief work of this Second Continental Congress was to make preparation for the war. 

One of its first important measures was the appointment of 

Colonel George Washington of Virginia as commander of the army which was then gathering near Boston. This 

Congress continued to meet from time to time during the war. It was the only general government the colonies had. 

 "Now WE MUST ALL HANG TOGETHER." The signing of the Declaration of Independence was a bold step for the colonists to take. The scene is reenacted in this picture.

It had very little authority. It made what provision it could for the army, voting money and supplies and appointing officers. Its chief weaknesses were that it had no power to force the people of the colonies to pay taxes or to obey its other measures. Congress could merely ask the colonies for money and soldiers, and each colony would then do as it pleased about complying with the request. Sometimes Congress tried to direct the movements of the army instead of trusting such matters to Washington and his generals.

The Declaration of Independence. At first, as we have seen, most American patriots took up arms against the

mother country to defend their rights as Englishmen. However, after a few months of war more and more of them came to agree with the views of such men as Samuel Adams, Thomas Paine, and Patrick Henry. It was impossible for the colonists to remain loyal to a king who was sending more soldiers to America to subdue them. Paine gave words to their thoughts when he wrote, ""Tis time to part!"

Soon the matter of independence was brought up in the 

Continental Congress, which was meeting in Philadelphia.

Richard Henry Lee, of Virginia, introduced a resolution on 

June 7, 1776, which declared "that these united colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states." 

Congress adopted Lee's resolution on July 2; a committee was at once appointed to draw up a Declaration of Independence which was presented to the assembly on July 4. 

The great document was the work of Thomas Jefferson, although Benjamin Franklin and John Adams, members of the committee, made a few changes in the wording. 

The Declaration was copied on parchment and signed by fifty-six members of Congress. There could be no turning back now. The rebellious colonists were committed to the cause of independence. As Benjamin Franklin is reported to have said, "We must all hang together now or we shall all hang separately." John Hancock, when he signed his name "without regard to cost of ink or paper," is said to have remarked, "I guess King George can read that without his spectacles!" Study the picture (page 163) of this famous event.

The original document is now carefully preserved in the 

Library of Congress at Washington, D. C. 

The important principles on which our government is founded are stated in the second paragraph of the Declaration of Independence, which begins, "We hold these truths to be self-evident." Americans should turn often to the

statement of these principles and thoughtfully read them. 

The Loyalists or Tories. Not all the colonists approved of the Declaration of Independence. Many remained loyal to England. Some of these defended the policies of the 

British government, while others, disliking what the king and his government were doing, nevertheless refused to fight against the mother country. Many of these persons were obliged to leave the colonies, fleeing to Canada or England and leaving behind them their property and possessions. Others entered the British armies and fought against the patriots. It is estimated that fifty thousand 

Americans fought on the British side in the war. The bitter feeling between the Tories and the patriots led to many cruel incidents in the course of the struggle.

CHAPTER IX  

It is not the purpose of this chapter to tell in detail the story of the War for Independence. We shall, rather, indicate some of the more important circumstances and events which aided the patriots in their struggle. You will learn how the leadership, devotion, and courage of men like George Washington and Benjamin Franklin overcame discouragement and defeat and at length won independence for the new nation. 

1. GENERAL GEORGE WASHINGTON 

You have read in the preceding chapter how George

Washington of Virginia was appointed by Congress to command the "Continental Army." As soon as he was appointed he hurried northward to take charge of the patriots who had gathered around the city of Boston which was held by the British soldiers under General Gage. A short time before Washington arrived, the British attacked the Americans on Bunker Hill about a half mile across the bay from the city. Though the British were driven back 167

three times, they finally compelled the colonial soldiers to give up the hill.

Organizing an army. Washington took command of the patriot forces at Cambridge, Massachusetts, a short distance from Boston. He found here about 16,000 men, gathered from the New England colonies. This body of men in their rude camps could scarcely be called an army.

There were the men from the fishing villages along the coast, the men in fringed buckskin from the backwoods settlements, and the men from the towns and farms of New England. The camps in which 

Washington found these troops were as ill-assorted as the men. 

Some were in tents of sailcloth, some in rude board shacks, and some in brushwood huts. 

These men not only needed much in the way of equipment, uniforms, arms, and ammunition, but also they needed training and discipline before they would be ready to engage in officers were available, and an officers can accomplish very It was a difficult task to provide food for an army of sixteen thousand men. Officers were appointed to look after these matters. They made arrangements with farmers and merchants, and soon loads of provisions were being delivered to the army and distributed. Herds of cattle were bought and driven into the camp to furnish a supply of meat. When an army was on the march in those days be-

fore railroads had come into use, great wagon trains and trains of pack horses followed along in the rear to convey the supplies and the sick and disabled soldiers. 

The British driven from Boston. Washington found so much work in organizing an army that it occupied all his time during the fall and winter of 

1775-76. The British troops, remembering Lexington and

Bunker Hill, did not trouble him. It is said that the women of New England found employment in winter evenings in melting lead and in running bullets for the soldiers. Not long after the war began, the 

British Fort Ticonderoga (tī-kon-der-ō'gȧ) on Lake Champlain was seized by the Green 

Mountain Boys under Ethan 

Allen. The Green Mountain 

Boys were a band of fighting men who lived in Vermont. Valuable supplies for

Washington's army were found at Ticonderoga. After snow fell, Washington had the big guns of the fort drawn by teams all the way to Boston to use against the British forts.

Washington felt that his army was ready to strike a blow. 

Suddenly one night he seized Dorchester Heights to the southeast of Boston. He threw up entrenchments there and mounted some of his big cannon. When the British saw those cannon frowning down on them in Boston they decided to leave the city. They took to their ships and sailed away. Great was the rejoicing in Boston when Washington's army came marching into the city. 

When the British troops left Boston in the spring of 1776 they sailed to Halifax (hăl'i-făks) in Canada. They waited there for more troops to come over from England to help them. The king hired several thousand troops from the prince of the German state, Hesse (hes). These troops were known as Hessians (hesh'ănz). The colonists and many people in England were indignant to think that foreign soldiers should be hired to fight against Americans.

Throughout the war the British depended on their ships to bring fresh troops and supplies from across the sea. 

The British army usually stayed near the coast and along the rivers so that such supplies and reenforcements could be easily secured from their ships. Most of the campaigns won by the British army were against coast cities. Whenever their armies sought to go far into the interior they met with disaster and defeat.

Strength and weakness of the Americans. The Declara tion of Independence, July, 1776, made it clear that the colonists meant to defy the power of England in a struggle to set up an independent nation. It may seem that the cause of the American patriots was almost hopeless. The population of England was three or four times as great as that of the colonies. Many of the Americans, the Loyalists, were not in favor of independence and gave help to the British. England had a trained army and the most powerful navy in the world. The Americans had no organized army 

1 In 1776 there were only twenty-eight post offices in all the colonies.

at the beginning of the war, and no navy. The men who fought at Lexington and Bunker Hill were from Massachusetts and the other New England colonies. They were put in the field by these colonies and not by the Continental Congress. This force was made up of volunteers, that is, men who enlisted in the army of their own free will and who could leave when their terms of enlistment expired. Many times during the war Washington found himself almost helpless as the men left the army at the end of their terms of enlistment. Later in the war Washington organized what was known as the "Continental Army." The men in this army stayed with their commander year after year.

The navy was made up of privately owned merchant ships whose owners volunteered for service. The owners of these ships were given the right by Congress to arm their vessels and put to sea to attack British merchant ships. 

They did great damage to England's trade during the war, but only occasionally did they fight against ships of the British navy. With the aid of the French a small number of well-armed ships were secured. One of these, the "Bonhomme (bōn hōm') Richard," engaged in battle with the

British man-of-war "Serapis (sê-rā'pis)." The American ship was commanded by Captain John Paul Jones, who had made a number of daring raids on British merchant ships. 

The "Serapis" was forced to surrender, but the American ship was so badly damaged that it could not be kept afloat. 

Captain Jones transferred his crew to the decks of the British ship and brought that vessel into a Dutch port. 

Perhaps the greatest weakness of the Americans was that they had no means of raising money with which to pay the costs of the war. The Continental Congress did not have the right to tax the colonies. It could only ask for money which a colony might pay or not as it pleased. 

When Congress was unable to secure enough money to

meet expenses, private citizens contributed funds. Robert 

Morris and Hayme Salomon, two wealthy men of Philadelphia, supplied members of Congress and generals in the field with money for their needs. These men pledged their private fortunes to support the War of Independence. 

Much of the money which was lent to Congress by these men was never repaid. Patriotic women raised money for the cause by selling their jewels and household silver.

 JOHN PAUL JONES. "I have just begun to fight." Does he look like a man who would use such words? 

England could not bring her full strength against the rebel lious colonists. Rivals in Eu rope, particularly France and

Holland, compelled England to keep strong forces on that side of the Atlantic. Such troops and ships as could be spared must carry on the war in America three thousand miles from the home country. Some of the 

English people opposed the war. They were against the policy of the king and his ministers in taxing the colonists.

Some did not think it right to send soldiers and ships to fight the Americans.

Fighting around New York and in New Jersey. In this book we cannot tell the complete story of the many battles and campaigns of the war. Many times the cause of independence seemed lost, and but for the unfailing courage of Washington the Americans might have given up. Here we can only glance at some of the more important events about which you may read more fully as you continue your study of American history.

In the summer of 1776 General Howe brought a strong

British army, by ship, against the city of New York. General Washington and his soldiers were defeated in a number of battles, and the city fell into the hands of the British. Many of Washington's men and officers were captured, and at one time it appeared as if the whole army might be lost. However, a dense fog at night enabled the

Americans to escape from Long Island and make good their retreat north into New York and later westward across New Jersey. All the forts around New York were taken by the British, including Fort Washington and Fort Lee above the city, and the ships of the British navy were free to pass up the Hudson River as they pleased.

The Americans were greatly discouraged; as their terms of service expired many of the soldiers left the American

army and went home so that Washington did not have sufficient forces with which to oppose the British. Winter was coming on and the American soldiers were short of food and clothing. It was with great difficulty that Washington kept his small army in the field. Indeed, he pledged his own private means for the purchase of supplies when Congress failed to provide for his men. 

The surprise at Trenton. The British generals Howe and 

Cornwallis (kôrn-wôl'is) thought they had won the war and were spending the Christmas holidays in New York 

City celebrating their victories. Washington seized this opportunity for a bold stroke against the British forces. On 

Christmas night he crossed the Delaware River which was full of floating ice, and, marching ten miles through a severe storm, he fell upon a Hessian force at Trenton and destroyed it, capturing one thousand men. Cornwallis hastened from New York with more British troops to retrieve this disaster. A few days later Washington outwitted this commander and defeated his force at Princeton. Washington then took up a strong position on Morristown Heights. 

His army was in a position to seize the British supplies which had to be brought from New York. The British commanders decided to withdraw their forces to New York for the winter. Thus in a brilliant campaign of a few weeks 

Washington undid all the British had accomplished in months. All the world realized that the task of winning 

American independence was in strong hands. The British generals learned to fear the skill and respect the courage of the American commander. Perhaps our own people appreciated him the least. 

1. Describe the patriot army which gathered near Boston after the Battle of Lexington. Tell of their equipment, arms, and tents. 

2. Give an account of Washington's work in organizing the army.

3. What happened at Trenton to show that in Washington the Americans had a capable leader?

BURGOYNE'S CAMPAIGN. The British under Burgoyne came up Lake 

Champlain and attempted to march across the wooded country to the 

Hudson River. Battles were fought at Saratoga and at Bemis Heights.

The British army was compelled to surrender to the Americans under 

General Gates, October 17, 1777. 

country from the north by way of Lake Champlain. Another British force under General Howe was to advance up the Hudson River and meet General Burgoyne's army at Albany. The purpose of the campaign was to cut New England off from the rest of the states. 

R. I

Burgoyne's army, made up of English troops, Hessians, Canadians, and Indians, moved up Lake Champlain without serious opposition from the Americans. Fort Ticonderoga on Lake Champlain was taken, and the British campaign seemed on the way to certain success. At this point, however, Burgoyne's difficulties began. 

In nearly all wars in early times in our country, Indians 

MATHAN HALE 

were employed on both sides. They were fierce fighters, but it was difficult to make them obey orders. War gave them a chance to loot and pillage the settlements and led to many acts of violence. The fact that white soldiers of all armies sometimes committed similar deeds did not lessen the anger of the American settlers over the depredations of the 

Indians of Burgoyne's army. Thousands of enraged settlers joined the 

American forces to fight against the British. Between the head of 

Lake Champlain and Fort Edward were twenty or thirty miles of dense forest and swamps. General Schuyler (ski'ler), one of the most skillful of the American generals, did everything possible to destroy the few roads through this region. His men felled trees across the roads, destroyed the bridges, dammed the streams, and flooded parts of the country. So difficult was travel that the best Burgoyne could do was to advance his army one mile a day.

British as a spy.

An expedition which was sent by General Burgoyne into Vermont to secure supplies for the British army was destroyed by Colonel Stark in the Battle of Bennington.

General Howe, who was expected to lead an army up the Hudson to help Burgoyne, did not appear. The British army attempted to fight its way southward toward Albany, but was defeated in two battles and compelled to surrender at Saratoga (săr-ȧ-to'gȧ), October 17, 1777. 

General Howe has been blamed for the failure of Burgoyne's campaign. He did not move his army up the Hudson as the British officials in London had planned. It is supposed that he did not clearly understand the British plans for the year. Instead of going to the aid of Burgoyne, Howe moved the main part of his army from New York southward for the capture of Philadelphia. General Washington marched his army to the defense of that city. The 

American army was defeated in the Battle of Brandywine in September, 1777, and Philadelphia fell to the British. 

This happened a few weeks before Burgoyne surrendered at Saratoga.

The capture of Burgoyne's army has been called the turning point of the war. The patriots were filled with new hope and courage. From that time on the British had little chance to defeat the Americans. Important results followed this victory. 

3. BENJAMIN FRANKLIN AND THE FRENCH ALLIANCE 

Benjamin Franklin, a native of Massachusetts who, when a boy, had moved to Philadelphia, was one of the wisest men of his time. By trade he was a printer, but he devoted much time to study, especially study of science. 

His experiments in electricity with key and kite had made him known to all scientific men in Europe. He gave a great deal of time and thought to public affairs also. He was one of the first Americans to see the need of some form of union among the colonies. As far back as 1754 he had proposed a plan known as the Albany plan of union. He went abroad several times in the interests of the colonies and was well known and popular in Europe.

Treaty of Alliance, 1778. Many of the French people sympathized with the Americans in their struggle for freedom, partly because they believed in the cause for which the Americans were fighting and partly because they wanted to see England lose her colonies in America. From the beginning of the war, the French had secretly aided the Americans.

Franklin, who was very popular with the French people, was sent over to France to obtain the help of that nation. 

The Americans wanted the French to recognize American independence and ally herself openly with the revolting colonies. When the great victory at Saratoga was won,

Franklin was able to persuade the French to come out into the open since it now looked as if the Americans might win. This important treaty which recognized American independence and promised aid was signed in February, 1778. France agreed to send ships and soldiers and, what was quite as important, lent a large sum of money. 

Congress was in sad need of money. The money which the states had been asked to provide had been paid only in small part, and Congress had no power with which to make them pay. So much paper money had been issued that it was practically worthless, and to issue more would be useless. About the only resource left was to borrow. The 

French loan was a great help.

About a year after the French treaty of alliance, Spain joined England's enemies. Somewhat later Holland came into the league to make war on England, an old commercial rival. England was thus beset on all sides and was unable to push the war against the American patriots. 

Valley Forge. The French alliance came at a critical time. It seemed as if the colonies were almost exhausted. 

Hard times faced the people everywhere. Washington with his little army at Valley Forge during the winter of 17771778 was in desperate straits. Both clothing and food were

scarce. Congress was weak and incompetent. Plots were formed to place another general in command of the patriot army. Washington paid little attention to his detractors. 

He went on with his difficult task, not only serving without pay but spending his own means to relieve the suffering of his men. The success won by Benjamin Franklin in France was no less important than those won by our armies on the battlefields. It is doubtful whether the American cause could have succeeded without the help of France. 

Other important help came to the Americans from Europe in the way of skilled generals who sympathized with the American cause and gave their services. One of the most important of these was the young French nobleman, Marquis de Lafayette (lä-fa-yet').  

Lafayette served with Washington throughout most of the war. He came to be a personal

BENJAMIN FRANKLIN. Do you think this picture of Franklin brings out his qualities of wisdom and common sense? friend of Washington and rendered many important services. Von Steuben (fon shtoi ben), an accomplished German officer, did a great deal in organizing and drilling Washington's soldiers. In the picture on page 167 the German officer is seen at work with a squad of Washington's men. A great deal of their later efficiency resulted from this work. Pulaski (pů-lăs'kĭ) and Kosciusko (kos-i-us'kō) were two Polish noblemen who gave their services to the American cause.

Monmouth. The effects of the French alliance were immediately felt. The British, afraid that they could not defend both Philadelphia and New York, decided to evacuate

Philadelphia and concentrate their forces at New York. As their army moved across New Jersey, Washington fell upon them at Monmouth and came near to winning a great victory. The mischief maker, General Charles Lee, who was in command of a portion of the American army, deprived Washington of this success by ordering a retreat at a critical moment. Lee, who had made trouble more than once, was dismissed from the army. 

An important result of the alliance with France came from the activities of the French fleet. After the treaty was agreed to, many warships came into American waters and so occupied the attention of the British fleet that it could do little to help the British armies in New York or in the South.

How the Northwest was won. Some years before the 

War for Independence, settlers crossed the Appalachian Mountains and made their homes in parts of what are now the states of Tennessee and Kentucky. In Chapter XI you will read the story of these pioneers. While Washington's army was fighting battles against the British in New York and New Jersey in 1776, these settlers were waging a successful war against the Indian tribes of the Tennessee Valley. Although these settlers were few in number, they were intensely patriotic. The region north of the Ohio River extending to the Great Lakes and Canada had been under the control of the British since the close of the French and Indian War in 1763 (p. 130). Only a few white people lived in this territory, they being largely of French blood and interested in the fur trade. The thought came to George 

Rogers Clark, a young pioneer of Kentucky, that this region might be won from the British and become a part of the new nation which was fighting for its independence. 

Clark appealed to the governor of Virginia, Patrick Henry, for aid in carrying out his plan. (Kentucky was a part of 

Virginia at that time.) Clark's plan was approved, but

little help was promised him. He was authorized to raise a force of 350 riflemen and was pledged $1200 to cover the cost of an expedition. Nothing daunted, the bold Clark took steps immediately to carry out his scheme. He raised a force of about 150 men, and early in the year 1778 embarked by boat down the Ohio River. THE SOUTH DURING THE WAR FOR INDEPENDENCE

4. HOW THE WAR WAS BROUGHT TO AN END 

The war in the South. In 1779 the scene of the war shifted to the South. The British generals thought it might be possible to overrun Georgia and the Carolinas as these colonies were somewhat remote from the more populous northern colonies. Under this plan the English expected, after winning back the South, to proceed northward and try to reconquer the entire country. There were many people in the South who were loyal to the British government. The British generals were able to secure the help of these loyalists or Tories, as they were called, and for a time it seemed as if that section might be won back to the British Empire. The invading armies, with the assistance of warships, captured important coast cities, including 

Savannah and Charleston. However, when their forces attempted to march into the country away from the coast, they met with little success, and though they won some battles, they were defeated in others. An American army under General Gates was defeated at Camden, South Carolina (August, 1780). The British were constantly harassed by surprise attacks of patriot bands under General Sumter and General Marion and others, and were not able to establish themselves securely at any point in the interior. Detachments of the British army were defeated at 

Cowpens and at Kings Mountain.

In 1781 Washington sent General Nathanael Greene to take command of the American forces in the South. General Greene conducted one of the most brilliant campaigns of the war. He outmaneuvered and outfought the British commander, General Cornwallis, who finally withdrew his army to Yorktown in Virginia. General Greene then moved farther into the South and freed that region from the remaining British and Tory forces.

Benedict Arnold. Before relating the closing events of the struggle for independence, we must pause for a moment to

relate one of the saddest incidents of the war. Benedict 

Arnold was a capable officer in the American army who had served brilliantly at Saratoga. In the early days of the war he led a mere handful of men through the Maine woods for an attack on Quebec. He had distinguished himself on many battlefields. Washington recognized his ability, but 

Congress passed him by time and again in the promotion 

L. C Handy Studios THE SURRENDER OF CORNWALLIS. The picture is from Trumbull's paint ing representing the famous event. The original is in the capitol at Washington. of officers. Arnold, at first hurt by these slights, at length became embittered. He had married a Tory woman, Margaret Shippen, in Philadelphia, and perhaps she influenced him. He had asked to be made commander of the fort at 

West Point, on the Hudson River, and the important post had been given to him. He decided to surrender this fort to the British. The plot was discovered, and 

Major Andre (än'drå) of the British army, who was concerned with arranging the plan, was caught and hanged as a spy. Arnold escaped to receive the reward of his treachery, a large sum of money and a high command in the British

army. Arnold counted his personal feelings above his duty to his country.

Yorktown. The war was brought to a close with a great victory for Washington. Cornwallis was at Yorktown, Virginia. Washington, who was at New York watching a British force there, was able to communicate his plans to the French admiral who was in the West Indies. Skillfully deceiving the British at New York, Washington with a combined American and French army moved by forced marches from the Hudson to Yorktown. The powerful French fleet occupied the harbor. The soldiers of Washington and the 

French general, Rochambeau (ro-shän-bō'), hemmed the British force in on land. The French ships of war cut off the chance of escape by sea. Cornwallis was trapped. He surrendered his army October 19, 1781. This brought the war to a close. Trumbull's famous painting, reproduced on page 

184, pictures this great event in American history. 

The treaty of peace. When the British army surrendered at Yorktown, King George and his ministers realized that the colonies could not be recovered. Ministers were appointed to confer with American representatives to settle the terms of peace. Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and 

John Jay were selected for this important work by the American Congress. The ministers of both countries met at Paris and after some delay agreed upon the terms that would bring the war to a close. The treaty, which was signed in 1783, is known as the Treaty of Paris. Great Britain recognized the independence of the United States of America. Boundaries were agreed upon. The new nation extended from the Atlantic coast on the east to the Mississippi River on the west and from the Great Lakes on the north to the thirty-first parallel on the south. England retained Canada. Florida was given back to Spain. These terms were fairly liberal, and for the most part acceptable to the American people.
