CHAPTER XIII  

This chapter tells the story of the extension of our nation westward and of our second war with England, sometimes called the "Second War of Independence." This war was caused by the violation of our rights on the sea by France and England, neither of which greatly respected the young, struggling republic. Though our country was not prepared for war, and for the most part conducted military matters very badly, we emerged from our difficulties with increased strength and self-respect. 

1. A NEW PRESIDENT AND A NEW CAPITAL 

Thomas Jefferson. The man who was inaugurated as president of our country on March 4, 1801, was, like Washington, a well-to-do Virginian. He was a tall, slim man with reddish hair and freckled face. He had none of the trim military bearing of Washington, and was inclined to be careless about his appearance. He knew a great deal about many things. He could talk with visitors about farming, 247

music, law, history, and almost any other subject that came up. His servants at Monticello loved him. 

This smiling gentlemanly man had fixed ideas about many of the questions of the day. He was sure the government under the Federalists was too formal and ceremonious. He believed the state and local governments should 

 THOMAS JEFFERSON. This is one of the best pictures we have of the author of the Declaration of Independence. be vigorous and that the central government should rule the people as little as possible. He wanted to keep down expenses. He believed that the common people had good judgment about political matters. 

In the fall of 1800 the seat of our government was removed from Philadelphia to 

Washington. John Adams was then president, and his wife, the intelligent and capable Abigail Adams, was the first mistress of the White

House. The White House was then a barn-like unfinished structure. Abigail

Adams became lost in the woods driving from Baltimore to the new capital. It was this woodland capital that saw the inauguration of Thomas Jefferson, the first ceremony of its kind in Washington. 

Jefferson's inauguration was a simple one. He merely left his boardinghouse and walked over to the Senate chamber to deliver his inaugural address. The open spaces were stumpy, there were undrained marshes, the new streets were muddy, and the paths which served as sidewalks were rough and strewn with litter from the unfinished buildings.

But the new capital, rough and unfinished as it was in 1801, was even then planned on a grand and imposing scale. The plan was made by a French landscape engineer, Major Pierre Charles L'Enfant (län-fän'). Today the city ranks as one of the most beautiful capitals in the world. 031

Paul's Photos MONTICELLO, THE HOME OF THOMAS JEFFERSON. Jefferson planned this fine residence himself. It stands on rolling ground outside the city of 

Charlottesville, Virginia. The Jefferson family lived here fifty-six years. 

Only a small crowd attended the first inauguration at the new capital. There was no music and no display. But the address of the new president was a ringing appeal to the people of our country to be loyal citizens. On that day, he said, our people were not Federalists, or Republicans, but Americans. Jefferson was a poor speaker, but everything he wrote was worth reading.

You already feel acquainted with this new president, as you remember him in connection with the Declaration of

Independence and with the disputes in Washington's cabinet. 

2. THE LOUISIANA PURCHASE 

Napoleon's whim. At this time Napoleon Bonaparte (bō'nȧ-pärt), who will be spoken of more in detail later on in this chapter, was rapidly becoming the greatest figure in France and, for that matter, in Europe. Already he dreamed of becoming the emperor of the French. He made a secret treaty with Spain, which gave him the city of New Orleans, the island where the city stands, and all the Louisiana territory. He had plans to build in the interior of North 

America a great French dominion. He sent an envoy to 

America to arrange for the coming of a strong French army to New Orleans. 

Jefferson's fears. You may be sure that President Jefferson was alarmed at the sudden turn affairs had taken. Our gratitude to France for her help in the Revolution had cooled. Besides, it was much better for our country to have weak, easy-going Spain as a neighbor on the west than France, the greatest military power in Europe, and led by a man like Napoleon. Emissaries were hurried to France to try to buy the Island of Orleans and the city of New Orleans, so that we might not lose our precious right to use the Mississippi freely.

The purchase. For several reasons the ambitious Napol eon suddenly changed his mind about his French dominion in America; and when the American envoys talked of buying the Island of Orleans, he told them they might buy the whole of Louisiana. He would not sell the island by itself. 

Our agents hesitated, because they had instructions to buy only the island. But Napoleon was offering a great bargain, and soon all was arranged and Louisiana was ours. It was a great stroke, and most Americans, even then, were well pleased at what had been done.

The Stars and Stripes go up. An interesting scene took

place at New Orleans a few months later. The flag of France had been flying over New Orleans only twenty days when the news came that the land was now not a province of France but a part of the United States. The Spanish and 

French people were bewildered by the sudden changes, and not at all pleased at the latest news. Most of them, being 

French, wanted to be under the French flag. They feared and disliked the Americans. On December 20, 1803, a force of American troops came marching up to the old city gates with the band playing first French, then American airs. 

Courtesy Louisiana State Museum 

NEW ORLEANS IN 1803. This is an old picture of New Orleans as it appeared in the year it became an American town. 

Here they were met by the Spanish garrison, which had not yet given up the forts, and escorted to the Cabildo, the main government building of the city. There copies of the papers showing that the country was now a part of the United States were read. The keys of the city were then handed over to the new American governor, and the Stars and Stripes were run up, while a military salute was fired.

The people were freed from their allegiance to France and were welcomed to the citizenship of the United States with full freedom. A French officer wrapped the beloved French flag around him and walked away. Thus ended the dreams of France to own the Mississippi Valley. The strong young 

American republic now possessed both banks of the great river, and the development of the West was assured.

The new domain. The great new domain stretched away to the north and west into regions then utterly unknown to Americans. Twenty states the size of Ohio could be carved out of it. The United States could hardly have had the history it has had nor be in any sense the United States we know today without this famous Louisiana Purchase. 

The southern part of the Purchase was given a territorial government until 1812, when, as Louisiana, it was admitted to the Union. 

1. Why was President Jefferson disturbed when he learned that Napoleon owned Louisiana? 

2. State the importance of the purchase. 

3. NEW TROUBLES WITH FRANCE AND ENGLAND 

England and France at war. During Jefferson's administration the struggle in Europe between France, under the leadership of Napoleon, and England was resumed. England's great naval victory at Trafalgar (trăf-ăl-gär') in 1805 made her mistress of the seas. On the other hand, the armies of Napoleon had conquered most of Europe with the exception of England. French armies could not cross the English 

Channel while the British fleet patrolled those waters. To injure his hated rival, Napoleon devised his "Continental System." Since England marketed a large portion of her manufactured goods in Europe, Napoleon decided to cut off that market by closing the ports of Europe to English goods. This he thought he could do since he was master of nearly every country of continental Europe except Russia, and that country was bound to him by treaty. England retaliated by declaring a blockade of the coast of Europe from Brest to the Elbe. That is, she declared the ports on that coast closed to ships with cargoes from neutral countries. Napoleon then declared the ports of England closed to neutral ships.

of the leading countries of Europe were at war, the United States was carrying on a large trade with these warring nations. You can readily see in what a plight our ships were.

There was scarcely a port in Europe to which they could sail without danger of being seized by the warships of one or the other of the countries at war. Our government protested vigorously, but France and England paid little attention to the young republic. The French had very few ships which kept the seas after Trafalgar; hence our ships suffered chiefly at the hands of the British. 

Impressment. Another practice of the British angered our people more than anything else. The pay on the American merchantmen was better than in the British navy. Accordingly many English sailors deserted to American ships. 

To recover such sailors British war vessels would stop American ships on the high seas, board them, and search for deserters. In many cases American sailors were taken off our ships and forced into the British navy. This impressment of our sailors caused great indignation. 

Jefferson's policy. President Jefferson was a peace-loving man. He did his very best to keep our country out of war. 

Though both France and England insulted us and disreregarded our rights on the seas, Jefferson would not retaliate. In fact, we had no force with which to fight back. Our government was being run on a very economical plan. Albert Gallatin (găl'a-tin) was Secretary of the Treasury.

Under his administration the national debt was rapidly reduced. Taxes were lowered. "Peace is our passion," said

Jefferson. Very limited funds were provided for the army and the navy, which were greatly reduced in size and efficiency. President Jefferson thought our coasts could be protected by small gunboats. Each boat was to carry one cannon and be manned by from five to seven men. About 150 of these boats were built. It was the unwise scheme of a man who knew little about such matters, and the whole plan failed.

Embargo Act, 1807. Our government thought it could punish England and France for the wrongs done us by shutting off American products from those countries. England was purchasing large quantities of food products, cotton, and naval stores. At President Jefferson's request

Congress passed an act in 1807 known as the Embargo Act. 

By this law all ships were prohibited from sailing from 

American ports to Europe.

This act proved disastrous. 

We needed a market for our products even more than

England needed these prodducts. Plantation owners were ruined. The price of farm products fell off onehalf. Thirty thousand sailors were thrown out of work. A storm of protest swept over the country. The act was repealed. 

 JAMES MADISON. AS a young statesman he was a leader in the drafting of our Constitution. This picture was made from an oil painting. 

President Madison, 18091817. These events occupied several years. Jefferson served out his second term and retired from the presidency in 1809. He was succeeded by James Madison, another noted 

Virginian, who had served his country well as a member of the Constitutional Convention. Madison attempted to continue Jefferson's policies. In spite of the president's wishes events carried us inevitably toward war. 

Bold young leaders from the new West were finding seats in Congress. Chief among these was Henry Clay from Kentucky, who was elected speaker of the House of Representatives. These Westerners had another grievance against

Great Britain. The Indians of the Northwest were restless and troublesome. They looked with jealous eyes upon the advance of the white settlers. British traders from Canada were supplying them with rifles and ammunition. The 

Westerners felt that Great Britain was arming these Indians against our settlers. The noted chief Tecumseh (tė-kum'sě) was at work stirring up and uniting the Indians. 

General William Harrison, governor of Indiana Territory, got together the fighting men of that region, marched against the Indians, and defeated them in the Battle of Tippecanoe (tip-ê-kȧ-noo') in 1811. To men like Clay, Tippecanoe appeared almost like a victory over the British themselves.

4. THE WAR OF 1812 

The causes of the War of 1812 dated back over many years, as you have learned in the preceding pages. Both 

France and England continued to interfere with our merchant ships. The efforts of President Jefferson and President 

Madison to avoid these difficulties had been in vain. The "impressment" of American seamen by the British navy made our people very angry. The British government claimed that since these men had been born in the British Isles they were still British subjects. Our government claimed, on the other hand, that these seamen were American subjects, since they were naturalized citizens of the 

United States. 

Other causes for trouble with England lay in the rivalry for the fur trade on the western frontiers. British fur-trading companies had now taken over the trade with the Indians which the French had formerly enjoyed. Two great companies, the North-west and the Hudson's Bay Com-

pany, became bitter rivals of the American Fur Company which had been organized by John Jacob Astor. The Indian war of 1811, about which you have just read, was a part of this struggle between the United States and the British.

The "War Hawks," as the strong advocates of war were called, under the leadership of Clay clamored loudly for war 

 AN OLD VIEW OF THE WHITE HOUSE. In 1825 the home of the presidents, at Washington, D.C., had this appearance. Compare this view with pictures of the White House as it appears today. against England. President Madison reluctantly abandoned his peace policy, and war was declared in June, 1812. 

We had suffered much at the hands of both France and England, but England seemed the chief offender, though it was a strange spectacle to see the liberty-loving Americans practically allying themselves with the despotic Napoleon. 

The western leaders were no doubt influenced by the belief that we could easily conquer Canada and thus punish England. Clay boasted that "the militia of Kentucky alone

are competent to place Montreal and Upper Canada at your feet." John C. Calhoun, another "War Hawk," boldly declared in Congress that within four weeks Canada would be ours.

Weakness of our army. Our country was wholly unprepared for war. Our army numbered only a few thousand men. We had few trained officers. The militia, as the state

These men had very little training and were not under the control of the United States government. Sometimes they refused to go out of their own states to fight. 

One disaster after another marked our efforts to invade Canada. In some battles our men fought bravely and won victories, but campaigns usually failed through mismanagement. After two years of fighting we were no nearer the

conquest of Canada than we were at the outset. Indeed, it was difficult for us to prevent British troops from invading the United States. In 1814 a small body of British troops landed on our eastern coast and by a rapid march seized 

Washington, our capital city. They burned the capitol building, the president's residence, and some other public buildings. During an enemy attack on the forts near 

Baltimore about this time, Francis Scott Key wrote "The 

Star Spangled Banner." 

Battle of New Orleans, 1815. One brilliant American victory marked the war. A strong force of British troops landed on our Gulf coast with the purpose of taking the important city of New Orleans. Andrew Jackson, one of our fighting Westerners, led the riflemen of the West to the defense of that city. Their deadly marksmanship won a decisive victory over some of the best troops in the 

British army.

Victories at sea. Our sailors on the ocean and on the 

Great Lakes gave a good account of themselves. Commodore Perry on Lake Erie, with a fleet built in large part from the timber growing on the shores of the lake, defeated a heavier British squadron. He announced his victory in the now famous words, "We have met the enemy and they are ours." On page 247 is a picture representing the most thrilling incident in this battle.

On the ocean we won a number of single-ship battles which astonished the world and not only won undying fame for our sailors, but did much to impress Europe with the idea that henceforth we were a nation to be reckoned with. One of the most celebrated naval victories was that of the American ship "Constitution," commanded by Commodore Isaac Hull, over the British frigate, “Guerriere.” 

In thirty minutes the American gunners shot the British ship to pieces and forced her crew to surrender, the ship going to the bottom shortly after the battle. Even in defeat

the American sailors won glory. The American ship "Chesapeake," commanded by Captain Lawrence, was defeated by the British ship "Shannon." Captain Lawrence was killed in the battle. His last words, "Don't give up the ship," became the watchword of the American Navy. 

Peace, 1814. Both sides tired of the war, and peace was 

INTERNATIONAL BOUNDARY UNITED STATES  A BOUNDARY MONUMENT. 

Concrete markers like this stand in pairs at the points where international highways cross the line between our country and Canada. finally made late in the year 1814.

The downfall of Napoleon in Europe about this time ended the long European war and made it easy for England and America to come to terms. The treaty ending the war did not settle the questions in dispute, but these issues were dropped with the coming of peace with Great Britain.

The affairs of our country during the war period were not well conducted. That lack of spirit of national unity which we noticed in the days following the Revolutionary War still showed itself. 

New England opposed the war bitterly, as her shipping was seriously injured. Some of her leaders went so far as to hold a convention in 1814, known as the Hartford Convention, for the purpose of taking steps to oppose certain measures of Congress. The delegates to the convention decided to ask 

Congress to submit to the states seven amendments to the Constitution. The purpose of the proposed amendments was to reduce the power of the United States government in such matters as the regulation of commerce and the conduct of war. Another purpose was greatly to increase the power and independence of the states. Thus the war

brought up in new form the old question of "states' rights" which was to go on troubling the nation for many years. 

With the coming of peace, however, and in the general rejoicing over the close of the war, the people of the country laid aside such questions as those raised at Hartford, and seemed more united in feeling than ever before. The victories of soldiers like Jackson and sailors like Hull and Perry aroused a feeling of national patriotism. For the first time our people came to think of themselves as a nation-one people.

Before this time affairs in our country had been largely influenced by events and conditions in Europe. From this time on the problems of our own growing country demanded the chief attention of our people. Although the War of 

1812 had been badly mismanaged, nevertheless the powers of Europe were taught to respect the vigorous young republic. Hence this war has sometimes been called "the 

Second War of Independence." Other important results of this war will be mentioned in the next chapter.

UNIT V THE NEW WEST AND THE OLDER EAST In Chapter XI we saw Daniel Boone and John Sevier and men like them plunging into the great wilderness beyond the Allegheny ridges. They carried long rifles, dressed like the red men, and built strong stockaded forts. They were trail blazers and Indian fighters.

Now we are to see a new class of pioneers pouring into that western country. To them a plow is much more important than a rifle. The Indian danger is gone. Farms are cleared; courthouses, schoolhouses, and churches are built. 

The dim trails are broadened into roads. 

Then the new West and the older East see that they need each other. They work together until wagon roads, canals, and railroads link the West and the East. 

Out of all this bustling activity comes a new, stronger nation with new ideas and new leaders.

In this unit we shall read how and why the early farm families made their homes in the West, how travel to the West was made easier, how new problems came to face the growing nation, and how new leaders rose to help solve them. 265

CHAPTER XIV FROM OLD EASTERN HOMES TO NEW HOMES IN THE WEST 

Chapter XI told how the early pioneers crossed the Appalachian Mountains and began their settlements in the valleys of the Ohio, the Tennessee, and other western rivers. You will now be led to see how this new part of our country grew and prospered as an increasing multitude of people from the older communities took up the westward march. This chapter describes the experiences and manner of life of those who thus sought and found new homes beyond the mountains. 

1. WHY THE EMIGRANTS TRAILED WESTWARD 

Changes in the West. Within twenty-five years after the close of the Revolutionary War much of the good land in Kentucky and Tennessee had been taken by well-to-do settlers who came in from Virginia and other southern states. Some of these new settlers brought their slaves with them. The primitive conditions and occupations of the 267

backwoods rapidly gave way to tobacco growing and stock raising on a large scale. The frontiersman grew restless under these new conditions. He began to miss the freedom of the wilderness and the happy-go-lucky life of early days.

He felt crowded. Glowing accounts of rich, cheap lands to

Kentucky and Tennessee began to move on to become the pioneers of new states. Some went westward across the

FORT DEARBORN, CHICAGO. The picture shows a reproduction of the original Fort Dearborn. The new fort stands on the shore of Lake Michigan, while the original fort was located on the bank of the Chicago River, in the heart of what is now Chicago's Loop District. In forts such as this, scattered along the frontier in early times, were stationed small companies of United States soldiers. In 1812 the original Fort Dearborn was destroyed by Indians, many settlers and members of the garrison losing their lives. loaded with men, women, children, and household goods passed his place on their way to the Ohio country. Other people in the state of New York, in western Virginia, and farther south along the western edge of the settled places have left us similar reports of the large number of emigrants streaming along the rutty roads, always toward the West.

What made these people hurry out into the new western

country? Stories of early settlers tell us that much hardship and suffering awaited them in the new homes they planned to set up. To be sure, there was little danger now from the 

Indians. The earlier pioneers such as Boone and Clark and military leaders such as Wayne and Harrison had attended to that. But poor roads and the gloomy forest and sickness and the lack of neighbors were enough to discourage timid people from trying to start homes in the West. 

Hard times in the older states. In the first place, those who went west were courageous people. They were willing to struggle with harsh frontier conditions if, in the end, they might find better opportunities for themselves and their children. For many people in the older states times were very hard in the years shortly before and after the 

War of 1812. You will remember the injury to trade caused by England and France when they seized our ships, and by the Embargo Law passed by our Congress. There was no work for the sailors. The farmers were unable to sell their crops. Then later, when the War of 1812 was over, people lost their places in the mills and factories because the owners could not find a market for their goods in the face of the cheap goods from England. The West promised relief from these evils. People abandoned their old homes and turned their faces westward where land was cheap and prosperity beckoned. 

1. Why did many Kentucky pioneers wish to move to less settled regions? 

2. In what ways, if any, were the lands farther west more attractive? 

2. CHANGES IN THE SOUTH 

Farther south the movement westward was based on the spread of the short-staple cotton plant and the plantation system. The invention of the cotton gin by Eli Whitney in 

1793 was one of the most important in a series of causes for the spread of cotton cultivation. Before Whitney's in-

FROM OLD EASTERN HOMES TO NEW IN WEST 271 

vention only a small amount of the short-staple, or greenseed cotton, was grown anywhere in the South. The longfibre cotton alone could be raised with profit in this country. This could be produced only on the sea islands along the shores of Georgia and South Carolina. Short-staple cotton could be raised in practically every section of the South, but separating the seeds from the lint or fibre took so long that there had been little or no profit to be made from it. 

The cotton gin with its revolving toothed cylinders could now get the seeds out easily and rapidly. With it one man could clean as much cotton in a day as could a hundred or more slaves working by hand.

Cotton raising becomes popular. The Southerners were turning eagerly to cotton raising at this time because of the sudden demand for more cotton. This demand came chiefly from England, where a series of inventions had transformed the whole process of spinning and weaving and had taken the business of making cloth from the home into great and growing factories. This change came at a time of decline in profits from rice, indigo, and tobacco in the older regions of the South.

Do you see, then, how the events in England and the work of Whitney combined to spread the raising of cotton over great areas in the South? If cotton could now be raised with any profit on the much-used soils of the older states of the South, how much more money could be made on the fresh, rich lands of western Georgia, of Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, and Texas. The recognition of these facts put other streams of emigrants on the roads leading toward the West. Many of the migrating planters took their slaves and a complete outfit of farming implements and household goods with them.

Advance of the plantation system. As the plantation system, with its cotton raising and its slaves, advanced into the interior of the South, many of the pioneers who

had settled there gave way before it. Some of these old settlers bought a few slaves and began raising cotton themselves. Many others sold out to the newcomers and moved on across the Mississippi, but in most cases they drifted back into the hilly country away from the richer lowlands. 

A BACK-BREAKING JOB. Churning day in the old farm home brought plenty of hard work to the housewife. This woman has finished the actual churning. She now has the fresh butter in a large wooden bowl and is working the moisture out of the butter and, probably, salt into it. There ought to be some good buttermilk somewhere about!

These people never owned slaves. They outnumbered the slave holders in the new regions which were being settled. 

On the rough hilly lands to which they moved, small farms were the rule. Crops of corn and small grains were raised. 

In parts of this region some cotton was produced. Remoteness from markets and the lack of a cash crop held back the development of these sections of the South. The log-cabin

FROM OLD EASTERN HOMES TO NEW IN WEST 273 

homes of these settlers were much like those to be found in the new settlements farther to the north. 

At least two important results came from this new southern interest in cotton raising: (1) practically all the influential people in the South were bound together, either directly or indirectly, in one common interest-cotton; (2) slavery, which had seemed to be dying out, now took on fresh life as the demand for cheap workers in the cotton fields increased.

2. State the reasons for the increased demand for cotton.

3. THE JOURNEY WESTWARD 

How the journey was made. The people who started on the western journey in those days had, first, a long hard journey in a wagon, unless they were willing, as some were, to go on foot or on horseback. Those from New England usually followed roads which crossed the state of New York. Farther south, roads were to be found that led across 

Pennsylvania toward Pittsburgh on the Ohio River. There was the old Forbes Road, and, coming up from the southeast, Braddock's Road. Still farther south the westwardmoving emigrants often moved along the route Boone had laid out through Cumberland Gap. Many of the planters with their slaves kept to the southward of the Appalachian ridges and in time developed passable roads across Georgia to the fresh cotton lands they were looking for. 

On the journey the poorer homeseeker often had a cow tied to the rear of his wagon, and crates containing geese and chickens dangling beneath the wagon rack. Those who were fairly well off sometimes had herds of cattle driven along behind the wagons. Camping out at night by the side of the road was one of the excitements of the journey. There were few taverns, or "stopping places," along the way.

Often these few were so dirty and ill-managed that selfrespecting people preferred to sleep on the ground by their campfires. 

The planter, of course, moved west in better style. Slaves drove the teams drawing his long train of wagons. They set up tents, cooked the meals, and made the long journey as comfortable as possible for the master and mistress. Often

the planters sent their force of field hands on ships around to some port on the Gulf of Mexico, or to some point on the Mississippi near to the new plantation. In most cases lands were cleared and the new plantation buildings erected by the servants long before the owner and his family reached the new home.

How the frontier passed on. The West was rapidly transformed by this flood of newcomers. The little clearings gave place to well-tilled farms. Towns and villages grew up as if by magic. Schoolhouses, churches, courthouses, even a

New, strong states entered the Union. By 1820 Kentucky, Tennessee, Ohio, Louisiana, Indiana, Alabama, Illinois, and Mississippi had all been granted statehood. The real frontier had passed on to Michigan and Wisconsin on the north, and to Missouri, Arkansas, and Iowa beyond the

4. MAKING NEW HOMES ON THE FRONTIER 

Much of the land to which the settlers went in the new West was heavily timbered. The timber provided the settlers with materials for the log-cabin homes. A new home was built of logs hewn smooth on the inside with an axe. 

When the timbers were ready the neighbors came to the "raising," and the walls of the house were laid up in a day or two. This house was built sufficiently high to make room for a loft where the family slept. At first there were no sawmills, and accordingly the lumber used was sawed out by hand with a saw called a whipsaw. An axe with a broad blade, called a broadaxe, was used in hewing out heavy. timbers and planks. On each side of the house openings were cut and covered with greased paper for windows. 

It was necessary to clear away the timber before crops could be raised. The trees were felled by the axemen and then cut into convenient lengths so that they could be piled and burned. Little stump-dotted clearings soon appeared around the cabins. Here the first crops were planted, usually corn and vegetables. There was plenty of meat, for the woods were full of deer and other wild game, but other food was scarce at times during the early years. Even Indian corn was fifty cents a bushel, which was a high price 1

when the settlers had little money and scarcely anything which they could sell for money. 

The settlers were obliged to produce nearly everything

Whenever a letter or a paper came to these people, it, too, must find its way by river and trail to its destination. 

There was not much chance for the children of the early settlers to go to school. A description of the school which 

Abraham Lincoln attended when he was a boy will perhaps help you to appreciate the splendid opportunities you have today. A school was located a few miles from the Lincoln home. It was a low log building of the same general style as the log cabins of the settlers. Split logs roughly hewn and set with flat side up on legs served as seats for the few pupils. The greased paper windows admitted only a little light and made it necessary to leave the door open. A crude fireplace partly heated the schoolroom.

Young Lincoln attended school for a few weeks when he was about ten years of age. He had neither slate nor pencil, paper nor pen. He learned to read the words in the first part of Webster's Elementary Spelling Book. Again, when he was fourteen years old, he attended school for a time. Conditions in his neighborhood were now getting better. He was provided with a pencil and a limited supply of paper. 

He learned to write and "cipher." Lincoln liked to study.

At home he read everything that came his way. He practiced "doing sums" in arithmetic on the wooden fire shovel. When the shovel was filled with figures, he shaved it off clean with a knife, and it was ready for a new set of figures.

The teachers were engaged for very short terms, for the settlers could spare little money to pay them. The teacher "boarded 'round" with the parents of the children, the

length of his stay in a family depending upon the number of children attending school.

CHAPTER XV  

You have learned how the country west of the Appalachian ridges was settled. You know how the early emigrants reached their new homes and what experiences awaited them there. But better means of travel were needed if the old East and the new West were to be firmly bound together in trade and in a common political life. Here you are to learn how men, east and west, turned to this problem of linking together the sections of our country. 

1. FLATBOATS AND STEAMBOATS 

As you have read about the rush of settlers to the West you have noticed how many of them used flatboats and other craft to go down the rivers on their way to their new homes. But it is necessary to understand, also, what an important part the river boats played after the settlers had built their homes and cleared their farms. 

Down the Mississippi on a flatboat. After a few years the farmers in the southern parts of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois, and in Kentucky were raising so much produce on their farms that they could not use all of it themselves. They wanted to send flour and bacon and hogs and cattle to 279

market. But where was there a market which they could reach? It would cost too much to send the things they had to sell back over the mountains to the East. The only other outlet was down the rivers to New Orleans. Great numbers of flatboats soon appeared on the western streams. THE "CLERMONT." This is supposed to be an exact replica of 

Fulton's famous vessel.

They were loaded with the products of the western farms and mills and were guided downward with the current toward New Orleans. Hundreds of strong young fellows made much of their living conducting the flatboats safely to the southern markets.

In the early years of this trade much of the produce brought down on the flatboats was reshipped to the West

Indies and to other outside markets. Later on the plantation owners near the lower Mississippi bought the larger share of it. 

Robert Fulton's steamboat. Robert Fulton's "Clermont" (klēr'mônt) proved the usefulness of the steamboat in 

1807 on the Hudson River. Within a few years steamboats were being used along our coasts and on many of our rivers. They were especially useful on the Mississippi and its branches. The fastest of them could make the run from St. Louis to New Orleans in six days, and back up against the current in fourteen days. They could take settlers up rivers to places which had been considered too far away to make attractive farms. Merchandise was now brought up the rivers, and stores were opened up. Heavy articles, such as gristmill stones, were now brought to the western millers by steamboat from New Orleans. As a writer put it in the flowery and exaggerated style of that time, "A steamboat coming from New Orleans brings to the remotest villages of our streams and to the very doors of the cabins, a little of Paris, a section of Broadway, or a slice of Philadelphia."

Growth of western towns. Many enterprising men in 

Cincinnati went into the business of building river steamboats. It was quickly learned that the deep, narrow hulls of ocean craft were out of place on the western streams. 

The river boats were constructed with flat bottoms to permit them to skim over shallow places in safety. Cincinnati called herself the "Queen City of the West." Beef and pork began to be packed in large quantities at both Cincinnati and Louisville. Cincinnati acquired the nickname, "Porkopolis." Pittsburgh, so long the "Gateway of the West," took on fresh distinction for its manufacture of iron products. Iron foundries, steam-engine shops, and nail factories were established there.

The steamboat was soon navigating the waters of the

Great Lakes, carrying emigrants to the shores of Lake Erie, Lake Huron, and Lake Michigan. Thus, a whole generation after settlers had taken up lands along the river banks, the shores of the Great Lakes began receiving those who were to settle the regions of the Northwest. Cleveland was soon a thriving lake port. Detroit, Chicago, Milwaukee-mere military posts or fur-trading stations up to this timebegan suddenly to thrive and grow. 

1. What important new use was found for the flatboats on the western rivers? 

2. Why was the steamboat so important to the new West? 

2. TURNPIKES AND CANALS 

Road building. In a great country like ours the need of improved means of communication and travel have always been important. We have seen the difficulties encountered by the pioneers in their rush westward across the mountains. Settlements clung closely to streams and lakes so long as means of easy travel were confined to waterways, but our people early turned their attention to building better roads. Large sums of money were spent for road building, and before the War of 1812 New England, New York, and Pennsylvania were fairly well supplied with turnpikes, as the better roads were called. At intervals along these turnpikes were toll gates or toll bridges where fees were collected from those making use of the roads. As these turnpikes were usually firm, hard roads, people were glad to pay to travel on them.

Along the turnpikes rolled stagecoaches carrying mail and passengers, and heavy wagons hauling freight. Between 

New York and Philadelphia five lines of stages ran daily coaches. One could travel by coach from Boston to New 

York in two days. Five days carried the traveler from Boston to Washington, part of the way being by boat. The

fare was thirty dollars. By coach and steamboat one could travel from New York to Quebec, Canada, in eight days at a cost of forty-seven dollars. A day's journey began at three o'clock in the morning and continued until nightfall. 

Horses were changed at stations along the way. 

The Cumberland Road. 

Soon after people began moving into the West in large numbers, as we have described, there came a demand for a 'turnpike leading to the Ohio country. Accordingly a route was selected and the work begun. The first section of the road ran from Fort Cumberland on the Potomac River to

across the state of New York from the Hudson River to Lake Erie. Congress considered for some time the matter of building such a canal. Some leaders, however, came to think that the national government had no right to build roads and canals since the Constitution said nothing about any such right. They argued that such internal improvements should be made by the states at their own expense. 

This idea finally prevailed. Even the Cumberland Road, which had been built by the United States Government,

was turned over before its completion to the states through which it passed. 

The Erie Canal. The state of New York, under the leadership of the enterprising Governor De Witt Clinton, took up the matter of canal building on its own account. 

Courtesy City Art Commission and Board of Education, New York City WHEN THE ERIE CANAL WAS COMPLETED. As a part of the celebration over the completion of the canal, water was brought from Lake Erie and emptied into New York Harbor. Here we see Governor De Witt Clinton carrying out the ceremony. 

The canal was built from Albany on the Hudson to Buffalo on Lake Erie, following the Mohawk River part of the way and making use of the small streams and the lakes of central New York. The canal was three hundred sixty-two miles long and cost about twenty thousand dollars a mile. 

Great celebrations were held at the opening of "Clinton's

Big Ditch." A fleet of canal boats proceeded from Buffalo to Albany and down the Hudson to New York City. This triumphal procession was greeted all along the way with the music of bands and the thunder of cannon. One of the boats carried two kegs of water from Lake Erie which were poured into New York Bay in a ceremony which was declared to be the wedding of the inland waters to those of the ocean. The picture on page 288 is an artist's idea of this scene.

The opening of this canal was indeed a great event.2 The products of the West which had access to the Great Lakes now found an easy and cheap means of transportation to the cities of the East. Hundreds of boats engaged in this trade carrying grain, flour, lumber, furs, and peltry from the West to Atlantic markets and machinery, tools, furniture, and merchandise of all kinds from the East to the people of the West.

The canal packets were soon loaded with passengers. 

These packets were rather interesting boats. They were seventy-five or eighty feet long and ten or twelve feet wide. 

On their low decks they carried long low cabins which were used as sitting rooms and dining rooms in the daytime and as bedrooms at night. Such a cabin was rigged up somewhat like our Pullman coaches of today. In fine weather the passengers would sit on the cabin roof and enjoy the sunshine and the scenery. The boat was drawn along the canal by a team of three horses hitched one before the other and driven along the towpath.

Other canals. In the country near the Great Lakes the people improved the streams and connected the natural waterways by means of canals. A canal was built from 

Cleveland on Lake Erie to Portsmouth on the Ohio River.

This canal followed the course of rivers for a good portion 2 The cost of transporting a ton of freight from Buffalo to New York City was reduced from one hundred dollars to five dollars as a result of the completion of the Erie Canal.

of the way. If you will look at the map on this page, you will see a few such canals that were built during this time.³ 

Many less important canals were built about the same time. 

The western farmer and the businessman were greatly helped by these improvements. Prices of farm products were much higher. Flour and grain doubled in price. At the same time, the farmer could get the things he needed for his own use from the eastern cities at much lower prices.

ROADS AND CANALS 

The pinched, hard times of frontier days were rapidly passing in these parts of the West. 

Travel and transportation by canal was cheap but slow. 

Canals could not be built in mountainous districts. They must follow river valleys and natural waterways. In winter canals could not be used at all. The Erie Canal, for example, freezes over for about five months of the year.

3. THE FIRST RAILROADS 

Philadelphia seeks more western trade.

A RACE BETWEEN STEAM AND HORSEFLESH. This famous race took place in 1830 between the steam locomotive, "Tom Thumb," and a horse-drawn vehicle. The horse won-but only because the engine broke down. The locomotive later proved its usefulness. drawing as it did this western trade to the city of New York, made that city almost at once the leading port of the United States, a position which it has held from that time to the present day. This threatened the prosperity of its rival city, Philadelphia. The enterprising citizens of the latter city were not willing to sit idly by and see the rich prize of western trade pass away from them. They set to work to connect Philadelphia with the West. A series of canals was

built following the course of the Susquehanna (sus-kwéhăn'a) River and its western tributaries to the mountains.

WHEN STEAM RAILWAYS WERE LESS THAN TEN YEARS OLD. Do you think that stagecoach construction influenced the builders of the early railway coaches? burgh. This railroad was a primitive affair. The rails were long wooden stringers with strap iron nailed on the upper side to strengthen and protect the rail. The cars were tiny, low affairs more like a pair of low trucks than anything else you perhaps can think of. This connection with the waters of the Ohio enabled Philadelphia to hold a good trade with the West. 

Baltimore's railroad. The merchants of Baltimore had connected that city with the Cumberland Road by a num-

ber of good turnpikes and had enjoyed a profitable trade with the West. With the completion of the Erie Canal and the canals in Pennsylvania, the cities of New York and Philadelphia bid fair to absorb much of Baltimore's western trade. Consequently the Baltimore merchants turned to the railroad, believing that as the canal had surpassed the wagon road as a means of transportation, so the railroad would surpass the canal. They began the building of a railroad westward from Baltimore and named it the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. By 1830 they had thirteen miles of track laid.

There was also a short railway in New York and one of 137 miles in South Carolina. All of them had been built for the use of horse-drawn coaches. George Stephenson of 

England had in the meantime exhibited a successful locomotive, the "Rocket." Soon a locomotive, the "De Witt 

Clinton," was in use on the New York railroad, the "Best

Friend" on the South Carolina line, and the "Tom Thumb" on the Baltimore and Ohio road. The latter ran the entire length of the railroad-thirteen miles—in an hour. The success of railroads was assured. By 1840 there were about three thousand miles, and by 1850 nearly ten thousand miles of railroad in the United States. 

The importance of these improvements in transportation can scarcely be overemphasized. They brought prosperity and growth for both East and West. The eastern cities began to displace New Orleans as the market for western products. The West was linked to the East.

CHAPTER XVI  

Great political and social changes were taking place in our country one hundred years ago. In the rapid developments of this stirring period the rising West played an important part. The older communities east of the mountains also responded to the spirit of change. A new era was dawning. What new problems arose? What men came forward to furnish the leadership in the attempt to solve them? This chapter answers these questions. 

1. HOW SAMUEL SLATER STARTED THE FACTORY SYSTEM IN AMERICA 

In Chapter XV the eagerness of business men in our eastern cities to link the East with the West was dealt with. 

Why were they so eager? This chapter furnishes an important part of the answer to that question. The East had new manufactured products it wanted to sell to the West. 

Samuel Slater was a boy who spent his early years in a little village in England. Near his home were great cotton and silk mills in which he worked and learned all about 295

spinning and weaving. The hum of mill machinery was music to his ears, and although only a boy, he suggested changes which were made to improve the machinery. 

Beginnings of cotton manufacture. When a young man, Samuel Slater heard of the wonderful opportunities in 

America, and he decided to go there. Not long after he landed in New York his skill and knowledge as to spinning and weaving became known to Moses Brown, a wealthy man of Providence, Rhode Island. Young Slater was invited to go to that place, where, in 1789, he set up, with Moses Brown's help, the first factory in America for the spinning of cotton yarn. You now have another reason for remembering this important date, for 1789 was also the year when George Washington became our first president. 

Slater had to make all his machinery from memory, for the laws of England would not allow anyone to take out of that country drawings of the machines used there. At first only spinning was done in the mills, the weaving being done in the New England farm homes with hand looms. Soon, however, the power loom was invented, and the manufacture of cotton cloth was established as an important industry.¹ 

Other manufactures. During those same years beginnings were likewise made in the factory production of many other things. America was eagerly following along the way English industry had already taken. Woolen cloth, leather goods, tools, machinery, and carriages were among the first articles to be made in factories in this country. Alexander 

Hamilton, who was Secretary of the Treasury in Washington's cabinet, made a report on the manufactures of the country. As we read this report today, we are surprised at the amount of goods made. Still, only a small part of our total manufacturing was done in factories, the larger portion being carried on in the households. 

1 A certain kind of cotton cloth which brought forty-two cents a yard in 1815 sold for seven and a half cents in 1830.

Factories developed very slowly. In 1804, fifteen years after Samuel Slater set up his first mill, there were only four cotton mills in America. This may well surprise you, for you might expect, with the abundance of water power furnished by the swift streams of New England and with the rapid growth of cotton cultivation in the South, that 

AT THE SPINNING WHEEL. This posed photograph shows the common use of the spinning wheel in the home before cloth was made by machinery. cotton manufacturing would grow very rapidly. Imported goods, however, could be bought more cheaply than such goods could be made in this country. Skilled labor was scarce here. Few people wanted to work in factories; they preferred to go into the West and take up land. The mills of England and Holland had been established a long time, and manufacturing processes in those countries were greatly improved. All these conditions enabled the Europeans to

manufacture goods more cheaply than they could be made in America. So it was that our people continued to import a very large portion of their manufactured goods for many years after Samuel Slater set the spindles whirring and the looms clacking in New England. 

William Thompson

MCCORMICK'S FIRST REAPING MACHINE. This machine cut the grain but did not bind it into bundles. Notice that the horses pushed the machine, instead of pulling it.

Samuel Slater has been called "The Father of American 

Manufacturing." In many ways he deserved the title. However, causes and circumstances with which this enterprising man had little to do were in the end largely responsible for the growth of manufacturing in this country. 

Our manufacturers aided by trouble with Europe. During the period from 1807 until the close of the War of 1812, our trade with the countries of Europe was almost wholly cut off. As our people could not buy things abroad, they were obliged to make them at home. In 1808, Samuel Slater

and his brother built a large cotton mill at Blackstone, Massachusetts. Other mills were soon built at Lowell, Fall 

River, and Lawrence, Massachusetts. Mills for the manufacture of woolen cloth, boots and shoes, hats, machinery, and hardware sprang up in many other places. In 1808 there were eight thousand cotton spindles in this country; in 1815 there were fifty thousand. In 1800 people of the 

South sold to manufacturers five hundred bales of cotton; in 1815 ninety thousand bales were sold. Growth in other lines was nearly as rapid. 

Protection for our manufactures. When peace returned in 

1815, trade with the countries of Europe was resumed. 

England had accumulated large quantities of goods during the war. Her merchants, after the return of peace, began shipping these goods to America in large quantities at low prices. Our manufacturers at once complained. They could not meet the prices of English goods. It cost more to make a yard of cotton cloth in America than it did in England, where labor was cheap and capital plentiful. To protect our manufacturers, Congress in 1816 passed a law which required cotton and woolen goods coming into this country to pay twenty-five per cent of their value in the form of a duty at the port of entry. Duties were also placed on carriages, leather goods, and several other kinds of articles. A little later a duty was placed on iron manufactures. You can readily see, can you not, how this would raise the price on imports and enable the American manufacturer to sell his products at a better price? A schedule of duties such as we have described is called a tariff. Until about 1830, this policy of using the tariff to protect our "infant industries," as they were called, was continued. During this period manufacturing grew rapidly.

A story is told of a visit paid Samuel Slater, then an old man, by President Andrew Jackson. "I understand," said the president, "that you have taught us how to spin so as

to rival Great Britain and that it is you who have set all of these thousands of spindles at work, which I have been delighted to see, and which are making so many people happy by giving them employment." "Yes sir," said Mr. 

Slater, "I suppose that I gave out the Psalm, and they have been singing the tune ever since."

We see, then, important changes growing out of the War of 1812. Until the period of this war our country was largely a land of farmers and merchants, with New England as the commercial section. But during this period, as we have seen, our trade with other countries was destroyed and our people took up the manufacture of the various things needed.

2. NEW NATIONAL LEADERS 

During the early years of the history of our country, as most of the people lived east of the Allegheny Mountains, our government was in the hands of men from the old states of the Atlantic seaboard. Down to 1828, all of our presidents came from the eastern states. Washington, Jefferson, Madison, and Monroe came from Virginia, while John' Adams and John Quincy Adams were from Massachusetts. 

With the settlement and development of the West, about which we have been reading for some time, it naturally came about that western men took a larger and larger part in managing the affairs of our government. Many of the matters in which our people were interested were questions which concerned the welfare of the West. 

Henry Clay. The West first spoke with the voice of Henry 

Clay, the great Kentuckian. In 1812, Clay, representing the 

West, asked for the destruction of British influence around

the Great Lakes and even for the conquest of Canada. Clay stood for all things western and things which would benefit that section. He became a great force in Congress. He was a leader of the House of Representatives. He was called "Harry of the West" and seemed to express the very spirit of that section. He was a bold, impulsive, high-spirited man, and he threw himself with great enthusiasm into whatever cause appealed to him. 

The American System. 

In the paragraphs, "Protection for our manufactures," page 299, you remember reading how, in 1816, a tariff was placed on goods which were brought into this country. Henry Clay was the author of this tariff system. He called it the "American System" since it had for its purpose the building up of American

Courtesy U. S. National Museum ELIAS HOWE'S FIRST SEWING MA- 

CHINE. The sewing machine was one of the most useful inventions of the nineteenth century. industries. He said that the building up of great manufacturing industries in the East should be encouraged, as thereby a "home market" would be created for western products. By home market Clay meant a market here in our own country for the wool, cotton, grain, and other products raised by American farmers.

Thus the West and the manufacturing interests of the Northeast supported the tariff. In 1824 a new tariff bill was passed which increased the rates on woolen and cotton goods, iron manufactures, and hemp.

At first the cotton-raising South thought that the tariff

might benefit that section as it would build up cotton manufacturing in this country, and thus supply a home market for cotton. It was soon discovered, however, that the price of cotton did not rise. Instead, as the tariff was made higher, and as the amount produced constantly increased, the price fell. On the other hand, the prices of cheap grades of cotton cloth, while still low, were raised by the tariff. The plantation owner used a great deal of this grade of cotton cloth for clothing for his slaves and for bagging for cotton bales. It was about the only "store bought" apparel the non-slaveholding masses could afford. The people of the South became dissatisfied with a tariff that increased their cost of living.

John C. Calhoun. As the West had its leader, Henry Clay, the champion of the tariff laws, so the South found, in John C. Calhoun, a leader in its opposition to these laws. Calhoun was of Scotch-Irish ancestry, descendant of sturdy, Indian-fighting frontiersmen. Friendly to the tariff in 1816, he became its bitterest opponent when he saw its failure to benefit his section of the country. 

John Quincy Adams. New England had its leader in John

Quincy Adams, who was Secretary of State during President Monroe's administration from 1817 to 1825. John 

Quincy Adams was a son of John Adams, who was president from 1797 to 1801. He had spent a great part of his life in the public service. He had lived many years abroad and had studied the problems of government in many lands. 

He had been called "the Puritan in politics." He was a cold, distant man, perfectly honest and an untiring worker. He made few warm personal friends.

There was only one political party at this time. The 

Federalist Party had made itself very unpopular by passing laws which the people did not like (p. 243). This party also opposed the War of 1812, and some of its leaders were concerned with the Hartford Convention (p. 260). Accord-

ingly, the party lost favor with the people, and we hear little of it after 1816. Nearly all American public men called themselves Republicans. This period has been called "The Era of Good Feeling." However, as we have seen, differences of opinion on important matters, such as the tariff, soon came about. 

John Marshall. While we are thinking about who the leaders of our people were in the time just after the 

War of 1812, we must not fail to give some thought to John Marshall. To be sure, he was not seeking votes in Congress for a favorite measure, nor was he campaigning to get votes for himself or others for some public office. But he was an important leader, nevertheless. Friendly, funloving John Marshall had been appointed chief justice of the Supreme Court by President John Adams. No one appeared to see any great importance in that court in the days when Marshall accepted his new position. But in Marshall's time questions came before the court which had to do with the nature of our government itself. Under Marshall's leadership the court met these questions squarely in a series of great decisions written, generally, by the chief justice. Every one of these decisions made the Constitution more important and added to the power of our national government in its dealings with individuals and with the states. 

17-18)

JOHN MARSHALL. The most famous chief justice of the Supreme Court.

In reading this chapter you have noticed that immediately after the War of 1812 the leaders, and the people

generally, felt proud of their country and were ready to do anything to make it grow and prosper. But when they got to thinking about whether the new laws and the new plans would help their particular state or section of the country, they often found their enthusiasm cooling. We have already noticed in John C. Calhoun an example of this. 

Daniel Webster, a northern leader, also changed some of his views at this time. When he saw that the new tariff laws were helping his section he was in favor of them, and of other plans to increase the power of the national government. To leaders like Calhoun and Webster and to thousands of others the welfare of the particular section of the country in which they lived appeared to be more important than anything else.

Now you can see the importance of the work of John Marshall. At the very time when the bonds intended to hold our people in a strong union seemed to be loosening, John Marshall and the Supreme Court were explaining our Constitution and attempting to make it clear that under it the Union was meant to be strong, permanent, and supreme over the people and over the states. 

Andrew Jackson. As the time approached for the election to choose someone to succeed Monroe as president in 1824, each section put forward its leading man as a candidate for the office. John Quincy Adams represented New England and favored the tariff. He believed in a strong central government. Henry Clay represented the West and favored the tariff and internal improvements at the expense of the national government. Calhoun was suggested as the candidate of the South. At the same time the friends of Andrew

Jackson began to urge his candidacy. The "Old Hero"was very popular throughout the West and South. He was a 

Westerner and a man of the common people. He had won the Battle of New Orleans at the close of the War of 1812; he had conquered the Indians of Florida and Alabama. The

West loved a fighting man. Also they said it was time the country had a president from west of the Allegheny Mountains. They were tired, they said, of aristocratic gentlemen from the old states and wanted a man of their own kind. 

People were enthusiastic about "Old Hickory," as

General Jackson was called. "Old Hickory" clubs were formed to aid his election. 

Members of these clubs wore silk vests with the picture of 

General Jackson stamped on them. 

Neither Clay nor Adams could secure many votes in the South because they both favored the tariff. Jackson's views on the tariff were unknown. William H. Crawford, of Georgia, the Secretary of War, was favored for the presidency by President 

Monroe and by many members of Congress. 

 ANDREW JACKSON. The famous 

Democratic president toward the end of his long career as pioneer, soldier, and statesman. 

Election of 1824. In the election Jackson received more votes than any other candidate but not a majority, and hence no one was elected. In such a case it was provided by the Constitution that the House of Representatives should elect the president from the three candidates receiving the highest votes. Since Jackson had received ninetynine votes, Adams eighty-four votes, Crawford forty-one, and Clay only thirty-seven votes, the House of Representatives could not vote for Clay. But as Speaker of the House, he had a great deal of influence in determining how the members of that body voted. He did not like Jackson and

thought him unfit for the presidency. He, therefore, threw his influence to Adams, who was elected. 

Election of Jackson, 1828. The friends of Jackson were very angry over the election of Adams. They said that 

Jackson had been unfairly beaten out of the presidency, that a "corrupt bargain" had been made between Adams and Clay by which Adams promised to appoint Clay Secretary of State in return for his aid in the election. This story was false, but many, including Jackson himself, believed it. 

It hurt both Clay and Adams very much. The Jackson men went immediately to work to secure the success of their candidate in the next election. So well was their work done and so popular was "Old Hickory" that Adams was easily defeated in 1828, and Jackson was proclaimed the people's president. And indeed the election of Jackson was an important political event. It meant the entrance of the young and vigorous West into a larger share in the government. 

Most of the Westerners were democratic in their views and felt sure that their hero, Jackson, would make great changes in the government. They were fond of thinking of themselves as the "Jacksonian Democracy." The "Jacksonian 

Democracy" asserted that the people were able to govern themselves and that education and training were not necessary to officeholding.

3. PRESIDENT ANDREW JACKSON 

The people's president in office. The inauguration of 

President Jackson was the occasion for a great celebration among his supporters from all parts of the country, and especially from the West. They came to Washington in

large numbers to see him take the high office of president of the United States. They packed the streets around the stand where General Jackson stood to take the oath of office, pledging himself to enforce the laws of the country and to uphold the Constitution. 

After the formal ceremonies of the inauguration were over, the friends of President Jackson conducted him to the president's residence, the White House. The crowd went cheering and shouting along the way. In their enthusiasm for their president, they invaded the White House itself, and men with muddy boots stood in the plush chairs in the best rooms of the president's mansion and drank their hero's health in the choicest wines the White House could provide. It was a gala day in Washington, and as you may well believe, a somewhat shocking one to the people of that city accustomed to the more formal ceremonies which had before this time inaugurated the scholarly men of the 

East into this high office.

The administration of Andrew Jackson has been called the "reign of Andrew Jackson" because he carried things with a high hand. He was a hot-tempered man and would not allow anyone to interfere with his purposes if he knew it. He was usually engaged in bitter quarrels with some of his opponents. Like most men of his temperament, he was both well hated and well loved.

Andrew Jackson grew up in the newer sections of South Carolina and Tennessee and received very little schooling. 

He had a high sense of duty and was personally honest, but he did not understand well the problems of government, and he was frequently misled by politicians who took advantage of his lack of experience in politics and often played on his high temper. Throughout his administration, he was surrounded by a group of personal friends known as the “kitchen cabinet," who did a great deal of the work of the presidency in Jackson's name.

The "spoils system." Jackson and his friends felt that those who had helped their party to win the election should be rewarded for their services. "To the victor belongs the spoils," a New York political leader, William Marcy, had exclaimed. The new leaders in the government gave these words real meaning when they said that the positions as clerks in the departments at Washington, as postmasters throughout the country, and as consuls and ministers in foreign countries should all be filled by Jackson men and that their opponents should be turned out of office to give them places. This idea, which has been followed more or less from that day to this, is known as the "spoils system." 

More tariff troubles. While Jackson was president, the trouble over the tariff came to a head. The South under the leadership of John C. Calhoun of South Carolina came more and more bitterly to oppose the tariff, the rates of which had been increased. They said the tariff was a means whereby the northern manufacturer took money out of the pockets of the southern planter. Southerners now held that the Constitution did not give Congress the right to lay duties for the purpose of protecting manufacturers; they said that since such duties were so unfair and worked such hardships on the South, they would disregard these laws in their states; that is, they would "nullify" all such laws. 

This doctrine of nullification, if put into practice, would change the nature of the Union. It would mean that our 

National Government would have slight power over the states, and in the end this might mean that the Union would be destroyed.

Daniel Webster. In 1830 this question of states' rights was debated in Congress by Daniel Webster of Massachusetts and Robert Y. Hayne of South Carolina. Webster made a great speech for the permanence of the Union in which he used the celebrated words, "Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable." Hayne argued that

the Union was only a compact among sovereign states from which any one of them might lawfully withdraw whenever it thought that the national government was violating the compact.

Nullification. In 1832 South Carolina brought matters to a climax by declaring the recent tariff law "null and void" and not binding upon the citizens of that state. South Carolina counted upon the well-known friendship of the president

The 1940 population is only an estimate. for the South. But President Jackson was opposed to the idea of nullification. He declared that the United States is a nation, not a league of free states. He met the crisis firmly and patriotically. In such a crisis as this Jackson was at his best. He sent notice to the South Carolina leaders that the laws of the United States would be enforced. He said, "My duty is emphatically pronounced in the Constitution. Those who told you that you might prevent the execution of the laws deceived you." He immediately prepared the army and the navy to enforce the laws in South Carolina. It seemed as if war would surely result. It was averted by 

Henry Clay, who introduced a new tariff measure which reduced the rates. South Carolina repealed her nullification ordinance against the tariff and further trouble was averted.

Democrats and Whigs. The struggle between the Jackson men and the Adams men for the presidency divided the Republican Party into two factions. Those who supported 

Jackson came to be called Democrats and those who opposed Jackson were called Whigs.

Jackson served two terms as president from 1829 to 1837. He was succeeded by Martin Van Buren, who was also elected by the Democrats. He carried out Jackson's policies.

The bank question. One of the big questions upon which the Whigs and Democrats differed was the question of the United States Bank which, as we have noticed, was first established by Alexander Hamilton in Washington's administration. President Jackson did not believe in this bank. 

He made many charges against it, one of which was that it oppressed the people by making them pay too high interest rates when they borrowed from it. Jackson also felt sure it was meddling in politics-and of course, as he saw it, on the wrong side of important questions. Jackson determined to destroy the "monster," as he called the bank, and a majority of the people supported him. The United 

States government deposited its money in this bank. Jackson removed the money, placing it in a number of state banks throughout the country, chiefly in the West. This was a serious blow to the United States Bank and was the chief cause of its failure.

Years of panic and business depression. During this period, as we have read, the West was being settled rapidly. 

The time was one of great business activity. Many people were making money and all others hoped to do so. Men were eager to build steamboats and own steamboat lines and buy lands and build towns. It took money to do these things, and such speculators borrowed wherever they could. 

They went to the banks which were well supplied with the government money deposited by Jackson. There borrowing

was easy, and too many speculative schemes were entered into. Many of these investments did not pay, and the banks could not get their money back. This situation put pressure on the banks which, in turn, tried to collect from others to whom money had been lent. Thus many speculators were forced to sell out whatever project they were engaged in and pay back to the banks whatever they could. Business grew dull. The banks were unable to collect many of the debts owed them. They failed. Not enough money could be secured to carry on business. Men were thrown out of work. Hard times in all lines resulted. These financial difficulties are known in our history as the "Panic of 1837."

2. What is meant by the spoils system? 

3. What were the opinions held by the Whigs? The Demo crats?

4. NEW CITIZENS IN A NEW SOCIETY 

Out of the many changes in the new ways of doing things and out of the great political episodes of the days of Clay and Jackson came new ideas about how people should conduct their lives, both as individuals and as members of society. Only a few can be mentioned here. In the first place, the new western states we have mentioned considered that a white man twenty-one years of age was entitled to vote and hold office. You will recall that most of the older states, even long after the Revolutionary War, clung to laws that barred the average poor man from the suffrage. When people began pouring into these liberal western states in numbers alarming to many Easterners, what idea do you suppose would occur to the leaders in the old states? Why, change their old, strict laws so that the discontented poor man would feel that he, too, was an important member of the commonwealth. That is exactly what was done; within

a few years white manhood suffrage became almost as general east of the mountains as west of them. 

It was at this time, also, that Americans turned their thoughts less and less often to Europe and its affairs, and gave their time and attention almost wholly to their own

Life in the factory towns. The new and growing factory towns which you read of in Chapter XVI, pages 298-299, also made our people think about some things they never had had to consider before. Was the owner of the factory responsible for the health of his workers or for their behavior outside working hours? Should small children be allowed to

go into the mills just because their parents were willing that they should? And if so, for how many hours a day?

Debtors. One old abuse, that of imprisonment for debt, was still allowed. What would we think today if people who owed a few dollars were thrown into jail on their failure promptly to pay their small debts? A hundred years ago thousands of people were lying in our jails awaiting the time when friends or relatives would come forward to take.

care of the debts and release them. As soon as poor men began to have the right to vote they speedily saw to it that this terrible old system was changed. At the same time these new voters began to interest themselves in making jails and prisons more sanitary, and in seeing to it that counties and states began maintaining asylums for the in-

sane. Dorothea L. Dix was a leader in this movement for prison reform and for more humane treatment of the insane.

Education. Just at this time, too, people, spurred on by leaders like Horace Mann and 

Henry Barnard, began to see that in our democratic communities it was as important for the children of the poor as for those of the rich to have some education.

Those views led to the starting of a system of free schools in the state of New York. Other eastern states followed this example. Here again the states east of the mountains were imitating the new western states where free schools had been encouraged from the first. 

About this same time there was agitation for more and better opportunities for women to get an education. The first seminary for girls was opened in 1821 at Troy, New York. The founder of this school was Emma Willard. The demand for an opportunity to secure an education was part of a general movement to secure additional rights for

women.2 Susan B. Anthony was a leader in this fight for women's rights. The women declared "that all men and women were created equal." In 1839 the state of Mississippi, and a little later, Texas and Indiana gave women the right to control their own property. In 1848 a convention was held in which it was demanded that women be given the right to vote.

American writers. During this period great American writers appeared for the first time. We have noticed how, following the War of 1812, our people gained confidence and self-reliance. This same spirit is shown in the field of literature. These writers wrote about American things. 

Washington Irving pictured America as a land of interest and beauty. In the "Leatherstocking Tales" James Fenimore Cooper used pioneer scenes and characters. 

The poetry of John Greenleaf Whittier and Henry W. 

Longfellow is rich in American themes.

The novels of 

Nathaniel Hawthorne describe Puritan New England. 

Many of the writings of Oliver Wendell Holmes and the essays of Ralph Waldo Emerson deal with American subjects. William Gilmore Simms, of South Carolina, wrote many novels dealing with southern life. Edgar Allan Poe and William Cullen Bryant, poets, belong to this period in American literature. Poe and Hawthorne were instrumental in developing the modern short story as a literary form. 

Many of our best known historians did their work at this time. In 1834 George Bancroft began publishing his great work on early American history. Francis Parkman wrote of the French in North America and William H. 

Prescott of the Spanish in Mexico and South America.

The interest of the reading public extended to newspapers and magazines. The New York Tribune, published by

UNIT VI NATIONAL EXPANSION AND ITS PROBLEMS In Chapters XVII, XVIII, and XIX our book tells the interesting story of the rapid expansion of our nation, southward to the Gulf of Mexico and westward to the Pacific Ocean. Within a period of forty years, between 1810 and 

1850, a series of events occurred which added to the United 

States, Florida, Texas, the Oregon Country, the far Southwest, and California.

Adventurous Americans led the way into the new lands. 

The quest for beaver pelts urged some of these pioneers forward. With others it was the need for fresh cotton lands, the desire for gold, or the longing for more freedom. Following the early trail blazers toward the west came those who laid the foundations for permanent settlements in the western territory. Never before had Americans pressed forward more eagerly toward the wilderness. Never before had our people seemed so sure of the great destiny of their country. 

The speed with which the nation expanded and grew strong is shown by the fact that men and women who had been born during the first years of the weak new nation were still active at the end of this period. 319
