CHAPTER XXI GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN THE NORTH AND THE SOUTH 

The war between the Union and the Southern Confederacy was a great and tragic event in our national history. On its outcome depended the whole future of our country. The story of the war is one of courage, steadfastness, and self-sacrifice. But it is a difficult story to understand. You will not be asked, in this chapter, to study the minor details of this struggle. Instead, you will be given the opportunity, as the chapter title suggests, to catch "glimpses" of some of its most memorable events. 

1. PEACE OR WAR? 

Why the southern states seceded. Chapter XX concluded by showing how the election of Abraham Lincoln as president, in November, 1860, was the signal for a number of southern states to leave the Union. Why did they do this? Alexander Stephens, a Georgian, said, "I will have 390

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 391 

equality for Georgia... in this Union, or I will look for new safeguards elsewhere." He went on to say that he believed those safeguards could still be found in the Union. 

Most southern leaders agreed with Howell Cobb and

Robert Toombs, who believed that the chances for the southern states to have "equality and safety in the Union are at an end." To these leaders the election of Lincoln appeared as the climax of a long course of events threatening the rights of their section. They believed their states had a right to secede, and they felt that the time to do so had come.

Shortly after his election Lincoln wrote a letter to 

Stephens. "Do the people of the South," he asked in that letter, "really entertain fears that a Republican administration would interfere with the slaves, or with them about the slaves? If they do, I wish to assure you, as once a friend, and still I hope not an enemy, that there is no cause for such fears. The South would be in no more danger in this respect than it was in the days of Washington." 

We can see from the quotations above the wide difference in the opinions of northern and southern leaders. In preceding chapters you have read of the many occasions for disputes between the leaders of the two sections over slavery and other questions and of the bitterness and misunderstandings which resulted. You will recall that on more than one occasion a state or a section of the country had threatened to withdraw from the Union when the people felt that their interests were being sacrificed. This happened in New England during the War of 1812 and in South Carolina over the tariff question in 1832. On such occasions those concerned made the claim that the government under the Constitution was merely a "compact" between the states and that a dissatisfied member could withdraw when it considered the compact violated. Others believed that "the Union is one and inseparable," to use

the words of Daniel Webster. This was an old question dating back to the organization of our government. 

Southern leaders saw in the election of Lincoln the triumph of a party, drawing its strength from the North, which was opposed to the extension of slavery. They felt sure that the new sectional party would not stop at merely 

 ABRAHAM LINCOLN. This is one of the best known and best loved pictures of President Abraham Lincoln. 

restricting slavery, but would go on with plans to abolish it entirely. Indeed, many people in the South thought of all Republicans as abolitionists. 

There was a widespread feeling in the South that the interests of that section were threatened by the result of the election of 1860. For this reason many southern leaders at once took steps to have the states in which they lived withdraw from the Union. 

Great numbers of people, in the South as well as in the 

North, felt that the division of our country into sections would be a great calamity.

They realized that there are no natural boundaries between the two sections. To them it was clear that we were really one people with a common history, a common language, and common ideals and institutions. Many leaders in the 

North, and some in the South, felt certain that separation would not remedy the difficulties facing the American people. If the nation broke up into sections, these men argued, many questions would remain to cause trouble. 

For example, who would then own the territories? Probably a majority of the northern leaders believed that the welfare

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 393 

of the American people depended on a united country, and that if necessary a war should be fought to keep the southern states in the Union.

Such were the beliefs of Abraham Lincoln. Those who agreed with him fought, during the first part of the war, to preserve the Union. As the war went on it became clear that if the Union cause won, slavery would cease to exist in all parts of the country.

The men of the South fought bravely for what they believed to be a just cause. They did not agree with the view that slavery injured their section, nor that a divided country would mean weakness and discord.

2. BEGINNING OF THE WAR 

The Confederacy formed. When Lincoln took office,

March 4, 1861, he found the nation in a perilous situation. 

Seven of the southern states had withdrawn (seceded) from the Union and a number of others stood ready to do so. 

The states already considering themselves out of the Union sent men to a convention in Montgomery, Alabama, to draw up a constitution. A government was organized which was known as the "Confederate States of America." The government at Washington did not recognize that any such government existed, nor did any foreign power. The Confederacy, however, exercised the powers of government in the southern states from 1861 to 1865 as best it could. It organized armies and a navy and directed the war against the Federal Government at Washington.

The constitution of the Confederacy was very much like that of the United States. But, unlike the National Con-

stitution, the constitution of the Confederacy forbade any laws against the holding of slaves and declared that there should be no protective tariffs. It provided for a term of six years for its president, but made this official ineligible for re-election. 

The capital of the Confederacy was for a short time at 

Montgomery, Alabama, but was soon removed to Richmond, Virginia.

Jefferson Davis. The Confed erate Congress elected Jefferson 

Davis of Mississippi president of the Confederate States of America.

He was inaugurated in the state capitol building at Montgomery.

Mr. Davis was an able and experienced statesman. Upon his graduation from West Point he had served for a time in the United States army and participated in the Mexican War. After retiring from the army he held many important positions in the national government. He represented his state in the United States Senate for a number of years and was a member of 

President Pierce's cabinet as Secretary of War. The president of the Confederacy was a man of high character and served both his state and his section with great ability. 

He was devoted to the cause of the Confederacy. 

L. C. Handywedd

JEFFERSON DAVIS. At the time this picture was taken he was president of the Confederate States. 

Lincoln's plea for peace. Throughout the North there was much hesitation and uncertainty in the months prior to Lincoln's inauguration. Southern leaders seized forts and arsenals located in their states. The men of the South were arming for the war which they expected to come. President

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 395 

Buchanan did little to prepare the North. Indeed, there were many northern men in those dark days who did not think the Union was worth fighting for. Horace Greeley, editor of the New York Tribune, expressed such sentiments when he wrote, "Let the erring sisters go in peace."

President Lincoln, too, wanted peace, but not at the price of a broken Union. In his inaugural address he pleaded for peace. To the southern people he said:

In your hands, my dissatisfied fellow countrymen, and not in mine, is the momentous issue of civil war. The government will not assail you. You can have no conflict without yourselves becoming the aggressors.... We are not enemies but friends. 

We must not be enemies. Though passion may have strained, it must not break the bonds of our affection. The mystic cords of memory, stretching from every battlefield and patriot's grave to every living heart and hearthstone all over this broad land, will yet swell the chorus of the Union when touched, as they surely will be, by the better angels of our natures. 

But peace was not to be. The national flag still waved over Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina.

The officials of the new Confederate Government determined that this place must be seized and the flag hauled down. Why should the flag of the United States fly over any part of South Carolina, which now considered itself a sovereign state outside the Union?

Fall of Fort Sumter. What to do about Fort Sumter was a difficult matter for both President Lincoln and President

Davis to decide. At one of the first cabinet meetings called by President Lincoln the matter was discussed. If the government sent more soldiers to help its commander, Major Anderson, hold the fort, then might it not appear that the Federal Government had made the first warlike move? But if the place were given up without an effort to hold it, would that not be admitting that the Confederacy was already, in fact, a separate nation and entitled to all

public property within its borders? President Lincoln finally decided it was time to send supplies, because the small garrison was almost without food. "We can wait, then," thought he, "and see what the southern leaders do about it."

The southern statesmen, sitting in their capital at 

Montgomery, Alabama, heard about the shipload of supplies. What was to be done? In spite of some good arguments by a few cool-headed men that the supplies should be allowed to land, the majority decided that the moment for action had come. A telegram flashed along the wires ordering General Beauregard (bō'rě-gärd) to open fire on the fort. In the early morning of April 12, 1861, a shell screamed out across the quiet waters of Charleston Harbor in the direction of Fort Sumter. War had begun. Thirty-six hours later Major Anderson surrendered the badly battered fort to the Confederacy. 

To arms! "You can have no conflict without yourselves becoming the aggressors," Lincoln had said to the men of the South. If you had been living in a northern state in the spring of 1861, would you have called the Southerners the "aggressors"? When Lincoln called for soldiers to help defend the Union from its enemies, after the fall of the fort, would you have felt the urge to go? That was the feeling that swept over the northern cities, towns, hamlets, and faraway wilderness communities. There was a wave of enthusiasm for war. Democrats forgot that they had voted against Lincoln only a few months before. Those who had before hesitated to oppose secession now had no doubts, since the flag of the Union had been fired upon. Flags fluttered out from one end of the northern states to the other, and to the beating of drums and the blare of bugles, men gathered in response to the president's call for troops. 

What about the men of the South? They saw in the fall of Sumter an act of defense against Lincoln's government,

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 397 

and a sign of the success of their cause. They, in response to their president's call, hurried forward to defend the Confederacy. Four more southern states whose leaders believed a state had a right to secede if its rights were violated now left the Union and joined the Confederacy rather than

Confederacy. They were North Carolina, Virginia, Arkansas, and Tennessee. The governor of North Carolina wrote this in reply to President Lincoln's call for volunteers: "I can be no party to this war upon the liberties of a free people. You can get no troops from North Carolina." Two interesting matters came up in connection with the secession of Virginia: first, the people of western Virginia favored

the Union and would not follow the majority of their fellow Virginians in secession. Union armies soon took control in the western counties of Virginia and enabled the people there to set up the separate state of West Virginia. Second, the secession of Virginia gave the Confederacy its finest general, Robert E. Lee. The picture on page 397 makes clear the esteem this Confederate general's soldiers had for him. Lee was a trained soldier and a loyal citizen, but he could not bear to think of serving in the armies of the Union against his beloved Virginia. Sadly he resigned his commission in the United States army and joined the soldiers of the Confederacy.

3. MAKING THE ARMIES 

Northern and Southern advantages. Leaders like President Lincoln and President Davis feared that the war would be long and bitter. But it was difficult for the masses of the people to realize, in 1861, that they were beginning a war which would continue for years and which would bring about so much suffering and cost so many lives. Twentytwo states remained loyal to the Union while but eleven joined the Confederacy. The population of the North was about four times as great as the white population of the Confederacy. In the North there was more property that could be taxed, more factories, better railways, a more stable government. But the Confederacy, also, had reasons to hope for success. In the southland there were many

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 399 

vigorous men, used to outdoor life, to firearms, and to matters connected with warfare. Many of the leaders were trained soldiers, even the Confederate president himself being a graduate of West Point. Then, too, if the Union was to be saved, the northern armies would be obliged to march into the South and defeat the southern armies on their own soil. Some of the military experts of Europe who came here to observe the progress of the war thought the 

South would not be beaten.

Enlisting for the war. In both North and South, from the 

Atlantic to the western plains, preparations for the war went on. Everywhere men-most of them young fellows between the ages of eighteen and twenty-five-hurried to the places where they could enlist, and from there by train¹ to camps where they were formed into companies and regiments and brigades. These recruits were given long practice marches and drilled by the officers to "present arms" and "right-shoulder-shift arms" at the word of command. 

Let us take the national capital, Washington, as an example, and see in our imagination what was going on in the way of building an army. 

We are struck, first of all, with the sight of throngs of young men who have volunteered to be soldiers in the armies of the Union. There are young farmer lads, "lumberjacks" from the north woods, clerks from the stores, sailors, mechanics, schoolmasters. One regiment of a thousand men, the first to arrive, has its quarters in the Senate Chamber at the capitol. The others make their homes in rude wooden camps, in barracks, or in tents. There are streets of tents and cities of tents-about Washington the hills and valleys are dotted with them. Everywhere men are in squads,

marching, drilling. Officers on horseback dash about on their many duties.

In the South, even before the war began, thousands of spirited young men formed themselves into companies and assembled military equipment.

On to Richmond! The Confederates had removed their capital from Montgomery, Alabama, to Richmond, Virginia, about one hundred miles south of Washington, on the James River. As northern congressmen and editors, and others not in the armies, watched the thousands of Union soldiers drilling day by day in and near the national capital, they became impatient to have these forces make an attack

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 401 

on the Confederacy. They did not know how long it takes to make an army. They set up the cry: "On to Richmond! 

On to Richmond!" President Lincoln and his generals gave in to the popular clamor, and in July, 1861, General Irvin

McDowell led thirty thousand soldiers across the Potomac River into Virginia. There were Confederate soldiers a few miles farther south on the road to Richmond, under General 

Pierre G. T. Beauregard, and still others farther west under 

General Joseph E. Johnston. General McDowell was supposed to beat these Confederates in battle and march on to the capture of Richmond. Thus on those hot July days the young soldiers from the North and those from the Souththe "Yanks" and the "Johnnies" as they came to call each other-were coming closer to each other, closer to the time when they would be ordered to spread out in long lines of battle, with shells from the cannon screaming overhead, and would be sent forward to shoot and bayonet one another in this the first hard battle of the war. Let us see how one of 

McDowell's "Yanks" or one of Stonewall Jackson's "Johnnies" looked as he trudged along in the heat and dust to fight his first battle.

The "boy in blue" of McDowell's army wore a dark blue coat and light blue trousers, coarse, ill-fitting shoes, and either a wide-brimmed hat with braid around it or a small cap with shiny leather visor. Over his shoulder as he marched was his musket, very long and heavy, slow in action but a good weapon. The bayonet for his musket hung at the soldier's side. It could be quickly fastened to the muzzle of the musket when the order to "fix bayonets" came. It was going to be used oftener as a handy tool around camp than as a weapon. The "Yank" carried a heavy load on his back-seventy-five pounds when in "full marching order." There was his blanket, and sometimes a piece of canvas so contrived as to make a sleeping tent for two men when it was fitted to another piece carried by another

soldier. Then there was his haversack containing rations for perhaps two or three days, his knapsack which held his personal belongings, and his leather-covered canteen.

1924-1963 

The "boy in gray" from the southland often had no uniform at all, although gray and butternut-brown were the most common colors in his apparel. But mixed with the regiments in gray were units from parts of the South in brightcolored uniforms. The gun carried by this soldier was quite likely to be one he had brought from home, not quite so good as the one his opponent carried, but he knew better how to use it. His outfit depended, perhaps, on the whim of his colonel or that of the governor of his state. In summer he slept under the stars far oftener than in a tent. 

His officers rode their own horses and wore the things they thought distinguished the soldier. Some of the regiments of the southern army in the later years of the war appeared in their nondescript outfits little like the well disciplined soldiers they really were. It sometimes seemed that the less like soldiers the men were clothed the better they fought.

Four years of war. It would be impossible for this book to tell you, or for you to learn here, the details of the terrible conflict that followed. Great armies-sometimes composed of as many as one hundred thousand men-were raised and equipped, and marched through the mud or dust to fight each other in battles which sometimes lasted two or three days. As the poor soldiers fell in battle or were captured or died of wounds or disease, fresh recruits were found to fill their places. When the men no longer came forward to volunteer for service they were "drafted" into the armies by their governments. Never, in all the wars that men have waged against one another, was greater courage shown than by the soldiers who fought in this war between the North and the South. We shall try to give you a few vivid "sidelights" on the conflict. 

1. Tell all you can about the forming and equipping of the northern and southern armies. 

2. What was the meaning of the northern cry, "On to Richmond!" and what battle came as a result of it? 

4. THE BLOCKADE 

Northern warships before southern ports. As you have learned, southern people raised great quantities of cotton to be sold abroad. The South bought from the North and from England and other countries a part of its food supply and practically all of the manufactured goods used. To cut off these supplies the Union government, very early in the war, decided to blockade southern ports. At the beginning of the conflict, the fleet was small, but ships of many kinds were purchased and hurried into the service. These war vessels patrolled southern coasts and seized incoming and outgoing ships. A fortune awaited the ship captain bold enough to carry a cargo of cotton past the blockade to an English port where it was in great demand. Likewise there were big profits for the shipowner who brought a cargo of

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 405 

rifles and ammunition or other needed supplies into a southern port. "Running the blockade" soon became a favorite venture of bold Southerners as well as of the venturesome ship captains of other countries. At first it was not difficult to slip past the Union vessels and land a rich cargo. But as the war went on the blockade became tighter, and the attempt to take a ship either into or out of a harbor in the South became a highly risky enterprise. Many an exciting race between the ships of the blockading squadrons and the swift blockade runners occurred.

It was often the practice of the commanders on board the blockade runners to load their ships with goods at some port in the West Indies or in the Bahama Islands. The cargoes usually consisted of supplies badly needed in the South. The ships would approach the coast of South Carolina or of Georgia or some other southern state just as darkness was setting in. If there was a thick fog, so much the better. Silently the blockade runners would glide in until their captains had learned the locations of the blockading vessels. Then there would be an order for "full steam ahead" and the runners would dash for safety under the guns of some southern fort while the northern gunners on the blockading ships were doing their best to sink the fastspeeding cargo ships. If good luck attended the blockade runners, a fortune awaited their owners at the end of their exciting run. If their ships were captured or sunk, that meant the total loss of the investment in the cargo and the vessels.

To make the blockade more effective the Union fleet attacked and captured most of the southern ports during the war. Admiral David Farragut, a native of Tennessee, won for himself a name in history by his capture of New Orleans in 1862 and, toward the end of the war, by his fight with the Confederate fleet at Mobile Bay.

The "Monitor" and the "Virginia." For a short time in the spring of 1862 it seemed that the northern blockade of southern coasts might be broken up. Although the South was woefully lacking in machine shops, mechanics, materials, and shipyards, some of her ingenious men contrived an ironclad ship which for a short time threatened to drive the Union vessels from the seas. The Confederates rebuilt the hull of the frigate "Merrimac," which had fallen into their hands, covered its sloping sides with sheets of iron, and renamed it the "Virginia." Suddenly one day this strange, ugly looking ship, without masts or sails, steamed into Hampton Roads, on the Virginia coast. Five proud ships of the Union navy lying at anchor there opened fire. 

Their heaviest shot bounded off the sides of the ironclad like hailstones. Without heeding the storm of shot which rained upon her, the "Virginia" headed straight for the frigate "Cumberland" and, driving her iron beak through the hull of the wooden ship, sent her to the bottom. She then turned on the "Congress" and destroyed her. The crews of the other vessels, to escape their assailant, ran their ships aground. The "Virginia" then withdrew, expecting to return and complete her work of destruction the next day.

This event filled the North with consternation as the news spread. It was expected that the ironclad would steam up the Potomac and shell Washington. 

But the "Virginia's" triumph was short-lived. When she returned the next day to attack the remainder of the Union fleet, what was her surprise to find awaiting her another ironclad, but of different type, the "Monitor," which had arrived during the night from New York. The "Monitor" was not more than one-fourth the size of the "Virginia.”

She was a low-lying vessel with her decks only slightly above the water. Her guns were mounted in a revolving steel turret on the deck. She had greater speed than the

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 

407 "Virginia." At once the combat began. Shot after shot was exchanged, but with little harm to either. In both cases the armor was superior to the gunfire. When the "Virginia" tried to ram her smaller opponent, being herself rather slow and unwieldy, the "Monitor" slipped away, receiving only a glancing blow which did no damage. After four hours of hard, close fighting, neither ship being able to injure the other seriously, the conflict came to an end. The "Virginia" could not go on with her work of destruction while the "Monitor" was there to protect the wooden vessels of the Union fleet. The 

Union navy was saved by the heroic fight of the little "Monitor." Its inventor, John Ericsson, had served his country well. 

Neither the "Virginia" nor the "Monitor" was a seaworthy ship. The "Virginia" was dismantled shortly after the battle to

However, this first use of armored ships showed that the days of the "oak-ribbed and white-winged" navies were over. This battle proved that these stately old ships must give way to steam power and steel hulls, and pointed the way for the construction of the future navies of the world.

5. FIGHTING FOR THE MISSISSIPPI 

Where the land battles were fought. Where were the great land battles of the war fought? If you think about this a moment you will see that the northern and southern armies would be likely to meet and fight along the border between the states which had seceded and the loyal states. 

You can easily name five or six states that would be likely battlegrounds. You will also remember that the northern armies were obliged to go into the South and defeat the armies there if they were to crush the Confederacy. From this you will conclude that there were more battles in the seceded states than in the Union states. 

Notice that the line separating the South from the North crosses the Appalachian Mountains. There was, then, a region east of the mountains where much fighting took place, and another larger area west of them where the armies also struggled with each other. Historians writing about the War between the North and the South often use the terms, "war in the East" and "war in the West."

You now understand what they mean. Let us talk about the war in the West first-keeping in mind all the time that there was fighting going on in both the East and the West throughout the war. 

Fighting in the West. You will remember that three of the 

Confederate states lay west of the Mississippi River. There was also Missouri, a slave state, which did not leave the Union but which furnished thousands of soldiers to the southern armies. The Mississippi is wide and its great valley was hard to cross in those days. If the Union armies could get control of that valley they would have the states to the west of the river cut off from the rest of the Con-

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 409 

federacy. The Confederates saw this and built forts along the river to hold possession. They built fleets of gunboats with which to patrol the river and strung great chains across the stream to prevent northern armies from advancing southward into Confederate territory. A great share of the fighting in the West had to do with this matter of seizing, or holding, the Mississippi River.

The first two years of the war in the West turned out favorably for the forces of the North. The armies fought great battles at Shiloh (shi'lō), and at Murfreesboro (mûr’frêz-bûr-ð), both in Tennessee; and scores of smaller battles and skirmishes. The northern armies did not always win, but they pushed the southern soldiers out of a great part of Kentucky and Tennessee. On the Mississippi and the other streams, the men of the northern navy, Farragut, Porter, Foote, and others, had taken all of the important Confederate forts with the exception of two- Vicksburg and Port Hudson. Study the map, page 412, and locate the battlefields mentioned, the captured forts, and the great stronghold, Vicksburg, still in the hands of the Southerners.

The strength of Vicksburg. Ulysses S. Grant was the 

Union leader in much of this western fighting. He was a graduate of West Point and had served in the Mexican War. As a Union commander he soon showed his ability. 

He would not give up when faced with discouragement and defeat. When men criticized him and wanted him removed from command, Abraham Lincoln said, "I can't spare this man. He fights.' 

It was this quiet, stubborn man who now planned to capture Vicksburg and free the Mississippi from the control of the Southerners. This was a hard task. Vicksburg was situated on a high bluff overlooking the river. Many cannons were mounted here, and an army of brave men was stationed in and around the city prepared to defend it.

The broad river and great swamps to the north and west were natural defenses. Grant's first attempts to take the city failed. But the commander and his soldiers kept stubbornly at their task, and after many months they drew near to the city and at last laid siege to it. 

The capture of Vicksburg. Soon the soldiers defending

Vicksburg, and the people who lived there as well, had a harder enemy to fight than even Grant's men. This was famine. The place held out for six weeks. 

Then the southern commander, Pemberton, surrendered to Grant, and his thirty thousand men marched out as prisoners. 

A few days later Port Hudson also surrendered.

The Mississippi now flowed "unvexed to the sea," as Lincoln said. The

6. GETTYSBURG 

Failures of the Union armies in the East. Although the 

Union armies seemed to be winning the war in the West, in the East it seemed that they were losing it. You have read about the fight at Bull Run and how it ended the first effort of the North to send an army across Virginia to

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 411 

capture Richmond. After that failure larger armies were raised and given months of training. But these splendid bodies of men, under such generals as McClellan and 

Burnside and Hooker, were unable to take the Confederate capital. Always the Confederate army, under its able general, Robert E. Lee, baffled them and turned them back. 

In the late summer of 1862 Lee was even able to invade the North, but was forced to retreat again into Virginia. 

The most brilliant of Lee's aids, "Stonewall" Jackson, was killed in one of the last and most famous of Confederate victories, Chancellorsville. By this time, the midsummer of 

1863, northern and eastern Virginia, marched over and fought over by hundreds of thousands of men, was almost devastated, with farms ruined, buildings burned, and railroads destroyed. Thousands upon thousands of fine young men, soldiers in blue and soldiers in gray, lay buried on the battlefields where they had fallen.

Lee's plans. After their many victories, General Lee and his army of veterans felt bold and confident. Lee knew how much greater the resources of the North were than those of the South. He knew what the blockade was doing to the South. He felt that if the Confederacy was to win the war it must win quickly. He saw the desolation in 

Virginia and thought about the rich farms and the populous towns and the fine factories of the North which had scarcely felt the blighting effects of the war. He determined again to lead his splendid army there, gather supplies, win a great victory if possible, march on some important northern city, threaten the capture of Washington, and win a peace that would give the Confederacy its independence. 

Lee's soldiers march north. The Confederate army hurried northward, crossed the Potomac into Maryland, and marched on into Pennsylvania. "Jeb" Stuart led the dashing southern cavalry. Herds of beef cattle were gathered in; clothing and shoes for the soldiers were taken and paid

for in the paper money of the Confederacy. At the village of Gettysburg some advance units of the northern army, which was moving up from the direction of Washington, met a part of the army of Lee. In the streets of the village there was hard fighting, the Union men being badly beaten.

For three days the struggle of the two great armies which met at Gettysburg went on. On the afternoon of the third day General Lee sent a body of his finest soldiers under

General Pickett straight across the open space between the two armies to attack the center of the Union forces. A colonel in the northern army gives us this description of 

Pickett's men as they swept forward: "Every eye could see his legions, an overwhelming resistless tide of an ocean of armed men sweeping upon us. More than half a mile their front extends; more than a thousand yards the dull gray masses deploy, man touching man, rank pressing rank, line supporting line. The red battle flags wave; their horsemen gallop up and down. The arms of 18,000 men, barrel and bayonet, gleam in the sun, a sloping forest of steel. All was orderly and still upon our crest. The click of the locks as each man raised the hammer to feel with his fingers that the cap was on the nipple, the sharp jar as a musket touched a stone upon the wall when thrust in aiming over it, were the only sounds that could be heard." 

The high tide of the Confederacy. The Union batteries opened fire, and then the infantry, but Pickett's men came on. They charged right up to the Union line and for a moment it seemed that they might pierce it. But at last they were driven back to the shelter of Lee's main army. The 

Battle of Gettysburg was over. General Lee had needed a victory if he was to go on with his invasion of the North; but a victory had been denied him. In a few days the Confederate army retreated into Virginia. 

This day, July 3, 1863, was the day before the one on which Vicksburg fell. The news of these two great victories

filled the North with rejoicing, though also with grief for the many brave men who had fallen. 

This date marks a turning point in the war. Before this battle the Confederate cause was at its high tide; from this time on its strength slowly ebbed.

7. WAR-TIME GOVERNMENT What about the President, Abraham Lincoln, during the dark and terrible days of the war? No man in the North suffered more than he and none carried so heavy and sad a burden. Lincoln was a tender-hearted man, and he felt great sympathy for the sorrow and suffering that the war brought upon both North and South. Many are the stories told of his kindly words and acts-in one case a letter of consolation to a mother whose son had fallen in battle, in another a reprieve to a soldier condemned for some breach of military discipline.

The officials of the government at Washington had many difficult problems to meet. From the outset many people in the North urged the president to use his power to free the slaves. These people did everything they could to force President Lincoln to adopt this policy. But the president was a wise and patient man who could see that the important matter was to save the Union. There were Union men who thought it unwise to free the slaves, and their help was needed to win the war. Many supporters of the cause of the Union in Kentucky and Maryland owned slaves. Lincoln wanted to keep these border states in the Union.

Freeing the slaves. As the war dragged on, however, it became clear that the slaves were a source of military strength to the South. For the most part they remained on

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 415 

the plantations and farms and raised the crops which fed the southern armies. Many negroes were employed in building forts and in doing other work in the Confederate camps. Finally, therefore, the president decided to declare free the slaves in those states that were at war against the Union. He believed he had a right as commander-in-chief 

 SIGNING THE EMANCIPATION PROCLAMATION. This famous painting by 

Carpenter shows Abraham Lincoln and the members of his cabinet at the moment when Lincoln issued the famous Proclamation. of the army to free the slaves as a military measure. This purpose he thought could be effected by a proclamation. 

In the fall of 1862 such a proclamation was issued to go into force January 1, 1863. This important document is known as the Emancipation Proclamation. As fast as northern armies conquered southern territory, the slaves held there were to be free. The proclamation led to the thirteenth amendment to the Constitution and the freeing of nearly four million slaves.

Great Britain and the war. Another matter which caused the national government much anxiety was that the

British government plainly sympathized with the South. 

The southern plantation owners were more like the English aristocracy than any other class in America. England needed southern cotton and did not like the blockade. 

Open sympathy for the South was shown in the "Trent" affair in 1861. It happened that two Confederate agents who were on their way to England and France, seeking to get those countries to recognize the South as an independent nation, were taken off the British ship "Trent" by a Union sea captain. The seizure was illegal, and Lincoln and Secretary of State William H. Seward promptly released the men. England's protest, however, was sharp, and she accompanied her demands with preparation for war. 

The British government did not prevent warships being built in English shipyards and turned over to the South to be used as commerce destroyers. One of the most famous of these vessels was the "Alabama," which destroyed many of the northern trading ships.

For the most part the working people of England sympathized with the northern states even though the loss of cotton shut down mills and left them without work. When 

Lincoln issued his Emancipation Proclamation many more Englishmen were won over to the cause of the Union, for England had come to oppose slavery and had done much to abolish it in many parts of the world. 

Criticism of the Federal Government. In the North there were people who held to the belief that the war to save the Union was wrong and was bound to fail. As the struggle dragged on and the loss of life mounted higher and higher, the number of these critics increased and it became easier for them to find sympathetic listeners. Organizations were formed seemingly for the purpose of discouraging enlistments in the northern armies and to interfere in other ways with the military plans of the Union. 

In war time even a liberal government must use harsh,

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 417 

stern measures to meet emergencies. The Union authorities were forced to put in prison many people who were charged with hampering the government. Some of these persons lay in prison for months without a trial. The government was charged with being "arbitrary," that is, From "Dixie," a Chronicle of America Photoplay-Yale University Press

BLANKETS FOR THEIR SOLDIERS. During the War between the North and the South, the women of the Confederacy did everything they could for their men at the front. This picture shows them cutting up their curtains in order to make blankets for the troops. unmindful of the civil rights of the people. Lincoln was called a "dictator." For a time it seemed likely that he would not even be renominated for a second term as president. But he was again named for the great office, and, in the presidential election of November, 1864, won over his Democratic opponent, General George B. McClellan. 

Difficulties of the Confederacy. The Confederacy, under its president, Jefferson Davis, was faced with many per-

plexing problems. The blockading fleets along the coast slowly shut off the South from the rest of the world. That section had put so much energy into raising cotton and tobacco for export that its people had come to depend on the North and on Europe for many of the necessaries of life. When the blockade cut these off, the people suffered extreme privation. The South not only had a great war to carry on, but also had to give attention to such questions as raising food for the army and for the people at home, and to developing factories for the manufacture of guns and ammunition, clothing, boots and shoes, and scores of other much-needed articles. 

As the northern armies pushed southward even such limited resources as the South possessed were destroyed or were lost to her. In time there were so few goods to be offered for sale in the South that even large stores did not find it worth while to keep open regularly. The people had to learn to go without many things and to use their ingenuity to invent substitutes. Salt became so scarce that it was sometimes used for money. Rye was sometimes used in making a pot of coffee, and raspberry leaves for brewing a cup of tea. People often found it necessary to wear wooden shoes. Such leather articles as old pocketbooks were cut up and made over into shoes for children. The southern people were brave and patient throughout the long struggle. 

Perhaps the picture on page 417 will still further illustrate the efforts of the southern people in the war. 

As the war began to go against the South, the paper money which had been issued by the Confederacy went down in value until it was almost worthless. Near the end of the war a good pair of shoes cost $150 in the Confederate paper money. Poverty and want spread to include all classes of people. The Confederate armies were being beaten by what lay behind them, in their homes and cities, as surely as they were being pressed back by the strong Union forces.

8. GRANT AND LEE-APPOMATTOX 

Grant commands the Union armies. One of the greatest causes for the failure of the Union forces during the first two or three years of the war had been the lack of cooperation among the various armies in the field. President Lincoln and Secretary of War Stanton often advised the Union generals in regard to military matters. At times they gave orders as to the conduct of campaigns. But campaigns could not be successfully directed from Washington, and oftener than not such orders and advice did more harm than good. Early in 1864 President Lincoln decided to place one general in command of all the armies. The choice for this high position fell upon General Grant, the hero of Vicksburg. Since the capture of that city he had further shown his ability. A Union army, after losing the great battle of Chickamauga (chik-ȧ-mô'gå), had been shut up in Chattanooga and besieged there by a strong Confederate army. Grant came to the relief of this army, now ably commanded by General George H. Thomas, with fresh forces and defeated the Confederates in the famous battles of 

Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge. 

General William T. Sherman was placed in command of the Union army which was stationed near Chattanooga, Tennessee. This army moved southward into northern 

Georgia to attack the Confederate army under General Joseph E. Johnston. After the Southern army had been driven back, General Hood took Johnston's place. The

Union army, greatly outnumbering Hood's forces, won a victory over the Confederates and captured the city of 

Atlanta. Sherman assembled his veterans and marched through Georgia "from Atlanta to the sea." As Sherman's men marched through the country they burned and de-

This was one of the best parts of the southland and had not been previously ravaged by the war. The destruction of the homes and property of citizens, leaving many families destitute, was harsh and ruthless and brought down severe criticism on the commanders of the Union armies who

planned the campaign and who ordered or allowed these acts. 

Grant and Lee in Virginia. All this time General Grant with a great army was hammering away at General Lee's veteran soldiers in Virginia. In the Battle of the Wilderness the northern army was checked, but, refusing to admit defeat, attempted to march around the Confederate army and move on toward Richmond. But General Lee, the master strategist, continued to block every maneuver of the Union commander. Grant could not defeat Lee in battle, but with his superior numbers he could wear him out. Though the northern armies lost more heavily in this campaign than the Confederate army, the North was able to supply more men while the South was nearly exhausted. 

Unable to reach Richmond from the north, General

Grant at last swung his army to the south and east and laid siege to Petersburg and Richmond. For many months 

General Lee defended these cities with his rapidly diminishing forces. The war was drawing to its weary end. Sherman's operations away to the southward, in Georgia and South Carolina, were destroying the dwindling resources of the South.

At last General Lee's hungry little army slipped out of the defenses of Richmond and hurried away to the westward in an effort to escape from the encircling Union armies. It was of no use. The twenty-five thousand men of 

Lee's once fine army were hemmed in with no chance to cut their way out. Lee sent word to Grant that he wished to surrender.

The end of the war. In a private home in Appomattox (ǎp-ô-mǎt'uks), Virginia, April 9, 1865, the two commanders met. It was a memorable scene: Lee, the conquered, resplendent in a new uniform with a jeweled sword at his side; Grant, the conqueror, in the wrinkled and none too clean uniform of a private soldier, with only the shoul-

der-straps of a lieutenant general to show his rank. This scene is pictured on page 420. Study the picture closely. 

While the terms of surrender were being discussed, the officers and common soldiers of the two armies were rapidly forgetting that for four years, and until that very morning,  THE WELL-LOVED GENERAL OF THE SOUTHERN CONFEDERACY. General 

Robert E. Lee is here shown mounted on his famous horse, Traveler. they had been doing their best to kill or capture each other on the battlefield. If the war was over, and the Confederates had lost, then the "Yank" and the "Johnnie" were, after all, citizens of a common country. Soon the former enemies were talking over their experiences as soldiers and sharing the contents of canteen and haversack. Grant sent to Lee's hungry men twenty-five thousand of the Union rations.

GLIMPSES OF THE WAR BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH 423 

General Lee was pleased with the generous terms given him and his defeated army. They were merely asked to agree not to fight again in the war. The Southerners were to take their private belongings, especially their horses, home with them. The horses, Grant said, would be needed for the spring plowing. Lee sadly said good-bye to his men, told them to be good citizens, and rode away toward his home.

Robert E. Lee. The great southern leader was not only a splendid general but a noble and gentle character as well. 

His fine qualities made such a lasting impression on those who knew him, and on those who have read the story of his life, that today, though he led the southern armies against the armies of the Union, he is a national idol. 

The other Confederate soldiers in the armies farther south soon surrendered. The war was over; the Union was saved; slavery was dead.

A wave of rejoicing swept over the North at the news from Appomattox. There were bonfires and illuminations; flags floated everywhere; the streets of northern towns and cities were filled with people who shouted, laughed, cheered, and wept, so great was their joy that the war was over. 

Also there were prayers of thanksgiving. As the poet,

Lowell, wrote: "There is something magnificent in having a country to love."

In the South, too, there was relief that the fighting was ended. The soldiers turned away from camp and battlefield to take up the tasks of peace. Sadly but bravely the southern people undertook the work of rebuilding a land devastated by four years of warfare. 

Death of Lincoln. But five days after Lee's surrender the rejoicing of the northern people was turned to grief by the assassination of President Lincoln. An actor, John Wilkes

Booth, who sympathized strongly with the South, shot 

Lincoln in a Washington theater, and the president died a

few hours later. The nation was plunged into deepest grief. 

The wise, kindly, sympathetic president was dead. Not only had the nation lost its president, but many citizens felt the loss of a personal friend, so near had Lincoln grown to the hearts of the people. The southern people also came to realize that in the death of Lincoln they had lost their best friend in the North.

UNIT VIII CHAPTERS IN PROGRESS 

With the close of the War between the North and the South, one chapter in the story of our country came to an end and another began. The spirit of change was everywhere. The Southland-without slaves but with millions of free colored people-had to build itself anew. In the 

North the blast of factory whistles grew louder, railway trains rumbled out along new lines, men in ever-increasing numbers plied axe and plow and pick and drill as they began a great assault on the wealth of the soil, the forest, and the mine. Men were making a new world, and they had to learn how to get on together in it. 

The story of this new world and its problems is an interesting one. It is told now in six "Chapters in Progress.' 

New ideas, new inventions, new ways of doing things soon made our country far different from what it was in the days of Andrew Jackson. New problems, often growing out of progress itself, faced our citizens. 427

Railroad Company at Birmingham, Alabama.

CHAPTER XXII  

The War between the North and the South settled difficulties which had long vexed the nation. But it created new problems, some of which have perplexed us from that day to this. Slavery was dead, but the negro still remained. The old plantation system disappeared. The mistakes and bitterness of the times are dealt with in the first section of this chapter. How the southern people built a new and better social and economic system is described in the second section. 

1. ONE NATION, ONE FLAG 

Reconstruction problems. Many grave questions faced the nation at the close of the war. The southern states must be restored to their places in the Union. Under what conditions should they be allowed to return? What should be 429

done with the men of the South, especially the leaders, who had been fighting against the Union? Should they be punished and, if so, how?

Some of the most serious questions concerned the negroes, who were now free but who did not have the rights of citizenship. What provisions should be made for their welfare? All such questions as these are usually referred to as "reconstruction" problems. 

Had President Lincoln lived he would have helped greatly, with his tact and sympathy, in solving these questions wisely and with justice. He had never admitted that the southern states had really left the Union. He had said that he wanted them to get back on the old footing with the rest of the country as soon as possible and with as little hardship to the southern people as possible. Before his death Lincoln had begun using a plan to restore the Union as it had been before 1860. He asked southern people to take an oath of loyalty to the Union, to set up loyal state governments, and to recognize the freedom of the former slaves. It was a mild and generous plan and was used with success in Louisiana, Tennessee, and Arkansas. In Lincoln's death the South, no less than the nation as a whole, lost a good friend and a wise leader. 

Thirteenth amendment, 1865. In what condition were the negroes during the months following the close of the war? The Emancipation Proclamation had freed some of them. To make this freedom lasting, and to free all other slaves in the whole country, and to do it in the most binding way, the thirteenth amendment to the Constitution was proposed and ratified, going into effect in December, 1865. It declared that slavery should not exist in any part of the United States. The people in the South, through their state governments, readily accepted the amendment. 

Freedmen's Bureau. The national government at Washington realized that the freedmen would probably be help-

less when thrown upon their own resources, as they had always depended on their masters for everything. So the 

Freedmen's Bureau was created by an act of Congress. 

Money was appropriated to help certain refugees, and especially the negroes, and men were appointed to distribute 

THE LOST CAUSE. The artist here pictures a Confederate soldier returning to his home at the end of the war. In what condition did he find his home? 

Do you imagine that the graves are those of southern soldiers? food and clothing to those in need. The Bureau attempted to regulate many phases of the life of negroes and refugee whites but was generally unsuccessful.

Black Codes. During the war the negroes for the most part had remained on the plantations except where the Union armies had occupied the country; but now that the war was over and they began to realize their freedom, many of them began to wander about depending on the Freedmen's Bureau for help. As might have been expected, "freedom" to many of these black men meant simply free-

dom from work. Idle and undirected negroes, when loitering about in crowds, became a nuisance and in some cases a menace in parts of the South. They would not work and in some instances resorted to thievery and other forms of lawlessness. To keep such persons within reasonable bounds and to induce them to work, several of the southern states passed laws known as the "Black Codes." These laws placed restrictions on the liberties of the negroes. Certain classes of negroes were required to make written contracts binding them to work, and if they left their employment they might be arrested and fined. Other unemployed negroes were arrested and fined as vagrants. Of course, they usually could not pay their fines. In such cases some white man needing labor paid the fine, and the court gave him the right to the negro's labor until the amount of the fine was earned. It was to the interest of the plantation owner to keep control of the negro whose labor he needed. Sometimes it took the colored man a long time to pay the court penalty, for he had also to earn the cost of food and clothing which the white man provided for him. Thus the effect of such laws or "Black Codes" in many cases was to return the freedman to the control of the white man. The Southerner said this was absolutely necessary if the plantations were to be tilled, since the negro was the chief labor supply in the southern states. He argued that it was of benefit to the negro himself as it was the only way to prevent him from becoming a tramp. He also believed that it was the best way to train the negro for the task of making his own living. 

Many leaders in the North, however, thought that such laws were returning the negro to a state of slavery and that steps should be taken to protect him. 

Andrew Johnson. Upon the death of Lincoln, Vice-President Andrew Johnson became president. He was a southern man but a stanch supporter of the Union. He was an honest man but was without tact and was very obstinate. Upon his

inauguration he immediately began making arrangements for the southern states to come back into the Union. He tried to follow Lincoln's plan which encouraged former Confederates to take the oath of loyalty to the United States and seek pardon for having taken part in the war against the Union. Many Southerners took advantage of the opportunity.

Attitude of Congress. When Congress met in December, 

1865, it disapproved of the arrangements made by President Johnson. In the first place, some of the members of that body held that the president had no right to arrange terms of reconstruction, that power belonging to Congress. 

Also they pointed to the Black Codes as evidence that greater security should be given the negro before giving to the southern states the complete management of their own affairs. Another thing that many Northerners did not like was that men who had lately been in arms against the government were not only pardoned for supporting the Confederacy but were now being elected to high offices in the southern state governments and even to seats in Congress. 

Some of the northern people felt that these men should be punished at least to the extent of being denied the right to vote and hold office.

Soon Congress, led in the Senate by Charles Sumner and in the House by Thaddeus Stevens, entered into a violent quarrel with the president over these matters which lasted to the end of Johnson's administration. In the course of the quarrel Congress passed laws which took from the president many of his usual powers. This clash between the president and Congress was very unfortunate, for the cooperation of all concerned was necessary if they were to meet successfully the many serious questions of the times. Many of the mistakes which were made might have been avoided except for this quarrel.

Fourteenth amendment rejected by southern states. One

of the first things done by Congress, in defiance of the president's wishes, was to propose the fourteenth amendment. 

This amendment provided that the negroes should become citizens of the United States. This provision would give them the right to hold property and assure them the protection of the United States courts so that no state could take their rights away. Many other rights as citizens would be secured. The amendment also attempted, in an indirect way, to secure the right to vote for the negro. It provided that if the right to vote was withheld from any portion of the inhabitants by any state, its number of representatives in Congress would be reduced in like proportion. It barred leaders of the Confederacy from holding office and declared that the debts of the Confederacy were never to be paid. 

This amendment was passed by Congress and was submitted to the states for their acceptance. It was rejected by all of the southern states except Tennessee. As it did not receive the necessary approval of three-fourths of the states, it failed of adoption. 

Leaders in Congress pointed to the rejection of the fourteenth amendment as an indication of the unwillingness of the southern states to give the negro his rights. They also argued that the southern leaders who had served in the Confederate armies and who were now resisting Congress should be punished in some way. There is no doubt that 

Congress also wanted to discredit President Johnson's plan. 

Reconstruction acts of Congress. Accordingly Congress adopted a plan of its own, very much more severe than that of the president. It passed acts in 1867 which took away the right to vote and to hold office from nearly all of those in the southern states who had taken a leading part in the war. At the same time the negro was given the right to vote. 

This was a revolution in the political conditions of the South. It took the reins of government out of the hands of those accustomed to manage such affairs and placed them

in the hands of those who only a few years before had been slaves. Most of the negro voters could neither read nor write. Many of them did not know their own names. In the city of Charleston, South Carolina, sixty-three Abraham 

Lincolns, forty-six George Washingtons, and more than thirty Andrew Jacksons registered as voters.

Of course the negroes by themselves were helpless, and accordingly the direction of affairs fell into the hands of certain white men, many of them unscrupulous, who saw here an opportunity to win high offices and advance themselves otherwise. Many of these men came from the northern states and were called "carpetbaggers" since it was said they carried all their belongings in a carpetbag. Some southern-born whites called "scalawags" joined the carpetbaggers and negroes in supporting the plan. Some of the 

Northerners who drifted into the South were worthy men who really desired to help the negroes to find their way to real freedom. Other leaders of the negroes were certain men of the South who had remained loyal to the Union and who were now brought into prominence. Both carpetbaggers and scalawags were thoroughly detested by the other whites of the South. One southern man was asked to tell what a scalawag was. "We mean by a scalawag," said he, "a meaner man than a carpetbagger." However, the carpetbaggers, scalawags, and negroes took charge of affairs in ten of the southern states and set up new state governments from which most of the southern whites who owned the property and paid the taxes were excluded. 

Fourteenth amendment passed, 1868. Then the fourteenth amendment was submitted to this body of new voters in the southern states and was, of course, accepted by them since it made permanent the rights which had already been granted them by act of Congress. 

The fifteenth amendment, 1869. The next year the fifteenth amendment was adopted. It said, "The right of

citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any state, on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." Thus was written into the highest law of the land the right of the negro to vote.

Many honest people in the North held that the negro needed the ballot to secure for himself the rights of citizenship, that without it he would be at the mercy of the southern white. Republican politicians in Congress saw in negro suffrage an advantage to their party. Most negroes have supported the Republican Party since that party gave them their freedom and the ballot. In recent years a considerable number have shown their independence by voting for candidates of other parties. When the government of the southern states was put in the hands of negroes and carpetbaggers, those states were placed in the control of the Republican Party. So far as this motive influenced 

Congress, its acts were unworthy. 

Many evil consequences followed in the wake of this policy of reconstruction.

Corrupt "carpetbag" government. The governments of the southern states were in incompetent and corrupt hands.

Money was wasted and stolen; nearly every form of extravagance and corruption ravaged the southern states, completing the ruin begun by the war. This condition lasted for a number of years. But the whites who had been deprived of their political rights would not put up with this state of affairs. They formed secret societies for the purposes of protection and revenge. The best known of these organizations was the Ku Klux Klan. Its members disguised themselves and rode through sections of the country terrorizing the carpetbaggers and negroes. Many northern whites were driven out. Negroes were whipped and frightened so that they did not dare to vote or hold office. 

Thus, by one means or another, sometimes violent, the

southern white men after some years regained control of the governments of the southern states. They thought this to be the only way to rid themselves of the evils put upon them by the policy of Congress in giving the negro the ballot.

You may wish to know the outcome of the quarrel between Congress and President Johnson. The struggle became so bitter that Congress finally impeached the president and tried to remove him from office. The attempt failed.

2. RISING FROM THE RUIN OF WAR 

"There was a South of slavery and secession-that South is dead. There is a South of union and freedom-that 

South, thank God, is living, breathing, growing every hour," said Henry W. Grady, a leading southern man, in 1886. 

When the war ended, our people, north and south, turned quickly from camps and battlefields to the activities of peace. A million men laid down their guns and sought their homes and the occupations that would give them a living. It was in the South that the problems of peace were almost as great as the problems of war had been. 

The ruin of war. The war had come very close to the southern people. It had called into service most of the ablebodied men; it had wrecked railroads and factories, ruined wagon roads, destroyed farm buildings, left towns and villages in smoking ruins. Weeds had taken the place of crops; the cattle in large areas had been driven off and butchered

by the armies. The poor people of the South found themselves in still greater poverty than before, while most of the well-to-do had been ruined. More than one fine lady or gentleman of the Old South now "kept the wolf from the door" only by the hardest kind of work. Turn back to the pictures, pages 417 and 431, and study them. They will help in giving an understanding of conditions in the South at the close of the war. There was no money and no credit, and the money lent to the Confederate government was never to be repaid. The carpetbag governments, as we have seen, piled up the debts of southern states and made taxes high. Plantations, which before the war had been worth $100,000, were now scarcely worth $10,000. Here is what one man says about the South as he saw it just after the war:

Window glass has given way to thin boards in railway coaches and in the cities. Furniture is marred and broken, and none has been replaced for years. . . . A complete set of crockery is never seen, and in very few houses is there enough to set the table... 

A set of forks with whole tines is a curiosity. Clocks and watches have nearly all stopped. . . . Hair brushes and tooth brushes have all worn out; combs are broken. . . . Pins, needles and thread. . . are very scarce. . . . Even candles, in some cases, have been replaced by a cup of grease in which a piece of cloth is plunged for a wick.¹

The people of the southern states had little left except their land. How to get crops planted and tended on these acres was a problem in itself. Southern landowners had grown accustomed to having negro slaves do all the plantation work. But now there were no slaves. Will the negroes work as free men and, if so, how shall they be paid? These questions troubled the "land-poor" southern white men.

Indeed, in 1865, the answer to the first question seemed to be "no." The negroes wandered about in droves, and 

1 From The Sequel of Appomattox by W. L. Fleming, Volume 32, "The 

Chronicles of America." Copyright Yale University Press.

waited for "gov'ment" to give them each "forty acres and a mule."

Breakup of the plantations. Plantation owners tried hiring the negroes for regular wages, but this did not work. 

Money coming at the end of the month or the end of the season would not keep the former slave busy in the cotton rows. Then the white men tried breaking up the plantations into small plots and leasing these to negroes or to poor white men. Many plans were tried. These varied from place to place and from time to time. Usually if the owner furnished the land, the seed, a mule, and the implements, he got half the crop. This plan worked better, and thus the days of the great southern plantation, with its mansion and its cluster of slave cabins, passed away, never to return. In time many of these small plots of ground were bought by the men who worked them. Cotton and tobacco still continued to be leading crops in this New South.2 But more corn, vegetables, and livestock were raised than in the old days before the war. New and better farming methods were gradually adopted in the South as well as in other sections. 

New ways to make money. But there were other ways than farming to make money in the southern states. These were neglected in the times of slavery, but received increasing attention after the war. There was plenty of water power in many of the southern rivers, and there was the cotton in southern fields. Eventually this led to great manufactures of cotton cloth, until in recent times more than half of the cotton cloth manufactured in the whole country is made south of Mason and Dixon's line. There were iron ore and timber in the South. The New South turned to these unused resources after the war. Today southern lumber and 

2 The South has gone on raising cotton in greater quantities than before the war. For example, over 2,000,000 five-hundred-pound bales were raised in 1850. But in 1880 the crop was over 8,000,000 bales, in 1925 over 

16,000,000 bales, and in 1937 over 18,000,000 bales.

southern steel and iron products are putting dollars in southern pockets. Even the southern climate is being "sold" today. Thousands upon thousands of people from all parts of the world spend their leisure in the brisk uplands of the South, or their winters in sunny Florida or along the Gulf Coast.

Better schools. The Old South failed to provide adequate free schools. The New South has planned schools for all children, both white and black. Both the common schools and the schools for higher education have made marvelous progress in recent years. There are some special schools for colored young men and women where they may get an industrial education, as well as schools for professional and cultural training. Booker T. Washington, who started the most famous of the industrial schools at Tuskegee, Alabama, believed that as the negroes became skilled in some useful work and capable of earning a good living, they would become more self-respecting and would win an increasing respect from their white neighbors.

2. Discuss the ways in which the New South of today differs from the Old South.

CHAPTER XXIII  

Not only did a new South develop after the War between the North and the South, as described in Chapter XXII, but a new North as well. In the present chapter you will learn how in New 

England and in the Middle Atlantic States the factory system of manufacture grew at an amazing rate, aided by protective tariffs and by a flood of immigrant labor. The use of machinery on the farm and the development of natural resources-soil, forest, and mine-transformed the Midwest from a pioneer section into rich and prosperous states. 

1. CHANGE AND GROWTH IN NEW ENGLAND AND THE MIDDLE STATES 

It is not the South alone that has seen changes since the war. Every section of our country, including the older states along the north Atlantic coast, has been transformed since then.

The New England factories. New England, as you read in an earlier chapter, was the first home of the modern 442

factory in our country.¹ This new system of gathering groups of workers in one place and having them turn out goods by the use of power machinery instead of with hand tools spread quickly to the near-by Middle Atlantic States. This entire northeastern section continued to put more and more of its money and energy into manufacturing down to the time of the War between the North and the South. Nearly every factory article that could be called American-made came from this part of the country.

WHAT FARM MACHINERY HAS DONE FOR THE GRAIN RAISERS. Notice the colonial hand tools. When the early machines came into use, how much was each farmer's "grain-raising ability" increased? What has the most modern machinery done for him? Try stating the facts of this chart in a written paragraph.

Factories increased by war. Did the war stop this development? No, it rather speeded it up. Northern soldiers needed almost everything in the way of equipment, uniforms, caps, shoes, guns, ammunition, tents, wagons, and a thousand other articles. The government bought lavishly and paid high prices. Those who could stay at home and run factories made money. 

¹ A smaller part of the area of New England is devoted to raising farm crops today than in 1850. Does this mean that there are fewer people in 

New England than formerly?

Then, too, our government, to secure funds during the war, put high tariffs on many manufactured articles. To save our factory owners from too much competition from abroad, the government greatly increased the duties on goods brought in at our ports. This enabled our manufacturers to go on making their high profits. When the war was over these men, liking the taste they had had of high protective tariffs, persuaded the government to keep them in force. Hence the factory owners, with plenty of capital with which to do business and with protection from competition because of the high tariffs, were in fine shape to go on expanding their factories and making still more goods. 

The belching smokestacks of hundreds of factories rose on every hand.

The new workers. Who were the workers in these new factories with their maze of whirring machinery? Were they the native New Englanders and the Pennsylvania Dutch and the Hollanders we met in earlier chapters? As the years passed fewer and fewer factory workers were descendants of the Americans of colonial times. More and more of them were new Americans from Europe, or the children of people born in Europe. By the year 1890 the people from Italy, Greece, Rumania, Poland, Russia, Portugal, and other southern and eastern European lands furnished a large share of the workers in the growing American industries.² 

In Lowell, Massachusetts, a recent census shows ten thousand Greek millhands. At New Bedford the old fisher folk have been displaced by thousands of Portuguese. 

Provincetown, near the first landing place of the Pilgrim

Fathers, seems more like a fishing town on the Mediterranean, with its dark-skinned people manning the boats and tending the shops, than a New England fishing village.

But you might well ask where are the native New Englanders and New Yorkers? Of course, thousands of them are still in their old homes. But other thousands left long ago.

He went where he could farm broad rich prairie lands or open a store or practice law, or, perhaps, become a lumberman in the forests of Michigan or Wisconsin, a cattleman on our great plains, or a miner in Colorado or Nevada, or take his chances in the South or Southwest.

It has been the development of factories, the rapid rise of manufacturing cities, and the displacing of old populations by new arrivals from Europe that have made of the old North Atlantic States a region so different from what it was in the days of Samuel Adams and John Hancock or even of Charles Sumner.

2. HOW THE MIDWEST Forged AHEAD 

By "Midwest" is meant the country north and west of the Ohio River and the region just to the west of the upper 

Mississippi. Let us see how this splendid area throve and grew during and since the war between the sections. 

A Century of Progress. In 1933 and 1934 the great city of Chicago celebrated a Century of Progress. This fine name for a world's fair was chosen because in 1933, Chicago was one hundred years old. But any one of the great states in that region—Wisconsin, or Michigan, or Illinois, or any one of the great cities like Milwaukee, or Detroit-could have used almost the same date for the celebration of its first hundred years of progress. Just about one hundred years ago this entire region of the Great Lakes and the upper Mississippi began to leave its wilderness days behind, and to forge ahead as a fair and prosperous land for civilized people to dwell in.³ 3 We have already noted how the pioneers poured into this area by way of the rivers; and how, later, when the 

Erie Canal had been completed and large ships had begun to move up and down the Great Lakes, it was the shores of these lakes that received an ever increasing share of new

settlers. This change was going on a hundred years ago. 

Then, too, with the defeat of Black Hawk and his warriors, in 1832, the fear of the red men vanished in most of the country east of the Mississippi. New lands were now taken up by settlers even faster than before. By the time of the 

War between the North and the South the vast region had been carved into states, and these thriving commonwealths
