Machinery for farmers. How did the war affect the Midwest? It caused the prices of things grown on a farm to rise. Farming was so profitable that the crops increased year by year. But with so many men away in the armies, how could these new crops be taken care of? There was only one way: by increased use of machinery. Until a few years before the war, only crude farm tools were used. Spades,

shovels, pitchforks, scythes, sickles, "grain cradles"-all of them hand implements and all heavy and clumsy—were in common use on every farm. But of horse-drawn machinery there was almost none except the plow. With sowing and planting and weeding and harvesting done by hand, the hardest-working farmer could care for only a few acres of 

Philip D. Gendreau

A WESTERN MINING CAMP. A scene in the film, Wells Fargo. What name would you give it? growing crops. It was the harvesting of the crops of grain that was most difficult for this "hand-tool" farmer. When the grain was ripe it had to be cut at once or go to ruin. 

What was the use in sowing more grain than could be harvested? To be sure, the farmer had been using the "cradle" in place of the ancient sickle for many years. With it he could lay the cut grain in a long smooth swath. But the fastest cradler did very well indeed to cut three acres of grain in a day. You can see, then, why only small amounts

of grain were raised on each farm in the old days. In 1831 a young man in Virginia, Cyrus McCormick, invented the reaper. This machine, drawn by horses, could cut several acres of grain in a day. This was a great help, but for many years the farmers failed to make general use of it. They saw no great object in raising more grain. But with the soaring grain prices of war times, all this was changed, and, by the time the war ended, there were 250,000 reapers cutting grain in American fields. Later John Appleby, a 

Wisconsin boy, invented a machine that would tie a knot; this machine was mounted on the reaper, and there was the "self-binder" of modern times.

Still more horse-drawn machinery came to the farms: machines to sow the grain, to disk and harrow the fields, to plant potatoes, to plant and harvest corn. Threshing machines, supplied with power by ten or twelve horses, moved from farm to farm after the grain had been harvested, threshing out all the grain the farmers could possibly grow.

Elevators for storing the grain were soon scattered along the railway lines. Larger elevators at ports on the Great 

Lakes poured their golden torrents of grains directly into the holds of great ships for eastern or foreign markets. 

As new grain-growing belts, especially those producing wheat, were developed far beyond the Mississippi, the farmers of the Midwest turned more and more to corn, hogs, and cattle. Meat packing became a great industry at such centers as Chicago, Illinois; Omaha, Nebraska; and Kansas

City, Missouri. Kansas took the lead in the production of beef cattle and wheat, while Iowa, with Illinois not far behind, outstripped other states in its yield of corn. Wisconsin soon became well known for its fine herds of dairy cattle. Minnesota, a great grain state, turned more and more to the dairying industry as the years passed. Labor-saving machinery also came to the aid of the dairy farmer. Ma-

chinery for milking the cows, for testing the milk, and for making butter and cheese, have lightened the work of the dairyman and his wife and thus made a large output of these products possible.

3. ABOVE THE SOIL AND BENEATH IT 

So far in our study of the New North we have discussed the factories of the East and the farming of the Midwest. 

But there were other things that helped to make the New North "new." 

The old pine forest. 

Stretching in a great dark-green band across the upper parts of Michigan, Wisconsin, and 

Minnesota there stood in early times a magnificent forest of pine trees. The strong, clean, durable lumber of the pine was in great demand after the War between the North and the 

South. Growing eastern cities, prairie villages, farmhouses and barns, docks and wharves, side

walks-pine lumber built them all. Thousands upon thousands of men were busily engaged in the "pineries" after 1865, transforming the millions of majestic trees of the old forest into boards, shingles, planks, and heavy squared timbers. The picture on page 450 gives a good idea of a part of the activities of the lumbermen.

In two or three decades the great pine forest was gone. 

Much wealth came out of it, and much more was wasted.

Great forest fires often completed the destruction begun by the eager but reckless lumbermen. When, a few years later, plans were formed to save our remaining forests and to replant forest areas, the worst example of the wanton waste of our old lumbering methods was to be found in this northern part of the Midwestern States.

Mesabi. "Indians no go near. White man go!" Two Indians, afraid that their gods would be displeased if they went a step farther, pointed along a trail that wound up from the northern shore of Lake Superior into the wild rough country. The five white men with the Indians hurried on and soon came to weird, red-tinted hills and gullies. 

It was the tint of iron ore, for the country there was almost a great mass of pure ore, lying just under a thin layer of soil. Philo M. Everett, the leader of the expedition, had

discovered, in 1845, the richest deposit of iron ore known in the whole world. Other rich deposits were later foundfive great "ranges" in all-but none so easy to mine as the first one discovered, Mesabi.

The first oil well. In 1859 the people of western Pennsylvania awakened to a new source of wealth right under their feet. A man named Drake drilled the first oil well. It had been known for some time that there was oil in that country: one creek was called Oil Creek because of the oil floating along on its surface. But Drake showed how to get the oil in quantities. Others learned how to purify the oil and make kerosene. Oil-burning lamps soon took the place of candles, and glass chimneys on the lamps made their light steady. There came a sudden demand for great quantities of kerosene, and in the days of the sectional war western Pennsylvania had a "boom" like that in California during the gold rush. More will be said about oil and about the men who built the great oil industry when we come to study the growth and development of large business enterprises. Do you understand now what forces were at work to make the title of this chapter so appropriate—“The New North"?

CHAPTER XXIV  

In this chapter you study the story of community and state building in the Far West. In 1865 this region was in great measure wild and undeveloped. Then a great railway system spanned it. 

The buffalo disappeared and the Indian was pushed aside. The cowboy, the miner, the lumberman, and the farmer spread across the land. Civilization claimed the Far West, and the old frontier vanished. 

1. OVER PLAIN AND MOUNTAIN 

A glance at the West in 1865. You have learned in earlier chapters how the history of our people in the Far West beyond the Mississippi began with the purchase of Louisiana, in 1803; how the fur trader and the soldier traced out the early routes and trails across the new lands; how the settlers poured into Oregon and won the land for the United States; how the Mormons fled into Utah and changed the desert into a land of homes; and finally, how the pioneers 456

and the soldiers added Texas and all of the great Southwest to our country. By 1853 the continental United States had the same form and size that it has today. 

But the region beyond the Missouri River, even at the close of the War between the North and the South, was still, for the most part, a wild and untamed land. We must now trace the story of its wonderful growth and development.

Frontier communities. In 1865 a solid tier of frontier states bordered the Mississippi on the west. Besides these, there were the states of Texas, Kansas, Nevada, California, and Oregon. The remainder of the Far West was composed of territories. The old trails westward from the Missouri 

River, which you have already studied about, were still in use. There were no railways in this entire region. The frontier line, beyond which there were fewer than two people to the square mile, ran irregularly across northwestern 

Minnesota, eastern Nebraska and Kansas, western Arkansas, and down across the center of Texas to a point near the mouth of the Rio Grande. But beyond this line there were "islands" of settlement, as in Utah, Oregon, and

California, which were surrounded by wide areas still roamed over by wild animals and the Indians. 

We have already noticed what a long, toilsome journey it was from Missouri or Iowa to Oregon or California.

Until about 1860 there was little improvement in far western travel. It was still a case of going on horseback or in a slow-moving prairie schooner.

The overland stage. By the year 1859, the year before 

Lincoln was elected president, both the railroad and the telegraph had reached eastern Kansas. Thousands of people were eager to move on farther into the west. The great need was for easier and quicker ways to reach the newer lands and to keep in touch with the older settlements. 

Others were concerned with the matter of getting mail

through rapidly from Kansas to California. In 1859 the 

Butterfield Overland Stage Company began running a stage between St. Louis and San Francisco. This company started a stage each way each day, over the longest stage route in the world. Stations were established where the exhausted horses were taken off and fresh ones attached, the stage whirling away again across the dusty plains. The route fol- திம் 

FOUR EARLY FAR-WEST OCCUPATIONS. Can you name the occupations represented here? Are the four figures placed in the right order? lowed was nearly the same as that taken by the wagon trains on their way to California. 

The pony express. To hurry the mails and dispatches along still faster, the pony express was established.¹ Horsemen on wiry ponies ran a sort of relay race across the country from the Missouri to California, each horse covering fifteen to twenty-five miles at a gallop. Fresh horses were substituted at stations along the route. By hard riding the distance was covered sometimes in eight or ten days. 

1 For old times' sake, the Pony Express was revived in 1923. Only one through trip was made. Two hundred forty-three horses were used.

But businessmen and statesmen felt that these means of carrying mail and passengers were only makeshifts until the railroads could be pushed out across the western prairies and mountains to bind together the East and the 

Farthest West.

The first railway to the Pacific. As soon as California became a part of the United States, men began to talk about a railroad to the Pacific. The war brought home to the government the fact that the Pacific Coast states might be hard to defend, and the opportunities for these states to hasten to the support of the rest of the country were seen to be limited and uncertain. Accordingly, during the progress of the war, acts were passed in Congress authorizing the building of two railroads, one to start in the east and one in the west, meeting somewhere about half way between. Work was soon begun at Omaha, Nebraska, and at 

San Francisco. The eastern section was called the Union 

Pacific and the western section the Central Pacific. The whole nation took an interest in the work, the government aiding the project with land and money. Up to this time most railways had been built to reach communities already founded; now the idea was that these roads would cause settlements to grow in places where there could be no settlements except for the railways. The main idea back of their construction was that the West would be developed and bound closely to the East.

When the Union Pacific approached the mountains, Indians sought to oppose its further progress, because the far-sighted chiefs saw that it meant a loss of their hunting grounds and that the white men would occupy all that country. But the work pressed on. 

Finally the two roads came together at Promontory (prom'un-tō-ri) Point, Utah. A crowd of important officials gathered there, and, amid impressive ceremonies, a gold spike was driven with a silver hammer to connect the last

rails in the transcontinental railroad. This was in 1869.2 

Enthusiastic people said that the way to the Indies, sought by Columbus, had at last been found. 

In 1870 a new railroad was planned to run from St. Paul and Duluth to Puget (pū'jet) Sound, passing through 

Minnesota, Dakota, Montana, and Washington. Hard

2. BUFFALOES AND INDIANS 

When the drivers of the overland stages were cracking their whips over the backs of four-horse teams and Buffalo 

Bill and "Pony Bob" Haslam were "riding" the pony express, there was a great area of plain and foothill yet as untamed as in the days of Lewis and Clark. It was twelve hundred miles wide. Millions of buffaloes roamed over it, beating hard trails into the prairies with their hoofs, gouging out great hollows where they wallowed in the mud of the river banks, and sometimes, when the ice broke with the weight of their marching columns, blackening the waters of the rivers for hundreds of miles downstream with their floating bodies. In 1865 one needed to go only a few days' journey west from where Omaha or Kansas City is today

before he began to see herds of these great, shaggy animals. 

One herd was called the "Eight-Mile-Square Herd." The interesting picture of the buffalo country in winter time, printed on page 460, gives a vivid impression of what the buffalo herds were like.

Twenty years later the almost countless buffaloes had been scattered into flying bands which sought safety from 

Courtesy National Park Service of the Dept. of the Interior 

BUFFALOES. All of the buffaloes found in the United States today are in parks or special buffalo preserves. At one time it looked as though the buffalo might disappear altogether; but today the buffalo population is increasing. their merciless pursuers in the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains. Thousands of them were shot to feed the crews of railroad builders. Then came men who hunted for sport. 

After them appeared the hide hunters who were still more wasteful. The buffalo hide, worth only a dollar or so then, was stripped from the dead animal and carried away, while the carcass, containing many hundreds of pounds of good meat, was left for the wolf and the vulture. Students of these matters state that never in the history of the whole world has wild life been so wantonly destroyed as in the

buffalo country in the years following the War between the North and the South.

In the early days of the old West the wagon trains toiling on toward Oregon or California were not greatly bothered by the Indians. Now and then wagons were pillaged, or the horses driven off, but there were no important Indian wars. 

It was not until the Indian of the plains and foothills saw the white men beginning to swarm over his ancient hunting grounds with the intention of occupying them permanently that he began to grow uneasy. When he saw the buffalo herds, which had meant food, clothing, and shelter for his people for generations, melting away before the inroads of the "palefaces," he grew sullen and ugly. The

Sioux (Soo) in the Dakotas, the Cheyennes (shi-ĕnz′) on the upper waters of the Platte, the Comanches (kô-măn’chêz) on the plains of Texas, and many less warlike tribes were ready to fight for their ancient hunting grounds. As a Sioux chief put it, "If you white men had a country which was very valuable, which had always belonged to your people, and which the Great Father had promised should be yours forever, and men of another race came to take it away by force, what would your people do? Would they fight?"

The government at Washington sought to protect the white men in the Indian country, and at Fort Laramie, in Wyoming, and at many other posts, soldiers were placed. 

Then the government, through its officers, tried to buy peace with the tribes by making them annual payments of money. Sometimes the money payment was for the tribal lands, the tribe agreeing to take up its home on a reservation set aside for it, where the Indians would be out of the way of the settlers, and where they would be fed and looked after by an Indian agent. This plan was not a good solution of the Indian problem. Most Indians like to remain near the graves of their ancestors and find it hard to accustom

Peace between the Indians and white men was secured for a little time, but distrust on the one hand and cruelty and bad management on the other brought on a series of Indian wars that lasted about twentyfive years. Out of the long list of battles and skirmishes, raids and massacres, only one or two can be told of here. 

Chief Joseph. In Idaho dwelt the Nez Perce (něz pûrs') Indians. Several treaties were made with that tribe by the government. One of these agreements, which only twenty of the 

Nez Perce leaders signed, gave to the white men a part of the ancient lands of the tribe where the city of Lewiston now stands. 

The other chiefs, including Chief 

Joseph, refused to be bound by the treaty. When, after a time, the troops came to force the 

 CHIEF SITTING BULL. This famous Sioux leader roused his tribesmen to fight the 

United States soldiers. In the war which followed, General 

George Custer and the men of his command-more than two hundred fifty-were surrounded and killed by the Indians.

Indians to give up their lands, large bands of the Nez Perce resisted. A number of small battles occurred, and the Indian warriors, although outnumbered, put up a brave fight under the leadership of Chief Joseph. At last the war came to an end, and Chief Joseph's followers, after first being taken to Indian Territory (now Oklahoma), were allowed to join their kinsmen in Idaho. 

Sitting Bull and Custer. Gold seekers were creeping into

the Black Hills, lands that belonged to the Sioux. When the 

Indians grew restless, the army officers, in order to prevent war, ordered the Sioux to disarm. Instead, many of the 

Indians resolved to fight. They were a bold, hardy race, the 

 INDIAN LEADERS ON THE WESTERN PLAINS. Chief Red Cloud sits in the center surrounded by his leading warriors. Notice the ceremonial pipes in the hands of the seated Indians. This picture not only gives an excellent idea of the dress and adornments of the Plains Indians, but brings out, also, much of the dignity so often seen in the bearing and in the faces of the red men. Red Cloud for many years opposed the coming of the whites. most fearless and warlike Indians on the Great Plains. 

They could muster several thousand fighting men. Sitting 

Bull was a capable Sioux chief. In him the warlike Sioux found a good leader.

Three armies were sent against the Sioux in 1876. Leading one of these armies went General George Custer, a dash-

ing leader who had won honors in the War between the North and the South. On the Little Big Horn River, in 

Montana, Custer and two hundred sixty of his men were surrounded and killed.

The battle of the Little Big Horn only prolonged the war. 

The Indians were finally subdued, but Sitting Bull and his own bands fled to Canada. Later they came back, in great destitution, and accepted the reservation life offered by the government. 

A new plan for the Indians. A new and more hopeful 

Indian policy was put into operation in the year 1887. Under this plan a farm of one hundred sixty acres and the privileges of full citizenship were given to each Indian man who would give up his tribal customs and try to live like a white man. In time more than half the Indians accepted the plan. Not all the Indians have been made happy and contented by this individual allotment policy. In many places soil is so barren that the Indian owners cannot make a living on the lands given to them. Then, too, the Indian idea of land ownership is tribal ownership. He is unaccustomed to individual ownership.

James Collier, who became Indian Commissioner in 1933, appreciated how the Indians feel about these matters. 

He restored land to some of the tribes, such lands to be owned and managed under old tribal customs. In other ways the commissioner attempted to give justice to our "first Americans." Indian schools are numerous. In these government schools the Indians are given a practical education and are encouraged to keep alive the ancient arts of their people. The outlook for the Indian people is now more hopeful than it has ever been since the coming of the white man.

3. COWBOYS AND PRAIRIE FARMERS 

The cattle kingdom. In the high plains east of the Rockies great herds of cattle speedily took the place of the vanishing buffalo. Wild cattle known as Texas longhorns were

He and his fellows gave the cowboys of the early days plenty of trouble. taken possession of by the early ranchers of Texas, cared for during the feeding season, and then driven slowly northward to the railway terminals in Kansas, from where they were shipped to eastern markets. Soon it was found that cattle would winter very well farther north than Texas, and the ranching area spread.³ The breed of cattle was later improved. 

The cowboy. The great ranches were unfenced. The herds were kept on certain feeding grounds, or were driven from one place to another by cowboys. These expert horsemen were a wild and rather picturesque lot in their broad hats, high boots, and jangling spurs. Some of them were so constantly in their big saddles that it was said that they almost forgot how to walk. They risked life and limb almost daily, riding into the herd to "rope" or lasso a steer, or dashing ahead to turn back a mad stampede of cattle. The wiry ponies of the cowboys were almost as skilled as were their 3 There are at the present time 68,000,000 head of cattle in the United States. The cattle outnumber the horses six to one.

Troubles of the cattlemen. The ranchers and their cowboys had many enemies. Sometimes there was trouble with the Indians. Often "cattle rustlers" or thieves had to be 

TEXAS CATTLE CROSSING A STREAM. Do you imagine there are other cow boys besides this single rider shown here? Do these "cows" look easy to manage? dealt with. Then, too, there was a never-ending war among them for water. In a dry country such as that was, the few streams and water holes were prizes, and the men fought for the possession of them for their cattle. 

Then at a later time the herders of sheep came into the country, and there was instant war between the sheep men and the cattlemen. Cattle will not feed where sheep have been, so the cattlemen were fighting for the very existence of their herds. But the business of raising stock for the markets grew and flourished for many years.

Growth of the states of the plains. The cattlemen of the plains with their great, free ranges in time gave way before the invasion of the farmers who came to till the soil. These followed the new railroads as the tracks were laid westward. 

From the famous Red River Valley in western Minnesota the farmers went out into the Dakotas, in the 1880's and later, and began to raise wheat. The settlers moved westward in Kansas and Nebraska and developed great wheat farms in those states. 

The Homestead Act, 1862. The movement of the farmers into the Great Plains was made possible by the Homestead Act of 1862, which enabled a person to get 160 acres of land for only a small fee, provided he lived on the land for five years and began improvements. There were few trees in this region, except on the narrow strips along the streams, so the government allowed settlers to get extra claims free when they had planted and cared for a certain number of trees. These were called "tree claims." The inducements were so great that thousands of families hurried westward from the older states, taking their horses, cattle, and household goods with them, or outfitting at the point where they left the railroad or steamboat. Once located on a homestead, the settler built a sod house and prepared some of the ground for the first crop of wheat. The invention of the barbed-wire fence enabled the farmer to fence his fields.5 

This helped him in his fight with the cowboys, whose roving herds would have destroyed the unfenced fields of growing crops. 

Sufferings of the pioneers. Here again our pioneers suffered great hardships. Terrible tornadoes swept the country in summer, and the families would run to their “cyclone cellars" for refuge. In winter, blizzards howled across the ers.

Along the railroads, crossing the northern parts of this new country, grain elevators sprang up, and a golden stream of wheat began to pour into the cities farther east. Minneapolis, with its water power, came to the front as the great flour-milling city, St. Paul, its sister city developed into a great railway center and shipping point for the Northwest. Duluth, on Lake Superior, became a great shipping point.

Farther south thousands of cattle were shipped to market from the railway terminals in Kansas, as we have seen. 

Later on the shipments of hogs were also important. Soon 

Kansas City, in Missouri, and Omaha, in Nebraska, were flourishing centers of the meat-packing industry. While cattle raising and grain growing continued to be important occupations in the near Southwest, important discoveries of petroleum and natural gas brought a quick transformation to much of that region and added greatly to its wealth. 

Kansas, Nebraska, and the Dakotas. Kansas became a state during the War between the North and the South. 

Nebraska has been a state since 1867; North and South

Dakota were admitted to the Union in 1889. 

Oklahoma. Oklahoma has had an interesting and unique history. You will recall how it was first called Indian Territory because many of the Indian tribes were sent there when their former homes were given up to the white settlers and miners.

In time, as the better lands of the plains were occupied, the settlers wanted Indian Territory opened for settlement. 

Accordingly, the Indians were given small farms, and the remainder of the land was made available for settlement by

white men. The date of opening the territory was fixed for 

April 22, 1889. Thousands of people were on hand to rush in to secure homesteads. In a single day fifty thousand persons moved into the western part of the territory, called Oklahoma. Guthrie grew to be a town of 5,000 population

4. PROSPECTORS AND MINERS 

The prospectors. After the trappers, the hunters, and the government explorers, the mining prospectors were the next men to wander through the Rocky Mountain area. It was felt that rich minerals might be found there as well as in California.

In 1859 silver was found in Nevada and there was a "rush" to the new "find." Soon Virginia City sprang up.

In 1864 Nevada was given statehood. Then both gold and silver were found in Colorado, and Denver and Leadville came into existence. A little later there was another new state. Montana owed its growth to the discovery of rich deposits of gold. Helena and, later, Butte, became centers of busy mining regions. The picture on page 473 is worthy of some study, because it shows what many of the "boom towns" were like. Men scoured Idaho and Wyoming but, finding few precious metals, many of them settled down to farming and ranching. The mountain states owed their beginnings largely to the miners.

Life in the scattered mining camps was much like that already described in California (page 357). There were few women and children; gambling, robbery, and murder were common. Town marshals and committees of the better men came to the front and finally, by harsh means, brought law and order to the camps. Family life then developed in the towns, schools were built, and orderly community activities took the place of the rough lawlessness of earlier days.

In the Southwest. Arizona and New Mexico have yielded a smaller return from mines than most of the Mountain States. Although containing a small white population from the early years of the Spanish conquests in America, these southwestern regions grew slowly. The lightness of the rainfall hindered the development of farming. Today in many places irrigation has overcome this handicap. The

dry, pure air of the region has in later years attracted thousands of people to the Southwest."

5. ALONG THE PACIFIC COAST 

California. As we have seen, California owed its early growth to the discovery of gold deposits along its rivers. 

But as time passed the people turned more and more to other pursuits. Oregon. The people of early Oregon, as we have seen, passed out to that country over the old Oregon Trail. The state has owed its steady growth and prosperity to its fine soil and climate, its great forests, and its opportunities for commerce. Portland, its chief city, is a beautiful and thriving place.

Washington. The state of Washington developed slowly until the railways came. Since then the development has been rapid. In the east, Spokane grew up to be the center of an "Inland Empire" of fruits, grain, cattle, and lumber; while on Puget Sound, the great arm of the Pacific on the west, there grew up two fine cities, Seattle and Tacoma.

This northwestern corner of our country is one of the busiest and most thriving places in the whole world. 

The territory of Alaska. Alaska was purchased from Russia in 1867. At that date it was considered by many people a useless addition to our territories. It contained enough land to make ten good-sized states, but at the time of the purchase had a population of only 10,000 people. The price paid was $7,200,000. For a time the fur and fisheries of the region gave it its chief value, but in 1897 gold was discovered near the boundary between Alaska and Canada, and mining adventurers, undaunted by the cold or the hundreds of miles to the new "diggings," flooded the country. Here, amid new surroundings, the incidents of the gold rush to California in 1849 were repeated.

Soon a brisk trade developed between the Pacific Coast cities, especially Seattle, and the Alaskan ports." In time the forests and coal deposits attracted attention, and it About 60,000 people now make their homes in Alaska.

was found that great areas were well adapted to farming. 

People at last realize that Alaska is not a frozen region, where ice and snow are perpetual, but a rich storehouse belonging to all the people of the nation. The government is taking steps to save this treasure-house for all Americans, rather than to let its riches be drained into the pockets of a few. UNITED ATES GULF OP MEXICO

6. THE VANISHING FRONTIER 

Farming on the prairies. Farming on the treeless prairies is carried on on a larger scale than in the older parts of the country. Hundreds of acres of wheat or corn are often found in one field. For this reason new types of machinery have been invented to care for the crops. Gang plows, turning many furrows at a time, are common. Great "combines,"

drawn by as many as thirty-two horses, or by tractors, cut, thresh, and bag the wheat all at the same time. Powerful machines for spraying the fruit trees in the orchards are in common use. In no other place in the world is so much of the farm work done by machinery. 

Irrigation in the dry lands. As has already been men- 

State Historical Society of North Dakota 

A SOD HOUSE on the prairies of North Dakota. Sod houses were often warmer and more comfortable than they looked. tioned, the greatest obstacle to farming in many parts of the Far West is the scantiness of the rainfall. But men have learned to overcome this handicap. We have already noted the success of the Mormons in raising crops in Utah by means of irrigation. Dams have been built to aid in storing up the waters of swift mountain streams in great storage basins, whence it is conducted to regions lying at lower levels. Here the water is led by means of open ditches or pipes to the parched land of the farmer or orchardist. The owner has then to conduct the water in little ditches down

between his apple or peach trees, or through his alfalfa field or garden. Under the magic effects of this moisture the most desert-like of places soon yield wonderful crops. 

The pictures on page 480 make the meaning of this statement clear.

But few men are wealthy enough to start irrigation projects by themselves. Sometimes private companies built the dams and reservoirs. The governments of western states lent their aid. In the year 1902 the United States took a hand in the problem of irrigation. In that year Congress passed the Reclamation Act, which provides federal money for the construction of dams and reservoirs. Such dams as the Roosevelt in Arizona, the Shoshone (shō-shō'ně) in Wyoming, and many others, have been constructed. In a book called The End of the Trail, E. A. Powell says this about the pioneer American who helped conquer the desert: 

Undismayed by the savageness of the countenance which the desert turned upon him, he laughed and turned up his sleeves, and spat upon his hands, and slashed the face of the desert with canals and irrigating ditches, and filled those ditches with water brought from deep in the earth or high in the mountains; . . . in the conquered and submissive soil, he replaced the aloe with the alfalfa, the mesquite with maize, the cactus with cotton. 

Irrigated farms are usually small farms. This brings the farm families close together, where better schools can be maintained and a more pleasant social life developed than in the average American farming region. 

Dry farming. In places where there is no irrigation as yet, or where it is impractical to irrigate, the wheat growers have discovered a way to get good crops. The wheat fields are allowed to lie unused every other year, the surface being kept well harrowed. In this way moisture is collected near the surface sufficient to raise a good crop of wheat the following year. The government, through the Department of 

Agriculture, has aided the farmers in selecting the seed best

Like our earlier frontiers, it was a wild barren region, unused except by the wild animals and the Indians. But in this chapter we read the story of how it was tamed and put to the uses of civilized people. 

No other wild area was ever subdued so quickly. A young man who moved out to this frontier in the year 1865, let us say, witnessed all these things before he reached the age of seventy: he saw Indians with bows and arrows on the

warpath, buffalo herds so large that they stopped trains, thousands of cattle feeding where the buffalo herds had been, herders watching vast flocks of sheep, farmers with their plows taking the place of both the cowboy and the sheep herder, government dams and irrigating ditches, grain and fruit trees where there had been only sand and sage brush, and railroads, telegraph lines, automobiles, and cities. During that time he saw thirteen new states added to the Union. There is no longer any frontier in the whole great area of the United States.

The frontier area influenced the American people in many significant ways. It made them more democratic, because on the frontier a man is valued for his own worth, and not for his family connections. Frontier conditions made 

Americans self-reliant and independent in spirit. While there was good free land, discontented people always had a place where they could go to start life over again. From now on the people of the United States will be obliged to go forward without the good influences brought to them by the frontier.

CHAPTER XXV  

We have noted in preceding chapters the rapid development of the different sections of our country in the years following the War between the North and the South. Your attention is now called to another kind of progress that was going on. Men everywhere were turning their minds to new ways of carrying on business, new methods of communication, new ways of living together in an increasingly complex world. In this chapter is told the story of accomplishments that soon brought about great changes in our country. 

You have all heard of Julius Caesar. He lived two thousand years ago. Yet, had this great Roman come back to earth when George Washington was living, he would have felt almost at home. He would have found the means of traveling, the methods of sending messages, and the ways 485

of making things and of working on the farms very much as they were in ancient Rome. But if Washington could have returned to this world after an absence of only fifty years, he would have found a world greatly different from the one he had known. And at the end of a hundred years the Father of His Country would have been completely bewildered by the change that had come. He would have found himself in a new world.

What was this new world, and how did it come about? 

Let us try to answer these questions. 

1. NEW WAYS TO DO THE WORLD'S WORK 

In the last three chapters studied we have often used the word "new." You could scarcely help noticing how many changes were coming to the South, the North, and the West; new factories, new farms, new industries, new mines, new states. But back of all those changes were new leaders with new ideas, new forces set to work. This chapter is a "peep behind the scenes." 

What is a pioneer? When you think of a pioneer, do you picture a person with a rifle, perhaps, or an axe, making his way through the woods or across the mountains? Yes, this person was a pioneer, and the story of our country shows that there were always men of this kind when the need arose. But now we must enlarge our idea of the pioneer and include the men and women who "pioneered" in inventing new machines, in finding new kinds of power, in arranging factories, in conducting businesses, in making new products and in improving old methods, and in a thousand other ways helping to create this new world of ours. 

Corporations formed. You learned in the chapter on "The 

New North" that after the War between the North and the South, there were businessmen with money to invest in promising enterprises. They had made money and they were eager to make more. If they owned a business they

wanted to see it grow. Many of them sought means to combine their capital, and the capital of others, in ways that would be fair and safe to all. Out of all this came the form of business which we call the corporation. This form of business organization had a charter and usually a board of directors to manage its business through appointed officers. The shares of stock of the corporation were sold to any one who would buy. A person who owned one or more shares was a stockholder and shared in the earnings of the corporation in proportion to the sum he had invested; if the concern was a failure he would lose his money, but was not "liable" for anything beyond that.

Paul's Photos 

How big business "squeezed" little business.

This corporation method of organizing business brought together great quantities of capital for use in rapidly extending business of all kinds.¹ As companies grew in size their managers found it easy and profitable to sell their products and services to the people at lower prices 

WALL STREET. If you were walking down Wall Street in New York City you would see these buildings. In front of you would be Trinity

Church and to the right would be the Sub-Treasury with the statue of 

Washington in front of it. 

¹ In 1930 two hundred great corporations conducted about half the business of the country. Millions of people own the shares of stock of these corporations.

than the small companies could offer. They could buy their raw products cheaper because they bought in such large quantities. They could put in better machinery and they could engage the help of more able men. They could employ more capable legal advisers, they could exercise greater influence in acquiring property and in influencing those who made and enforced the laws, and they could open up markets and increase the uses of what they had to sell through expensive advertising.

As business was done on a larger and still larger scale, the small concerns of the country found it harder and harder to stay in business at all. In many lines the owners of small businesses were forced to give up or to sell out to the growing corporations. We have a picture then of business as a whole getting bigger and bigger, but the number of separate businesses growing smaller and smaller. Many men operating small shops in the manufacture of shoes, hats, or clothing found it necessary to close their doors and go to work for a daily wage or for a salary in the large factories which had crowded them out. Things much like this are still going on. For example, more automobiles can be built now than ever before, but the number of corporations making automobiles is much smaller than a few years ago. And just now we see the bus lines in the country rapidly growing in mileage, while the number of the companies operating buses grows smaller. 

John D. Rockefeller and his Standard Oil Company. In this new "Age of Big Business," as it is sometimes called, the first John D. Rockefeller played a leading part. He was a hard-working young man and he saved his money. He watched keenly the struggles of the many little concerns that were trying to get a start in the new "oil" business.² (You read of the first oil well on page 454.) Mr. Rockefeller 

2 It has been said that "kerosene put an end to whaling." What does this mean?

got other shrewd, skillful men to join him, and they began the building of the great Standard Oil Company. Some rival oil companies were driven out of business; others were frightened into joining the fast-growing Standard Oil Company. Then Mr. Rockefeller saw a chance to control the entire industry. Why not get all the companies in the oil

The Standard Oil Company was to become a union of corporations, a "trust." The story of this trust, what the people thought about it, and what our government did about it, belongs in a later chapter. 

How Cornelius Vanderbilt built a good railway system.

In New York City there was a man who had made a name for himself before and during the War between the North

and the South by operating lines of steamboats. This man was "Commodore" Cornelius Vanderbilt. He saw that the railroads were a rather jumbled lot of short lines, poorly operated and managed, and failing to give either the shippers of freight or the passengers who rode on their trains as good service as might be rendered. Vanderbilt went into the railroad business. Before his day a passenger changed cars seventeen times on a trip from Chicago to New York. 

Think of buying seventeen tickets and having your baggage transferred seventeen times on such a trip! It took more than fifty hours to make the journey. Mr. Vanderbilt was rough in his business methods, and some of his practices would not be tolerated today. But he straightened out and completed a real railway system between New York and Chicago. He joined small railways end to end. He built good stations. He "double-tracked" some of his system. He made better roadbeds and introduced powerful engines and more comfortable cars. When Mr. Vanderbilt got through with his improvements one could ride straight through on one ticket and make the journey in less than twenty-five hours. 

What Cornelius Vanderbilt did with his railway system others were soon doing with scores of other short and disconnected little lines.³ 

Andrew Carnegie (kär-nā'gi) and the "Age of Steel." Another good example of "big business" is to be found in iron and steel making. Men had used iron for a long time, and steel could be made by a slow, laborious process. About the time other changes and improvements were coming so rapidly, two men, William Kelly, an American, and Henry 

Bessemer, an Englishman, learned how to use air to blow the impurities out of red-hot iron and thus make steel. 

Andrew Carnegie was a young Scotchman who had come 3 Between 1880 and 1900 enough new railway track was laid in the United States to encircle the earth four times at the equator. Almost a third of the world's railway mileage is in this country.

to America as a boy. He worked at many things and grew rapidly in ability and in the esteem of people who knew him. 

He saw the great chance there was in the new Bessemer process of making steel. Like Rockefeller, he was clever enough to select other capable men to help him with his plans. He was fond of saying 

 later that his success was due to the fact that he surrounded himself with men who were more able than he. He soon had working with him one man who was a genius at keeping accounts, another who knew all about iron and steel, another who knew how to handle great masses of men. 

Carnegie himself was one of the greatest salesmen the world has ever seen. These men got control of some of the iron deposits near Lake Superior, built steel mills at 

Pittsburgh, near the coal needed for the smelting of the iron, built fleets of lake boats, and began "bringing the ore to the coal." Steel suddenly became plentiful and cheap. Andrew Carnegie went out and convinced the railroad men, the builders of factory machines, and the building contractors that his steel-steel made in America-was better and cheaper than any other. 

He taught Americans how to use steel in place of other materials. Carnegie, and men like him, brought in what people are fond of calling the "Age of Steel." 

ANDREW CARNEGIE. This eager, hard-working Scotch immigrant became a great manufacturer of steel products. He did more than any other one man, probably, to usher in in America the "Age of of Steel."

Other great businesses were built in ways similar to those used in the three examples we have given. In lumbering,

mining, salt manufacture, the making of new farm machinery, expanding of department stores, and scores of other activities, men organized and operated business on a large scale. They were making "big business." They organized huge corporations with their shares of stock, their thousands of workers, their constantly improved methods and machines. They searched for wider and wider markets; they advertised to induce people to buy and use such a wide variety of useful and beautiful articles that even the humblest home was transformed by the coming of this new world. 

But the coming of "big business" brought evil as well as good. Corporation managers often tried to make profits not through good management but by gaining monopolies in their respective fields and then raising the price of their commodity far above what was fair and just. They often bribed judges and lawmakers into giving them unfair advantages. They used recklessly and wastefully the resources they controlled. They gave money to the political parties so that whichever one was in power would pass laws favorable to their plans. Often they fought against all efforts to raise the wages or to shorten the working day of their employees. "Big business" gained the reputation of being selfish and unpatriotic in its methods.

SOME OF THE LEADING RAILWAY SYSTEMS OF THE UNITED STATES

States, a person wishing to send a message to some one beyond the reach of his voice sent a letter, a note, or a special messenger.5 Samuel F. B. Morse brought about the first great change in sending messages. In 1838 he sent the first telegram over a three-mile wire. A few years later our government gave him money to build a longer line. This line was built from Washington to Baltimore, and the first message sent over it, in 1844, was "What hath God wrought."

By 1860 every state in the Union had telegraph lines. 

Ocean cable. Almost from the first day of the telegraph, men thought what a fine thing it would be to have a telegraph line across the ocean. Cyrus W. Field went to work on this problem. Men with money aided him, and again and again the great cable containing the wires was unwound from the decks of ships and lowered to the sea floor, but each time it parted. Field did not become discouraged. 

Finally, in 1866, a successful cable was laid, and since that time telegraphic communication has been maintained with the rest of the world.

The human voice on a wire. The next great pioneer in the field of communication was Alexander Graham Bell. 

He worked on the problem of carrying the sound of the human voice over an electric wire. At the Centennial Fair at Philadelphia in 1876, he exhibited a successful telephone. 

But people were skeptical about Bell's invention, and some one told him that, while his contrivance was an interesting toy, any man would be crazy to invest money in it as a business affair. At last, however, it began to dawn on people that here was one of the greatest conveniences for the home and the office that had ever been devised. Soon 

5 The Indians, by means of smoke signals, and some natives of Africa and the Pacific islands, by means of drums, had made more progress than civilized people in this matter of rapid communication. • Americans are the greatest telephone users in the world. The six per cent of the world's population that live in the United States have sixty-one per cent of the world's telephones.

there were many people with money to help Bell carry out his plans. One day in the winter of 1915, Mr. Bell stood in an office in New York City and talked with an old friend in San Francisco. It is now possible to telephone to people beyond the ocean. 

Messages without a wire. 

The fourth great name in this story of communication is the name not of an American but of an Italian. In 1896 Marconi (mär-kō'ne) invented an instrument for telegraphing through space without wires.

Rapid improvements were made and soon wireless messages were sent across the ocean, from the land to a ship in midocean, and from one ship to another." Today there are 250,000 miles of railway lines in our country-much more than in all the countries of Europe combined. The great areas of the nation lying away from the navigable rivers and especially the regions of the West could never have been developed without the aid of the railways.

Ocean steamships. We have seen what a great convenience the steamboat was for handling river traffic in the early days. It was not long after the coming of the river steamboats that steam-propelled ships were also crossing

the oceans. Today great steamers carrying two or three thousand passengers and equipped with every comfort and convenience that could be imagined cross the ocean in five or six days.

Highways. In Chapter XV, page 282, you learned of the building of better country roads in the eastern states about one hundred years ago and of the many good results which such roads brought to the people. If you have read the stories of early travel in our country, you have learned that in most parts of the United States, however, roads were very much neglected and traveling was very slow and difficult. The reasons for this may be found, perhaps, in the fact that the distances were so great and the population so widespread that road building was a very large and expensive undertaking. Another reason for the slow improvement in highways was that for many years the leading public men were interested in canals as a means of transportation. Before canal building had gone very far many of our financiers became interested in railway building, and for a long time this great enterprise absorbed the public interest.

In recent times popular interest in the improvement of our highways has been greatly stimulated by the use of the automobile. From 1890 to 1910 the automobile was in an experimental stage, but after the latter date the automobile came into general use by the American people. Many millions of automobiles are manufactured each year, and their use has become a part of the everyday life of most classes of our people. You will be interested in the picture on page 498 of the first automobile show in America.

The use of the automobile made necessary improved highways. Towns, counties, states, and even the federal government, began appropriating money for the construction and improvement of roads. In 1916 the United States

Solving the problem of flight. Men had from ancient times dreamed of an invention by means of which a person might travel through the air like a bird. Some did more than dream, but their efforts to make a "flying machine" always failed and the would-be inventors were laughed at as "cranks." Balloons were in use in the eighteenth century, but, of course, they were at the mercy of every wind. 

With the coming of the gasoline engine, however, and the development of construction materials and mechanical skills, there was more chance for the invention of a workable "flying machine." The gasoline engine was already being used to run many kinds of machines, including the automobile. It was both light and powerful. Why not use it to propel a vessel through the air? On both sides of the ocean men went to work on the problem. In our country the Wright brothers of Dayton, Ohio, worked patiently, and finally, in 1905, they had a successful flying machine, or airplane. During these years great progress in flight was made in Europe. In the World War men learned more about building and operating the new airplanes than would have been learned, perhaps, in twenty-five years of peace. 

You know the story of Charles A. Lindbergh and his great flight across the Atlantic from New York City to Paris in 1927. Since that time the daring exploits of other aviators have excited wide interest. It would be impossible to live today and not know these things and be in touch with the new and wider uses in science and in commerce to which the "heavier-than-air" airplane and the "lighter-than-air" airship are being put.11 

11 In 1927 the average cost of air travel per mile was twelve cents. By 

1935 this had been reduced to 5.5 cents. In 1934 there were 461,743 persons who made journeys by airplane in the United States. By the next year the number reached 746,946.

3. MAKING AMERICAN LIFE MORE ATTRACTIVE Lifting burdens. Recent chap ters in this book have led you to see how new factories, by the use of water power or steam power, were lifting age-old burdens from the shoulders of the people. Two new "servants" were then set to work to lighten still further the jobs that human muscles had done for so long. These were gasoline and electricity. Enough has been said about the former when automobiles and airplanes were discussed. The story of "pioneering" in the uses of electricity needs more attention. 

New servants at work. Benjamin Franklin, you will recall, was interested in electricity. You no doubt remember his "kite" experiment. In 1878 Charles F. Brush invented a system of arc electric

lighting. About the same time Thomas A. Edison, the greatest inventor the world has seen, showed how a good light could be produced by means of an electric current running through a wire in a glass bulb from which the air had been expelled. This was the beginning of our modern systems of lighting homes and cities. Within a few years, in all civilized lands, the darkness of night was giving away to the brilliant effects of millions of electric lights.12 

Soon other work was found for electricity. It took the place of horses on street-railway systems, went to work in the offices of dentists and surgeons, made possible the improvements in communication we have already noticed, and went into the home to sweep floors and wash dishes.

It has been estimated that all the new power devices that have been set to work would, if equally divided among us all, be the same as if each family had a dozen slaves working for it. "America the Beautiful." With new ways to set money to work producing more wealth, and with new means at hand for doing the work of the country, the United States soon became a far different land from what it had been in the days before the war of 1861-1865. It grew in wealth and population faster than it grew in ideas about culture and beauty. But even here there was improvement. Private houses and places of business were becoming increasingly attractive as American architects brought more skill to their tasks. American sculptors, working in bronze and marble, were creating statues and monuments having dignity and beauty. Landscape experts were turning ugly places into beauty spots. Both the states and the nation were each year adding new parks and playgrounds in the mountains and forests for all Americans to enjoy. Not only

CHAPTER XXVI  

Changes create new problems. This truth was never more clearly shown than in the period we are studying. As old problems were solved, new ones arose. Four of these important problems are discussed in this chapter: the rising tide of immigration, the growth of our cities, the new labor unions, and the rapid exhaustion of our natural resources. We now turn to a study of these problems and of the efforts of our people to solve them. 

1. THE STORY OF IMMIGRATION 

Who are the immigrants? All of us, except the Indians, are immigrants or the descendants of immigrants. Perhaps the ancestors of some of you came to this country in the "Mayflower" of the Pilgrims; perhaps the fathers and mothers of others of you came in an immigrant ship only 506

a few years ago. In either case the earliest home of your people was in some country beyond the sea. In a way, then, we are all immigrants. 

America has received three main classes of immigrants: people of the white race from Europe, people of the yellow race from Asia, and people of the black race from Africa. 

Those from Africa, in general, came because they were forced to come, and perhaps should not be called "immigrants" at all. Those from Asia, industrious though they have usually been, have had little permanent influence on

THE COMING OF THE IMMIGRANTS. Which were our greatest immigration years? Why has the immigration to this country dropped to such low numbers in more recent years? our history. Our story of immigration will have to do chiefly with the people coming to us from Europe. 

Colonial immigrants. In colonial days most of the people living along the Atlantic shore from Maine to Georgia were from England. In and around New York there was quite a sprinkling of Hollanders; in some colonies there were a few 

French people and a few Scotch Highlanders. Two of the largest and most interesting groups of colonists were the Germans (Pennsylvania Dutch) in Penn's colony, and the Scotch-Irish (Scotch people who had lived for a time in the north of Ireland) who were scattered along the frontier from Pennsylvania to South Carolina. But after the English captured New Amsterdam the English language and English customs and ideas and laws prevailed in all the thirteen colonies.

The rising of the immigrant tide. After we became an independent nation, fresh groups of people from beyond the sea came to our shores. The stream of immigration, however, was small until between 1830 and 1850. Then immigrants poured into this country¹ mainly from Ireland and Germany.

Why did Irishmen suddenly make up their minds to come to America? There were two reasons. In the first place, the

Irish were in rebellion against harsh and unjust treatment by the English government. In the second place, the Irish potato crop-and most of the Irish people depended on the potato for their food—was ruined for two years in succession. Relief ships from America were crowded with Irish immigrants on the return voyage. Thousands of others followed as soon as they could get away from that stricken country. In America the Irish immigrants first took up the heaviest and hardest kind of work, for they were too poor to buy farms or start businesses and were forced to work for wages. They loaded ships, built wagon roads, built roadbeds for new railways. Because they were poor they stayed mostly in the east, and, in time, many of them became energetic and popular leaders in many an eastern city. 

Germans of a fine type began coming to this country about 1840. They had struggled to make for themselves a larger place in the government at home. Failing in this they fled from the old homeland to find a new home in America. 

Carl Schurz (shoorts), who aided the Union so vigorously in the War between the North and the South, and who later held a cabinet position, was one of these German exiles. 

Later on, and for many years, many thousands of Germans came to America to try to make a better living than seemed possible in Germany.

Unlike the Irish, the Germans moved out toward the 1 Between 1820 and 1935 more than 38,000,000 immigrants sought homes in America.

west. They wanted good land for farms, good water and timber, and a chance to take part in the affairs of the communities where they settled. The states nearest the Great 

Lakes got the largest share of these newcomers. Many of the educated and thrifty Germans quickly took to city life in the growing towns of the Midwest. Milwaukee, Wisconsin; Cincinnati, Ohio; and St. Louis, Missouri, are among the large cities which profited most by the coming of the Germans.

Behind the Germans came the Norwegians, Swedes, and Danes. They pushed out into Minnesota, the Dakotas, and other midwestern states. Most of them took up farms or went into business. Some worked in the lumbering areas for a time. They made the finest kind of people for developing the newer parts of the states they settled in. 

The new immigration. Gradually, during the years from 

1880 to 1890, there was a slackening in the tide of immigration from the countries we have named. Old abuses in the homelands had largely gone, and new opportunities had come; the need to seek new homes had largely passed away. 

But the places of these earlier immigrants were filled by fresh waves of people from Italy, Poland, and the other lands of eastern and southern Europe. These new immigrants had had small opportunity for education and for experience in political matters at home. They were usually in great poverty when they arrived in our country. Had they wanted to farm or to start small, independent business enterprises, they would have found far less opportunity than had the Irish and Germans who had arrived fifty years earlier. As you will remember, by 1880 the stirring 'Age of Big Business" had arrived, with its giant factories, its masses of workmen, its direction in the hands of far-off boards of directors. But "big business" wanted workers, and these new immigrants took what they could get-usually the hardest jobs, requiring the least skill and 66

paying the lowest wages. Since the growing factories were usually located in the cities, the new immigrant naturally became a city dweller. And when he climbed to a better job, or made a success of some new line of work, he felt that the big, growing city of his adoption was the best place for him to live. 

Millions of Population 1790 131 12 10 3 2 1810 1830 Stemming the tide. In the earlier years our people had thought little about the immigrant except as a means to get certain hard work done cheaply. But in the 1870's people began asking: Are the steamship companies and the factory owners coaxing people to come to America by giving them false notions about the opportunities here?

Do many of them arrive so poor that they must soon fall back on public or private charity? Are the immigrants likely to bring disease into the country? Do they become citizens as soon as possible after their arrival? Do they know anything about the questions we are trying to settle by means of the ballot? You readily see that such questions arose in connection for millions of pop- with this newer immigration from southern and eastern Europe, and not in connection with the older peoples from northern and western Europe.

Congress interested itself in these matters. What was learned about immigration practices and some of the effects of the coming of the immigrant was discouraging. It was clear that the time had come to drop the old policy of "open arms" to all comers and to begin sifting out and sending back to Europe such immigrants as were unlikely to make good citizens here in our country.

Laws restricting immigration. Within a few years Congress had taken steps to regulate the flow of immigrants toward our shores and to allow entry to only the better classes. Here are some of the laws that were passed: a law forbidding all efforts to stimulate immigration by the offer of work; a law that said the immigrant must have a certain amount of money in order to be admitted; laws forbidding the entry of idiots, insane people, those unsound physically, and those who tried to enter the country that they might carry on criminal or immoral practices. Some years later another "hurdle" was raised before the would-be immigrant: he could not enter unless he could read, and show that he understood, a few lines of print in some language. 

But the problem of the immigrant was not yet solved. 

We had all the laborers we needed. We learned during the 

World War how ignorant of the English language and of our history and government many new Americans were. It was feared, too, that fresh millions would attempt to come here to share in our great prosperity following that war. So a new law was passed which differed greatly from all the earlier laws on immigration. The earlier laws had sought only to sort out the immigration "wheat" from the "chaff," with no thought as to how much of the "wheat" might enter, or from where. The new law, called the National Origins 

Law, stated what the total number of immigrants admitted each year was to be, and the maximum number that was to be allowed to enter from each country as well.2 This maximum from each country was based on the number of that nationality already here. The number of immigrants, or quota, from any country is limited to a small percentage of the number of people from that country already living in the United States. The larger the number of people in the 

2 Under the new immigration law Great Britain and Ireland together are allowed about 65,000 immigrants annually. But in a recent year only 2,000 came. More than forty small nations, islands, and dependencies are each allowed a maximum of 100 immigrants per year.

United States whose national origin was a particular country, the larger the quota of immigrants permitted from that country. The total for any given year is not to exceed 

150,000. The purpose of this law is to let in large numbers of immigrants from northern and western Europe and small numbers from the other parts of Europe. The former countries have, of course, supplied us with a much greater part of our population than have the latter. 

At present immigration from Europe is almost at a standstill, and it seems likely that there will be no immigrant "problem" for some time to come. 

1. Account for the increase in immigration about the years 1840-1850. 

2. What change did immigration show about 1880? 

3. What questions about the immigrants began to come up about this time? 

4. What laws have been passed to aid in controlling the kind of immigrants to be allowed to come here? To control the numbers allowed to come here? 

2. LIVING IN THE CITIES 

The growth of our cities. It is not surprising that Lincoln, Grant, Lee, Jefferson Davis, and other prominent leaders at the time of the War between the North and the South were born in small country communities. When they were born they had scarcely one chance in fifteen of being born anywhere else. When the very old men of today were born they had about four chances out of five of finding themselves in a country family. Babies born nowadays have fewer than two chances of being born in the country against more than three chances of being born in a city. 

You have already learned how fast the population of this country has increased. Perhaps it will surprise you to learn that the population of our cities has increased three and a half times as fast as the population of the whole country. Chicago, our second largest city, today, together

with its suburbs, has about the same number of people as there were in the whole United States when George Washington became president. Do these "facts and figures" give you some idea of how fast has been the growth of our 

American cities? Why have our cities grown so fast? 

A CROWDED TENEMENT DISTRICT. Such scenes as this are not hard to find in our great cities. This is Orchard Street, New York City, in the crowded slum area. Market day has come.

Why the cities grew. The chief explanation of the growth of cities lies in the revolution in industry which you studied in Chapter XXV. The greatest of our manufacturing estab lishments are usually found in and about cities. We could say, perhaps, that the factory was located at a certain point because there was a city there; and that the city grew to be a greater city because that factory had been built there.

Factories furnish employment for thousands of workers. 

But other thousands must be on hand to house and feed and clothe and amuse and transport those who work in the factories. In some such way as this, only much less simply, of course, have our cities grown.

But what has made it possible for factories to gather in raw materials for manufacture from great distances, and for city dwellers to get to and from their work which is sometimes thirty or forty miles from where they live? One explanation is rapid and cheap transportation. Without our railways, streetcar systems, paved streets, subways, elevated lines, and city buses, our great businesses could never have built our great cities. A little thought will also make it clear that new lighting systems, skyscrapers, modern water systems, sewage-disposal arrangements, and alert health departments have each contributed a part in the growth of our cities.

When we say a place "grows" we mean that more people live there than formerly. Growth is caused in just two ways: (1) natural increase, that is, more people are born there than die there; (2) people move in from elsewhere to make their homes. Of course there was natural increase in the. population of cities. But a far greater cause of growth was the stream of new arrivals from foreign lands and from the villages and farms of our own country. Generally they went to live in a city because they thought they could make more money there than elsewhere, or the same amount at more agreeable work. Good city schools, city amusements, and the supposed gaiety and excitement of city life compared with life on a farm have also acted as magnets to draw millions of people cityward.³ 

The depression beginning in 1929 seems to have stopped the movement of people from the farms to the cities. In 1932 a million left the farm and moved cityward; but in the same year 1,500,000 went from the cities to the country. Federal work projects to relieve unemployment, mainly in cities, later slowed up the movement to farms.

Fighting the evils of city life. One writer has spoken of our cities as "the hope of democracy. "It is surely true, since our cities make up so great a part of our national life, that, if they fail to govern themselves well, our entire scheme of democratic government will be likely to fail. Perhaps we should not be greatly discouraged when we learn that so far American cities have not managed their affairs any too successfully. 

Cities have grown fast; they have sometimes had clumsy and outgrown systems of government to work with; they have had most of the burden of trying to Americanize the millions of immigrants who have come to them. 

MICHAEL PUPIN. Pupin, a Serbian immigrant boy, became one of our most famous inventors. Many of our newest citizens have quickly become leaders in American life.

Among the special evils that have shown themselves in our cities are the following: dishonesty among the elected officials of the city; tenement houses, for the city's poorer people, unfit for human beings to live in; inefficient police and fire departments; children swarming on city streets with no place to play and often turning to lives of crime; the rise of a new type of murderous "gunman," fighting one another in gangs and often cowing city officials into ignoring the doings of the underworld; a growing number of crimes of violence, and the rise of such new crimes as "racketeering"; bad health conditions, due to crowded tenements, bad water, im-

pure milk, and poor systems of disposing of garbage. 

Many of these evils of city life have passed away, and others are passing. The worst of the tenements are gone. 

Playgrounds have grown in number and size. Many of our fire departments are among the best in the world. Today a person has a better chance to remain healthy in the city than in the country. Our great cities today give us many more things to be proud of than to be ashamed of. 

1. Why have our cities grown so rapidly? 

2. What have been leading causes of the evils in city life? 

3. THE WORKERS AND THEIR UNIONS 

owner,

The story of the Thomas family. Frank Thomas was born in 1818. In his home town there was a small shop where wagons were repaired and new wagons were made. When 

Frank was sixteen he went to work there. Besides the 

James Wilson, five or six men were usually employed. Frank soon learned much about wagon-making, for the whole process was carried on right there in a single large room: the wooden parts turned out and fitted, the iron parts. bolted into place, and the painting done. All the men helped in turning out each wagon. The men worked hard and the wages were not very good. But Mr. Wilson was a good man to work for; he worked right along among his men; he was kind and thoughtful when sickness or death came to the home of one of his workers. Whenever one of the men felt that he should have more wages, or that the corner where he did some of his work was too dark, or that better tools were needed, he went direct to Mr. Wilson and talked the matter over with him. Frank Thomas liked his job. He found the work agreeing with him, and he was healthy and strong. He took great pride in the Wilson 

4 In 1935 the most healthful cities in which to live were found to be 

Detroit, Michigan; Oakland, California; Brookline, Massachusetts; and 

Hibbing, Minnesota.

wagons. He married and settled down in that town and spent thirty years in the wagon shop.

Joe Thomas was Frank Thomas' son. He was born in 

1845. He eventually went to work in the Wilson plant-the same one where his father had spent all his working years. 

This was in 1870. What a change had come since the senior 

Photo by U. S. Forest Service "HELP PREVENT FOREST FIRES." This picture gives a good idea of the complete destruction of forests often caused by fires. 

Thomas' day! The Wilson wagons had been good wagons.

From finding purchasers among the near-by farmers the Wilson wagons had gone on to establish first a state-wide market and finally a nation-wide market. Not only wagons but all sorts of wheeled vehicles were made by Wilson now: coaches, carriages, gigs, etc. Joe Thomas learned that a great corporation, called the Wilson Manufacturing Company, now owned not only this great plant in the old town but other branch factories here and there. James Wilson,

now an old man, was president of the company. The main offices of the company were in New York City, five hundred miles away. There was a plant manager here where 

Joe went to work, and there were foremen on all floors of the big plant. None of them was a Wilson. Three thousand men were working there. 

Joe did not "make wagons" as his father had done. He stood all day in one place operating a lever on a machine that punched square holes in long strips of sheet iron. His wages were higher than his father's had been, but it cost him much more to live. His corner in the plant was a dangerous one, for a belt whipped by close to his elbow, and a saw hummed, unguarded, just back of him. Dust gathered thick in that corner, and it was hard to breathe. Joe became thin and pale.

Joe tried to talk to his foreman about these things, but the foreman said Joe could quit if he did not like his job. 

The manager would listen to no complaints from the men. 

The thousands of stockholders of the Wilson Manufacturing Company were scattered all through America and wanted most of all a big dividend, and the manager knew he must help make it or lose his position. So he drove the men hard.

About this time Joe went to an evening meeting of workingmen. Here he heard much talk about the grievances of workingmen and many threats against even the employers who tried to be fair and just. He learned about a great new organization which planned to unite all classes of workmen in a union. The chief speaker stated that the capitalists owned the factories, the machinery, and the product. All the workers had was their labor. It was time for the workers to combine and defend themselves. "You men, each by himself," said the speaker, "can never get these capitalists to listen to you. If we combine they will be forced to listen to the collective voice of ten thousand of us." Joe Thomas

then and there joined the Knights of Labor, this new organization of workers. Later he became a member of the still greater American Federation of Labor. 

Demands of the labor unions. Does this story help you to understand why labor unions grew the way they did after the War between the North and the South? Under the calm
