This is a scene in Oregon. guidance of Samuel Gompers (gom'perz), the union labor movement grew until there were several million members. 

Better wages, shorter work days, safer conditions in the factories, and laws to prevent children from being employed in industry were leading demands of the unions. 

The factory owners did not like these labor unions. They preferred to deal with the workers individually. They were alarmed at the almost warlike talk of some of the union leaders. Some of them tried to ignore the representatives of the unions who came to discuss their problems. Soon em-

ployers and laborers were bitterly opposed to each other. 

There followed a series of great strikes, the men walking out of the factories or mines by the thousands. The owners fought back by hiring strikebreakers, or by the "lockout, or closing down of the plants for months. There was much rioting and some bloodshed. Two of the worst of the early 

Photo by U. S. Forest Service A FOREST RANGER'S STATION IN NORTH CAROLINA. From such high points as this the forest rangers watch for fires in the forests they guard. strikes were the Pullman strike of 1894, at Chicago, and the Homestead strike in Pennsylvania, in 1892.

The public is interested. Gradually the people began to realize that these struggles injured the public as a whole. 

Was it right for people to shiver through a winter, or for factories and offices to close, just because a strike was going on in the coal fields a thousand miles away? The national government, particularly in Theodore Roosevelt's time, began to take a hand in forcing a settlement of the matters in

dispute. Boards of arbitration to settle labor quarrels have also been set up.

In one way and another, often through state laws, most of the earlier demands of the workmen have been granted. 

Conditions of labor in factories today are safe and healthful. 

You can scarcely help knowing, just at this time, how rapidly the working day is being shortened. 

For many years it seemed that the "war between capital and labor" had seen its worst days. But new and violent disputes have again occurred, and it is hard to foresee the final results of these unfortunate affairs. These matters will come up for a short discussion in Chapter XXXII.

4. SAVING THE NATION'S WEALTH 

A nation of wasters. Another serious problem grew for the most part out of our "Age of Big Business." The new organization of business, with its speeding machines and its fresh millions of workmen, made startling inroads on the storedup wealth of the nation. The forests were fast stripped of their virgin timber; coal, iron, copper, and oil were brought from below the surface of the land in ever increasing quantities. In many regions our rich soil was being exhausted. 

The wild life of forest and prairie and stream grew scarcer year by year.

The worst feature of it all was that much of this natural wealth was being wasted. From the pioneer hunter who killed a fifteen-hundred-pound buffalo and took only its tongue for his supper to the great corporation which got only a fraction of the coal that it mined to our furnaces, we were a nation of wasters. 

Theodore Roosevelt and conservation. Thoughtful Amer icans saw all this and tried to call a halt.

But it was only

when Theodore Roosevelt became president that much was done to save and to use wisely the natural wealth of the country. Mr. Roosevelt was keenly interested in the problem. As president he was able to do something about it. 

As a forceful leader he was able to stir up a wide public FO 13 11

This movement, made so popular by Theodore Roosevelt, is called the "conservation" movement. It has had a fine effect on businessmen even in the handling of the natural wealth of their own private properties. There is no longer the reckless wastefulness that was once so common. President Franklin D. Roosevelt made the conservation of

our basic wealth one of his major aims. Even the Boy Scout, when he takes care in putting out his campfire, or refuses to shoot a songbird, has learned to be a "conservationist."

The wastage of the soil. Great floods in the Ohio and 

Mississippi River valleys, in the years 1927 and 1937, and repeated dust storms in the West and Southwest, have centered the attention of our people on another form of 

EFFECT OF EROSION. In dry western areas good examples can be found of how rock surfaces are being worn away by wind and water. waste which has long been going on. Millions of tons of the best soil on America's farms is annually being carried away by the winds or by the rushing waters of our rivers.5 What is happening to the soil in many areas is shown in the picture on page 523. sands upon thousands of American farms. The Soil Conservation Service of our national government is taking the lead in looking for the solution of this serious problem. 

Each year more farmers are following the advice and guidance of this government agency in planting and caring for their crops. In the Concho (kon'chō) River Valley, in western Texas, the farmers decided to cooperate with the government in seeing what could be done to save the soil from washing away. In the summer of 1936 that area had one of the heaviest rainfalls on record. But skillful diking, proper plowing, and maintaining of areas of grassland in the right places had the effect of preventing all soil erosion. 

The new methods of fighting soil wastage are now spreading rapidly to other regions.

Much remains to be done in conserving our natural resources and in repairing the damage already wrought by our wasteful methods.

CHAPTER XXVII  

In this chapter we again turn our attention to the political life of the nation. What questions concerned the voters during this period? What attitude did the political parties take toward the issues of the day? What men came forward to contest for the presidency and other high offices? What matters were occupying the attention of Congress, and what new laws were put upon the statute books? Answers to these questions will now claim our attention.

We now turn our attention to the political activities of our people during the years of growth and development from about 1870 to 1914, a period of more than forty years. 

As you have read about the industrial age we were entering and the changes which were taking place, you have noted how, time and again, some department of our government was concerned with events which were taking place. Congress passed the new immigration laws; our government helped finance the building of the first transcontinental rail- 528

way. One president took an active part in helping settle labor disputes and another did much to arouse interest in conservation.¹ You understand, then, that our government played an important part in the great changes which took place in our country during this period. 

1. LOW STANDARDS IN OUR POLITICAL LIFE 

The chart on this page will show you that the Democratic Party was not successful in many of the presidential elections of this period. In the elections for seats in Congress the Democrats did better. None of the presidents during this period except Andrew Johnson came from the South, and none came from west of the Mississippi River. 

Corruption in high places. Grant, the first president after

Johnson, was nominated by the Republicans because of his splendid military record in the war. He was better as a general than he proved to be as a president. He was so honest and straightforward himself that he could not see dishonesty in others. He. felt flattered when wealthy men courted his friendship, no matter how they had made their money. Such men easily deceived him.

99 It was not an easy time in which to be president. Large numbers of dishonest and greedy men had gained power both in politics and in the world of business. Politics and business became more mixed than ever before in our history. 

In New York City a political group, the "Tweed Ring,' managed the affairs of the city in such a way as to pour millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money into the pockets of members of the ring. The "Whiskey Ring" was a group of liquor manufacturers who avoided paying the tax on liquor by bribing the government tax collectors. In western railway building a scandal grew out of the activities of the "Credit Mobilier." This organization had bribed a number of congressmen to vote a certain way by giving them shares of stock in the concern. Even Grant's Secretary of War took bribes from men who wanted to be agents on the Indian reservations and who expected to get their money back by cheating the Indians. The people were startled when they learned about these dishonest acts. Grant's failure to see what was going on caused him to lose much of his popularity and led the voters in large numbers to lose confidence in the Republican Party. The panic of 1873 brought on hard times when factories closed and men were thrown out of work. President Grant allowed the harsh treatment of the 

South to continue. The voters grew more and more ready to make a change in the administration of national affairs. 

An exciting election. In 1876 a successor to President 

Grant was to be chosen. The Republicans nominated 

Rutherford B. Hayes and the Democrats nominated Samuel 

J. Tilden. Owing to the conditions which existed in some of the southern states on account of the reconstruction policy, the election returns of several of these states were in dispute between the two parties. A special commission, called the Electoral Commission, was appointed to decide the matter. This commission of fifteen men included eight 

Republicans and seven Democrats. It decided by a vote of

eight to seven that Mr. Hayes had been elected. This decision caused great dissatisfaction. But Hayes gave the country an honest and capable administration in spite of corrupt politicians. In 1880 the Republicans placed James 

A. Garfield in the White House. He was shot by a disappointed office seeker a few months after his inauguration, and Chester A. Arthur, the vice-president, finished the presidential term. 

The fight against the "spoils system." For many years one of the worst features of our politics was the "spoils system." When a mayor or governor or president was elected he, of course, had the duty of appointing many men to offices below him. Instead of seeking the most capable men for these positions, it was the common practice in all parties to name "friends" for these places. By “friends” was meant the men who had done the most in getting votes for the successful party.

Under a system like that, capable and experienced persons were continually being turned out of their positions while vote-getting politicians took their places. The public service suffered, and successful candidates were almost overwhelmed by the swarms of place seekers who crowded forward. It is said that in the midst of a war to save the Union, Abraham Lincoln's time was so taken up by these men that he was almost in despair over the really important questions that needed his attention. He is said to have remarked that politicians were clamoring for places in a house while the house was on fire.

One wing of the Republican Party had been asking for some time that the party "clean house." One thing they wanted was a reform of the civil service, that is, they asked for the destruction of the spoils system. The death of President Garfield at the hands of Charles Guitteau, an office seeker who failed to get what he wanted, aided the cause of the reformers. The Pendleton Act was passed by Con-

gress in 1883 and provided for a Civil Service Commission which was to arrange examinations to determine the fitness of people for government positions. Slowly the plan was worked out and a few thousand of the lower positions in the government service were filled under the "merit" system. In spite of the hostility of many politicians, later presidents, notably Grover Cleveland and Theodore Roosevelt, greatly extended the list. Today a vast army of government workers hold their positions because they have shown their fitness for the work by means of civil service examinations. Cities and states are also making wide use of this common-sense system. 

1. Why is the spoils system likely to give us poorly trained men in important government positions? 

2. What was the Pendleton Act of 1883? 

2. GROVER CLEVELAND AND THE TARIFF QUESTION 

One of the most interesting men in public life at that time was Grover Cleveland, the successful Democratic candidate for the presidency in the election of 1884. He had been the "veto" mayor of Buffalo, New York, and the "veto" governor of the state of New York. In the White House he went on courageously vetoing any measure he did not like. 

He had decided views on his duties and responsibilities as president, and he asked for little advice from even the leaders of his own party. The people liked him far better than the politicians did.

President Cleveland noticed that each year there was a surplus in the treasury, and that the Republicans when in power were eager to spend this money in dredging out harbors, deepening streams to make them navigable, or for army posts in the West or for increases in soldier's pensions. 

Many of these projects were a waste of money, but they helped congressmen who got money spent in their districts to remain popular with the voters. Cleveland wanted to

run the government economically. If too much money was coming into the treasury, why not lower the taxes? thought

Cleveland. He was sure the taxes on goods coming in from foreign countries were too high. He believed these rates were being kept up to please our manufacturers who, of course, could get a larger profit on the sale of their own articles when "protected" against competition by these high tariff rates. He felt that the cost of living should come down, and that lowering the duties would accomplish this. He began a campaign to lower tariff rates that had been high ever since the War between the North and the 

South. In 1887 he devoted an entire annual message to arguing for a lower tariff. At once the tariff question became an issue between the two political parties. The 

Republican orators used the "full dinner pail" argument. 

They said, "If you lower the tariff our manufacturers will not be able to sell goods as cheaply as the European manufacturers, who have 'pauper' labor. Then our factories will close and our workmen will be out of jobs." They asked, "Which is better: to have the cost of living high and to have a job, or to have the cost of living low and have no job at all?" 

 GROVER CLEVELAND. The coura geous Democratic president of the 

1880's and 1890's.

The Republicans out-argued the Democrats, and Benjamin Harrison won the presidency in 1888. The triumphant party then passed an even higher tariff measure, known as the McKinley Tariff. This law clearly injured large groups

of people, and in 1892 Grover Cleveland was again elected president. The tariff question will be discussed in a later chapter. 

1. How did President Cleveland's idea about the surplus in the treasury differ from that of the Republicans? 

2. What brought up the question of the tariff as an issue between Democrats and Republicans? 

3. What was one of the most convincing of the Republican arguments? 

4. Can you account for the many bitter strikes during the years when the manufacturers claimed high tariffs were beneficial to laborers? 

3. A TIME OF UNREST AND POLITICAL STRIFE 

Distress among the people. In the days of Cleveland's second administration three important classes of people were sure they were suffering from evils the government could correct if it only would. First, there were the laboring men. They began to think of themselves as "wage slaves." 

The government had interfered with some of their strikes and seemed to be helping the corporations against them. 

Hard times came on again in 1893, mills closed, and banks failed. More goods were being made than could be sold. 

Men out of work walked the streets and grew sullen and bitter.

The small businessmen were also dissatisfied. Prices were falling, and the farmers and workingmen who came to their stores bought fewer goods than formerly. Very often they could not pay for what they did purchase. These businessmen found it more difficult as time passed to pay their bills to the manufacturers and the wholesalers for goods purchased. They blamed the great financiers of the East and were certain the great business organizations, or "trusts," would ruin them.

The farmers, especially those on the newer farms of the West and Southwest, were also discouraged. The railroads,

on which they depended so much, were combining to keep up the freight rates, granted big shippers lower rates than the small ones, and granted rebates, or a return of a part of the freight charged. The prices of everything raised on a farm were falling; most of the farmers were in debt and often could not even pay the interest on the debt. Mortgages were being foreclosed, and farm families were losing all they had struggled so hard to get. They, also, felt that the government was to blame for their plight. 

Photo by U. S. Forest Service 

EFFECT OF EROSION. A forest once grew here. Now the trees are gone and running water is wearing away the land. 

This period of hard times is known in our history as the "Panic of 1893."2 During these years the policies of our government were largely concerned with attempts to find remedies for the many difficulties of the times. 

The government acts. After the farmers had tried unsuccessfully to correct the railway abuses through laws passed by their state legislatures, Congress took up the matter. Our 

2 Our country has gone through several periods of business panic and hard times. Among the severest were those of 1837, 1873, and 1893, and the long period of depression beginning in 1929.

Constitution says that Congress is to regulate "interstate" commerce. The railroad companies that had lines extending in more than one state were engaged in interstate commerce. 

Congress passed the Interstate Commerce Act in 1887. 

The law aimed to correct several evils of railway management, and, while it did not do much good at the time, it at least showed that the national government was willing and able to take hold of the business problems of the country.

Three years later Congress passed the Sherman Anti- Trust Law. It failed to keep "big business" from growing bigger, but the people were pleased that their government had taken a step in what they felt was the right direction. 

What kind of money? More and more people came to feel that something was wrong with our money. The lack of a good money system, millions became convinced, was the true cause of all their distress. You must go back in our history to get the beginning of this story. As business grew and expanded after the War between the North and the South, and more people were buying and selling goods and receiving wages, more money was needed. The question was, what kind of new money shall the government make? 

There were several hundred million dollars in paper money called "greenbacks" which had been issued by the government in war time and which were still being used. Why not continue to use them and print even more of them? To be sure, they were only promises to pay, and at one time it took nearly three one-dollar greenbacks to buy what one gold dollar would buy. Many debtors, especially western farmers, had borrowed this kind of money. "Suppose,' said one of them, "I had borrowed a thousand bushels of wheat valued in this greenback currency at one dollar a bushel. Now if the government draws in all these greenbacks, there will be, say, only half as much money in use as there was before. Then wheat will drop to fifty cents a 99

bushel because there will be just as much wheat as before and only half as much money. Now if I pay my debt in wheat it will take two thousand bushels to do it." So this man wanted the greenbacks kept in use, while the man to whom he owed money hoped the government would take them out of circulation. The discontented farmers organized the Farmers' Alliance. In 1892 this organization with other groups of dissatisfied citizens joined with labor unions to form the Populist Party. James B. Weaver was nominated for president. He received more than a million votes. 

In the end Congress withdrew part of the greenbacks from circulation. Those left in circulation were soon at par, that is, they were considered as good as gold dollars. You can identify them today as they have the words "United 

States Note" printed on them. 

Silver dollars. Great deposits of silver had been recently discovered in the West. The owners of these mines now wanted the government to begin coining silver dollars, as this would make our mints heavy purchasers of their silver.

People having debts were not satisfied with the way the greenback matter had been settled. As we have seen, all sorts of people who were distressed over money matters, and particularly those troubled by low prices for farm products, had come to believe that if the government would furnish a greater supply of money, prices would go up, the wage earners would go back to work, farmers could pay off their mortgages, and everybody would be happy. 

It was easy for the silver-mine owners to get these people to join them in asking the government to begin coining great numbers of silver dollars.

Congress responded by passing a law that provided for the purchase of about thirty million dollars' worth of silver each year and later another law that said fifty million dollars' worth was to be bought yearly. But this did not satisfy the "silverites." They demanded the "free and un-

unlimited" purchase and coinage of silver by the government. 

The "free silver" election. The exciting presidential campaign of 1896 was fought on the silver question. It was largely a battle between the people who were prospering and those who were not prospering. The Republican Party, with William McKinley as its candidate, took the side opposed to "free silver." But many Republicans voted with the Democrats, while Democrats, especially in the 

East, voted for the Republican candidates. William Jennings Bryan, who captured the Democratic nomination for the presidency, said: 

ade

WILLIAM JENNINGS BRYAN.

McKinley won the election.

Times soon grew much better and much of the discontent of those days passed away.

4. THE TIMES OF THEODORE ROOSEVELT AND AFTER 

A new kind of president. President McKinley was assassinated by an anarchist shortly after the beginning of his second term of office. Theodore Roosevelt, the vice-president, completed that term and served one term in his own right-seven and one half years in all. We had never had another president quite like this man. In the first place, he was born into a well-to-do family, was a city boy, went to a great university as a matter of course, and did not have to worry about earning a living. In the second place, he was energetic and felt it to be his business as president to plan what ought to be done, get the people back of him, and force Congress along roads he wished it to take. He said and did more interesting things and had more interesting things said about him than almost any president we had ever had. He made of the presidency a more important and powerful office than it had been except perhaps in the days of Andrew Jackson and Abraham Lincoln.

We have already seen how Roosevelt aided in starting the great conservation movement. The people saw the fighting qualities of their new president and expected him to make a strong fight against two evils which still troubled them. These had to do with railroads and trusts. You will recall that Congress had passed laws on these matters earlier, but little had resulted from them. In Theodore 

Roosevelt's time certain railroads were combining in such a way as to enable them to control rates over entire sections of the country. The trusts had kept on growing until now the greatest of them were far larger than any other business concerns in the entire world. The people were fearful that

these mighty combinations would destroy all opportunities in our country for small businesses. 

The "trust buster." As was expected, President Roosevelt used the force of the government against some of the evil practices of "big business." He won the title of "trust buster." But he declared that the great business concerns were here to stay, and that they should contribute to the well-being of all of us. He said that the long, strong arm of the government should at all times be ready to reach out over the world of business to control and regulate it to the good of all. While business continued on a large scale, its practices became less open to criticism. 

The Progressives. In Theodore Roosevelt's time questions about ballots,³ nominations for office, the duties of lawmakers, and similar matters began to be widely discussed. There was a growing feeling that a few strong politicians in each party were really nominating our candidates, conducting our elections, and making our laws. Those who had these feelings began calling themselves "progressives" and began demanding that the voters as a whole be given more control over the political parties and over lawmaking. 

The progressives also wanted laws to assist the laboring man, to protect women who worked in industry, and still further to control business. 

Making voters more important. In recent years a number of changes have been made in the method of electing officials. (1) The seventeenth amendment was added to our Constitution stating that United States Senators must be elected directly by the voters. (2) Direct primaries are used, in the place of conventions, to nominate candidates for office. (3) A short ballot, with fewer names on it, and therefore The Australian ballot first came into general use in the election of 

1892. It is the one you are familiar with.

less confusing to the voter, is being tried in some cities and states. (4) Plans to allow the voters themselves to begin the making of laws, or to approve or reject those already made by their representatives, are being tried in some states. (The "initiative" and the "referendum," these are called, respectively.) (5) In a few places plans have been suggested and tried that attempt to give minority groups (fewer than half) as well as majority groups (more than half) a hand in managing government matters. (6) The total number of voters was practically doubled when the nineteenth amendment to the Constitution was added giving women the same voting rights that men already had.

He was not the fighting type of president the people had grown accustomed to. He was sincere in his desire to administer the government fairly and honestly. The Progressives, most of whom still called themselves Republicans, wanted the new president to hurry on with the reforms they favored. Taft disappointed them. There was a split in the ranks of the Republicans, and when the time came for the election of 1912 they went to the polling places under two

banners: Taft had been renominated by those Republicans who did not care to see many changes in the way national affairs were conducted, while Theodore Roosevelt had placed himself at the head of the Progressives as their candidate. Woodrow Wilson, who had been nominated by the Democratic Party, won by a large majority of the electoral votes.

5. THE LEADERSHIP OF Woodrow WILSON 

The new president was very different from the men who have usually occupied the White House. He had been a college professor for many years, and had been president of Princeton University, in New Jersey. After that he had served as governor of the state of New Jersey, attracting nation-wide attention to himself by his courageous battles for reforms in that state.

When George Washington was president he went to Congress and talked directly to the members whenever he had advice to give them. But Thomas Jefferson began the practice of sending written messages to Congress. This plan was followed down to the year 1913. Then Mr. Wilson startled the country by reviving Washington's plan. He thought he could place his views before Congress better in spoken words than in writing. In his first message the president spoke of what he called "the new freedom" and urged many reforms.

President Wilson invited all "forward-looking" men to help him in his work. He made it clear to his party that he would hold it to all the pledges it had made before election day. The Democrats had promised to lower the tariff rates, which, you will remember, had remained high for many years. A new law, called the Underwood Tariff Act, was

passed in 1913. The tax on a long list of imported articles was made lower by the new law. 

Congress next turned to banking problems. A law was passed providing for a federal reserve board which was to supervise the banks of the country. The country was divided into twelve areas, in each of which there was to be a federal reserve bank. All national banks were required to be members of the federal reserve system. Perhaps you have seen the sign displayed in some bank you have visited: "Member of Federal Reserve." The new law was intended to spread money and credit more evenly over the country, and to provide, when conditions warranted it, a new kind of currency in the form of Federal Reserve bank notes. 

People still feared the great business organizations, or trusts, which, they thought, might control the prices of many necessities of life, and which seemed to have it in their power to crush small businesses. Theodore Roosevelt, you recall, believed that great business concerns had come to stay, but that they must be forced by the government to treat the public and the small companies fairly. Woodrow 

Wilson felt that they were dangerous to the prosperity of the country. Congress, under his leadership, passed a new anti-trust law, the Clayton Anti-Trust Act of 1914. The law stated what acts of the trusts were harmful to smaller businesses, forbade them, and fixed penalties for those found guilty of carrying on the harmful practices. A commission was set up to watch the trusts and to bring complaints against those using unfair methods. Business continued to be done on a large scale in our country, but those who managed the affairs of the trusts became more careful about their business practices. 

From time to time hard struggles occurred between the labor unions and the owners of mills, factories, and mines. 

The unions felt bitter toward the courts because they seemed to favor the owners. The Clayton Act declared that

"the labor of a human being is not a commodity or an article of commerce" and said that the law applying to trusts did not apply to the organizations of labor. The new law limited the right of the courts to interfere in labor disputes. 

Brown Brothers SAMUEL GOMPERS ADDRESSING A LABOR MEETING. The scene is in 

Cooper Union, New York City.

During the first few years that President Wilson and the Democratic Party were in power, other laws were passed which were in the interests of working people. One provided that a money payment, or compensation, should be granted to any government employee injured while on duty. 

Another law forbade the employment in industry of children under a certain age, but the Supreme Court declared this law to be unconstitutional. A third law granted coal

miners in Alaska an eight-hour day, and laid down rules for the health and safety of the miners. These laws showed that workers in the industries of the country were receiving more sympathetic treatment by the government than ever before. Events in Europe prevented Woodrow Wilson from urging upon Congress other laws which he thought necessary to bring about a "new freedom" in America.

UNIT IX WORLD PROBLEMS AND NATIONAL LIFE 

The next chapters in our book tell the story of how the United States assumed responsibilities as one of the leading nations of the world. Here will be told the story of the tragedy of the first World War, our part in it, and how it proved to be only the prelude to a new and greater World War.

As we review our relations with other countries, in these later years, we shall better understand the many interests held in common by the liberty-loving people of all lands and shall appreciate more fully the importance of our efforts to promote friendly relations among them. 

As we study these final chapters our attention will be called to the many difficult problems our country has had to face, the many questions to which our leaders have not yet found the answers. We shall note, too, the steady effort of our government to promote the general welfare of the people through all the changes that have come. 

In closing the story, let us make a survey of this land of ours and estimate its possibilities as a home for the many millions who call it "my country." At the end let us turn our thoughts to the finer and deeper currents of our national life. In reviewing them we may gain a fuller appreciation of the duties and responsibilities of our citizenship. 549

CHAPTER XXVIII  

We must now observe how our country was led to reach out beyond its natural boundaries and to assume new responsibilities in world affairs. The reasons that caused the United States to give up its older policy of keeping to itself must be studied. In this chapter will be told the interesting story of how we acquired new possessions beyond the seas, how we met the new problems they brought to us, and how we began to play our part as a nation among nations. 

1. A LOOK BEYOND OUR BOUNDARIES 

Our people busy with their own problems. It is not surprising that the United States gave little attention to questions of world-wide political interest during all the years that followed the close of the great wars of Napoleon in 1815. Our nation had been busy expanding into the west, 551

clearing the land, building homes and cities, perfecting new inventions, and laying the foundations of a great prosperity. 

More than this, the agitation over slavery and the problems raised by the terrible war between sections centered the attention of the people on their own affairs. So it had come about that the United States had lived its life in its own way and had been regarded by the other nations as having no great concern with affairs of world-wide importance. 

 WILLIAM MCKINLEY. During 

McKinley's administration as president our country engaged in the short and successful war with Spain. 

A new interest in world affairs.

But after 1885 one matter after another came up which tended to press the nation forward until it took a place among the other great nations of the world. Some of the events which caused our country to take this step must now be noted.

Samoa. Our first venture toward outlying possessions was made in the Pacific. The Samoan (sä-mō'ån) islands are far out in the South Pacific, 4,700 miles from San Francisco. German,

English, and American traders had established themselves there. Once, when there was a native revolt, the islands had been offered to the United States. We refused the offer, but soon we did take a coaling station, Pago-Pago (päng'o päng'ō) and promised to protect the islands. The islands were of little use to us unless we intended to reach out for other possessions in the Pacific. 

However, we clung to our foothold there and objected to the encroachments of Germany and England in that quarter. At one time the warships of the United States,

Germany, and England, which lay in the same harbor there, were almost ready to open fire on one another when a great hurricane came up, wrecked several of the hostile vessels, and scattered the others. The matter of influence or control there was settled when England withdrew from the islands, leaving the United States in possession of the island of Tutuila (too-too-e'lä) and Germany of the other islands of the group. Thus our country took its first step out beyond the continent of North America. 

The Venezuela matter. Another step towards becoming an important world power came in connection with Venezuela (věn-e-zwē'lȧ), a South American country. When you look at a map of South America you will see that British Guiana (gê-ä'nȧ) borders on Venezuela. For years there had been a dispute between England and Venezuela over the boundary between their lands. Venezuela wished to arbitrate, or have judges from other countries settle the matter, but England refused. Later, our country asked England to settle the matter by arbitration. But England had taken up a position on an island near the mouth of the Orinoco (ō-ri-nō'kō) River, from which she could control the interior region, and it looked as if she meant to take the disputed strip. Then President Cleveland, in his annual message in December, 1895, declared that the Monroe Doctrine (p. 325) applied to the case, and, as England refused to arbitrate, it was our business to send a commission to South America to decide on the right boundary. After that, the president said, the United States would resist any effort to break down the decision of our commission. He hinted that this might mean war with Great Britain. England then agreed to arbitrate, and the dispute was soon peaceably settled.

The Venezuela dispute showed the great nations that we meant to keep the Monroe Doctrine alive as a real force in the affairs of the western world. The president's strong

stand caused them to regard our country with increased respect. England cooperated in such a way as to strengthen the good will between the two great English-speaking nations.

Hawaii. Far out in the midst of the Pacific Ocean lie the 

Hawaiian Islands. American merchants, as well as those of Courtesy Corporacion Nacional del Turismo, Havana, Cuba HAVANA, CUBA. Perhaps the picture suggests why so many thousands of 

Americans visit the Cuban capital each year. other nations, traded there; in 1820 the missionaries arrived, and the gentle natives came easily under their influence. 

But after 1891 a restless Hawaiian queen came to the throne. She wished to rule without limits on her power, and a series of internal quarrels arose. Marines from our ships aided those who were opposing the queen. She was forced to give up her throne, and annexation to the United States was planned. The plan failed. Later President Cleveland tried to restore the government of the deposed queen.

In 1898 came the Spanish-American War, and with it 

Admiral Dewey's victory at Manila Bay (p. 556). Now the need for military posts and coaling stations in the Pacific was evident, and Hawaii was annexed as “a part of the territory of the United States." In 1900 a regular territorial government was set up.

2. What uses did we have for Samoa and Hawaii? 

2. CUBA AND THE WAR WITH SPAIN 

Spanish oppression of Cuba. After revolt had taken from 

Spain all her possessions on the mainland of America, Cuba and Puerto Rico (pwěr'tō rē'kō) remained to her. The lot of the people on these two islands was not a happy one. 

Spain learned nothing from her earlier losses of colonies and continued to rule her possessions unwisely. All laws for the government of the two islands were made in Spain; men from Spain held the important offices; native Cubans and 

Puerto Ricans could not speak or write their views with safety. Spain took the revenues and in return did not give safety, prosperity, or education.

Cuban revolt. In 1895 a final desperate revolt against 

Spain began in Cuba. The people of our country had long been interested in the near-by island. John Quincy Adams had once said that Cuba was of more importance to our national interests than any other foreign territory. Parties of Americans had often landed in Cuba to aid in her revolts. 

When the struggle of the Cubans was renewed in 1895, Americans generally sympathized with the revolutionists. 

For a time Cuban men, women, and children were gathered by the Spanish authorities in great camps, where bad food and poor sanitation brought thousands of them to their graves. A widespread demand went up in the United States for our government to step in and stop this struggle by forcing Spain to yield more rights to the Cubans, by recognizing

Cuban independence, or even by aiding them with our army and navy. But the government waited patiently for matters to improve. 

Destruction of the "Maine." Then, on the night of 

February 15, 1898, one of our battleships, the “Maine,” while on a friendly visit, was blown up in Havana Harbor, Cuba. Two hundred sixty-six officers and men went down with the ship.

War declared on Spain. The American people felt certain that the Spaniards had caused the sinking of the "Maine." 

They were eager to have our country go to war with Spain. "Remember the 'Maine'!" was the cry that went up throughout the United States. President McKinley could not resist the clamor for war. In April Congress put the army and navy at the president's disposal for the purpose of driving Spain from Cuba. 

Dewey's victory. The first important event of the war took place thousands of miles from our shores and from Cuba. Spain's colonists in the Philippines were also in revolt against her, and a Spanish fleet of war vessels was stationed at Manila Bay. Our Pacific Squadron was at 

Hong Kong, China. Commodore George Dewey, its com mander, got orders to find and destroy the Spanish fleet. 

Our new navy of steel vessels, which the government had been building since about 1880, was to be given a chance to prove its merit. Dewey's ships slipped into Manila Bay and in a brisk naval battle destroyed the Spanish fleet. 

Fighting in Cuba. Now Cuba and Puerto Rico became the scene of war. Our warships kept a Spanish fleet "bottled up" in the harbor of Santiago (sän-tê-ä'gō) de Cuba, on the southeastern shore of the island. Lieutenant Hobson and seven seamen made a gallant effort to sink a coaling ship across the narrow neck of the harbor. The effort failed and Hobson and his men were captured by the Spaniards. 

Near Santiago an army of regular soldiers, national guards-

men, and volunteers was landed and moved forward to attack the Spanish soldiers entrenched on the hills back of the town. The battle which followed, at the El Caney blockhouse and on San Juan (săn hwän') Hill, was wretchedly managed, but the men fought with the usual bravery

About this time the Spanish fleet steamed out of the harbor and made a desperate attempt to escape. The ships were all destroyed by the guns of the waiting American fleet. Spain, a loser at all points, soon asked for peace, and the war came to an end after only a few months of fighting. 

A badly managed war. While our navy proved that it

was efficiently organized, army affairs, in general, were managed so badly that it almost seemed as though we had forgotten how to fight a war. The equipment was bad: our men were in Cuba in the summer time, but they had to wear uniforms suited to the climate of the northern part of

But our government learned a lesson that it made good use of later, as we shall see.

Results. As a result of the war, Spain was forced from

Cuba and Puerto Rico in the Atlantic, and from Guam and the great Philippine group of islands in the Pacific. We gave Spain $20,000,000 for the Philippines, and took possession of all our new "conquests," promising, however, that we would leave Cuba as soon as she could manage her own affairs as an independent nation.

3. OUR FLAG IN NEW PLACES 

Following the Spanish-American War came a number of events that have ever since kept our country interested in the West Indies and in the nations along the shores of the 

Caribbean (kǎr-i-bē'ăn) Sea. Our next new interest there had to do with canal building at the Isthmus of Panama. 

The war with Spain and its outcome strengthened the idea our people had long held that a canal across the isthmus was desirable. But there were many obstacles in the way of our building or controlling such a canal. An old treaty with England stood in the way, and the claims of a French company which had tried and failed to unite the two oceans had to be disposed of. The South American and 

Central American countries owning the narrow part of the isthmus would have to be dealt with. 

Digging the Panama Canal. Under the leadership of an energetic president, Theodore Roosevelt, our government attacked these problems. One by one the difficulties were disposed of.

The State of Panama, a part of Colombia, revolted from that country when it seemed that plans for the canal were going to fail. We soon gained control of the Canal Zone

after President Roosevelt hastened to deal with the new nation, Panama. This action by the president was severely criticized. Later our government paid Colombia $25,000,000 as compensation for what that country claimed as damages caused by our action.

PANAMA 

THE PANAMA CANAL. The canal is almost fifty miles long. Ships coming in from the Atlantic end are lifted, by means of locks, to the level of Gatun Lake. From the lake the ships enter the section of the canal where it passes through the mountains. The Pedro Miguel and the Miraflores locks bring ships to the level of the Pacific. major problems to take care of: (1) Who was to build the canal-private companies or the United States Government? (2) Should it be a sea-level canal, or should locks be used? (3) How should the Zone be made healthful so that white men could work there? It was decided that "Uncle

Sam" himself should carry out the project, and that it should be a lock canal.

The third problem was the most difficult. The old French company had failed largely because of the high death rate among the workers. The climate in the Panama region had long been regarded as one of the deadliest in the world for white men. Yellow fever and malaria were the twin scourges of that wet, hot land. But for three years our army men had been in Cuba, fighting the filth and disease there. 

They made a great discovery: that the diseases of yellow fever and malaria are caused by the bites of certain mosquitoes. Dr. Jesse W. Lazear gave his life in the experiments leading to the discovery. Armed with this new knowledge Dr. William Gorgas and his assistants set to work at Panama. Slowly they won their battle against the mosquito. The engineers of the government under G. W. 

Goethals (gō'thălz), together with an army of skilled men and common laborers, set to work digging the canal. In ten years it was finished.

The Panama Canal has been a wonderful help to world commerce, shortening the voyage from New York to San Francisco by 8,000 miles. It adds greatly to the protection our navy could give us in time of war. The total cost was nearly $400,000,000, but the money paid for its use by steamship companies makes it a good investment. Two views of the canal are shown facing pages 562 and 563. You will be interested in studying them. 

Governing our new possessions. It was one thing for our country to purchase the Louisiana Territory, to add Oregon by treaty, or even to purchase Alaska, but it was quite another thing to add such lands as Puerto Rico and the Philippines to our possessions. The former were unoccupied lands, for the most part, and well suited for development by our own people. But in the latter lands there are teeming populations wholly different from our own in race,

language, and customs. When people in 1899 heard that we had taken the Philippines, many of them had to search a long time in their atlases even to locate that group of islands. If they read farther, they learned that almost ten million people lived there some of them quite cultured and

Now that these new lands were ours, what should be done with them? Should they be treated as Louisiana or Oregon had been treated, with the idea that states in our Union should some day be created there? This was a new situation.

The new lands have ever since been treated as possessions rather than as parts of the United States. All of them have received much careful thought and attention and have prospered under our flag even though they do not come under our Constitution. 

Today Puerto Rico and Hawaii have governors and judges appointed by the president with legislative bodies elected by the people themselves. In other words, these islands have governments much like those of our territories before their admission to the Union as states. The 

Philippines were governed in much the same way for many years, but it was generally understood that in due time they were to be given their independence. A strong sentiment grew up among the Filipinos for independence, and in 1935 our government made provision that the islands should have an independent government after a period of years. 

Small islands here and there are ruled directly by officers appointed by the president.

Cuba and the small Caribbean countries mentioned earlier in this chapter have been referred to as our "protectorates." They are really independent nations, except that our government has at times insisted on supervising their general concerns when it has been deemed necessary as a means of preserving the Monroe Doctrine or of safeguarding our interests.

4. TAKING Rank as a WORLD POWER 

George Washington advised his country to avoid becoming entangled in the affairs of the Old World. As soon as our young nation could do so, it "turned its back on Europe" and interested itself primarily in what was going on on this side of the Atlantic. 

How we became active in world affairs. But the world had grown “smaller" since the Father of His Country had advised his fellow Americans to avoid entanglements with European countries. American dollars were invested in many countries. We now had possessions not only in the 

Atlantic, but in the far Pacific as well. It was becoming more difficult for our country to cling to its "hands off" policy of earlier times. The easily won war with Spain, while it had angered and disturbed some of the friends of Spain in Europe, had brought us recognition as a strong nation in world affairs. We became a "world power," that is, one of the six or seven leading nations of the world to be consulted in all great international matters. Let us look at a few examples of what all this meant. 

Until about the year 1900 the powerful nations had been sending to us, as their representatives, men with the rank of "minister," but among themselves they were exchanging officials of a higher rank, called "ambassadors." Now these countries hastened to send to us only their representatives of the highest order, or ambassadors. We created for ourselves this new class of foreign representatives, or diplomatic officers, in order to return the compliment. 

China. Nothing shows our new place in world affairs more clearly than a series of events which took place in China. It seemed, in 1899, as though the nations of Europe intended to cut that ancient land into pieces and parcel it out among themselves. John Hay, our Secretary of State, sent notes to the nations most concerned suggesting that China be left as it was and that other nations have com-

plete freedom of trade with all parts of that great country. 

This was called the "open door" policy. In China there was at this time a society of natives who called themselves the Boxers, and who were bent on driving out of their country all foreigners and foreign influence. The Boxers began a war which imperiled the lives of thousands of missionaries and other Europeans and Americans then in China. It took a combined army of American and European soldiers to quell the Boxers.

After this China's situation seemed worse than before. 

The countries that had sent soldiers were determined that China should pay a fine, or "indemnity" for what had happened. But they wanted the indemnity to be in the form of pieces of Chinese territory. Again Secretary Hay stepped in. He got the nations to take money payments instead. Our part of the indemnity amounted to $24,000,000. 

We found that our actual expenses for our part in putting down the Boxers was only $11,000,000. What do you suppose was done with the thirteen-million-dollar balance?

It was handed back to China as a token of our good will, and China has been spending that money in educating young Chinese in American universities.

A nation among nations. Other events, such as President 

Theodore Roosevelt's successful effort to get Russia and Japan to end the war between them, and the prominent part we played in conferences held at The Hague, in Holland, in efforts to prevent war, showed how well we were doing our part as a nation in the family of nations.

CHAPTER XXIX  

The purpose of this chapter is to explain the causes and circumstances which drew the United States into the World War. A brief account is given of how our nation was organized to do its part in that conflict, but no attempt is made to follow the armies in the field. With the war ended, the difficult task of making peace was undertaken. We shall see how the hatred and suspicion bred by the war prevented the adoption of satisfactory terms of peace. 

1. HOW THE United StaTES CAME TO ENTER THE WAR 

The events narrated in Chapter XXVIII show how, as time passed, our country as a world power was coming to have closer relations with other nations. In spite of our time-honored "policy of isolation" it was seen that it would be impossible for the United States to keep clear of world affairs. You have learned of our cooperation with other 567

nations in dealing with affairs in China. Our statesmen had taken part from time to time in conferences with the leaders of other nations for the purpose of finding ways and means of solving difficulties between nations without going to war. The United States declared strongly in favor of arbitration as a means of settling controversies. 

Outbreak of the World War. Efforts to establish a permanent peace among nations failed with the outbreak of the World War in 1914. It is not possible for us to show here the underlying causes of this terrible struggle which involved nearly all the nations of the civilized world and brought to all peoples untold misery. In general it may be said that the war grew out of the age-old rivalries of European powers. The United States had no part in the causes of the war. At the outset this war was between the "Central Powers" (Germany and Austria) on one side and the "Allies" (France, Belgium, Great Britain, Russia, and Serbia) on the other. As the war went on, other nations were drawn in until it was indeed a World War. Let us see how America became involved and what part this nation took in the struggle. 

America neutral. Not only did the United States have no part in causing the war; it was the deep desire of our people to avoid taking part in it, and President Wilson made. every effort to keep us out of the conflict. So it was that 

American neutrality was declared soon after the war broke out, and President Wilson advised the American people to be neutral in thought as well as in deed. As many of our people or their parents had been born in one or the other of the countries engaged in the conflict, it was quite impossible for them not to sympathize with their people in the home country. From the beginning of the war the governments of the nations engaged attempted to enlist the interest and support of our people by publicity campaigns designed to appeal to the natural sympathies and preju-

dices of our population. Those in charge of this propaganda were frequently guilty of gross exaggeration and misrepresentation of facts. But in spite of all these circumstances there was a sincere and earnest desire on the part of the American people to keep out of the war. 

Difficulties with Great Britain and Germany. The war was only a few months old when troubles began to arise between our country and both Great Britain and Germany. 

The British navy was the most powerful in the world and controlled the seas. Germany did not raise enough food to supply its population and its armies. Great Britain immediately took advantage of this situation and ordered its war vessels to stop ships bound for German ports with cargoes of food and other supplies. Ships to neutral countries like Holland, Norway, and Sweden were also halted on the plea that goods landed in those countries would ultimately find their way across the border into Germany. 

American mail was opened and read by order of the British authorities. President Wilson protested against this interference with our trade. The controversy grew very bitter, and Great Britain finally agreed to arbitrate the points in dispute. However, this did little to relieve the situation since the British navy continued to stop American ships. 

You see Great Britain was determined to deprive Germany of these supplies and thus make it more difficult for her to carry on the war.

The problems arising out of the commercial relations of neutrals and nations at war have always proved difficult to solve. You will remember that similar questions arose in the 

War of 1812 and again in the War between the North and the South. International law seems not to be clear on many points of neutral rights, and as new conditions arise no rules are found to cover questions which come up. We shall now see how difficulties arose between our country and Germany. Since the British navy controlled the seas, it was

THE UNITED STATES AS A WORLD POWER

possible for the Allies to purchase and transport all kinds of supplies and war munitions. This, of course, placed 

Germany at a great disadvantage, and the German government protested that the United States should not allow such purchases to be made. Our government maintained the right to sell to whatever purchasers offered to buy.

The submarine. It was the use of the submarine by 

Germany which brought matters to a crisis. With Great 

Britain supreme on the surface of the ocean, Germany turned to the only effective weapon remaining to her in naval warfare, the submarine. The purpose of the German government was similar to that of Great Britain, that is, to destroy the commerce of her enemy. German leaders believed that if they could cut off from Great Britain the vast quantity of food supplies and other materials coming into that country from America, the British government would not be able to carry on the war and must be forced to give up the struggle. Germany had a number of these dangerous undersea boats, and in 1915 they were ordered to attack shipping bound for British ports. 

Immediately a new situation presented itself. To operate successfully the submarine had sometimes to sink vessels without warning. From the very nature of the submarine attack no provision could be made for the safety of passengers and crew on the vessels attacked. If a warship was sunk no complaint could be made, but when a merchant ship was torpedoed and sent to the bottom of the sea with a loss of life, the matter was quite different. 

President Wilson protested against the use of the submarine. It was maintained that its use violated international law and was contrary to the rules of civilized warfare. The German government retorted that the submarine was a new kind of weapon and that international law must take into account its peculiar character. It was argued that merchant ships bound for British ports usually

included in their cargoes war munitions, and that the proper way to protect American citizens was to prevent them from taking passage on vessels bound through the submarine war zone-that is, those waters surrounding the British Isles. 

 OUR COUNTRY ENTERS THE WORLD WAR. President Woodrow Wilson is reading his War Message to Congress in April, 1917.

In May, 1915, the "Lusitania," a British merchant ship, was sunk off the coast of Ireland with a loss of nearly 1,200 lives including men, women, and children. Among the victims were 114 American citizens. Many of our people demanded that an immediate declaration of war be made against Germany. Our president, however, still held out against war. He continued to protest to the German government and demanded that damages be paid and that

the use of the submarine against merchant vessels cease. 

After months of tedious correspondence the German government finally agreed that submarines would sink no more ships without warning and without saving the lives of those on board. For a moment the danger of this country's becoming involved in the war seemed averted. 

Failure of peace efforts. During all these months President Wilson was endeavoring to stop the conflict in Europe. 

He made many proposals to the warring nations in an effort to straighten out their difficulties but met with no success.

The armies of the nations engaged in the war fought with desperation on a hundred battlefields. Airships flew over cities far behind the lines and dropped bombs destroying property and killing people. In nearly all the warring countries there was a shortage of food, and people were starving. 

The situation was becoming particularly serious in Germany, and the leaders of that country realized that they must win the war quickly if they were to win at all. With the British navy commanding the seas, the Allies were better able to secure munitions and food supplies, and hence time was running against Germany. Confronted with this situation the German government decided on unrestricted submarine warfare and announced in January, 1917, that neutral vessels in waters around the British Isles would be sunk on sight with no effort being made to save the lives of those on board. German leaders believed that in a short time the submarine would sink such a large number of merchant ships that the British people would be starved into surrender. No doubt the German government realized that this declaration of unrestricted submarine warfare might bring America into the war. They took this risk counting on the well-known unpreparedness of America for war, believing that Great Britain would be brought to terms before America could do anything effective. Ger-

many planned also to give the United States something to worry about closer at hand. She proposed an alliance with 

Mexico against this country in case we entered the war against Germany.

War declared. Though our president had striven valiantly to keep this country out of the struggle, he now saw that his efforts were in vain. He could not give up the principle for which he had contended since the outbreak of the war in 1914. On April 6, 1917, at the request of the president, Congress declared war against the German Imperial Government and shortly thereafter against Austria. 

On page 572 is a picture of Congress as the president delivered his war message. 

We have now related the events which drew our country into the terrible World War. The decision to enter was difficult to make. President Wilson delayed for many months before he asked Congress to make the declaration. 

There were numerous points and issues to consider in our relation with the Allies and with Germany. It is not easy to apply laws and rules to the conduct of a war. War is cruel and lawless. Men and nations resort to fighting when law and order and justice are forgotten. 

1. Was it possible for the American people to be indifferent to the war?

2. OUR PART IN THE WAR 

As soon as it was decided that we should take part in the war our government set itself vigorously to work to organize the nation for the struggle. A publicity campaign was organized, similar to that carried on by the European countries, to inform the people about war work and to arouse

the enthusiasm of the nation. Unfortunately those in charge of this campaign were frequently guilty of misrepresentation in order to gain their ends. War has few scruples. Two of the slogans were "A war to end war" and "A war to make the world safe for democracy."

Defeating the submarine. One of the first tasks undertaken by our government was that of helping the British navy beat the submarine. English shipping was going to the bottom of the sea at an alarming rate. Our warships went immediately to the aid of the British navy. Fleets of merchant ships were organized and under the convoy of naval vessels passed through the submarine zone with few losses. New methods were devised for fighting the submarines. Swift, light cruisers, called submarine chasers, scoured the ocean and by the use of depth bombs and other means hunted the submarine down. During this time our country built ships by the thousands to replace those that had been sunk, and for a time the United States was the greatest ship-building nation in the world. 

The National Army. Our government realized that if we were to make war on Germany, a large and effective army must be created. Our regular army numbered only a few thousand men, and it, together with the state militia, or National Guard, was seen to be wholly inadequate to the task of fighting a war against armies such as Germany had in the field. These military forces were increased and, in 

May, 1917, Congress passed a General Conscription Law by means of which all men between the ages of 21 and 31 registered for military service. From this vast number were selected men to make up the new National Army. The selection was based on fitness to perform military service. 

Unmarried men and those who could be best spared from industry were in general given the first call. By the end of the year upwards of 2,000,000 men had been added to the fighting forces. Vast military camps called "cantonments"

were built at which these men were trained for war. In 1918 the age limits for the draft were changed. Under the new law men between the ages of 18 and 45 were subject to conscription.

The army which was sent to Europe was called the 

American Expeditionary Force (A.E.F.). General John J. 

Pershing was made Commanding General of these forces.

In May, 1917, the first American soldiers reached France, but the number crossing the ocean rapidly increased, and by the end of the year they were going over at the rate of more than 50,000 per month.

War work. The whole American nation was organized to support the army. The management of many industries, including the railroads, was taken over by the government. 

A Food Administration was created with Mr. Herbert 

Hoover as commissioner, the purpose of which was to raise more food and to save food so that our armies might be supplied and also that we might have a surplus to send to our allies in Europe. A Fuel Administration, the War 

Industries Board, and other agencies were set up to aid in winning the war.

How war expenses were paid. It was necessary for our government to levy heavy taxes to raise money for war expenses. Taxes were put on all sorts of things including show tickets, ball game admissions, and other amusements, railroad tickets, profits on business, and the like. A large share of the money required to carry on the war was raised by borrowing. The people were asked to subscribe to "Liberty Loans," and a great amount of money (over twenty billion dollars in all) was raised from these five loans, the last of which was called the "Victory Loan." 

1 The amount of money borrowed by means of Liberty Loans and the number of lenders was as follows: First Liberty Loan, four million persons lent two billion dollars; Second, 9,400,000 persons lent $3,808,000,000; 

Third, 18,376,000 persons lent $4,176,000,000; Fourth, 22,777,000 persons lent $6,992,000,000; Victory Loan, 11,803,000 persons lent $4,498,000,000.

All classes of people, rich and poor, were included in the campaign to make these loans. In some cases people were unwilling to lend their money because of limited means or because they were not in sympathy with the war. Such persons were often persuaded to lend by citizens' committees which did not always use gentle methods. This was a war in which all the people were engaged to a greater extent than in any previous war. We must not suppose, however, that all were in favor of the war and entered into its activities willingly. 

The objections of most of those who opposed were stilled by the noise of popular enthusiasm, but a few paid the penalty of opposition by serving prison terms. 

How the citizens at home helped to carry on the war. 

Thousands and thousands of our citizens, men, women, and children, entered some form of war work to aid the government. Great numbers who had never before taken an interest in the work of the Red Cross now joined that organization and aided it in the work of preparing hospital supplies, serving as nurses, operating trucks, and relieving the refugees of the war-stricken areas in Europe. Men gave up good positions and went to Washington to serve the government. Women took positions in factories left vacant by men who had gone to the war. Throughout the nation children planned and cared for "war gardens.” 

What it meant to be at war was brought home to the people in other ways. "It is not an army that we must shape and train for war," said the President; "it is a nation." Citizens learned to live in their houses when heated to a temperature of 65 degrees, instead of 72 or more. They learned to leave their cars at home except when these were needed in business affairs. The coal and the gasoline were needed to help win the war. The Food 

Administration, headed by Herbert Hoover, taught people to go through each Tuesday "wheatless" and each Thursday "meatless." The amount of sugar a family could buy

was limited by law. The wheat, meat, and sugar were needed by the soldiers in Europe.

Besides the Red Cross, other organizations active in war work included the Young Men's Christian Association, the Young Women's Christian Association, the Knights of 

Columbus, the Salvation Army, and the Jewish Welfare Board. On all sides there was enthusiasm for the war because people believed it was a war to save democracy and hoped it was a war to end war itself. 

Our army in France. As we have seen, our government was sending soldiers across the ocean to France in ever increasing numbers. Many of these units were only partly trained and were obliged to put in weeks and months of intensive training in France before they were ready to take part in battles against the veteran enemy troops. Many items of equipment for the troops could not be provided in our country, and during the first months of our preparation in the war it was necessary for us to purchase from the French and the British many things necessary on the battlefield. 

Great delay was experienced in the manufacture of effective machine guns, important weapons in modern warfare. Perhaps the greatest failure of our government in providing war equipment was in the matter of airplanes. Even though our entry into the war was anticipated for some time, only twenty-three airplanes were available at the time our soldiers entered battle. It was necessary for our fliers to use, for the most part, airplanes secured from the French and the British armies. You may be surprised to learn that in our country, noted for the mechanical genius of its people, failures like these could occur. Failure to equip our troops fully was due in part to the need for haste in sending them hurriedly overseas, and in part to the inexperience of some of our officials and the desire for huge profits on the part of some manufacturers.

However, to the surprise of the whole world, more than 1,000,000 American soldiers were landed in France by July, 1918. When the German High 

Command discovered that this large movement of American troops was under way, the decision was made to launch a general attack against the British and French forces. 

Early in the year 1918 the German commanders had

available large numbers of troops on the Western Front, that is against the French and English. Russia had withdrawn from the war because of a revolution in that country, and Italian armies had been defeated so that it was possible to move large bodies of German and Austrian troops to France.

The great German drive was started in northeast France in March, 1918. The British army was forced back toward the Channel. Then, in May, the Germans drove against the 

French, straight toward Paris. Here American troops, men of the Second Division, were thrown into battle for the first time. By this time the Allies came to realize the necessity of a unified command, and accordingly the French general, Ferdinand Foch (fôsh), was given supreme command over all the allied armies. By June 1, a considerable body of American troops was in the front line and aided the French in checking the German attack at Chateau-Thierry (shä-tō-tyĕ-rē'). Later the American troops attacked the 

Germans and in three weeks of bitter fighting drove them from Belleau (bě-lō') Wood.

The turning point of the war. In the middle of July, the 

German army started its last desperate thrust to win the war in the vicinity of Rhiems (rēmz), northeast of Paris. 

After a severe battle the German advance was stopped in what is known as the Second Battle of the Marne. In this battle 85,000 American troops were engaged. This was the turning point of the war. On July 18, General Foch launched his great offensive with a large number of American troops taking part. In the months that followed, the German armies were gradually rolled back. In September, 500,000 

American troops under the command of General Pershing drove the German forces out of the St. Mihiel (săn mē-yĕl') salient near Verdun. In September and October American armies numbering over 1,000,000 men engaged in what is

known as the Meuse (mûz)-Argonne (år-gôn') offensive, finally breaking the German lines near Sedan. 

The end of the war. The end of the war was approaching. 

Allied armies won important victories in other fields, in Bulgaria and Turkey. Exhausted Germany could not go on, and her leaders asked that the fighting cease. A revolting

Germany deposed the Kaiser, and a republican form of government was set up. On November 11, 1918, an armistice was arranged, and the fighting of the terrible war was over.
