3. MAKING PEACE 

The cost of the war.

The cost of the war staggers the

imagination. No figures which may be given can bring home to us the cost in human life destroyed. Thirteen million men were killed in the battles of this great struggle and millions more maimed and crippled for life. We shudder with horror at the dreadful results of this combat. A whole generation of men wiped out! The world filled with the pitiful human wrecks of war!

The property damage was beyond our ability to comprehend, and the debts incurred by the nations engaged in the war are so great that they will not be paid for long years to come, if ever.

Our country was in the war for only a short time compared with other countries, and as a consequence our direct losses were not so heavy. Yet thousands of homes lost a son or a father and many thousands more suffered the tragedy of a loved one crippled for life.

This was a "war to end war" and it was the fervent desire of thoughtful persons that with the close of this conflict, means would be found to prevent future war. 

Peace. With the struggle ended, the great task of making peace among the nations was undertaken. For many reasons this was a difficult problem. War, besides exciting enthusiasm and arousing idealism, breeds hatred and suspicion. 

Among the victorious nations there was a strong desire to punish Germany. Usually at the close of a war the peace treaty is not made on the basis of justice to the nations concerned, but rather to the advantage of the victor. 

Conference at Paris. The leaders of the Allied nations met in Paris in January, 1919. Delegates from thirty-two nations were present. Germany and the nations which had supported that country in the war were not represented at this meeting. The leaders of the allied nations decided that the terms of the peace treaty should be drawn without consulting the defeated nations.

The making of this treaty was of such great importance

to America, as well as to the rest of the world, that Presi- Ident Wilson decided to attend the conference himself. No president of our country had ever done such a thing before, and in some quarters President Wilson was criticized for his action. The people across the ocean were glad to see our president, as the picture on page 581 seems to show. He was accompanied by a number of other statesmen and a large corps of experts. The prime ministers of Great Britain, France, and Italy headed the delegations from those countries: Lloyd George for Great Britain, Georges Clemenceau (klē-män-sō') for France, Count Orlando for Italy. These statesmen, with President Wilson, were called the "Big Four" of the conference, and it was they who settled most of the important points. 99 

The "Fourteen Points." During the war President Wil son had submitted his celebrated "Fourteen Points.'

These now became the basis of the discussion for the terms of peace. They included, among other provisions, (1) righting the wrong done by Germany to France; (2) restoring

Belgium; (3) open, or public, treaties between nations; (4) free use of the seas; (5) changes in many of the national boundaries in Europe. President Wilson declared, "We have no selfish ends to serve; we seek no conquest, no dominion."

It was soon evident that the nations would have great difficulty in coming to an agreement. Many differences of opinion arose. After months of dispute a compromise treaty was arrived at. The terms of this treaty were not fully satisfactory to any of the nations, but seemed the best that could be made under the circumstances. Many of the ideas of President Wilson were disregarded in the terms which were finally agreed upon. 

Provisions of the peace treaty. We may summarize the leading provisions of the treaty as follows: Germany was declared to be responsible for starting the war. That coun-

try was required to make large money payments extending over a long period of years to pay for the devastation of France and Belgium by the invading armies of Germany. 

Germany's colonies and possessions in Asia, Africa, and the islands of the seas were taken from her. Germany was 

 FOUR STATESMEN OF THE WORLD WAR TIMES. These four men had most to do with arranging terms of peace at the end of the World War. From left to right they are Signor Orlando, of Italy; Lloyd George, of England; 

M. Clemenceau, of France; and President Woodrow Wilson of the United

States. 

obliged to turn over to the Allies a large number of her war vessels, and a limitation was placed on her naval and military forces in the future. A new map of Europe was made, several new nations being established: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Jugoslavia, Finland. The boundaries of many other nations were changed. A League of Nations was established.

The League of Nations. When President Wilson found

that he could not get all of his "Fourteen Points" adopted, he concentrated on his idea of a League of Nations and finally secured its adoption as a part of the peace treaty. 

The central idea of this plan is a League of Nations to prevent war. Every nation which signed the peace treaty became a member of the League. The plan provided that delegates of member nations should meet regularly to discuss world affairs. A Court of International Justice was to be set up by the Council of the League. Its work was to hear and judge cases of dispute between nations. It was provided that all boundaries described in the peace treaty should be maintained. Penalties were set up to be applied to any nation which might violate the terms of the constitution of the League.

The treaty of peace was signed June 28, 1919, in the Hall of Mirrors in the Palace of Versailles (vĕr-sä'y'). The German delegates were called to this meeting and the completed treaty was presented. After some small changes had been made, the German representatives signed. This is known as the "Peace of Versailles." The League of Nations was set up in June, 1920.

President Wilson signed the treaty, but as the United States Senate shares with the president the treaty-making power, it was necessary for that body to accept the treaty before it would be binding on the United States. When 

President Wilson returned home he presented the treaty to the United States Senate for its approval. Opposition immediately sprang up, particularly to the League of Nations. Republican senators, led by Senator Lodge of 

Massachusetts and Senator Borah of Idaho, attacked the League of Nations. They argued that membership in the 

League would involve the United States in Old World politics and would lead us into European wars; that it was contrary to the policy of our government laid down in Washington's time and as expressed in the Monroe Doctrine.

´

President Wilson and those who supported him argued that the world was now closely knit together and that whatever affected one nation was pretty certain to affect others, as the World War had shown; that the only way to prevent troubles among the nations was to set up a central organization like the League of Nations. 

The president toured the country seeking to rally support for his idea. He had been working under a heavy strain for months and his strength finally gave out. He was stricken by a grave illness in September, 1919, from which he never recovered. He died in 1924. 

The Peace Treaty was defeated in the United States Senate. The United States refused to enter the League of Nations.

Later on our government made separate treaties with 

Germany and Austria.

CHAPTER XXX  

As the world is today, our country cannot be a hermit nation. Our citizens and the citizens of other countries have many interests in common-political, commercial, intellectual, and social. In many respects the world is a unit. This chapter relates incidents in our relations with other countries in recent years and tells of the failure of all efforts to bring about lasting peace among the nations. 

1. NEW-WORLD NEIGHBORS 

Who are our New-World neighbors? Besides Canada and

Newfoundland to the north of us, there are, to the south, twenty independent nations. These twenty countries, with a few scattered colonies in or near the Caribbean Sea, make up what is spoken of as Latin America. This name comes 588

from the fact that the languages spoken there-chiefly Spanish and Portuguese are derived from the Latin tongue of the Romans. The independent states are all republics. They differ greatly in size and importance: Panama

HIP DE LA CONDESA MEX IN THE CAPITAL OF OUR SOUTHERN NEIGHBOR. Mexico City, Mexico, has a population of over one million people. This view is in Hippodrome Park. has half a million people while Brazil has over thirty million.

Mexico. There have been times when Mexico, like other 

Latin-American countries, has been a republic in name only. During one of these periods, Porfirio Diaz (dē'ǎs) ruled Mexico. He invited foreign capitalists to invest their money in the riches of Mexican mines and oil fields and made it easy for these outsiders to make handsome profits from their enterprises. But Diaz did little for the poor

people of his country. Most of them remained landless laborers on the estates of the rich. The aging dictator harshly put down every attempt to broaden either the economic or the political freedom of his people. 

At last, however, the revolution grew so strong that Diaz was unable to stamp it out. He fled from the land he had ruled so long. Political leaders quickly came forward and fought among themselves for power. They seemed to have forgotten that Mexico had a frame of government that might be followed. The strife and confusion went on for years.

Our government and Mexico. Conditions in Mexico greatly disturbed our own government and American business interests. Hundreds of millions of American dollars were invested in Mexico. Would the investment be lost as a result of all this bloodshed and confusion? Was it the duty of the United States government to try to protect 

American investments in that country? Troubles were. likely to arise along the border between citizens of the two countries. President Woodrow Wilson tried the policy of "watchful waiting," with the hope that the people of Mexico might settle down under a firm but liberal government of their own choosing. The plan was upset more than once. Once our sailors took and held the Mexican port of 

Vera Cruz (va'rä croos') in the effort to get Huerta (wer'tä), then in power, to show a proper respect for our government. 

At another time an army marched into northern Mexico in pursuit of the bandit Villa (vē'yä), who had been carrying on his raids on the American side of the international boundary line.

At last law and order began again to assert themselves in Mexico. Elections were held and the conditions of the peons, or poor laborers, were somewhat improved. There had long been much uncertainty about the safety of American investments in Mexico. The better leaders of the

Mexican people resented the easy terms on which Diaz had permitted foreigners to come into Mexico to exploit its resources. Dwight W. Morrow, sent by President Coolidge as ambassador to Mexico, won its leaders over to a more friendly view. In more recent years Mexico has shown in many ways that she is glad to stand beside the United States against the aggressor nations of the Old World. 

Around the Caribbean Sea. You will recall that at the close of the Spanish-American War our country took possession of Puerto Rico in the Caribbean Sea. When Spain was driven out of Cuba the United States assumed certain rights of guardianship over that island. The Virgin Islands were purchased from Denmark in 1917. In 1904 our government acquired a strip of territory across Panama as a site for the Panama Ship Canal. This canal was completed in 1914. 

Thus, step by step, this big republic of ours took a hand in matters around the shores of the Caribbean Sea. Once started on a policy of expansion, it seemed difficult for us to stop. There was the Dominican Republic occupying the eastern part of the second largest of the West Indian Islands. 

Its finances became tangled and its debts remained unpaid. 

Could we stand back and allow some European nation to dictate the financial and other affairs of the little republic? We sent a part of our fleet there, and for years our naval officers supervised the affairs of the Dominican Republic and our marines kept order. Under our control the well-being of the inhabitants was improved, but the people of the country resented the presence of our officers and soldiers.

The western end of the island is controlled by the black republic of Haiti (hā'ti). Our relations with the Haitians have been very much like those with the Dominican Republic at the other end of the island. Here, also, general conditions have been improved. There are better highways, railroads, and schools; the people enjoy better health because

of our work in sanitation. But here again, our assistance has been forced upon an unwilling people.

Haiti and the Dominican Republic has been repeated. Our officials and marines have taken charge of the administration of affairs, supervising elections and attempting to straighten out the financial difficulties of the country. This policy of our government has been sharply called in question by American leaders in Congress. Americans have made large

investments in other small Latin-American countries. Some of these countries have borrowed heavily, and have been unwilling or unable to pay these debts. These and other causes have brought several of these countries, at one time or another, partly under the economic control of our government. In recent years our government has adopted a "hands-off" policy toward these small neighbors. 

Feelings of Latin-America toward the United States. The people of Latin America felt grateful for our Monroe Doctrine, which enabled them to keep their independence in earlier times and to develop within as they saw fit. But when they noticed what was going on in Panama and Nicaragua and Haiti and saw that their strong northern neighbor sometimes took control of the smaller American nations, their feelings of suspicion often grew stronger than any feelings of gratitude. 

Our country is so large and powerful in comparison with most of these countries that their statesmen wondered whether we were really friendly or whether our Monroe Doctrine and our investments in their lands were not disguises masking an intention to gain control of them. We have helped create the Pan-American Union, an organization to promote cordial relations among all the countries of North and South America. Its headquarters are in Washington, D. C., in a handsome building erected by Andrew Carnegie expressly for the Union. We have sent some of our best men to travel about in Latin America to help toward a better understanding. "Ambassadors of good will" like Colonel

Charles Lindbergh have spent much time among our southern neighbors. A long succession of conferences has been held. 

The early meetings usually failed to mend the relations between our country and the nations of Latin America. 

Often these neighbors of ours seemed to desire closer ties with certain Old-World countries than they did with us.

They produced many articles for export that found readier markets across the Atlantic than in the United States. Beef produced in Argentina is a good example of this. We produce more than enough for ourselves, and so many citizens of this country were against the idea of allowing Argentine beef to be shipped to the United States. In Europe, on the other hand, countries like Germany wanted this product. How, then, could we keep the friendship and trade of Argentina without buying her meat products? You see, it is a difficult question.

Strong groups of Germans and Italians, in particular, make their homes in South American countries. Many of these people work hard at the task of breaking down our ties of friendship and commerce with Latin America and in knitting more strongly the bonds between these southern lands and their own home countries. At last the governments in the southern countries began to see that these alien groups among them were trying to interfere in political matters, and to stir up revolts in the countries where they made their homes. It was clear that the most violent among them were trying to help the schemes for conquest of the European dictators. As the South American leaders saw all this they turned more and more toward our country as their best friend. They saw that the countries of the Western Hemisphere must stand together against those countries of the Old World which were trying to break down their unity and undermine their governments. A conference of all the New 

World nations, held in Rio de Janeiro in 1941, bound the twenty-one American nations together more firmly than ever before.

Canada, our northern friend. Not a soldier, a fort, or a warship guards the more than three thousand miles of boundary between our country and Canada. For a century and a quarter this has been true, and yet there has been no war along that border for all those years-an example to all

Canada, a part of the British Empire, is really a great sister republic of the United States. The two governments are on the most friendly terms. A recent reciprocity treaty was entered into whereby certain tariff rates in effect between the two countries were lowered with the expectation that the people on both sides of the line would be benefited.

Thousands of Americans have migrated to Canada, while thousands of Canadians have found homes in the United States. Speaking a common language, the two peoples have met and mingled freely. In the years of turmoil and war, following the outbreak of war in Europe in the fall of 1939, our country and Canada began cooperating in all measures that would aid in their common defense, and in assisting their friends and allies throughout the world in the effort to defeat the nations bent on conquest.

2. EFFORTS TO BUILD A PEACEFUL WORLD 

Substitutes for war. Men often quarrel with each other today. It may be a question of where a line fence should run between two farms; or it may be rivalry for some office; or the quarrel may occur over a collision between their cars. 

But almost never do men fight and kill each other over causes such as these. Why not? Because they have a substitute for "war." They have courts to which they turn to settle their difficulties.

The nations as yet have no fixed body of laws to fall back on, no system of courts to which they may appeal, and no set plan for calling in some outside authority to take up their disagreements and make decisions binding upon all the parties concerned. For a time it seemed that some progress was being made in solving this hard problem. But the opening of a new world war made it necessary to put all such questions to one side until peace in the world is again restored.

Arbitration. In many ways serious attempts have been made to build a lasting peace among nations. One method

of handling disputes between nations is called arbitration. 

Our country has led the world in the settlement of disputes by arbitration. This means that when a question arises between two countries, a committee of three or five men is selected usually from other countries to take up the question in dispute, go over the entire matter, and settle it once for all. The two nations which have asked for the arbitrament of the case then abide strictly by the decision. By this means we have settled difficult matters with England, such as the "Alabama" claims, the fisheries, question in the Newfoundland waters, and boundary disputes between this country and Canada. In some cases the decisions have been favorable to us and in some unfavorable; but, whether the decision was for us or against us, there has never been any thought of disobeying the arbitrators. 

The countries belonging to the League of Nations agreed to use this plan whenever they could. Many special agreements to arbitrate disputes have been made, from time to time, by our country and others. 

The Hague Tribunal and the World Court. It was easy for nations that saw the advantages of arbitration to take the next step. Why not have a permanent court made up of judges who devote all their time to settling, in a judicial way, the disputes among nations? A partial answer to this question came in The Hague (hāg) Tribunal, with its meeting place at The Hague, Holland, in a beautiful building erected for its use by Andrew Carnegie, the retired "steel king." Efforts were made by the League of Nations to create a real court, superior in judicial power to The Hague Tribunal. Our country did not become a member of this new court, but some of our best citizens consented to serve, from time to time, as World Court judges.

Destroying the causes of war. Governments and peoples often learn to hate and fear each other. Sometimes these feelings come down from quarrels or injuries of past cen-

turies; sometimes they spring from more recent causes, such as disputes over colonies, trade rivalry, the size of armies and navies, or interference with each other's internal affairs. 

Destroying the causes of war, and thus stamping out war 

 TRYING TO DISARM. Statesmen from many powerful nations met at Wash ington, in 1921-1922. One of their objects was to end the race for larger and larger navies then going on among the nations. Few lasting results came from the meeting. The picture shows one of the sessions of the conference. itself, is one of the most important, and at the same time one of the most difficult questions facing our world today. 

The Treaty of Versailles and the causes of war. Woodrow 

Wilson felt that if the map of Europe could be so redrawn that national groups could come together under governments of their own choice, many of the hatreds and jealousies in Europe would disappear. A partial attempt was made to carry out his ideas; but the new map of Europe made almost

as many new causes of trouble as it corrected. Italians, Rumanians, Germans, Poles, Austrians-they were all left dissatisfied by the arrangements included in the treaty. 

The League of Nations and war. You know, of course, that we did not join the League of Nations. But the United 

States often worked with the League for peace. The League sought to remove the causes of war by working for the limitation of armaments, by condemning secret treaties, and by helping settle quarrels that arose over trade or colonial possessions. In spite of hopeful beginnings, the League of 

Nations, as we shall see, lost its popularity and its power to bring about a more peaceful world.

Limitations of armaments. The idea of limiting the size of armies and navies, and of other means of waging war, came up at the first Hague Conference in 1899. As far as land forces are concerned, the efforts to limit armaments were fruitless. The nations that forced Germany to limit her army to 100,000 men generally kept their armies as large as ever. The reasons and excuses for this were many, and varied from country to country. Europe continued to be an armed camp.

The Washington Arms Conference. Our government, during the administration of President Harding, called together representatives of the countries having large navies. 

Our leader in this conference, Charles Evans Hughes,

Secretary of State, and later Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, startled those present by suggesting that fighting craft of certain classes be scrapped. An agreement was reached among the United States, England, France, Japan, and Italy by which seventy ships, then in use or being built, were to be put out of commission. After 1931 these nations were to be allowed to build new ships, but only in a certain relation to the number of ships in the navies of the other nations in the arrangement. This agreement has sometimes been called the "ten-year naval holiday." But

as it applied only to certain kinds of large ships, it did not have much effect in checking the building of newer, and perhaps more dangerous, classes of fighting vessels. The disarmament agreement was not renewed at the end of the ten-year period, and the race in shipbuilding was resumed. 

Other later meetings, held at Geneva, Switzerland, and at London, failed to end the fears and jealousies among the nations. They began arming themselves for war on land, on the sea, and in the air, more feverishly than before. 

European debts and reparations. A good part of the money borrowed from the American people by our government by selling bonds during the World War was lent to England, France, Italy, and other allied nations. After the war the statesmen of these nations argued that these war debts should be canceled. They said that all this money should be considered as our contribution toward winning the war. 

But the statesmen of our country steadfastly refused to look at these obligations in any other light than that they were ordinary business arrangements. 

In spite of the stand taken by our leaders, however, much was done to lighten the debt burden of the other countries. 

The rate of interest was reduced; the payments were spread out over a period of sixty-two years; in 1931 we allowed a one-year postponement of all payments on the debt. The nations continued year after year to postpone payments on these debts. It is believed by many, now that a second world war has added so many new problems, that the old debts left from the first great war will never be paid. For a long time little Finland was the only country that met its debt payments promptly.

From the day the armistice was signed, a main point in the minds of many European statesmen was thạt Germany should be made to pay for the damages to property of the citizens of allied countries. France said, for example, that hundreds of her villages and scores of mines and factories

had been ruined because the German armies had occupied much of northern France for such a long time during the war. Then why should not the German government pay the "repair" bill? "Reparations," they called it.

The leaders in Europe went further. They said to our government, "How can we pay our debts to you unless 

Germany makes these reparations payments?" In this way we were forced to interest ourselves in the matter of the reparations. Two commissions, the first headed by General 

Charles G. Dawes and the second by Owen D. Young, both eminent Americans, tried to decide how much Germany was capable of paying each year. Later the European powers decided on an entirely new plan of settlement. They were careful, however, to link reparations with the question of their debts to our country. Later events have made it clear enough that all questions about debts and reparations would have to be postponed for many years or dropped completely.

Outlawing war. "The High Contracting Parties solemnly declare in the names of their respective peoples that they condemn recourse to war for the solution of international controversies, and renounce it as an instrument of national policy in their relation to one another." Thus runs Article I of the Kellogg-Briand (brê-äN') Peace Pact, first put in form by our Secretary of State, Frank B. Kellogg, and Aristide

Briand, Foreign Minister of France. Many nations actually signed the pact, and others agreed to do so. But the pact was silent on the question of what to do with a nation that broke its pledge and went to war anyway. This, in the minds of many, destroyed the pact's usefulness and value. In the tragic years following 1939 little or nothing was heard about this famous agreement to consider war an "outlaw." 

Punishing the disturbers of world peace. Those nations belonging to the League of Nations agreed to protect the territory of their members against any nation seeking to

seize lands belonging to any of them. They also agreed to cut off financial and trade relations with any member of the League that failed to live up to its promises. This last agreement took the name of "sanctions," and went on to state that members of the League were to contribute war forces to aid in enforcing the covenants of the League. In other words, the members of the League of Nations agreed to stop their regular trade relations with an offending member, and threatened to use force to make good all 

League arrangements. 

The ability of the League of Nations to prevent wars soon began to have some severe tests. A later chapter will tell about the rise of the dictator, Mussolini (moos-so-lē'ne), in Italy, and about the efforts of Italy to extend its possessions in 

Africa. In this matter the 

League declared Italy to be guilty of aggression against another nation. The League then set in motion its plan to punish an aggressor. The members of the League were to band together and refuse to carry on certain kinds of trade with Italy. It was thought that if Mussolini could not get oil and certain metals needed in war, he would have to give up his plans in Africa. The United States, even though not a member of the League, worked with its members to try to prevent the African war. But Mussolini went on with

his plans, the League members did little more than threaten, and Italy succeeded in conquering the ancient kingdom of Ethiopia. 

When Japan attacked China, the League again threatened, but could not seem to back up its threats with force. The warlike leaders in Japan, like Mussolini, went on with their plans with almost no interference from the League or any of its members.

Year by year it became clearer that all the plans to stop war and all the machinery set up to punish aggressor nations failed when faced by questions which seemed vital to the stronger nations of the world. It began to seem that all the years of work for a peaceful world had gone for nothing. It became clear to thoughtful people, as they watched the changes that were taking place, that a period of strife and war, not an era of peace among the nations, was again at hand.

CHAPTER XXXI  

This chapter makes clear how deep an interest Americans have always felt in the subject of education. From early colonial times, as we have already seen, provision was made for schools. With 

America independent, and with democracy broadening year by year, there grew a desire for freer and better schools. Here we learn how much we owe to thoughtful leaders, to earnest teachers, and to generous local, state, and national governments for the good schools we have today. 

We should not have a complete story of our country if we did not make a study of the development of our schools and other educational agencies. For a glance at our schools at almost any time in our history-what they were like, how they were supported, and what people thought of 605

them gives us a fair idea of what conditions in general were like at that particular time. 

1. EARLY IDEAS ABOUT EDUCATION 

In colonial New England. The Puritans believed in education, especially for boys. They did not think so much about the value of education in making good citizens as they did about its value in making good Puritans. They began a system of common schools to help all children in gaining some education, and Latin schools to help a few of the brighter ones to get ready to enter college. Harvard College was founded, and, a little later, Yale and other schools of higher learning.

The common schools. Often at first the schools were held in some farmer's kitchen. Later log schoolhouses were built. 

They were crude and uncomfortable, with great fireplaces in one end, the teacher's desk in the middle, and the splitlog benches for the pupils ranged around the walls. The teacher, usually a man, did his teaching "at the end of a hickory stick." The "scholar" was as likely to get a cut from the rod for not knowing his lesson as he was for bad conduct. Pupils started their learning by means of the "hornbook," which was not what we should call a book at all. It was a single sheet of paper tacked to a thin piece of wood and protected with a light sheet of horn, not as transparent as a piece of glass but making it possible to read the words and letters beneath it. On the sheet of paper were the alphabet, some simple syllables, and, at the bottom, the Lord's Prayer.

When pupils had finished with the hornbook they went on to the famous colonial schoolbook, The New England Primer. With its help the student was supposed to learn to read and spell. In these early schools there were a few slates, a small quantity of paper, no blackboards, charts, maps, or globes.

The New England people taxed themselves to support these schools. But the salaries of the teachers were so low, there was so little equipment, and the school terms were so brief that the total cost of such schools was low. 

In the South. Here there were no tax-supported schools 

Courtesy of The Edison Institute INTERIOR OF HENRY FORD'S SCHOOL. Notice the wood stove, the stove pipe, and the oil lamps in brackets on the wall. in early times. Few children of poor parents had a chance for an education. The well-to-do planters and merchants sometimes paid for the support of small "field" schools, built in an abandoned field. Generally the planters hired. tutors for their own children. Some of the boys were sent back to England to complete their education, while others were educated in the American colleges.

2. THE SPIRIT OF DEMOCRACY IN THE SCHOOLS 

In Chapter XVI you read of the new spirit that was coming into American life in the early nineteenth century. 

Our country was at last becoming a democracy. The new democratic movement touched our schools also. 

When this movement began, the schools as a rule were about as they had been in colonial times. The children who went to school were studying the new subjects, geography and history, but the schools were still largely controlled by the churches and were often supported only by those interested. At best this support was meager and irregular. 

As Americans developed their democracy, they realized that better schools were necessary to make it successful. "What shall be done about education?" they asked. Men began to see that there were three possible courses open to those interested in schools: to allow the churches to struggle on with the problem; to go without schools for the children of common people; and to begin supporting schools for all children by taxation. 

What was the best course to take? At least three forces were at work, one hundred years ago, to lead people to give the third answer to the problem. 

1. The number of immigrants coming to our shores was rapidly increasing. It was clear that education would help to make of them and their children good American citizens. 

2. Our new factories were building up a class of wageearners who as a class wanted free education for their children. 

3. There had arisen a group of devoted men and women who spent their lives working for free schools. Among these was Horace Mann. He pleaded with the voters in state after state to support plans for taxes for the schools. Others were 

Henry Barnard, Emma Willard, Mary Lyon, and Frances

Wright. They argued in favor of more money for the schools and pointed out that it was the duty of all, those who had children and those who were childless, to aid in plans that would give every child in America a chance to go to school at the expense of the community and the state.¹ 

Free education in the Northwest and in the South. In the Northwest we should expect free schools to flourish, if anywhere.

We recall that in that region Congress set aside a section of land in each township for the support of education. But often this school land had been sold or leased on terms that brought little money to the schools. Generally, the schools were free, but they were often miserable affairs, with little money and poor teaching. In Chapter 

XIV we noticed the kind of school that boys like Abraham Lincoln had to attend in the rough wilderness communities. The leaders of the Old South scarcely felt the new spirit in education. 

It was not until after the War between the North and the South that the southern people made great progress in the building of tax-supported systems of public education. 

 HORACE MANN. He spent much of his life urging upon the people of his time the need for a system of free public schools.

High schools. It was about one hundred years ago, also, that the first free high schools were established. It was even harder to convince people of the need of these than it was to get them to see how badly the free elementary schools were needed. Scattered through the country already were a number of academies which seemed, to many people, to supply all that was needed in the way of education for any 1 There are now about 250,000 schoolhouses in the United States.

pupils who might want to go on beyond the common schools. "Why should the children of poor people expect to go to school after they have learned their 'three R's' in the common schools? If they haven't money enough to go to the academies, why should we be taxed to help them carry out their foolish notions?" Thus argued the well-todo. Probably many poor people were also indifferent to the high-school idea in those days. 

In spite of strong opposition, free high schools gained a footing here and there. The courses were what we today should call "practical," and no attempt was made to fit the boys who attended them for college. The boys in the academies were inclined to "look down on" the public-highschool boys. 

Education for girls. The academies, the high schools, and the colleges were still closed to girls and women a hundred years ago. Why should, a girl need to go to school more than a year or so? If she could read and do the simplest “sums, if she could sew and cook and make butter and do well the other tasks around the house, what else was there for her to learn that would be useful to her? Could she learn the things boys learned in academy or college? Many people doubted it.

Slowly the old barriers gave way. Academies for women were opened in many places. In a few cases schools opened their doors for women as well as for men. But not until after 1865 did the women go on to win for themselves the same opportunities in education as enjoyed by the men. 

Gradually the idea spread through the land that education was something too precious, too valuable a support of democratic institutions, to be denied to any young person, rich or poor, boy or girl, in the republic.

3. EDUCATION MEETING MODERN NEEDS 

If your grandfathers and grandmothers were in this country when they were children, most of them probably went to school. The chances are that they attended school five or six months each year for several years. Since a great majority of our people lived in the country at that time, they probably went to a one-room school beside some country road. Perhaps it was three or four miles from

where many of them lived. They carried their noonday meals to school and ate around the big stove in the middle of the schoolroom when the weather was cold, or out under the shade of the trees if the weather was warm. 

When elderly men visited this school of your grandfather's, they must have noticed several improvements over the schools they themselves had attended. The light was better. The stove was an improvement over the fireplace of their own time. There were many more books, and they were much more attractive and interesting than those of earlier times. It is likely that the teacher spent more time with the books and lessons and less with the "rod" than in the earlier schools. The older boys and girls would be found studying some new subjects, such as physiology and civil government, while more time than formerly was being given to such studies as geography and history. 

Some weak points in the old schools. But, after all, the schools of sixty years ago were not very good. The larger boys usually attended them only during a few winter months.2 They went over the same lessons, in the same books, winter after winter. The teachers had so many classes in the one-room, ungraded schools that the recitation periods were not more than ten or twelve minutes in length. Even those who were enrolled in the schools stayed at home almost as many days as they attended school. 

What would your teacher think of that? Play at such schools was simple, though sometimes dangerous, as shown in the picture on page 613. 

Attendance was much better in the village and city schools than in the country. The question of going on to high school and college concerned few of the boys and almost none of the girls sixty or seventy years ago. 

2 Pupils, of course, attend school much more regularly than they once did. In 1870 the average daily attendance was fifty-nine per cent of those enrolled; in 1934, the average was eighty-five per cent. Cities do better than country sections in this respect.

The colleges and universities: the Morrill Act. There was a growing list of schools of higher education after the middle of the nineteenth century. Many of the betterknown institutions were supported by private means. But state universities were springing up in many of the states, and the enrollment in these grew rapidly. They usually owed their beginning to grants of land by the federal

Growth of our modern school system. After about the year 1880 the schools rapidly improved. High schools began to appear even in the smaller towns. Courses in manual training, cooking, sewing, and agriculture were soon to be found in many of these schools. Some of these courses were

offered in the graded schools as well as in the high schools. 

School libraries and playground equipment were provided.³ 

Musical organizations among the pupils, particularly in the high schools, and debating and athletic teams representing the schools in competition with other schools helped to make school life far more varied and interesting than college life had been only a few short years before. School attendance became far better than it had been before. Highschool attendance grew at an amazing rate. In many cities. junior high schools came into existence. Still more recently junior colleges have been created by local school boards, thus making it possible for the graduates from high schools to gain two years of college education in their home communities. In the country districts, in many places, consolidated schools have been built to take the places of the small and poorly equipped one-room schoolhouses.

Federal aid. In recent years the Federal Government has provided aid for certain types of education. In 1917 the

In our own times the national government has provided money for the assistance of high-school and college students. During the years of the depression many young people in our country were without the means of continuing in school. The National Youth Administration was organ ized in 1935. Funds were set aside under this plan to provide paid employment for college and high-school students while attending school.

Newspapers, magazines, books. No one needs to go without education merely because he cannot go to school. 

There are many ways open to all to improve their education outside the classroom. Even the least intelligent of people can gain useful knowledge by means of the radio, illustrations, and moving pictures. To the many who are ready readers the range of newspapers, magazines, and books is so wide that the tastes and abilities of every class of readers can quickly be met. Before the great newspapers of our time could come into existence, two things had to

occur: (1) publishers had to be sure of a sufficient supply of cheap paper; (2) new and rapid means of printing had to be invented.

The Arabs learned from captured Chinese how to make paper by making a pulp from fibrous plants and then drying it in thin sheets. Centuries passed, however, before this slow process was sufficiently improved to assure the world of a large and cheap supply of paper. One of the greatest improvements came when the Fourdrinier (foordrin'i-er) brothers invented their machine for making paper in an endless roll. A few years later it was shown that wood pulp would furnish a suitable supply of raw material. 

Now the publishers were ready to turn out great quantities of printed matter, provided they could make machines to do the work of printing rapidly and well. 

Power printing. Before the days of Columbus, as you have learned, John Gutenberg invented movable types to be used in printing. As these could be set up for the printing of a piece of composition and then reset again and again for other pieces, they were a wonderful improvement. 

Making these types was a job in itself, of course, but new and better methods were employed until today type can be turned out by the thousands of pieces each hour, if necessary.

But setting the type and printing the page continued for three hundred years to be a slow, costly process. This fact helps to explain why there were so few books and newspapers even small ones-in the America of colonial days. 

Finally a man made a cylinder-shaped press. A little later a steam engine was attached to revolve the cylinder. Now the publishers were on the right road to rapid printing. 

The Hoe press. A man named Hoe learned how to attach the type to one cylinder, at the same time bringing the paper up against the type by means of another cylinder. 

With both cylinders revolving at a good speed, pages of

print began "coming off the press" at unheard-of speed. 

Before 1850, twenty thousand copies could be run off in an hour. The day of the penny and two-cent daily papers, sold by the hundreds of thousands, was at hand. Books, magazines, pamphlets, as well as newspapers, were at last within the reach of all. Thus it happened that at the very time the ability to read was becoming almost universal among us, reading matter within the reach of the pocketbooks of all was pouring from the presses of the country. 

Photography and new, cheap processes of making plates from which pictures could be printed enabled the publishers to become lavish in illustrating their papers and books. 

New and interesting discoveries are being made almost every year in the arts of printing and engraving. 

If a man like Benjamin Franklin, the wise old printer of 

Philadelphia, could come back to earth today, he would no doubt be particularly amazed at the way in which the modern printer has loaded the shelves of our libraries, the tops of our school desks, and the reading tables in our homes with newspapers, magazines, and books. He would revel in the clearness of the print and the beauty of the illustrations.

CHAPTER XXXII CITIZEN AND NATION IN THE WORLD OF TODAY 

This chapter attempts to give a clear picture of the events and movements which make up the history of these later years. The political contests of the time and other important matters which have risen to interest and excite the American voter are described. The activities of the government in its attempts to keep its citizens from want and to restore to them their opportunities to make a living are narrated. Disturbances growing out of long years of hard times and unemployment are discussed in the final pages of the chapter. 

1. POLITICAL QUESTIONS OF OUR OWN TIMES 

The right to vote. In 1888 the state of Massachusetts adopted the Australian ballot system. This method of voting has since come into general use. You are familiar with the form of ballot which is used: a large sheet containing the names of the candidates which the voter gets as he goes 621

inside the polling place and which he marks in secret in a curtained booth. The adoption of this method was a great step forward in free and independent voting by our citizens.

Corruption in elections. Efforts are being made to correct other evils connected with our elections. Most states have "corrupt practices" laws to prevent the "stuffing" of ballot-boxes (putting in more than one ballot) and to keep "repeaters" (those who vote more than once in an election) away from the polls. Some states have laws to prohibit corporations from contributing money to help pay for political campaigns. Other laws have been passed to limit the contributions which individuals may make to campaign funds. Laws have been enacted to require publication of all campaign expenditures.

One of the serious problems about voting is not due to evil practices at the polls. It lies in the fact that too few of our citizens go to the polls to vote. Often fewer than half of the qualified voters in a particular election cast their ballots. Why? That is a hard question to answer. Let us review a few matters in an effort to understand why this is true.

Extending the right to vote. You will remember that in 

Washington's day only about one white man in six had the right to vote. This right was looked upon by most men as a rare privilege. As we grew more democratic in our ideas, about one hundred years ago, state after state granted the right to vote to all white men over twenty-one years of age. 

Then later, following the War between the North and the South, colored men were given the ballot. In 1920 the nineteenth amendment was added to the Constitution. By this amendment the women, after a long struggle, gained the same voting privileges as were enjoyed by men. This all means that today we have in this country about fifty million persons who have a right to vote.

CITIZEN AND NATION IN THE WORLD TODAY 623 

The confused voter. But while we were busy increasing the number of those who may vote, we were also making the matter of voting intelligently much more difficult. 

People felt that in order to have democratic government, most of the officeholders should be elected by the voters. 

So it came about that in most states and cities even judges and administrative officials are elected by the vote of the people. Then, too, as governments, state and local, took on increased duties, the number of officers to be elected greatly increased.

All this made the problem of voting difficult for the average voter. In the meantime political parties and political bosses and political conventions were being used to select candidates for office, write party platforms, and influence elections. Soon the voter began to feel that he had very little to say about who the candidates for office were to be or what worth-while principles these stood for. Bewildered and disgusted, he often decided that there was no use in going to the polls at all.

Many attempts have been made to interest the voters in elections. The short ballot—that is, a ballot with few names on it has been suggested. This, so it was said, would allow the voter to center his attention on only a few candidates and would enable him to be more intelligent in his choices. Primary elections and plans to make elected officials more responsive to the wishes of those who elected them have been tried. The purpose of these plans is largely to keep the voters interested in public affairs. Woman suffrage, it was felt, would result in better-conducted elections and in a more general interest in politics. 

Today interest in public questions is growing. People see more clearly than ever before how much their governments, local, state, and national, have to do with their own comfort and prosperity. This is a hopeful sign of the times. A country such as ours justly puts the ballot in the hands of

all normal adults. But the number of voters is, after all, much less important than the kind of voters. Intelligence, alertness, independence, and interest in public affairsthese are the qualities required in good citizens. Voting is a duty as well as a priv-

The Civilian Conservation Corps (C.C.C.) was organ ized, and, in 1936, enrolled about 500,000 young men. 

Through this plan jobless young men were taken off the streets of our cities and away from many poorer farm areas and were employed by the government in projects for conserving forests and farm lands. 

Aid to the farmers. A measure for the relief of farmers¹ was enacted by Congress. This was known as the Agricul tural Adjustment Act (A.A.A.). By the provisions of this act it was hoped that the farmer would secure a reasonable income from his farm. As a large surplus of farm crops had piled up, plans were made to limit the production of wheat, cotton, and other important crops. The government arranged to pay farmers rent for that part of their lands which was not put into crops, and to make other payments to farmers to induce them to cut down farm production. 

Many farmers were deeply in debt. In some cases, when mortgages were foreclosed, farmers resisted the officers who came to put them off their lands. To aid the farmers the 

Farm Credit Administration was created, whereby loans were made at low rates of interest. 

Money for the New Deal. Where did our government get the money with which to carry out this program? Taxes were increased in order to bring a larger amount of money, into the treasury. However, only a small part of the huge sums required could be raised by taxation. It was necessary for the government to borrow billions of dollars. Bonds were sold to investors at low interest rates. By this plan

the costs of the recovery program will be paid gradually in future years as the country returns to prosperity. 

These and many other acts and plans comprised the recovery program of the administration which is known as "The New Deal."

Several of the acts of Congress extending the functions of the national government under the New Deal were brought before the United States Supreme Court; at the close of 1935 and the beginning of 1936 the National Recovery Act and the Agricultural Adjustment Act were declared unconstitutional. These decisions of the Supreme 

Court have served to direct the attention of our people to our highest judicial body and have emphasized the important power this court holds in shaping the affairs of our nation.

The Supreme Court and its work. Our people have generally held the Supreme Court in great respect. Its function has been to use the Constitution as a sort of measuring stick for laws made by Congress and by state legislatures. 

If a law does not agree with the meaning of the Constitution, as interpreted by the Supreme Court, it is declared unconstitutional. It has seemed to many that this power of our highest court has sometimes been used to destroy good laws which had been passed to promote the well-being of the people. 

Amendments to the Constitution. Six amendments, the sixteenth to the twenty-first inclusive, have been added to the Constitution in recent years.

Article Sixteen gives Congress the power to lay and collect taxes on incomes from whatever source derived. 

Article Seventeen provides for the election of United States senators directly by the voters instead of by the legislatures of the states. 

Article Eighteen prohibited the manufacture, sale, or

Article Nineteen says, "The right of citizens of the United

States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any state on account of sex."

Article Eighteen proved to be difficult to enforce, and a great many citizens were never in sympathy with it. After much agitation it was repealed by the adoption of a new amendment, Article Twenty-One.

3. OUR GOVERNMENT FACES OTHER NEW PROBLEMS 

The government and the railroads. Soon after the World 

War, Congress felt it necessary to deal again with the problem of the railroads. We have already noted how rapidly railway lines spread over the country in the years 18701900. The railroads were everywhere recognized as essential to the development of the country. But in time railway management became unpopular, particularly in many of the western states. It was claimed that the roads were unfair to many shippers and to many towns and localities. 

Laws had been passed in an effort to correct these abuses. 

During the World War the government took over the management of the railroads. In 1920, when these roads were handed back to private management, Congress passed the important Transportation Act. In this act the Interstate 

Commerce Commission, comprising eleven members, was given great power over the railroads. It could fix the highest and lowest rates the roads might charge. It had control of the new stock or bond issues of roads. It could make plans for combining some of the lines and was given power to use part of the earnings of the stronger roads as loans to weaker lines.

In spite of the good times after 1920, the railroads failed to earn fair returns. The amount of freight and the number of passengers carried seemed to show that the railroads were declining in usefulness. Automobiles, trucks, and a growing use of river and lake boats were taking business away from the railroads. However, in more recent years the roads have recaptured some of their lost trade by improving their services and equipment. Electric-driven streamlined

CITIZEN AND NATION IN THE WORLD TODAY 633 

trains have thundered along the rails at a speed of nearly two miles a minute.2 Steam has answered the challenge of electricity. Modern steam locomotives draw air-condi tioned coaches across the land at breath-taking speeds.³

Water power. Dams put in the right places on rapidly flowing rivers can be used to make tremendous amounts of electric power which can be conveyed hundreds of miles over transmission wires to be used in turning the wheels of industry. But the development of water power is an expensive undertaking. The dams built are useful in controlling the flow of rivers, while raising the level of the water behind the dams often makes possible the irrigation of large tracts of land. For these and other reasons our government has gone actively into this work of building great hydroelectric plants, particularly in the South and West. The 

Tennessee Valley (T.V.A.) project and the practical completion of the Grand Coulee Dam on the Columbia River show the interest of our government in these vast enterprises. 

Hundreds of millions of dollars are being spent in such work. 

In some cases the government is not only manufacturing electricity but producing it for sale to consumers.

This raises important questions. Would it be better to depend on private companies to build these plants and supply these services as has been done in the past? Is it proper for our government to go into business and compete with private concerns already in this field? These matters are now receiving much serious thought and discussion. 

Tariffs. Often in our history the subject of tariffs has claimed attention. What duties should be paid on the many kinds of articles coming into our country has been a question on which our people have not agreed. Our two leading political parties have often argued over tariff matters. When Woodrow Wilson and the Democratic

"9 It was claimed that foreigners could not ship goods into this country because our tariffs were so high. "If others cannot sell goods to us, they cannot buy goods from us,' ran the argument. As the South American and North American nations drew closer together, in these later years, their leaders have planned to lower the tariff walls that have so often hampered the trade between them. 

Adjusted compensation for veterans of the World War. 

The soldiers who took part in the World War received much smaller pay than the men who worked in the factories and shops during the war. To the veterans this seemed unfair, and they asked the government to make up the difference to them. This additional pay asked for was called a bonus or adjusted compensation. In 1924, each veteran was given a paid-up insurance policy, the value of which was determined by the time he had served in the army during the war. These policies were to be payable in 1945. During the depression the veterans asked for immediate payment, and in 1936 arrangements were made to exchange the insurance policies for bonds which could be immediately cashed at any bank for an amount somewhat less than the value of the payment to be made in 1945. The total sum of money needed for this purpose was over two billion dollars. 

The presidential election of 1936. In preparation for the presidential election of 1936, the Democratic Party, without dissent, nominated President Franklin D. Roosevelt to succeed himself. The choice of the Republican party fell on 

Governor Alfred Landon of Kansas. A spirited campaign followed.

The Republicans called in question many of the policies of the "New Deal" (pages 626-631). The increasing public debt was pointed out as indication of unwise spending by the Roosevelt administration; the charge was made that the powers of the federal government were being extended over matters which properly belonged within the control

of state governments. The Republicans contended that a "balanced budget" was essential to the sound administration of the government. 

The Democratic Party stood squarely on the record of the "New Deal." Democrats claimed for the Roosevelt SODA REALE

They justified the extension of federal powers as essential to the welfare of the nation.

The election was a "landslide" for the Democratic candidates. President Roosevelt was re-elected by the greatest vote ever polled in the history of our country. In only two

CITIZEN AND NATION IN THE WORLD TODAY 637 

states, Maine and Vermont, was the electoral vote recorded for Governor Landon. The result of the election indicated an overwhelming endorsement of the policies of President Roosevelt. 

Continuance of depression. For many months following the presidential election in 1936 the signs on every hand indicated that times were growing better. Then once more the mills and factories found the orders for the goods they made diminishing. Their owners began again to lay off workers. The number of those who could find no employment became almost as great as during 1932 and 1933. The administration at Washington believed it to be necessary again to "prime the pump," that is, to take billions of dollars of the public money and distribute it to destitute families in the form of direct relief, or as salaries and wages to workers on many public projects. It was hoped that this money, once in the hands of the needy, would be spent by them for a great variety of necessary goods and services. 

This in turn, it was hoped, would again give the factories many new orders and would cause them to re-hire the men they had discharged. Thus business in the country, in factories and stores, would again become brisk. It was necessary for the government to continue its policy of borrowing money through the sale of bonds to meet the cost of its program. 

Party contests. During Franklin D. Roosevelt's second term as president several questions arose which caused bitter debates in Congress and much excited discussion throughout the nation. The president desired to reorganize the Supreme Court and make provision for an increase in its membership. In the debates on this question many of the members of the president's own party took the side opposed to changing the Court. The plan failed. 

As other plans were put forward by the president, it became more and more clear that the people were thinking

less about whether they were Democrats or Republicans, and more about whether they favored the New Deal plans or were against them. The president and his aims continued to be popular with those who felt that his plans for fighting the depression were wise and that the laws he favored would bring more justice and more prosperity to the poorer classes in the nation. Opposed to the president's plans were those who felt that the business of the country would thrive better without interference by the government and that, with business free from such interference, times would soon become good. They said that the first need for a sound, prosperous nation was to "balance the budget."

New laws. The Seventy-fifth Congress (1937-1938) took much time debating about the Supreme Court and about other proposals of President Roosevelt. In its first sessions it passed few laws. Before the end of its final session, however, it enacted some important laws. One of these was a wages-and-hours law, which sought to provide fair wages for all workers and to set limits to the number of hours in a working day or week.

In a further effort to help the farmers, a crop-control law was passed. By means of this law the government, with the help of the farmers themselves, tried to regulate the amount of grain and cotton and other farm crops produced, in order to keep prices at a more even level and to make the farmers more prosperous.

Fresh labor-union troubles. In Chapter XXVI we noticed the rise of strong labor unions, and especially the steady growth in power and influence of the American 

Federation of Labor under its wise leader, Samuel Gompers.

After his death William Green became the president of the Federation. His views of labor unions were much like those of Samuel Gompers. The Federation continued to do all it could for the security of its groups of skilled workers. 

John L. Lewis, the leader of a powerful organization of

CITIZEN AND NATION IN THE WORLD TODAY 639 

mine workers, argued that unskilled workers of all classes should receive the benefits of unionism. He also contended that the union to which a worker might belong should be determined by the industry in which he was employed rather than by the craft or trade at which he worked. Thus, under his plan, all employees of a motor manufacturer would belong to the same union. Under the organization of the American Federation of Labor, the tool-makers have their own union, whether they are employed by a motor manufacturer or a boilermaker; the painters have a separate union. So, under the Federation, a dozen or more different unions might be represented among the workers of one automobile plant. 

A bitter quarrel soon developed between Green and 

Lewis. The Lewis Committee for Industrial Organization 

(the C.I.O.), later known as the Congress of Industrial 

Organization, began a campaign to organize the workers in steel mills and automobile factories. The early months of the year 1937 witnessed many disturbances in industrial districts, and scenes of violence and bloodshed were common.
